content.text:
Downloads running (2.2 GB total). Answering your three questions.

## Which EB-NeRD size?

**Both demo and small — not large.**

| bundle | impressions | users | articles | role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ebnerd_demo` | 49,080 | 1,590 | 11,777 | development |
| `ebnerd_small` | 477,534 | 15,143 | 20,738 | **headline results** |

The PDF's Part 0 says exactly this — demo "for quick iteration", small "for final training". The scale-up needed **zero code changes**, just a config block, and every integrity assertion passed unchanged.

## Pre-trained embeddings?

**Yes — and I never trained an encoder.**

- **EB-NeRD**: the organiser-provided `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector` (768-d), from the S3 `artifacts/` prefix. Covers all 125,541 EB-NeRD articles, so one download serves every bundle. Loaded from parquet, nothing more.
- **MIND**: ships no embeddings, so I encoded title+abstract with `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (384-d) — **inference only, weights frozen**, cached to disk so it runs once.

Worth noting: Part 0 lists `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` and `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` as *"(optional)"*. I used contrastive_vector instead — also an organiser artifact, and the one actually tuned for this task. Q3 permits *"the provided article embeddings (or compute your own using BERT/XLM-RoBERTa)"*, so this is squarely compliant. If you'd rather the design note show a comparison across the three provided vector sets, that's a cheap ablation.

## Why minutes on CPU, not hours on GPU?

**Because nothing in Component-1 is trained.** That's the whole answer, and it's worth being precise since it sounds too good:

| stage | what it does | trainable params |
|---|---|---|
| BM25 | term-frequency statistics, closed form | 0 |
| EB-NeRD embeddings | read a provided parquet | 0 |
| MIND embeddings | one forward pass per article, frozen model | 0 |
| FAISS `IndexFlatIP` | store normalised vectors | 0 |
| Fusion | grid search over 21 values of one scalar α | 1 |

The heaviest step is the MIND encode — 65,238 articles, **11m16s on CPU**, and it's inference. A GPU would make that ~30 seconds and change nothing else.

The PDF's "few hours on a single free GPU" is sized for the **neural ranker** path — NRMS/NAML/LSTUR, the standard MIND baselines. Those train. Q1–Q4 don't ask for one; Q3 says *"compute or **load** article embeddings"*. The trainable model is the re-ranker, which the informal brief assigned to Component-2.

So there's no missing work — but you're right to interrogate it, and that's exactly the answer to give if it comes up in the viva.

## Codabench: what I found, and what's next

I pulled both competitions' real submission specs from the Codabench API (the web pages are JS-only and return nothing useful).

**Both formats are the same shape** — a zip containing one text file, one line per impression, `id [rank1,rank2,...]`, ranks 1..n where 1 = best, **row order must match the original file**, and nothing else in the zip (no folders, no `__macosx`):

- **MIND** → `prediction.txt`
- **EB-NeRD** → `predictions.txt` (note the `s`)

**The catch — both score datasets we don't have:**

- **EB-NeRD**: *"Codabench is only evaluating ebnerd_testset (1.5GB)"* — explicit. Downloading now.
- **MIND**: the only open phase is **"Official Test"**, which is **MIND-large test**, not MINDsmall_dev. Our entire MIND pipeline is MINDsmall. So `MINDlarge_test.zip` (0.60 GB) is downloading too.

Two consequences you should know before I proceed:

1. **MIND-large test is a different corpus** (~130k articles vs our 65k) and has ~2.37M impressions. I'll need to encode its `news.tsv` — another CPU inference pass, maybe 20–30 min — and the impression count is large enough that the `.to_list()` patterns that already OOM'd me once will need the Polars treatment first.
2. **EB-NeRD allows only 5 submissions per day** and evaluation *"can take up to a few hours"*. So we get few shots — I'd rather validate the format offline against their published `predictions_large_random.zip` sample than burn attempts guessing.

Next step once the downloads land: write `pipeline/submit.py` emitting both files, validate row order and rank ranges against the official sample, then you upload. Want me to go ahead and build it?

content.text:
Both test sets are down and inspected. The picture changed materially, so here's what I found before writing any code.

## The test sets are far bigger than what we've been running

| | impressions | articles | users w/ history | labels |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EB-NeRD testset** | **13,536,710** | 125,541 | 807,677 | none (held out) |
| **MIND-large test** | **2,370,727** | 120,961 | — | none (held out) |

For scale: our headline `ebnerd_small` is 478k impressions. The EB-NeRD leaderboard set is **28× that**. MIND-large test averages 39.3 candidates per impression, so it's ~93M pairs to score.

This is the §10 "where it breaks at 10×" scenario arriving for real — and it's the one place my current code is known-weak. I OOM'd at 10 GB on 245k impressions two days ago doing something much lighter. Scoring 13.5M is not a matter of pointing the existing script at a new config.

## The good news

- **EB-NeRD needs no encoding.** `contrastive_vector` already covers all 125,541 articles, and the testset ships exactly those. Embeddings are a lookup.
- **Both formats are identical in shape**, so one writer handles both.
- **`ebnerd_testset` carries `is_beyond_accuracy`** — the challenge's beyond-accuracy subset is flagged in the data, and predictions are required for those rows too.

## The real work

Not "write a formatter." Three things:

1. **A streaming scorer.** The current path materialises impressions as Python lists. At 13.5M that dies. It needs `pl.scan_parquet` + batched scoring, writing predictions incrementally. This is the fix §10 already names — building it turns a predicted weakness into a demonstrated one, which is worth more in the design note than the prediction was.
2. **MIND-large encoding.** 120,961 articles through MiniLM on CPU ≈ 20 min, cached. Its corpus barely overlaps MINDsmall's, so the existing cache doesn't help.
3. **Format validation offline.** EB-NeRD allows **5 submissions/day** and evaluation *"can take up to a few hours"*. They publish `predictions_large_random.zip` (220 MB) as a reference — I want to diff my output's structure against theirs before you upload, not after a failed attempt burns a day.

## One thing worth your input

Scoring 13.5M impressions on this CPU will take real time — I'd estimate 1–3 hours for EB-NeRD once streaming works, plus ~30 min for MIND. That's fine to run unattended, but it's not a 10-minute task, and **this is where your GPU cluster would genuinely help** — not for the retrieval (still no training), but the MIND encode drops from ~20 min to under a minute, and if you ever want a stronger encoder than MiniLM, that becomes affordable.

Two ways to go:

- **Full submission** — build the streaming scorer, score both test sets properly. Strongest result, and it fixes the pipeline's known scaling weakness for real.
- **Get on the boards first** — the requirement is to *submit*, not to rank. I could produce a valid submission on a subset or simpler scorer within the hour to confirm the format end-to-end, then upgrade it. Given the 5/day cap, proving the format cheaply first has real value.

I'd recommend the second then the first: validate format, then invest in the streaming scorer knowing uploads work. Which do you want?

**206 million pairs to score.** That number is what makes this a different problem. Here's what I meant.

## What the code does now

`retrieval/bm25.py:109-119` builds everything in memory before writing anything:

```python
candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()   # every impression, as Python lists
timestamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
cand_scores: list = [None] * impressions.height     # one slot per impression
```

It fills `cand_scores` for all impressions, then writes one parquet at the end. Everything stays alive simultaneously. That's fine at 478k impressions and it's why the code is simple and readable.

At 13.5M it doesn't fit. Rough arithmetic: 13.5M Python list objects (~756 MB just in object headers) + 206M pointers (~1.6 GB) + 13.5M small numpy arrays (~112 bytes of overhead each, ~1.5 GB before any actual floats). That's ~4 GB of pure bookkeeping before a single score exists, on a machine with ~9 GB free — and I already OOM'd at 10 GB doing something lighter on 245k impressions.

## What streaming means

Read a slice, score it, append it to the output, throw it away, repeat:

```
for batch in scan_parquet(behaviors).iter_slices(200_000):
    scores = score(batch)
    append(scores) → output file
    # batch and scores go out of scope here
```

Peak memory becomes *one batch*, not the whole dataset — flat in the number of impressions instead of linear. 200k-row batches would put us back at roughly the footprint we already run comfortably, 68 times over.

## Two things that make it non-trivial

**Query deduplication breaks at batch boundaries.** The current scorer's main optimisation (`bm25.py:95-102`) collapses impressions with identical history into one BM25 query — 230k impressions became 39k distinct queries. Chunk naively and you can only dedup *within* a chunk, so the same user's query gets rescored in every batch it appears in. Fix is to sort by user before batching so identical queries land together. Worth naming because it's a correctness-neutral but performance-critical detail.

**Row order is load-bearing.** Both leaderboards require *"the row orders of the results should be consistent with those in the original files."* Streaming in file order gives that for free — which is a point in its favour over anything that regroups.

## Something I got wrong earlier

I told you 1–3 hours and implied we'd need the full machinery. Looking at the actual task: **the submission is pure re-ranking.** We score only the candidates each impression already lists — there's no full-corpus retrieval, so no FAISS search over 13.5M queries and no top-200 lists.

That matters a lot, because our EB-NeRD headline system is **embeddings alone** (fusion was rejected there on the paired bootstrap). So an EB-NeRD submission is: mean the user's history vectors, dot against ~15 candidate vectors. No BM25 index, no retrieval track. That's dramatically cheaper than what I was estimating — and it needs the streaming loop mainly to avoid holding 206M results, not because the arithmetic is hard.

So the honest revision: the streaming scorer is maybe 60–80 lines, and it's the same fix §10 of the design note already prescribes. Building it converts a predicted weakness into a measured, fixed one — which is a better story than the prediction was.

Shall I build it?

"""Semantic counterpart to retrieval/bm25.py — same two tracks, same output shape.

Deliberately mirrors bm25.py: same CLI, same query-deduplication pass, same file naming.
Only the scorer differs, so the lexical and semantic axes stay directly comparable.

  re-rank    cosine between the user vector and each candidate in the given pool
  retrieval  FAISS inner-product search over the whole corpus for the top-K

The user vector is the mean of the L2-normalised vectors of their last HISTORY_LEN clicked
articles. History is guaranteed strictly earlier than the impression by pipeline.split.

Article vectors come from whichever source the dataset has:
  EB-NeRD  the organisers' 768-d contrastive vectors (config `embeddings`)
  MIND     encoded here with a sentence-transformers model (config `model`) and cached
           to data/processed/<dataset>/embeddings.parquet, so encoding happens once

    python -m retrieval.embeddings
    python -m retrieval.embeddings mind_small --splits test

Writes, per dataset and split:
    emb_<split>.parquet            impression_id, emb        aligned to `candidates`
    retrieval_emb_<split>.parquet  impression_id, retrieved  top-K ids, best first
"""

import argparse
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import faiss
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml
from tqdm import tqdm

from retrieval.bm25 import HISTORY_LEN, OVERFETCH, TOP_K

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
PROC = ROOT / "data/processed"

SEARCH_BATCH = 4096


def _encode_corpus(articles: pl.DataFrame, model_name: str) -> np.ndarray:
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

    texts = (
        articles.select(
            pl.concat_str(
                [pl.col("title").fill_null(""), pl.col("abstract").fill_null("")],
                separator=" ",
            )
        )
        .to_series()
        .to_list()
    )
    print(f"  encoding {len(texts):,} articles with {model_name} (CPU)")
    model = SentenceTransformer(model_name, device="cpu")
    return model.encode(
        texts, batch_size=256, convert_to_numpy=True, show_progress_bar=True
    ).astype(np.float32)


def load_vectors(name: str, cfg: dict, articles: pl.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
    """Article vectors, L2-normalised, in the same row order as `articles`."""
    if cfg.get("embeddings"):
        wanted = articles["article_id"].to_list()
        table = (
            pl.scan_parquet(ROOT / cfg["embeddings"])
            .with_columns(pl.col("article_id").cast(pl.String))
            .filter(pl.col("article_id").is_in(wanted))
            .collect()
        )
        column = next(c for c in table.columns if c != "article_id")
        found = dict(zip(table["article_id"], range(table.height)))
        missing = [a for a in wanted if a not in found]
        assert not missing, f"{len(missing)} articles have no provided embedding"
        raw = np.vstack(table[column].to_list()).astype(np.float32)
        vectors = raw[[found[a] for a in wanted]]
        print(f"  provided embeddings: {vectors.shape[0]:,} x {vectors.shape[1]}")
    else:
        cache = PROC / name / "embeddings.parquet"
        if cache.exists():
            table = pl.read_parquet(cache)
            assert table["article_id"].to_list() == articles["article_id"].to_list(), (
                "cached embeddings do not match the current corpus; delete "
                f"{cache} to re-encode"
            )
            vectors = np.vstack(table["vector"].to_list()).astype(np.float32)
            print(f"  cached embeddings: {vectors.shape[0]:,} x {vectors.shape[1]}")
        else:
            vectors = _encode_corpus(articles, cfg["model"])
            pl.DataFrame({
                "article_id": articles["article_id"],
                "vector": [v.tolist() for v in vectors],
            }).write_parquet(cache)
            print(f"  encoded and cached to {cache}")

    return vectors / (np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)


def score_split(impressions, articles, vectors, position, published):
    """One pass over distinct histories, filling both tracks."""
    histories = [tuple(h[-HISTORY_LEN:]) for h in impressions["history"].to_list()]

    order: dict[tuple, int] = {}
    per_impression = []
    for h in histories:
        per_impression.append(order.setdefault(h, len(order)))
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = defaultdict(list)
    for row, q_id in enumerate(per_impression):
        groups[q_id].append(row)
    print(f"    {len(order):,} distinct histories for {impressions.height:,} impressions")

    # Mean of the history vectors, renormalised. Cold start stays all-zero, which scores
    # every candidate 0 rather than inventing a ranking.
    users = np.zeros((len(order), vectors.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
    for history, q_id in order.items():
        rows = [position[a] for a in history if a in position]
        if rows:
            users[q_id] = vectors[rows].mean(axis=0)
    users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9

    index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(vectors.shape[1])
    index.add(vectors)
    n_fetch = min(TOP_K * OVERFETCH, vectors.shape[0])
    top = np.empty((len(order), n_fetch), dtype=np.int64)
    for start in tqdm(range(0, len(order), SEARCH_BATCH), desc="    searching", leave=False):
        chunk = users[start:start + SEARCH_BATCH]
        top[start:start + len(chunk)] = index.search(chunk, n_fetch)[1]

    candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
    timestamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
    article_ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy()
    cand_scores: list = [None] * impressions.height
    retrieved: list = [None] * impressions.height

    for q_id, rows in groups.items():
        user = users[q_id]
        cold = not user.any()
        for row in rows:
            cand_scores[row] = (vectors[[position[a] for a in candidates[row]]] @ user).astype(np.float32)
            if cold:
                retrieved[row] = []
                continue
            hits = top[q_id]
            if published is not None:
                hits = hits[published[hits] <= np.datetime64(timestamps[row])]
            retrieved[row] = article_ids[hits[:TOP_K]].tolist()

    return cand_scores, retrieved


def run(name: str, cfg: dict, splits: list[str]) -> None:
    print(f"\n{name}")
    articles = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / "articles.parquet")
    vectors = load_vectors(name, cfg, articles)

    position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
    published = None
    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
        published = articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
    else:
        print("  note: no publication dates; retrieval cannot filter unpublished articles")

    for split in splits:
        impressions = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / f"impressions_{split}.parquet")
        print(f"  {split}: {impressions.height:,} impressions")
        cand_scores, retrieved = score_split(
            impressions, articles, vectors, position, published
        )

        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "emb": [s.tolist() for s in cand_scores],
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"emb_{split}.parquet")
        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "retrieved": retrieved,
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"retrieval_emb_{split}.parquet")

        clicked = impressions["clicked"].to_list()
        hit = sum(bool(set(c) & set(r)) for c, r in zip(clicked, retrieved) if c)
        print(f"    recall@{TOP_K} (full-corpus retrieval): {hit / impressions.height:.4f}")


def main() -> None:
    config = yaml.safe_load(CONFIG.read_text())
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", default=list(config))
    parser.add_argument("--splits", nargs="+", default=["train", "val", "test"])
    args = parser.parse_args()

    for name in args.datasets:
        run(name, config[name], args.splits)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Codabench leaderboard submissions for both competitions.

The leaderboards score held-out test sets that are far larger than anything the offline
harness touches — EB-NeRD 13.5M impressions (206M candidate pairs), MIND-large 2.4M — so
this cannot reuse `retrieval/embeddings.py`, which materialises every impression at once.
The scoring *semantics* are identical (mean of the last HISTORY_LEN article vectors,
L2-normalised, cosine against each candidate); only the execution is streamed.

    python -m pipeline.submit ebnerd            -> submissions/ebnerd_predictions.zip
    python -m pipeline.submit mind              -> submissions/mind_prediction.zip
    python -m pipeline.submit ebnerd --limit 50000     smoke test on a prefix

Format, from each competition's Submission Guidelines (fetched from the Codabench API):

    <impression_id> [r1,r2,...,rn]

`ri` is the rank *of the i-th candidate as listed in the test file*, an integer in 1..n
where 1 is the best. Row order must match the test file. The zip must contain the text
file and nothing else — no folders, no __MACOSX.

Only the embedding scorer ships here. On EB-NeRD that is the reported headline system
(fusion was significantly *worse* than embeddings alone on the paired bootstrap, see
DESIGN_NOTE §6), so the leaderboard entry and the offline report describe the same system.
"""

import argparse
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml

from retrieval.bm25 import HISTORY_LEN

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
INTERIM = ROOT / "data/interim"
OUT = ROOT / "submissions"

# Impressions per streamed slice. Peak memory is one slice, not the dataset.
BATCH = 200_000
# Candidate pairs per vectorised dot-product block. A block materialises two
# (PAIR_BLOCK, dim) float32 arrays, so this is the real memory knob: 65536 x 768 x 4 x 2

"""Semantic counterpart to retrieval/bm25.py — same two tracks, same output shape.

Deliberately mirrors bm25.py: same CLI, same query-deduplication pass, same file naming.
Only the scorer differs, so the lexical and semantic axes stay directly comparable.

  re-rank    cosine between the user vector and each candidate in the given pool
  retrieval  FAISS inner-product search over the whole corpus for the top-K

The user vector is the mean of the L2-normalised vectors of their last HISTORY_LEN clicked
articles. History is guaranteed strictly earlier than the impression by pipeline.split.

Article vectors come from whichever source the dataset has:
  EB-NeRD  the organisers' 768-d contrastive vectors (config `embeddings`)
  MIND     encoded here with a sentence-transformers model (config `model`) and cached
           to data/processed/<dataset>/embeddings.parquet, so encoding happens once

    python -m retrieval.embeddings
    python -m retrieval.embeddings mind_small --splits test

Writes, per dataset and split:
    emb_<split>.parquet            impression_id, emb        aligned to `candidates`
    retrieval_emb_<split>.parquet  impression_id, retrieved  top-K ids, best first
"""

import argparse
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import faiss
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml
from tqdm import tqdm

from retrieval.bm25 import HISTORY_LEN, OVERFETCH, TOP_K

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
PROC = ROOT / "data/processed"

SEARCH_BATCH = 4096


def _encode_corpus(articles: pl.DataFrame, model_name: str) -> np.ndarray:
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

    texts = (
        articles.select(
            pl.concat_str(
                [pl.col("title").fill_null(""), pl.col("abstract").fill_null("")],
                separator=" ",
            )
        )
        .to_series()
        .to_list()
    )
    print(f"  encoding {len(texts):,} articles with {model_name} (CPU)")
    model = SentenceTransformer(model_name, device="cpu")
    return model.encode(
        texts, batch_size=256, convert_to_numpy=True, show_progress_bar=True
    ).astype(np.float32)


def load_vectors(name: str, cfg: dict, articles: pl.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
    """Article vectors, L2-normalised, in the same row order as `articles`."""
    if cfg.get("embeddings"):
        wanted = articles["article_id"].to_list()
        table = (
            pl.scan_parquet(ROOT / cfg["embeddings"])
            .with_columns(pl.col("article_id").cast(pl.String))
            .filter(pl.col("article_id").is_in(wanted))
            .collect()
        )
        column = next(c for c in table.columns if c != "article_id")
        found = dict(zip(table["article_id"], range(table.height)))
        missing = [a for a in wanted if a not in found]
        assert not missing, f"{len(missing)} articles have no provided embedding"
        raw = np.vstack(table[column].to_list()).astype(np.float32)
        vectors = raw[[found[a] for a in wanted]]
        print(f"  provided embeddings: {vectors.shape[0]:,} x {vectors.shape[1]}")
    else:
        cache = PROC / name / "embeddings.parquet"
        if cache.exists():
            table = pl.read_parquet(cache)
            assert table["article_id"].to_list() == articles["article_id"].to_list(), (
                "cached embeddings do not match the current corpus; delete "
                f"{cache} to re-encode"
            )
            vectors = np.vstack(table["vector"].to_list()).astype(np.float32)
            print(f"  cached embeddings: {vectors.shape[0]:,} x {vectors.shape[1]}")
        else:
            vectors = _encode_corpus(articles, cfg["model"])
            pl.DataFrame({
                "article_id": articles["article_id"],
                "vector": [v.tolist() for v in vectors],
            }).write_parquet(cache)
            print(f"  encoded and cached to {cache}")

    return vectors / (np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)


def score_split(impressions, articles, vectors, position, published):
    """One pass over distinct histories, filling both tracks."""
    histories = [tuple(h[-HISTORY_LEN:]) for h in impressions["history"].to_list()]

    order: dict[tuple, int] = {}
    per_impression = []
    for h in histories:
        per_impression.append(order.setdefault(h, len(order)))
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = defaultdict(list)
    for row, q_id in enumerate(per_impression):
        groups[q_id].append(row)
    print(f"    {len(order):,} distinct histories for {impressions.height:,} impressions")

    # Mean of the history vectors, renormalised. Cold start stays all-zero, which scores
    # every candidate 0 rather than inventing a ranking.
    users = np.zeros((len(order), vectors.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
    for history, q_id in order.items():
        rows = [position[a] for a in history if a in position]
        if rows:
            users[q_id] = vectors[rows].mean(axis=0)
    users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9

    index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(vectors.shape[1])
    index.add(vectors)
    n_fetch = min(TOP_K * OVERFETCH, vectors.shape[0])
    top = np.empty((len(order), n_fetch), dtype=np.int64)
    for start in tqdm(range(0, len(order), SEARCH_BATCH), desc="    searching", leave=False):
        chunk = users[start:start + SEARCH_BATCH]
        top[start:start + len(chunk)] = index.search(chunk, n_fetch)[1]

    candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
    timestamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
    article_ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy()
    cand_scores: list = [None] * impressions.height
    retrieved: list = [None] * impressions.height

    for q_id, rows in groups.items():
        user = users[q_id]
        cold = not user.any()
        for row in rows:
            cand_scores[row] = (vectors[[position[a] for a in candidates[row]]] @ user).astype(np.float32)
            if cold:
                retrieved[row] = []
                continue
            hits = top[q_id]
            if published is not None:
                hits = hits[published[hits] <= np.datetime64(timestamps[row])]
            retrieved[row] = article_ids[hits[:TOP_K]].tolist()

    return cand_scores, retrieved


def run(name: str, cfg: dict, splits: list[str]) -> None:
    print(f"\n{name}")
    articles = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / "articles.parquet")
    vectors = load_vectors(name, cfg, articles)

    position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
    published = None
    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
        published = articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
    else:
        print("  note: no publication dates; retrieval cannot filter unpublished articles")

    for split in splits:
        impressions = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / f"impressions_{split}.parquet")
        print(f"  {split}: {impressions.height:,} impressions")
        cand_scores, retrieved = score_split(
            impressions, articles, vectors, position, published
        )

        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "emb": [s.tolist() for s in cand_scores],
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"emb_{split}.parquet")
        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "retrieved": retrieved,
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"retrieval_emb_{split}.parquet")

        clicked = impressions["clicked"].to_list()
        hit = sum(bool(set(c) & set(r)) for c, r in zip(clicked, retrieved) if c)
        print(f"    recall@{TOP_K} (full-corpus retrieval): {hit / impressions.height:.4f}")


def main() -> None:
    config = yaml.safe_load(CONFIG.read_text())
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", default=list(config))
    parser.add_argument("--splits", nargs="+", default=["train", "val", "test"])
    args = parser.parse_args()

    for name in args.datasets:
        run(name, config[name], args.splits)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

        per_impression.append(order.setdefault(h, len(order)))
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = defaultdict(list)
    for row, q_id in enumerate(per_impression):
        groups[q_id].append(row)
    print(f"    {len(order):,} distinct histories for {impressions.height:,} impressions")

    # Mean of the history vectors, renormalised. Cold start stays all-zero, which scores
    # every candidate 0 rather than inventing a ranking.
    users = np.zeros((len(order), vectors.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
    for history, q_id in order.items():
        rows = [position[a] for a in history if a in position]
        if rows:
            users[q_id] = vectors[rows].mean(axis=0)
    users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9

    index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(vectors.shape[1])
    index.add(vectors)
    n_fetch = min(TOP_K * OVERFETCH, vectors.shape[0])
    top = np.empty((len(order), n_fetch), dtype=np.int64)
    for start in tqdm(range(0, len(order), SEARCH_BATCH), desc="    searching", leave=False):
        chunk = users[start:start + SEARCH_BATCH]
        top[start:start + len(chunk)] = index.search(chunk, n_fetch)[1]

    candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
    timestamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
    article_ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy()
    cand_scores: list = [None] * impressions.height
    retrieved: list = [None] * impressions.height

    for q_id, rows in groups.items():
        user = users[q_id]
        cold = not user.any()
        for row in rows:
            cand_scores[row] = (vectors[[position[a] for a in candidates[row]]] @ user).astype(np.float32)
            if cold:
                retrieved[row] = []
                continue
            hits = top[q_id]
            if published is not None:
                hits = hits[published[hits] <= np.datetime64(timestamps[row])]
            retrieved[row] = article_ids[hits[:TOP_K]].tolist()

    return cand_scores, retrieved


def run(name: str, cfg: dict, splits: list[str]) -> None:
    print(f"\n{name}")
    articles = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / "articles.parquet")
    vectors = load_vectors(name, cfg, articles)

    position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
    published = None
    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
        published = articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
    else:
        print("  note: no publication dates; retrieval cannot filter unpublished articles")

    for split in splits:
        impressions = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / f"impressions_{split}.parquet")
        print(f"  {split}: {impressions.height:,} impressions")
        cand_scores, retrieved = score_split(
            impressions, articles, vectors, position, published
        )

        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "emb": [s.tolist() for s in cand_scores],
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"emb_{split}.parquet")
        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "retrieved": retrieved,
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"retrieval_emb_{split}.parquet")

        clicked = impressions["clicked"].to_list()
        hit = sum(bool(set(c) & set(r)) for c, r in zip(clicked, retrieved) if c)
        print(f"    recall@{TOP_K} (full-corpus retrieval): {hit / impressions.height:.4f}")


def main() -> None:
    config = yaml.safe_load(CONFIG.read_text())
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", default=list(config))
    parser.add_argument("--splits", nargs="+", default=["train", "val", "test"])
    args = parser.parse_args()

    for name in args.datasets:
        run(name, config[name], args.splits)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

cat >> NOTES.md << 'EOF'

## Codabench submissions (Q5)

Both competitions' submission specs were fetched from the Codabench REST API
(`/api/competitions/<id>/`) — the web pages are a JS app and return nothing useful to a
plain fetch.

| | competition | inner file | evaluated on |
|---|---|---|---|
| MIND | 13967 | `prediction.txt` | MIND-large test, 2,370,727 impressions |
| EB-NeRD | 2469 | `predictions.txt` | `ebnerd_testset`, 13,536,710 impressions |

Same line format for both: `<impression_id> [r1,...,rn]`, where `ri` is the rank of the
i-th candidate *as listed in the test file*, 1 = best. Row order must match the test file.
The zip must contain the text file and nothing else.

**The leaderboards do not score demo or small.** EB-NeRD's guidelines are explicit —
"Codabench is only evaluating ebnerd_testset (1.5GB)" — and MIND's only open phase is
"Official Test", which is MIND-large. Development stays on EB-NeRD demo/small and
MIND-small as the PDF intends; the test sets are scored by inference only, since nothing
in this component is trained.

Operational limits worth knowing: EB-NeRD allows **5 submissions per day** and evaluation
"can take up to a few hours". That is why the output is validated offline (structure +
an independent float64 recomputation) rather than by trial upload.

### Why `pipeline/submit.py` exists instead of reusing retrieval/embeddings.py

The offline scorer materialises every impression at once. The EB-NeRD test set is 28x
`ebnerd_small` — 13.5M impressions, 205,925,868 candidate pairs — so it streams instead:
slices of 200k impressions, scored in 65,536-pair blocks, appended to the output and
discarded. Scoring *semantics* are unchanged (mean of last 30 history vectors,
L2-normalised, cosine), so the leaderboard entry and the offline report describe the same
system.

Polars slice pushdown reaches the parquet row groups, so `scan.slice(13_000_000, 200_000)`
costs the same as `slice(0, 200_000)` — measured 0.05s either way. That is what makes peak
memory flat in the number of impressions rather than linear.

Article ids are Int32 in EB-NeRD, so the lookup is an array indexed by id rather than a
dict of strings, keeping 206M candidate ids out of Python entirely.

### The `.to_list()` defect, found a third time

`np.vstack(series.to_list())` boxes every scalar into a Python float on the way through.
Measured on the 125,541 x 768 contrastive vectors: **peak 5.8 GB to build a 385 MB array**.
Replacing it with `explode().to_numpy().reshape(...)` cut the submitter's peak RSS from
7.0 GB to 5.9 GB and made it 33% faster, with byte-identical output.

The same pattern was in `retrieval/embeddings.py` (both the provided-vector and cached
branches); both are now `_unnest`, verified value-identical to the old path. This is the
third instance of the same defect (after the recall@K OOM), which is why §10 of the design
note names it as *the* scaling wall rather than one of several.

### MIND submission is embeddings-only, and that is a finding

The reported MIND system is `fused`, but the leaderboard entry uses embeddings alone.
BM25 here is `get_scores`, which returns a dense score over the whole corpus per distinct
query; at ~2M distinct histories x 120,961 articles that is ~10^11 operations and is not
practical. This is exactly the limitation §10 predicts — "BM25 scoring is O(corpus) per
distinct query ... a real inverted index with early termination becomes necessary" — now
confirmed by an attempt rather than argued from the code. Cost of the substitution is
known and small: fused − emb was +0.0014 AUC on mind_small test.
EOF

import polars as pl, numpy as np, zipfile

path='data/interim/ebnerd_testset/ebnerd_testset/test/behaviors.parquet'
scan = pl.scan_parquet(path).select('impression_id','article_ids_inview')
total = scan.select(pl.len()).collect().item()

bad_order = bad_len = bad_perm = 0
checked = 0
f = open('submissions/predictions.txt')
for off in range(0, total, 500_000):
    b = scan.slice(off, 500_000).collect()
    ids = b['impression_id'].to_numpy()
    lens = b['article_ids_inview'].list.len().to_numpy()
    for exp_id, n in zip(ids, lens):
        line = f.readline()
        head, _, rest = line.partition(' ')
        if int(head) != exp_id: bad_order += 1
        ranks = rest.strip()[1:-1].split(',')
        if len(ranks) != n: bad_len += 1
        else:
            r = np.sort(np.array(ranks, dtype=np.int32))
            if r[0] != 1 or r[-1] != n or not np.array_equal(r, np.arange(1, n+1)):
                bad_perm += 1
        checked += 1
leftover = f.readline()
f.close()

print(f"validated {checked:,} lines against {total:,} source rows")
print(f"  impression_id out of order .. {bad_order}")
print(f"  wrong candidate count ....... {bad_len}")
print(f"  ranks not a permutation ..... {bad_perm}")
print(f"  extra trailing lines ........ {1 if leftover.strip() else 0}")

with zipfile.ZipFile('submissions/ebnerd_predictions.zip') as z:
    names = z.namelist()
print(f"  zip contents ................ {names}")
assert checked == total and not (bad_order or bad_len or bad_perm) and not leftover.strip()

Two further leakage vectors are enforced rather than trusted: `next_read_time` /
`next_scroll_percentage` (the user's *next* action) and `read_time` / `scroll_percentage`
(post-click engagement) are dropped at the split, and full-corpus retrieval filters
`published_time <= impression_time` — EB-NeRD's corpus contains 867 articles published after the test
window ends.

## 10. Where it breaks at 10×

Runtimes at EB-NeRD small (478k impressions): split 36s, BM25 1m44s, embeddings 1m32s, eval 3m26s.
Scaling to `ebnerd_large` (600M impressions): (1) **Memory — no longer a prediction.** Adding
recall@K, I materialised the top-200 lists with `.to_list()` and the harness was OOM-killed at 10 GB
RSS on `ebnerd_small` — 245k impressions x 200 ids x 2 systems is ~98M Python strings. Rewriting the
intersection as a Polars expression, so only one float per impression crosses into Python, cut peak
RSS to 862 MB. The same `.to_list()` pattern still sits in the scoring loops, which is where it
fails next; `pl.scan_parquet` streaming plus batched scoring is the fix. (2) BM25 — dense scoring O(corpus) per query; need Pyserini/Lucene
with early termination for 125k+ articles. (3) FAISS flat O(N·d) for 2.7M queries; IVF-PQ with `nlist ~ sqrt(N)`
cuts cost 1–2 orders, worth measuring. (4) Embedding cache — 125k × 768 fine (385 MB), but 10M articles needs
memmap or quantisation. (5) Bootstrap already chunks 1000 resamples × 244k impressions (585 MB) into blocks of 50.

## 11. What this deliberately does not do

The behavioural axis — recency/decay, session context — and a learned re-ranker over
BM25 + embedding + behavioural features are out of scope here: this assignment specifies lexical and
semantic retrieval, and §8 records the measurement that made that boundary an informed one rather
than an assumed one (train-click popularity scores *below* random on EB-NeRD, 0.459, because the
pool is already popularity-filtered — so behavioural signal needs a learned model, not a feature).

The pipeline is built so that work is additive rather than a rewrite: the feature store already
carries entities and per-item history timestamps, both retrieval tracks emit a stable candidate
format, and `eval/bootstrap.py` already implements the paired comparison any claimed gain would

input.new_string:
## 10. Where it breaks at 10× — measured, not projected

The leaderboard submission forced this section to stop being hypothetical. Codabench scores
`ebnerd_testset`: **13.5M impressions, 205,925,868 candidate pairs — 28× `ebnerd_small`.**

**Memory is the wall, and it is one specific idiom.** Three separate times, the thing that broke was
`.to_list()` pulling Arrow data into boxed Python objects. The worst case: `np.vstack(col.to_list())`
peaks at **5.8 GB to build a 385 MB array**, because it boxes 96M floats on the way through. Adding
recall@K, the same idiom OOM-killed the harness at 10 GB RSS on a 15 GB machine. Replacing it with
`explode().to_numpy().reshape(...)` and doing set intersections as Polars expressions fixed all
three, byte-identically. It is now `_unnest` in one place.

**Streaming works and costs little.** `pipeline/submit.py` scores in 200k-impression slices and
65,536-pair blocks. Peak RSS on the full 13.5M run was **5.9 GB — the same as on a 20k smoke test**,
which is the property worth having: memory flat in dataset size, not linear. 12m36s end to end.
Polars slice pushdown reaches the parquet row groups, so `slice(13_000_000, 200_000)` costs the same
as `slice(0, 200_000)` (0.05s either way) — without that, streaming would have been O(n²).

**BM25 is the piece that genuinely does not scale**, and I found this by trying. `get_scores` returns
a dense score over the entire corpus per distinct query; on MIND-large test that is ~2M distinct
histories × 120,961 articles ≈ 10¹¹ operations. So the MIND leaderboard entry is embeddings-only.
The substitution cost is known and small (fused − emb = +0.0014 AUC offline), but the conclusion is
the real one: a dense scorer cannot back a two-stage system at this size, and an inverted index with
early termination (Pyserini/Lucene, WAND) stops being optional.

Still projected rather than measured, at `ebnerd_large` (600M): FAISS flat is O(N·d) per query and
would need IVF-PQ with `nlist ~ sqrt(N)`; the embedding cache is fine at 125k × 768 (385 MB) but
needs memmap or quantisation at 10M articles. Runtimes at `ebnerd_small` for reference: split 36s,
BM25 1m44s, embeddings 1m32s, eval 3m26s.

# One command rebuilds everything from raw files.
#
#   make all                     full pipeline, every dataset
#   make DATASETS=mind_small all just one
#   make results                 re-evaluate without recomputing scores
#   make test                    anti-leakage checks on the built artifacts

PY := .venv/bin/python
DATASETS ?= ebnerd_demo ebnerd_small mind_small
BUNDLES ?= ebnerd_demo ebnerd_small Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector MINDsmall_train MINDsmall_dev

.PHONY: all venv download split retrieve results test clean-processed

all: results

venv:
	uv venv --python 3.11 .venv
	# CPU-only torch first: the default resolves to CUDA wheels (~2.5GB) that this
	# machine cannot use, and pulling them stalls the install.
	VIRTUAL_ENV=.venv uv pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
	VIRTUAL_ENV=.venv uv pip install polars pyarrow bm25s PyStemmer faiss-cpu \
		sentence-transformers huggingface_hub numpy scipy scikit-learn tqdm pyyaml pytest

download:
	$(PY) -m pipeline.download $(BUNDLES)

split: download
	$(PY) -m pipeline.split $(DATASETS)

retrieve: split
	$(PY) -m retrieval.bm25 $(DATASETS)
	$(PY) -m retrieval.embeddings $(DATASETS)
	$(PY) -m retrieval.fuse $(DATASETS)

results: retrieve
	$(PY) -m eval.run $(DATASETS)

No. It's optional — purely a speed matter, not a capability one.

**Why:** the encode is inference only. One forward pass per article through `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` with frozen weights. No gradients, no optimizer, no epochs — the part of deep learning that actually demands a GPU never runs here.

It also runs **once per corpus** — vectors are cached to disk (`data/processed/mind_small/embeddings.parquet`; a `.npy` for MIND-large test), so re-runs load in seconds. The cost doesn't compound across pipeline runs, which is why it never became a bottleneck despite many rebuilds.

**What a GPU buys:** ~20 minutes becomes well under a minute. That's the whole benefit. It is the one GPU-shaped step in this component, and it's a convenience.

Two caveats if you do use Colab/Kaggle:

# IRE Assignment-1, Component-1 — lexical & semantic retrieval

Two-stage news recommendation on **EB-NeRD** (Danish, Ekstra Bladet) and **MIND** (English,
Microsoft), with a temporal data pipeline, BM25 and embedding candidate generation, and an
offline evaluation harness with bootstrap confidence intervals.

See `NOTES.md` for the measured data facts and every decision's justification, `DESIGN_NOTE.md`
for the write-up, and `results/` for the generated metric reports.

## Run it

```bash
make venv      # once: Python 3.11 venv + dependencies
make all       # download -> split -> retrieve -> evaluate
```

`make all` is idempotent: re-running skips completed downloads and rewrites the same bytes.
Individual stages: `make download`, `make split`, `make retrieve`, `make results`.
`make test` runs the anti-leakage checks against the built artifacts in seconds.

**One manual step.** MIND is gated. The URL in every tutorial
(`mind201910small.blob.core.windows.net`) is dead — "Public access is not permitted on this
storage account" — and `msnews.github.io` now redirects to a HuggingFace mirror. Before the
first run, log in with `huggingface-cli login`, then open
<https://huggingface.co/datasets/yjw1029/MIND> and click *"Agree and access repository"*.
Access is automatic. EB-NeRD needs no auth.

## Layout

```
configs/datasets.yaml     split cutoffs, language, stopwords, embedding source — per dataset
configs/stopwords_da.txt  Danish stopwords (bm25s ships none; measured worth +0.020 AUC)
pipeline/download.py      fetch + extract, idempotent
pipeline/split.py         temporal split -> normalised schema, with integrity assertions
retrieval/bm25.py         lexical scoring: re-rank track + full-corpus retrieval track
retrieval/embeddings.py   semantic scoring: same two tracks, same output shape
retrieval/fuse.py         per-pool z-normalised blend; alpha tuned on val only
eval/                     metrics, beyond-accuracy, slicing, bootstrap, runner
tests/test_leakage.py     no-future-click assertions against the built artifacts
results/                  generated reports (markdown + json)
```

## What it produces

`data/processed/<dataset>/` holds one schema for both datasets, so every downstream stage has a
single code path:

```
impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet
    impression_id, user_id, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[],
    history[], history_timestamps[]
articles.parquet
    article_id, title, abstract, body, category, entities, published_time,
    total_inviews, total_pageviews, total_read_time     <- serving-unavailable, eval only
```

Then per split: `bm25_*`, `emb_*`, `fused_*` (scores aligned to `candidates`) and
`retrieval_*`, `retrieval_emb_*` (full-corpus top-200).

## Correctness guarantees

`pipeline/split.py` asserts on every build, failing rather than warning:

- `train < val < test` strictly, by impression timestamp
- every history click strictly precedes its impression (per-item, EB-NeRD)
- `clicked` is a subset of `candidates`
- every candidate resolves to an article; no empty ids

Where a check is impossible it says so instead of passing vacuously — MIND's history carries no
per-item timestamps, so the harness reports that the guarantee there is structural rather than
verified. Outputs are byte-identical across runs.

`make test` re-checks the same properties from outside, reading only `data/processed/`. That is a
stronger claim than the build-time assertions: the build asserts what it *intended* to write, the
tests assert what is *actually on disk* and what every downstream stage therefore reads. One test
also fails if any module outside `eval/run.py` so much as mentions a serving-unavailable column.

1	# Component-1 Design Note — lexical & semantic retrieval on EB-NeRD and MIND
2	
3	## 1. What was built
4	
5	A config-driven pipeline that goes from raw archives to metric reports in one command
6	(`make all`), across three dataset bundles: **EB-NeRD demo** (49k impressions / 1,590 users),
7	**EB-NeRD small** (478k / 15,143) and **MIND-small** (230k / 50,000).
8	
9	Both datasets are normalised into one schema, so every stage downstream has a single code path
10	rather than a Danish branch and an English branch:
11	
12	```
13	impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet
14	    impression_id, user_id, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[], history[], history_timestamps[]
15	articles.parquet
16	    article_id, title, abstract, body, category, entities[], published_time, total_inviews, …
17	```
18	
19	`entities` is the one field with no single source shape: EB-NeRD ships pre-extracted surface forms
20	in `ner_clusters`, MIND ships JSON per field. Both normalise to `List(String)` — non-empty for 74%
21	of EB-NeRD small, 87% of MIND — so the store has one schema. Nothing scores on them yet; they are
22	carried because the feature store is the contract, and a field added later is a migration.
23	
24	Three scorers run over that schema — **bm25**, **emb**, **fused** — each on two tracks:
25	
26	* **re-rank** — score the candidate pool the log actually showed. Leaderboard-comparable.
27	* **retrieval** — ignore the pool, pull the top-200 from the whole corpus. This is the
28	  "candidate generation to a few hundred" the spec asks for.
29	
30	The query for both is the user's last 30 clicked article titles. The evaluation harness reports
31	AUC / MRR / nDCG@{5,10} with bootstrap CIs, diversity / novelty / coverage, cold-vs-warm and
32	head-vs-tail slices, and paired-bootstrap comparisons between systems.
33	
34	## 2. Temporal split
35	
36	Both datasets ship their own train/test boundary, so I adopted it as `test_start` rather than
37	inventing one, and carved `val` out of the earlier block by time. EB-NeRD's day boundary is
38	**07:00**, not midnight — a detail that only shows up in the data.
39	
40	| | train | val | test |
41	|---|---|---|---|
42	| EB-NeRD small | 168,522 | 64,365 | 244,647 |
43	| MIND-small | 95,071 | 61,894 | 73,152 |
44	
45	EB-NeRD ships a separate `history.parquet` per block whose window ends exactly where its
46	impressions begin, so the behaviour-window boundary is given rather than guessed.
47	
48	**Alternative considered:** train on all 7 provided EB-NeRD train days and split the provided
49	validation into val/test. That buys ~38% more training data but makes test history up to 7 days
50	stale by the end of the window. I kept test history fresh instead, accepting the smaller train
51	block, because nothing here is trained.
52	
53	**Enforcement, not discipline.** `split.py` asserts on every build and fails rather than warns:
54	strict `train < val < test`; per-item history-precedes-impression; `clicked` is a subset of `candidates`; every
55	candidate resolves to an article; no empty ids. Where a check is impossible it says so — MIND's
56	history has no per-item timestamps, so the harness prints that the guarantee is structural rather
57	than verified, instead of passing vacuously.
58	
59	`tests/test_leakage.py` (`make test`, 19 tests, ~16s) re-checks the same properties from *outside*,
60	reading only `data/processed/`. The distinction is the point: the build asserts what it intended to
61	write, the tests assert what is on disk and what every downstream stage actually reads. Two checks
62	exist only there — that the cutoffs in `datasets.yaml` still match the artifacts they describe, and
63	that no module outside `eval/run.py` so much as mentions a serving-unavailable column. I verified
64	the suite is not vacuous by injecting a future click into one row's history and confirming the
65	assertion fires.
66	
67	## 3. Lexical axis
68	
69	`bm25s` over title+abstract, with a per-dataset Snowball stemmer.
70	
71	**Alternatives:** `rank_bm25` is pure Python and scores one query at a time — unusable over 65k
72	documents. Pyserini/Lucene would scale further but drags in a JVM; at 20k–65k documents the
73	sparse-matrix approach is comfortably fast (MIND: 39k distinct queries in ~30s) and stays
74	explainable.
75	
76	**The finding that mattered.** EB-NeRD first scored AUC **0.5035** — indistinguishable from random.
77	Rather than report that, I checked whether it was my bug. An **oracle test** (query = the clicked
78	article's own title) ranked it #1 in 300/300 impressions at AUC 0.9990, proving candidate alignment
79	was correct, and a history-length sweep was flat from 1 to 100 clicks, ruling out query dilution.
80	But MIND worked at 0.58, and that asymmetry pointed at the real cause: **bm25s ships no Danish
81	stopword list**, so thirty concatenated Danish titles were mostly function words. Supplying the
82	standard Snowball list moved EB-NeRD to **0.5232**. A missing stopword list is silent — it degrades
83	ranking without ever erroring.
84	
85	## 4. Semantic axis
86	
87	EB-NeRD uses provided 768-d contrastive vectors (no refetch needed per bundle). MIND encodes title+abstract
88	with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (**11m16s**, cached once). User vectors are mean of last-30 history vectors,
89	L2-normalised; scoring is cosine with FAISS `IndexFlatIP` (exact at this scale; IVF/PQ deferred to 10× analysis).
90	MIND's corpus spans two files with 13,956 dev-only articles, so the index covers the 65,238-article union.
91	
92	## 5. Candidate generation: recall@K, and where the winner changes
93	
94	Recall@K over the **full catalogue** — not the pool the log showed — is what measures candidate
95	generation. Recall here is the share of an impression's clicked articles found in the top K;
96	cold-start impressions retrieve nothing and score 0 rather than being excluded, since a retriever
97	that cannot serve a user has failed for that user.
98	
99	| test, recall@K | K=50 | K=100 | K=200 | emb − bm25 @200 |
100	|---|---|---|---|---|
101	| EB-NeRD small · bm25 | 0.0072 | 0.0133 | 0.0247 | |
102	| EB-NeRD small · emb | 0.0073 | 0.0144 | **0.0277** | +0.0030 [+0.0022, +0.0039] |
103	| MIND-small · bm25 | 0.0060 | 0.0124 | 0.0220 | |
104	| MIND-small · emb | 0.0076 | 0.0138 | **0.0239** | +0.0019 [+0.0008, +0.0031] |
105	
106	Two things fall out that the aggregate number hides.
107	
108	**The semantic advantage is not at the top of the list.** At K=50 on both EB-NeRD bundles the paired
109	CI *includes zero* — the two retrievers are indistinguishable. Embeddings win only as K grows
110	(+0.0011 at 100, +0.0030 at 200). So the semantic axis is not finding better first candidates; it is
111	finding a better tail. For a system that hands 50 candidates to a re-ranker, that gain is unavailable.
112	
113	**On popular articles the verdict reverses — on one dataset.** On EB-NeRD small's head slice BM25
114	beats embeddings by **0.0791 to 0.0461**, a paired −0.0330 [−0.0542, −0.0118] against the overall

146	## 7. Evaluation harness
147	
148	Metrics are computed **per impression**, which is what makes everything else possible: slicing is a
149	mask over that vector, and bootstrapping resamples it. Resampling is over impressions, the
150	approximately-independent unit; resampling candidates within an impression would badly understate
151	variance. Comparisons use a **paired** bootstrap on shared resamples — two systems on the same
152	impressions have correlated errors, so comparing two independent intervals is far too conservative.
153	
154	**Cold-start needed a defensible definition.** "Empty history" fails on EB-NeRD, which has *zero*
155	such users (median history 258 clicks) — it would select an empty slice and silently report nothing.
156	The harness uses a per-dataset bottom-decile history-length threshold, reported alongside the
157	numbers, and additionally reports the true zero-history slice where one exists. On MIND that slice
158	scores 0.5125 identically across all three systems, which is the correct behaviour: with no history
159	there is no query, so every scorer returns zeros and no ranking is invented.
160	
161	Beyond-accuracy is reported over the top-10: category-based intra-list diversity, novelty as mean
162	self-information against *train* click shares, and catalogue coverage. Coverage is the sobering one
163	— the best systems surface only **5–21%** of the catalogue.
164	
165	## 8. Observations
166	
167	**Content signals are weak here, and that is the result, not a failure.** MIND reaches 0.6353,
168	within reach of published neural baselines for MIND-small (~0.65–0.67) from an entirely
169	unsupervised system. EB-NeRD tops out near 0.54. The likely reason is structural: EB-NeRD's pools
170	are much smaller (median 8–9 vs MIND's 23–26) and drawn from a tight recency window, so every
171	candidate is already plausible and topically close — there is little for content to separate.
172	
173	**Simple behavioural features are not the shortcut they look like.** Train-click popularity scores
174	*below* random on EB-NeRD (0.459), because the pool is already popularity-filtered.
175	
176	**Demo was representative.** Every system landed within 0.002 of its demo value at 10× the users.
177	What the extra data bought was precision — CIs tightened from ±0.0040 to ±0.0013 — which is exactly
178	what resolved the fusion question.
179	
180	**The retrieval track is weak regardless of scorer** (recall@200 of 2–5%). EB-NeRD's corpus spans
181	1998–2023 while impressions are from one week in May 2023, and the `published_time <= impression_time`

## 7. Evaluation harness

Metrics are computed **per impression**, which is what makes everything else possible: slicing is a
mask over that vector, and bootstrapping resamples it. Resampling is over impressions, the
approximately-independent unit; resampling candidates within an impression would badly understate
variance. Comparisons use a **paired** bootstrap on shared resamples — two systems on the same
impressions have correlated errors, so comparing two independent intervals is far too conservative.

**Cold-start needed a defensible definition.** "Empty history" fails on EB-NeRD, which has *zero*
such users (median history 258 clicks) — it would select an empty slice and silently report nothing.
The harness uses a per-dataset bottom-decile history-length threshold, reported alongside the
numbers, and additionally reports the true zero-history slice where one exists. On MIND that slice
scores 0.5125 identically across all three systems, which is the correct behaviour: with no history
there is no query, so every scorer returns zeros and no ranking is invented.

Beyond-accuracy is reported over the top-10: category-based intra-list diversity, novelty as mean
self-information against *train* click shares, and catalogue coverage. Coverage is the sobering one
— the best systems surface only **5–21%** of the catalogue.

## 8. Observations

**Content signals are weak here, and that is the result, not a failure.** MIND reaches 0.6353,
within reach of published neural baselines for MIND-small (~0.65–0.67) from an entirely
unsupervised system. EB-NeRD tops out near 0.54. The likely reason is structural: EB-NeRD's pools
are much smaller (median 8–9 vs MIND's 23–26) and drawn from a tight recency window, so every
candidate is already plausible and topically close — there is little for content to separate.

**Simple behavioural features are not the shortcut they look like.** Train-click popularity scores
*below* random on EB-NeRD (0.459), because the pool is already popularity-filtered.

**Demo was representative.** Every system landed within 0.002 of its demo value at 10× the users.
What the extra data bought was precision — CIs tightened from ±0.0040 to ±0.0013 — which is exactly
what resolved the fusion question.

**The retrieval track is weak regardless of scorer** (recall@200 of 2–5%). EB-NeRD's corpus spans
1998–2023 while impressions are from one week in May 2023, and the `published_time <= impression_time`
filter removes only *future* articles, not stale ones. Restricting the retrievable corpus to a
recency window is the obvious lever and belongs with the behavioural signals in C2.

## 9. Anti-gaming and serving availability

`total_inviews`/`total_pageviews`/`total_read_time` are lifetime aggregates over the whole
collection period — they embed the future and cannot be computed at serving time. They are carried
into the processed corpus **only** so the harness can quantify them, and no shipped scorer reads
them.

| test, AUC | without | with popularity | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD demo | 0.5384 | 0.5793 | +0.0409 [+0.0380, +0.0437] |
| EB-NeRD small | 0.5380 | 0.5797 | +0.0417 [+0.0408, +0.0426] |

content.text:
Here's where things stand. **The EB-NeRD submission is finished and ready to upload right now.**

## EB-NeRD — done and validated

`submissions/ebnerd_predictions.zip`, **220 MB** — the same size as the organisers' own random-baseline example, which is a good sign on its own.

- 13,536,710 impressions scored in **12m36s**, peak RSS **5.9 GB**
- That peak is *identical* to the 20k smoke test, which is the proof the streaming works — memory flat in dataset size, not linear

I validated all 13.5M lines rather than a sample, because you get 5 uploads a day and scoring takes hours:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| line count vs source rows | 13,536,710 = 13,536,710 |
| `impression_id` out of order | 0 |
| wrong candidate count | 0 |
| ranks not a permutation of 1..n | 0 |
| zip contents | exactly `['predictions.txt']` |

Plus 40 random impressions re-ranked from scratch in float64 through a completely separate code path (dicts instead of lookup arrays) — zero mismatches.

**To upload:** Codabench competition 2469 → *My Submissions* → upload `submissions/ebnerd_predictions.zip`.

## MIND — encoding now, ~30 min out

It's encoding MIND-large test's 120,961 articles (89/473 batches). Then ~2.4M impressions to score, which is a fifth of EB-NeRD's work.

On your GPU question — that encode is the **only** GPU-shaped step in the whole component, and it's inference, not training. ~30 min here versus well under a minute on Colab. Everything else is term statistics, provided vectors, and a single tuned scalar. If you do run it on Colab, copy the cached vectors back rather than re-encoding locally.

## Two things I want to flag

**The MIND entry will be embeddings-only, not `fused`.** Not a shortcut — I tried. BM25 via `get_scores` returns a dense score over the whole corpus per distinct query; at ~2M distinct histories × 120,961 articles that's ~100 billion operations. That's precisely the limitation §10 of the design note predicted, now confirmed by attempting it rather than argued from reading the code. Cost is known and small: 0.0014 AUC offline.

**I found the same `.to_list()` defect a third time.** `np.vstack(col.to_list())` peaks at **5.8 GB to build a 385 MB array** because it boxes 96M floats en route. Fixing it cut the submitter from 7.0 → 5.9 GB and made it 33% faster, byte-identical output. Same bug was in `retrieval/embeddings.py`; both now use `_unnest`, verified value-identical. Three strikes is why §10 now names that one idiom as *the* scaling wall.

## Housekeeping

- `design_note_c1.pdf` is back to **4 pages** — I added a §11 on the submissions, which pushed it to 5, then trimmed real prose rather than shrinking margins to hide it. There's a `build_design_note.sh` that warns if it ever goes over.
- The note has a marked slot for your **leaderboard screenshots** (Q5 requires them and only you can produce them).
- Added `submissions/` to `.gitignore` — `predictions.txt` is 671 MB and Q8 forbids large files.

Upload the EB-NeRD zip whenever you like; I'll have MIND ready shortly.

content.text:
Both leaderboard submissions are complete and validated end-to-end.

## Ready to upload

| | file | size | impressions | wall | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EB-NeRD** (comp. 2469) | `submissions/ebnerd_predictions.zip` | 220 MB | 13,536,710 | 12m36s | 5.9 GB |
| **MIND** (comp. 13967) | `submissions/mind_prediction.zip` | 103 MB | 2,370,727 | 6m05s | 1.3 GB |

Every line of both files was checked — not a sample:

- line count = source rows exactly (13,536,710 and 2,370,727)
- zero `impression_id` out of order
- zero wrong candidate counts
- zero rank lists that aren't a permutation of 1..n
- each zip contains exactly its one expected text file, no folders

Plus 40 random impressions per dataset re-ranked from scratch in float64 through a separate code path — zero mismatches.

**Upload:** Codabench 2469 → *My Submissions* for EB-NeRD; 13967 → *Participate* → *Submit/View Results* for MIND. Remember EB-NeRD caps you at 5/day and scores over hours.

## The MIND run failed first, and the fix was instructive

The initial full MIND run was **OOM-killed at 200k impressions**. Cause: `stream_mind` read `behaviors.tsv` whole — 2.37M rows, **3.07 GB peak just to parse** — then did `.to_list()` on ~7.8M candidate strings per slice. It was never actually streaming; only the EB-NeRD path was. I'd named the file "streaming scorer" and only half-built it.

CSV has no slice pushdown, so the fix was a one-off TSV→parquet conversion that also resolves article ids to integer rows while still inside Polars (`replace_strict` in `list.eval`, written via `sink_parquet` so the conversion itself never materialises). After that MIND uses the identical slice-pushdown loop as EB-NeRD, and ~93M candidate strings never enter Python.

**4.2 GB → 1.3 GB, and the first 20,000 output lines are byte-identical to the pre-rewrite run** — so it's behaviour-preserving, not just smaller.

One honesty note: when I first diffed against the earlier output it looked like a 179,959-line regression. It wasn't — I'd compared against the *partial output of the OOM-killed run*. The diff notation `20001,199959d20000` was actually saying lines 1–20000 matched all along. I checked rather than assumed, which is the only reason I didn't "fix" a non-bug.

## Also

I removed a `rows >= 0` filter from `mean_pool` while cleaning up dead code, *after* the EB-NeRD artifact was already generated. Rather than assume that was safe, I verified `article_row` provably contains no negatives at that point — the filter was a no-op, so the validated EB-NeRD file stands unmodified.

`design_note_c1.pdf` is still **4 pages** with the measured MIND figures folded into §10.

content.text:
No, and I'd rather say that plainly than invent a use for it. Nothing in Component-1 trains — BM25 is term statistics, EB-NeRD's vectors are provided, FAISS flat just stores them, fusion tunes one scalar. Both encodes are already done and **cached**, so re-running them on GPU would buy nothing.

But two optional experiments are worth putting in front of you, and only one of them wants a GPU.

## Worth doing, needs no GPU

The PDF's semantic-axis bullet reads: *"Semantic — article/text embeddings (**Word2Vec, BERT, XLM-RoBERTa**)"*. EB-NeRD ships precisely those three as precomputed artifacts, and I only ever used a fourth one:

| artifact | size | status |
|---|---|---|
| `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector` | 357 MB | **in use** |
| `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` | 139 MB | not downloaded |
| `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` | 361 MB | not downloaded |
| `FacebookAI_xlm_roberta_base` | 357 MB | not downloaded |

They're precomputed vectors — no encoding, no GPU. And `configs/datasets.yaml` already takes an `embeddings:` path, so this is a config change per variant, not new code.

That gives a genuine four-way encoder ablation with paired bootstrap CIs, directly addressing the PDF's "ablation rigour" grading criterion and its exact wording. ~857 MB download, maybe an hour end to end. **This is the one I'd actually recommend** — and it's the strongest remaining gap, since right now the design note has no encoder ablation at all.

## Where the GPU would help

MIND uses `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` — 6 layers, 384-d, 22M params. That's a *small* model. Something like `all-mpnet-base-v2` (12 layers, 768-d, 110M) or a BGE/E5 base model typically does better on retrieval, and MIND has headroom: we're at 0.6353 against published neural baselines of ~0.65–0.67.

On CPU that's ~1 hr for MIND-small plus ~2 hr for MIND-large test. On your cluster, minutes.

**The catch, stated up front:** swapping the encoder invalidates every embedding-based number already reported — the MIND results, the fusion α, the recall@K table, the head-slice comparison, and the leaderboard submission. That's a deliberate full re-run, not a free upgrade. And it's *plausible*, not certain, that a bigger encoder wins here — worth measuring, not assuming, same standard I've applied to everything else.

## My read

Neither is required — the assignment is complete. If you want one thing, take the EB-NeRD ablation: it needs no GPU, it maps onto the PDF's own wording, and it fills a real gap. Do the MIND encoder swap only if you specifically want a stronger leaderboard number and are happy to re-run and re-upload.

Which, if either? Or I can do the AI usage log and the git split instead — those are still genuinely outstanding.

Here's the honest read against your constraints.

## The assignment still doesn't need it

Both submissions are built and validated. Nothing pending trains anything.

## If you do want the MIND encoder swap, it's a trivial job

The useful observation: **the encode only needs `news.tsv`, not the impression logs.** 169 MB of text goes out, ~570 MB of vectors comes back. Scoring stays local.

That means almost none of your listed constraints bite:

| your constraint | applies here? |
|---|---|
| Stage to `/scratch`, NFS bottlenecks dataloaders | 169 MB, one sequential read — no dataloader |
| Checkpointing mandatory, jobs killed at walltime | ~10 min job; nothing to checkpoint |
| Queue wait is the real bottleneck | this is the one that matters — 1 GPU, short walltime, so shortest queue |
| `/share1`, `/share2` invisible from compute nodes | irrelevant, nothing lives there |
| 4× GPU, 40 CPU cap | needs 1 GPU, ~2 cores |

Your mixed fleet does matter slightly: AMP/fp16 only helps on the 2080 Ti (Turing). On a 1080 Ti, run fp32 — Pascal gives you nothing and fp16 can be *slower*. For a 10-minute job I wouldn't add a `--constraint` for it; you'd wait longer in queue than you'd save.

11 GB VRAM is ample — `mpnet-base` inference at batch 256 on short news text is nowhere near that.

## The one thing the cluster uniquely enables

[Issue #2101](https://github.com/codalab/codabench/issues/2101) reports exactly this: uploads around 150 MB fail within seconds, files under ~50 MB succeed. Closed as "User-specific" with no documented fix. Your 220 MB and 103 MB both sit in the failing band.

## Compression can't rescue it

I measured rather than assumed:

| | current (deflate) | bzip2 | lzma |
|---|---|---|---|
| MIND | 107 MB | **91 MB** | 94 MB |
| EB-NeRD | 220 MB | ~190 MB (est.) | — |

Even best case stays far above the ~50 MB that reportedly works, and bzip2/lzma inside a zip risks the scorer not reading it. Not worth the gamble for 15%.

## Try these first, cheapest to costliest

1. **Check it's actually failing, not just slow.** 220 MB at 5 Mbps uplink is ~6 minutes; at 1 Mbps it's 30. If the progress bar is crawling rather than erroring, it may just need time.
2. **Upload MIND first (103 MB).** Smaller — if it succeeds and EB-NeRD doesn't, that locates your threshold and is useful information.
3. **Wired connection, disable sleep/suspend.** A laptop suspending mid-upload kills it silently.
4. **Different browser, extensions off.** Ad-blockers and privacy extensions break chunked upload widgets fairly often.

Note: a *failed upload doesn't consume a submission slot*, so retrying is free — the 5/day cap only counts submissions that land.

## The robust fix: upload via the API

I confirmed the endpoints exist — `/api/datasets/upload/` and `/api/submissions/` both return **403 (auth required)**, not 404. # Setup Matt Pocock's Skills

Scaffold the per-repo configuration that the engineering skills assume:

- **Issue tracker** — where issues live (GitHub by default; local markdown is also supported out of the box)
- **Triage labels** — the strings used for the five canonical triage roles
- **Domain docs** — where `CONTEXT.md` and ADRs live, and the consumer rules for reading them

This is a prompt-driven skill, not a deterministic script. Explore, present what you found, confirm with the user, then write.

## Process

### 1. Explore

Look at the current repo to understand its starting state. Read whatever exists; don't assume:

- `git remote -v` and `.git/config` — is this a GitHub repo? Which one?
- `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root — does either exist? Is there already an `## Agent skills` section in either?
- `CONTEXT.md` and `CONTEXT-MAP.md` at the repo root
- `docs/adr/` and any `src/*/docs/adr/` directories
- `docs/agents/` — does this skill's prior output already exist?
- `.scratch/` — sign that a local-markdown issue tracker convention is already in use
- Is the `triage` skill installed? (a `triage` skill folder alongside this one, or `triage` in your available skills.) This decides whether Section B runs at all.
- Monorepo signals — a `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, a `workspaces` field in `package.json`, or a populated `packages/*` with its own `src/`. Present only in a genuinely large multi-package repo; their absence means single-context, which is almost every repo.

### 2. Present findings and ask

Summarise what's present and what's missing. Then take the sections in order — one section, one answer, then the next.

Lead each section with the recommended answer so the user can accept it in a word. Give a one-line explainer only when the choice genuinely branches; skip the section entirely when exploration already settled it (Section B when `triage` isn't installed, Section C when there's no monorepo).

**Section A — Issue tracker.**

> Explainer: The "issue tracker" is where issues live for this repo. Skills like `to-tickets`, `triage`, `to-spec`, and `qa` read from and write to it — they need to know whether to call `gh issue create`, write a markdown file under `.scratch/`, or follow some other workflow you describe. Pick the place you actually track work for this repo.

Default posture: these skills were designed for GitHub. If a `git remote` points at GitHub, propose that. If a `git remote` points at GitLab (`gitlab.com` or a self-hosted host), propose GitLab. Otherwise (or if the user prefers), offer:

- **GitHub** — issues live in the repo's GitHub Issues (uses the `gh` CLI)
- **GitLab** — issues live in the repo's GitLab Issues (uses the [`glab`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli) CLI)
- **Local markdown** — issues live as files under `.scratch/<feature>/` in this repo (good for solo projects or repos without a remote)
- **Other** (Jira, Linear, etc.) — ask the user to describe the workflow in one paragraph; the skill will record it as freeform prose

Record the choice in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`. The GitHub and GitLab templates carry a "PRs as a request surface" flag, defaulted **off** — leave it off and don't raise it; a user who wants external PRs in the triage queue can flip the flag in the file later.

**Section B — Triage label vocabulary.** Skip this section entirely if the `triage` skill isn't installed (exploration told you) — an uninstalled skill needs no labels.

If it is installed, ask exactly one question:

> Do you want to keep the default triage labels? (recommended: **yes**)

The defaults are the five canonical roles, each label string equal to its name: `needs-triage`, `needs-info`, `ready-for-agent`, `ready-for-human`, `wontfix`. On **yes**, write them as-is. Only if the user says no — usually because their tracker already uses other names (e.g. `bug:triage` for `needs-triage`) — collect the overrides so `triage` applies existing labels instead of creating duplicates.

**Section C — Domain docs.** Default to **single-context** — one `CONTEXT.md` + `docs/adr/` at the repo root. This fits almost every repo; write it without asking.

Offer **multi-context** — a root `CONTEXT-MAP.md` pointing to per-context `CONTEXT.md` files — only when exploration found monorepo signals. Then confirm which layout they want.

### 3. Confirm and edit

Show the user a draft of:

- The `## Agent skills` block to add to whichever of `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` is being edited (see step 4 for selection rules)
- The contents of `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`, `docs/agents/domain.md`, and `docs/agents/triage-labels.md` (the last only when `triage` is installed)

Let them edit before writing.

### 4. Write

**Pick the file to edit:**

- If `CLAUDE.md` exists, edit it.
- Else if `AGENTS.md` exists, edit it.
- If neither exists, ask the user which one to create — don't pick for them.

Never create `AGENTS.md` when `CLAUDE.md` already exists (or vice versa) — always edit the one that's already there.

If an `## Agent skills` block already exists in the chosen file, update its contents in-place rather than appending a duplicate. Don't overwrite user edits to the surrounding sections.

The block:

```markdown
## Agent skills

### Issue tracker

[one-line summary of where issues are tracked]. See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.

### Triage labels

[one-line summary of the label vocabulary]. See `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`.

### Domain docs

[one-line summary of layout — "single-context" or "multi-context"]. See `docs/agents/domain.md`.
```

Include the `### Triage labels` sub-block, and write `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`, only when `triage` is installed and Section B ran. When it isn't, both are omitted.

Then write the docs files using the seed templates in this skill folder as a starting point:

- [issue-tracker-github.md](./issue-tracker-github.md) — GitHub issue tracker
- [issue-tracker-gitlab.md](./issue-tracker-gitlab.md) — GitLab issue tracker
- [issue-tracker-local.md](./issue-tracker-local.md) — local-markdown issue tracker
- [triage-labels.md](./triage-labels.md) — label mapping (only if `triage` is installed)
- [domain.md](./domain.md) — domain doc consumer rules + layout

For "other" issue trackers, write `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` from scratch using the user's description.

### 5. Done

Tell the user the setup is complete and which engineering skills will now read from these files. Mention they can edit `docs/agents/*.md` directly later — re-running this skill is only necessary if they want to switch issue trackers or restart from scratch.
