# Issue tracker: Local Markdown

Issues and specs (you may know a spec as a PRD) for this repo live as markdown files in `.scratch/`.

## Conventions

- One feature per directory: `.scratch/<feature-slug>/`
- The spec is `.scratch/<feature-slug>/spec.md`
- Implementation issues are one file per ticket at `.scratch/<feature-slug>/issues/<NN>-<slug>.md`, numbered from `01` — never a single combined tickets file
- Triage state is recorded as a `Status:` line near the top of each issue file (see `triage-labels.md` for the role strings)
- Comments and conversation history append to the bottom of the file under a `## Comments` heading

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a new file under `.scratch/<feature-slug>/` (creating the directory if needed).

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Read the file at the referenced path. The user will normally pass the path or the issue number directly.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a file with one **child** file per ticket.

- **Map**: `.scratch/<effort>/map.md` — the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body.
- **Child ticket**: `.scratch/<effort>/issues/NN-<slug>.md`, numbered from `01`, with the question in the body. A `Type:` line records the ticket type (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`); a `Status:` line records `claimed`/`resolved`.
- **Blocking**: a `Blocked by: NN, NN` line near the top. A ticket is unblocked when every file it lists is `resolved`.
- **Frontier**: scan `.scratch/<effort>/issues/` for files that are open, unblocked, and unclaimed; first by number wins.
- **Claim**: set `Status: claimed` and save before any work.
- **Resolve**: append the answer under an `## Answer` heading, set `Status: resolved`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far in `map.md`.
=================== domain.md
# Domain Docs

How the engineering skills should consume this repo's domain documentation when exploring the codebase.

## Before exploring, read these

- **`CONTEXT.md`** at the repo root, or
- **`CONTEXT-MAP.md`** at the repo root if it exists — it points at one `CONTEXT.md` per context. Read each one relevant to the topic.
- **`docs/adr/`** — read ADRs that touch the area you're about to work in. In multi-context repos, also check `src/<context>/docs/adr/` for context-scoped decisions.

If any of these files don't exist, **proceed silently**. Don't flag their absence; don't suggest creating them upfront. The `/domain-modeling` skill (reached via `/grill-with-docs` and `/improve-codebase-architecture`) creates them lazily when terms or decisions actually get resolved.

## File structure

Single-context repo (most repos):

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/adr/
│   ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│   └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

Multi-context repo (presence of `CONTEXT-MAP.md` at the root):

```
/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
└── src/
    ├── ordering/
    │   ├── CONTEXT.md
    │   └── docs/adr/                  ← context-specific decisions
    └── billing/
        ├── CONTEXT.md
        └── docs/adr/
```

## Use the glossary's vocabulary

When your output names a domain concept (in an issue title, a refactor proposal, a hypothesis, a test name), use the term as defined in `CONTEXT.md`. Don't drift to synonyms the glossary explicitly avoids.

If the concept you need isn't in the glossary yet, that's a signal — either you're inventing language the project doesn't use (reconsider) or there's a real gap (note it for `/domain-modeling`).

## Flag ADR conflicts

If your output contradicts an existing ADR, surface it explicitly rather than silently overriding:

> _Contradicts ADR-0007 (event-sourced orders) — but worth reopening because…_

Good — this is the most useful thing we can do. I'll start with the big picture, then you pick what to go deeper on.

---

# 1. What the assignment actually asks

A news website shows someone a short list of articles. They click one. That moment — the list shown, plus what got clicked — is one row of your data. There are millions of them.

**Your job:** given the list that was shown, put those articles in order so the one the person actually clicked ends up near the top.

That's the whole task. It's a sorting job.

You're allowed to use two things to help you sort:
- **What that person read before** (their reading history)
- **The text of each article** (headline, summary, body)

**Why it's harder than it sounds:** the articles in the list were *already* chosen by the news site's own system. They're all recent, all newsworthy, all plausible. You're not separating good from rubbish — you're separating good from good.

---

# 2. What we built

Two different ways to guess, plus a tool to check how well each guess does.

**Way 1 — matching words.**
If someone reads a lot about football, and one of the choices has "football" in the headline, that's probably a decent bet. So: count the words shared between what they read before and each article on offer. More overlap = higher rank.

The standard recipe for doing this counting properly is called **BM25**. It's decades old and very well understood. It's just word counting with sensible adjustments (rare words count more, very long articles don't get an unfair advantage).

**Way 2 — matching meaning.**
Word matching breaks when different words mean the same thing. "Car" and "vehicle" share no letters but mean nearly the same. So we also turn each article into a long list of numbers that captures *what it's about*. Articles on similar topics get similar numbers.

Those number-lists are called **embeddings**. We compare number-lists instead of words.

**Then: measure.**
We take articles where we already know what was clicked, run both methods, and count how often the clicked article ended up near the top.

---

# 3. The one number you need to understand

It's called **AUC**. Here's what it means, plainly:

> Pick one article the person clicked, and one they didn't. How often does your method rank the clicked one higher?

- **0.5** = you're guessing. A coin flip.
- **1.0** = perfect, every time.
- **0.6** = right 60% of the time.

That's it. That's the whole idea.

---

# 4. What we actually got

| dataset | word matching | meaning matching |
|---|---|---|
| MIND (English news) | 0.56 | **0.64** |
| EB-NeRD (Danish news) | 0.51 | **0.54** |

**Meaning beat words on both.** That's the main result.

**But be ready for this question: "why so low?"** Your answer is a good one, and it's honest:

On the Danish data, the lists shown were tiny — often only 8 or 9 articles, all published in the same few hours, all about similar things. There's very little for *any* text-based method to grab onto. On the English data, lists were longer and more varied, so there was more to work with — and the score is higher, 0.64.

For comparison: published research on this English dataset, using trained neural networks, gets around 0.65–0.67. We got 0.64 **without training anything at all**. That's a genuinely respectable answer.

---

# Where do you want to go next?

Pick any of these and I'll do the same treatment:

1. **How we split the data by time** — and why doing it wrong would be cheating (this is worth a lot of marks)
2. **How word matching works** — and the bug I found that was silently ruining the Danish results
3. **How meaning matching works** — where the numbers come from
4. **How we measure properly** — and why we report a *range* instead of a single number
5. **The anti-cheating checks** — the assignment specifically demands these
6. **The mistakes I made and fixed** — good viva material, since markers like hearing about real debugging

I'd suggest **1** first — it's the foundation everything else sits on, and it's the single thing most likely to come up in your viva. But your call.

# Glossary — every term in this assignment, in plain English

Written for someone new to the subject. Terms are grouped by what they're for, not alphabetically,
because that's the order they make sense in.

Tags: **[used]** we built it · **[named]** the brief mentions it, we didn't use it ·
**[tooling]** not from the course at all

---

## 1. Words for the data itself

**Impression** **[used]**
One moment when a list of articles was shown to one person. Your data is millions of these.
Each one records: who, when, what was shown, what was clicked.

**Candidates** **[used]**
The articles in that shown list. These are what you have to put in order.

**Click history** **[used]**
The articles that person read *before* this moment. Your main clue about what they like.

**Session context** **[named]**
Extra details of the moment — time of day, device used. We didn't use these.

**Corpus** **[used]**
All the articles you have. The whole collection.

**Catalogue** **[used]**
Same thing as corpus. Used interchangeably.

---

## 2. The three kinds of clue (the "three axes")

The brief keeps saying "all three modelling axes". It just means these three kinds of clue:

**Lexical** **[used]**
To do with the actual *words*. Matching because two texts share the word "football".

**Semantic** **[used]**
To do with *meaning*. Matching "car" with "vehicle" even though they share no letters.

**Behavioural** **[named]**
To do with what people *do* — what's popular, what's recent, what they clicked lately.
This is the follow-up assignment, not this one.

---

## 3. Matching on words

**BM25** **[used]**
A recipe for scoring word overlap between what you're searching with and each document.
Two sensible adjustments over naive counting:
- rare words count for more than common ones
- long documents don't win just for containing more words

It's the standard baseline in search — decades old, very well understood.

**TF-IDF** **[named]**
An older, simpler version of the same idea. TF = how often a word appears here.
IDF = how rare that word is overall. Multiply them. BM25 is the refined descendant.

**Inverted index** **[used]**
A lookup table from *word* → *which documents contain it*. Exactly like the index at the back of
a textbook. It's what makes word search fast — you never scan every document.

**Stopwords** **[used]**
Extremely common words — "the", "and", "is" — that carry almost no meaning, so they get thrown
away before matching. **This caused the biggest bug in the project:** no Danish stopword list
existed, so the Danish results were almost random until I supplied one.

**Stemming** **[used]**
Chopping words back to a root so "running", "runs" and "ran" all match each other.
Has to be done per-language.

---

## 4. Matching on meaning

**Embedding** (also called a **vector**) **[used]**
A long list of numbers standing in for a piece of text, arranged so that texts about similar
things get similar numbers. Ours are 768 numbers per article (Danish) or 384 (English).

**Word2Vec** **[named]**
An older way to make embeddings — one fixed vector per word.

**BERT** **[named]**
A neural network that reads a whole sentence and produces embeddings that depend on context,
so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank account" come out different.

**XLM-RoBERTa** **[named]**
Like BERT, but trained on many languages at once. Useful for Danish.

**MiniLM** **[used]**
The small, fast embedding model we actually used for the English data.

**Cosine similarity** **[used]**
How we compare two embeddings. Gives a number where higher = more alike. It compares *direction*
only, ignoring size — so a long article and a short one about the same topic still match.

---

## 5. Finding the good ones quickly

**Top-K** **[used]**
The K best results. "Top-200" = the 200 highest-scoring articles.

**Nearest neighbour** **[used]**
The most similar item to the thing you're holding.

**ANN — Approximate Nearest Neighbour** **[used]**
Finding the most similar items *quickly*, by accepting "very close" instead of insisting on
"provably the closest". You need this when there are millions of items, because checking every
one is too slow.

**FAISS** **[used]** / **ScaNN** **[named]**
Software libraries that do that search. FAISS is Meta's, ScaNN is Google's. We used FAISS.

**Flat index / brute force** **[used]**
Checking every single item, no shortcuts. Exact, but slow at large sizes.
At our size it was fast enough, so that's what we used.

**IVF / PQ / quantisation** **[named]**
Tricks to make the search faster by being slightly less exact. We didn't need them, but the
report explains when you would.

**Candidate generation** **[used]**
Stage one: narrowing the whole collection down to a few hundred worth a closer look.

**Re-ranker** **[named]**
Stage two: carefully ordering those few hundred with a trained model. **Not this assignment.**

**Two-stage retrieve-then-rank** **[used]**
The overall pattern: cheap narrowing first, expensive careful ordering second.

**GBDT — Gradient Boosted Decision Trees** **[named]**
A kind of machine-learning model that works well on table-shaped data. Suggested for the
re-ranker in the follow-up.

---

## 6. Scoring how good you are

**AUC** **[used]** — *the headline number*
Pick one article they clicked and one they didn't. How often do you rank the clicked one higher?
- 0.5 = coin flip
- 1.0 = perfect

**MRR — Mean Reciprocal Rank** **[used]**
If the clicked article lands at position 1 you score 1; position 2 scores ½; position 3 scores ⅓.
Averaged over everything. Rewards getting the right answer *very* near the top.

**nDCG@5 / nDCG@10** **[used]**
"How good is my ordering in the top 5 (or 10), compared with the best possible ordering?"
1.0 = perfect. The @5 / @10 is just how far down the list you look.

**Recall@K** **[used]**
Of the articles the person actually clicked, what fraction did you manage to get into your top K?
This measures whether stage one is even finding the right things.

---

## 7. Measures that aren't accuracy

The brief calls these **beyond-accuracy**. The point: a system can score well and still be bad.

**Diversity** **[used]**
Are your ten recommendations all about the same thing, or a mix? Ten football stories = not diverse.

**Novelty** **[used]**
Are you showing obscure things, or only what everybody already reads?

**Coverage** **[used]**
Across everything you recommend to everyone, what share of the whole collection did you ever show?
Ours was 5–21% — meaning most articles never get shown to anyone, by any method.

---

## 8. Looking at subgroups

**Slice / slicing** **[used]**
Checking your score for one subgroup instead of everybody, because an average can hide that
you're terrible for some people.

**Cold-start** **[used]**
Someone you know almost nothing about — a brand-new user with no reading history.
There's nothing to match against, so it's the hardest case.

**Warm** **[used]**
The opposite: plenty of history to work with.

**Head vs tail** **[used]**
Head = popular items. Tail = rarely-touched items. Most items are tail.
Systems usually look good on head and bad on tail.

---

## 9. Splitting the data, and cheating

**Temporal split** **[used]**
Dividing your data by *time*: earliest chunk to build on, middle to tune with, latest to test on.

**Random split** **[forbidden]**
Dividing rows randomly. **Banned in this assignment**, because it lets you learn from the future
to predict the past. That inflates your score and means nothing.

**Train / validation / test** **[used]**
Three chunks. *Train* = build on it. *Validation* = tune your choices on it.
*Test* = your final honest score — you look at it once, at the end.

**Leakage** **[used]**
Using information you couldn't possibly have had at the time. Cheating, usually by accident.

**Future-click leakage** **[used]**
The specific version here: using a click that happened *after* the moment you're predicting.

**Behaviour-window boundary** **[used]**
The cut-off line. History must come from before it, predictions from after it.

**Serving time** **[used]**
The moment a real system would have to make this recommendation, live.
If a piece of information doesn't exist yet at that moment, you're not allowed to use it.

**Serving-unavailable feature** **[used]**
Data that only exists later. Example: an article's total lifetime view count — that's only known
after the fact. Using it inflates your score dishonestly. The brief demands you report your
numbers both with and without such features. Ours: it was worth +0.041 AUC, more than our entire
meaning-matching method gained.

**Anti-gaming** **[used]**
The brief's rules to stop you inflating your numbers, accidentally or otherwise.

**Ablation** **[named]**
Removing one piece and re-measuring, to prove that piece actually mattered.

---

## 10. Being sure your numbers are real

**Bootstrap** **[used]**
A way to find out how much your score would wobble if you'd happened to collect slightly
different data. You re-draw your data at random (with repeats allowed) many times — we did 1,000 —
and watch how much the answer moves.

**Confidence interval (CI)** **[used]**
The resulting range. "0.64, somewhere between 0.63 and 0.65."

**Paired bootstrap** **[used]**
Comparing two methods on the *same* re-drawn data each time. Fairer, because both methods face
identical luck.

**"the CI excludes zero"** **[used]**
Means an improvement is real rather than noise. If the range of the *difference* between two
methods includes zero, they might genuinely be equally good and you can't claim a win.

---

## 11. Admin words

**Leaderboard** **[used]** — a public ranking of everyone's submissions.
**Codabench** **[used]** — the website hosting the two leaderboards you must submit to.
**Design note** **[used]** — the report you hand in, 4 pages maximum.
**10× scale** **[used]** — "what would break if this got ten times bigger?"
**Viva** — the live conversation where you explain and modify your own code.

---

## 12. Tooling words — NOT from your course

You don't need these for the assignment. Listed only because they've come up.

**ADR — Architecture Decision Record** **[tooling]**
A short note recording why a technical choice was made. It came from a plugin, not your course.

**Parquet** **[tooling]** — a file format for tables. Smaller and much faster than CSV.
**Polars** **[tooling]** — the library we use to handle tables. Like pandas, but faster and lighter.
**Streaming** **[tooling]** — processing data in chunks rather than loading it all at once.
**OOM (Out Of Memory)** **[tooling]** — the program asked for more memory than existed and was killed.

# Glossary — every term in this assignment, in plain English

Written for someone new to the subject. Terms are grouped by what they're for, not alphabetically,
because that's the order they make sense in.

Tags: **[used]** we built it · **[named]** the brief mentions it, we didn't use it ·
**[tooling]** not from the course at all

---

## 1. Words for the data itself

**Impression** **[used]**
One moment when a list of articles was shown to one person. Your data is millions of these.
Each one records: who, when, what was shown, what was clicked.

**Candidates** **[used]**
The articles in that shown list. These are what you have to put in order.

**Click history** **[used]**
The articles that person read *before* this moment. Your main clue about what they like.

**Session context** **[named]**
Extra details of the moment — time of day, device used. We didn't use these.

**Corpus** **[used]**
All the articles you have. The whole collection.

**Catalogue** **[used]**
Same thing as corpus. Used interchangeably.

---

## 2. The three kinds of clue (the "three axes")

The brief keeps saying "all three modelling axes". It just means these three kinds of clue:

**Lexical** **[used]**
To do with the actual *words*. Matching because two texts share the word "football".

**Semantic** **[used]**
To do with *meaning*. Matching "car" with "vehicle" even though they share no letters.

**Behavioural** **[named]**
To do with what people *do* — what's popular, what's recent, what they clicked lately.
This is the follow-up assignment, not this one.

---

## 3. Matching on words

**BM25** **[used]**
A recipe for scoring word overlap between what you're searching with and each document.
Two sensible adjustments over naive counting:
- rare words count for more than common ones
- long documents don't win just for containing more words

It's the standard baseline in search — decades old, very well understood.

**TF-IDF** **[named]**
An older, simpler version of the same idea. TF = how often a word appears here.
IDF = how rare that word is overall. Multiply them. BM25 is the refined descendant.

**Inverted index** **[used]**
A lookup table from *word* → *which documents contain it*. Exactly like the index at the back of
a textbook. It's what makes word search fast — you never scan every document.

**Stopwords** **[used]**
Extremely common words — "the", "and", "is" — that carry almost no meaning, so they get thrown
away before matching. **This caused the biggest bug in the project:** no Danish stopword list
existed, so the Danish results were almost random until I supplied one.

**Stemming** **[used]**
Chopping words back to a root so "running", "runs" and "ran" all match each other.
Has to be done per-language.

---

## 4. Matching on meaning

**Embedding** (also called a **vector**) **[used]**
A long list of numbers standing in for a piece of text, arranged so that texts about similar
things get similar numbers. Ours are 768 numbers per article (Danish) or 384 (English).

**Word2Vec** **[named]**
An older way to make embeddings — one fixed vector per word.

**BERT** **[named]**
A neural network that reads a whole sentence and produces embeddings that depend on context,
so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank account" come out different.

**XLM-RoBERTa** **[named]**
Like BERT, but trained on many languages at once. Useful for Danish.

**MiniLM** **[used]**
The small, fast embedding model we actually used for the English data.

**Cosine similarity** **[used]**
How we compare two embeddings. Gives a number where higher = more alike. It compares *direction*
only, ignoring size — so a long article and a short one about the same topic still match.

---

## 5. Finding the good ones quickly

**Top-K** **[used]**
The K best results. "Top-200" = the 200 highest-scoring articles.

**Nearest neighbour** **[used]**
The most similar item to the thing you're holding.

**ANN — Approximate Nearest Neighbour** **[used]**
Finding the most similar items *quickly*, by accepting "very close" instead of insisting on
"provably the closest". You need this when there are millions of items, because checking every
one is too slow.

**FAISS** **[used]** / **ScaNN** **[named]**
Software libraries that do that search. FAISS is Meta's, ScaNN is Google's. We used FAISS.

**Flat index / brute force** **[used]**
Checking every single item, no shortcuts. Exact, but slow at large sizes.
At our size it was fast enough, so that's what we used.

**IVF / PQ / quantisation** **[named]**
Tricks to make the search faster by being slightly less exact. We didn't need them, but the
report explains when you would.

**Candidate generation** **[used]**
Stage one: narrowing the whole collection down to a few hundred worth a closer look.

**Re-ranker** **[named]**
Stage two: carefully ordering those few hundred with a trained model. **Not this assignment.**

**Two-stage retrieve-then-rank** **[used]**
The overall pattern: cheap narrowing first, expensive careful ordering second.

**GBDT — Gradient Boosted Decision Trees** **[named]**
A kind of machine-learning model that works well on table-shaped data. Suggested for the
re-ranker in the follow-up.

---

## 6. Scoring how good you are

**AUC** **[used]** — *the headline number*
Pick one article they clicked and one they didn't. How often do you rank the clicked one higher?
- 0.5 = coin flip
- 1.0 = perfect

**MRR — Mean Reciprocal Rank** **[used]**
If the clicked article lands at position 1 you score 1; position 2 scores ½; position 3 scores ⅓.
Averaged over everything. Rewards getting the right answer *very* near the top.

**nDCG@5 / nDCG@10** **[used]**
"How good is my ordering in the top 5 (or 10), compared with the best possible ordering?"
1.0 = perfect. The @5 / @10 is just how far down the list you look.

**Recall@K** **[used]**
Of the articles the person actually clicked, what fraction did you manage to get into your top K?
This measures whether stage one is even finding the right things.

---

## 7. Measures that aren't accuracy

The brief calls these **beyond-accuracy**. The point: a system can score well and still be bad.

**Diversity** **[used]**
Are your ten recommendations all about the same thing, or a mix? Ten football stories = not diverse.

**Novelty** **[used]**
Are you showing obscure things, or only what everybody already reads?

**Coverage** **[used]**
Across everything you recommend to everyone, what share of the whole collection did you ever show?
Ours was 5–21% — meaning most articles never get shown to anyone, by any method.

---

## 8. Looking at subgroups

**Slice / slicing** **[used]**
Checking your score for one subgroup instead of everybody, because an average can hide that
you're terrible for some people.

**Cold-start** **[used]**
Someone you know almost nothing about — a brand-new user with no reading history.
There's nothing to match against, so it's the hardest case.

**Warm** **[used]**
The opposite: plenty of history to work with.

**Head vs tail** **[used]**
Head = popular items. Tail = rarely-touched items. Most items are tail.
Systems usually look good on head and bad on tail.

---

## 9. Splitting the data, and cheating

**Temporal split** **[used]**
Dividing your data by *time*: earliest chunk to build on, middle to tune with, latest to test on.

**Random split** **[forbidden]**
Dividing rows randomly. **Banned in this assignment**, because it lets you learn from the future
to predict the past. That inflates your score and means nothing.

**Train / validation / test** **[used]**
Three chunks. *Train* = build on it. *Validation* = tune your choices on it.
*Test* = your final honest score — you look at it once, at the end.

**Leakage** **[used]**
Using information you couldn't possibly have had at the time. Cheating, usually by accident.

**Future-click leakage** **[used]**
The specific version here: using a click that happened *after* the moment you're predicting.

**Behaviour-window boundary** **[used]**
The cut-off line. History must come from before it, predictions from after it.

**Serving time** **[used]**
The moment a real system would have to make this recommendation, live.
If a piece of information doesn't exist yet at that moment, you're not allowed to use it.

**Serving-unavailable feature** **[used]**
Data that only exists later. Example: an article's total lifetime view count — that's only known
after the fact. Using it inflates your score dishonestly. The brief demands you report your
numbers both with and without such features. Ours: it was worth +0.041 AUC, more than our entire
meaning-matching method gained.

**Anti-gaming** **[used]**
The brief's rules to stop you inflating your numbers, accidentally or otherwise.

**Ablation** **[named]**
Removing one piece and re-measuring, to prove that piece actually mattered.

---

## 10. Being sure your numbers are real

**Bootstrap** **[used]**
A way to find out how much your score would wobble if you'd happened to collect slightly
different data. You re-draw your data at random (with repeats allowed) many times — we did 1,000 —
and watch how much the answer moves.

**Confidence interval (CI)** **[used]**
The resulting range. "0.64, somewhere between 0.63 and 0.65."

**Paired bootstrap** **[used]**
Comparing two methods on the *same* re-drawn data each time. Fairer, because both methods face
identical luck.

**"the CI excludes zero"** **[used]**
Means an improvement is real rather than noise. If the range of the *difference* between two
methods includes zero, they might genuinely be equally good and you can't claim a win.

---

## 11. Admin words

**Leaderboard** **[used]** — a public ranking of everyone's submissions.
**Codabench** **[used]** — the website hosting the two leaderboards you must submit to.
**Design note** **[used]** — the report you hand in, 4 pages maximum.
**10× scale** **[used]** — "what would break if this got ten times bigger?"
**Viva** — the live conversation where you explain and modify your own code.

---

## 12. Tooling words — NOT from your course

You don't need these for the assignment. Listed only because they've come up.

**ADR — Architecture Decision Record** **[tooling]**
A short note recording why a technical choice was made. It came from a plugin, not your course.

**Parquet** **[tooling]** — a file format for tables. Smaller and much faster than CSV.
**Polars** **[tooling]** — the library we use to handle tables. Like pandas, but faster and lighter.
**Streaming** **[tooling]** — processing data in chunks rather than loading it all at once.
**OOM (Out Of Memory)** **[tooling]** — the program asked for more memory than existed and was killed.
**RSS** **[tooling]** — how much memory a program is actually using right now.
**SLURM** **[tooling]** — the job scheduler on your university GPU cluster.

def recall_at_k(retrieved: pl.Series, clicked: pl.Series, ks: tuple[int, ...],
                keep: np.ndarray) -> dict[int, np.ndarray]:
    """...
    Stays in Polars deliberately. Materialising these lists in Python costs ~5 GB per
    system at ebnerd_small (245k impressions x 200 ids) and OOMs a 15 GB machine; the
    set intersection runs in Rust and only the one float per impression crosses back.
    """
    rows = pl.DataFrame({"retrieved": retrieved, "clicked": clicked}).filter(keep)
    truth_size = pl.col("clicked").list.len()
    return {
        k: rows.select(
            pl.col("retrieved").list.head(k)
            .list.set_intersection(pl.col("clicked"))
            .list.len() / truth_size
        ).to_series().to_numpy().astype(np.float64)
        for k in ks
    }
```

2. **`list.unique()` default is hash-ordered** — would have broken byte-identical rebuilds. Caught before trusting it; fixed with `maintain_order=True`.

# Glossary — every term in this assignment, in plain English

Written for someone new to the subject. Terms are grouped by what they're for, not alphabetically,
because that's the order they make sense in.

Tags: **[used]** we built it · **[named]** the brief mentions it, we didn't use it ·
**[tooling]** not from the course at all

---

## 1. Words for the data itself

**Impression** **[used]**
One moment when a list of articles was shown to one person. Your data is millions of these.
Each one records: who, when, what was shown, what was clicked.

**Candidates** **[used]**
The articles in that shown list. These are what you have to put in order.

**Click history** **[used]**
The articles that person read *before* this moment. Your main clue about what they like.

**Session context** **[named]**
Extra details of the moment — time of day, device used. We didn't use these.

**Corpus** **[used]**
All the articles you have. The whole collection.

**Catalogue** **[used]**
Same thing as corpus. Used interchangeably.

---

## 2. The three kinds of clue (the "three axes")

The brief keeps saying "all three modelling axes". It just means these three kinds of clue:

**Lexical** **[used]**
To do with the actual *words*. Matching because two texts share the word "football".

**Semantic** **[used]**
To do with *meaning*. Matching "car" with "vehicle" even though they share no letters.

**Behavioural** **[named]**
To do with what people *do* — what's popular, what's recent, what they clicked lately.
This is the follow-up assignment, not this one.

---

## 3. Matching on words

**BM25** **[used]**
A recipe for scoring word overlap between what you're searching with and each document.
Two sensible adjustments over naive counting:
- rare words count for more than common ones
- long documents don't win just for containing more words

It's the standard baseline in search — decades old, very well understood.

**TF-IDF** **[named]**
An older, simpler version of the same idea. TF = how often a word appears here.
IDF = how rare that word is overall. Multiply them. BM25 is the refined descendant.

**Inverted index** **[used]**
A lookup table from *word* → *which documents contain it*. Exactly like the index at the back of
a textbook. It's what makes word search fast — you never scan every document.

**Stopwords** **[used]**
Extremely common words — "the", "and", "is" — that carry almost no meaning, so they get thrown
away before matching. **This caused the biggest bug in the project:** no Danish stopword list
existed, so the Danish results were almost random until I supplied one.

**Stemming** **[used]**
Chopping words back to a root so "running", "runs" and "ran" all match each other.
Has to be done per-language.

---

## 4. Matching on meaning

**Embedding** (also called a **vector**) **[used]**
A long list of numbers standing in for a piece of text, arranged so that texts about similar
things get similar numbers. Ours are 768 numbers per article (Danish) or 384 (English).

**Word2Vec** **[named]**
An older way to make embeddings — one fixed vector per word.

**BERT** **[named]**
A neural network that reads a whole sentence and produces embeddings that depend on context,
so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank account" come out different.

**XLM-RoBERTa** **[named]**
Like BERT, but trained on many languages at once. Useful for Danish.

**MiniLM** **[used]**
The small, fast embedding model we actually used for the English data.

**Cosine similarity** **[used]**
How we compare two embeddings. Gives a number where higher = more alike. It compares *direction*
only, ignoring size — so a long article and a short one about the same topic still match.

---

## 5. Finding the good ones quickly

**Top-K** **[used]**
The K best results. "Top-200" = the 200 highest-scoring articles.

**Nearest neighbour** **[used]**
The most similar item to the thing you're holding.

**ANN — Approximate Nearest Neighbour** **[used]**
Finding the most similar items *quickly*, by accepting "very close" instead of insisting on
"provably the closest". You need this when there are millions of items, because checking every
one is too slow.

**FAISS** **[used]** / **ScaNN** **[named]**
Software libraries that do that search. FAISS is Meta's, ScaNN is Google's. We used FAISS.

**Flat index / brute force** **[used]**
Checking every single item, no shortcuts. Exact, but slow at large sizes.
At our size it was fast enough, so that's what we used.

**IVF / PQ / quantisation** **[named]**
Tricks to make the search faster by being slightly less exact. We didn't need them, but the
report explains when you would.

**Candidate generation** **[used]**
Stage one: narrowing the whole collection down to a few hundred worth a closer look.

**Re-ranker** **[named]**
Stage two: carefully ordering those few hundred with a trained model. **Not this assignment.**

**Two-stage retrieve-then-rank** **[used]**
The overall pattern: cheap narrowing first, expensive careful ordering second.

**GBDT — Gradient Boosted Decision Trees** **[named]**
A kind of machine-learning model that works well on table-shaped data. Suggested for the
re-ranker in the follow-up.

---

## 6. Scoring how good you are

**AUC** **[used]** — *the headline number*
Pick one article they clicked and one they didn't. How often do you rank the clicked one higher?
- 0.5 = coin flip
- 1.0 = perfect

**MRR — Mean Reciprocal Rank** **[used]**
If the clicked article lands at position 1 you score 1; position 2 scores ½; position 3 scores ⅓.
Averaged over everything. Rewards getting the right answer *very* near the top.

**nDCG@5 / nDCG@10** **[used]**
"How good is my ordering in the top 5 (or 10), compared with the best possible ordering?"
1.0 = perfect. The @5 / @10 is just how far down the list you look.

**Recall@K** **[used]**
Of the articles the person actually clicked, what fraction did you manage to get into your top K?
This measures whether stage one is even finding the right things.

---

## 7. Measures that aren't accuracy

The brief calls these **beyond-accuracy**. The point: a system can score well and still be bad.

**Diversity** **[used]**
Are your ten recommendations all about the same thing, or a mix? Ten football stories = not diverse.

**Novelty** **[used]**
Are you showing obscure things, or only what everybody already reads?

**Coverage** **[used]**
Across everything you recommend to everyone, what share of the whole collection did you ever show?
Ours was 5–21% — meaning most articles never get shown to anyone, by any method.

---

## 8. Looking at subgroups

**Slice / slicing** **[used]**
Checking your score for one subgroup instead of everybody, because an average can hide that
you're terrible for some people.

**Cold-start** **[used]**
Someone you know almost nothing about — a brand-new user with no reading history.
There's nothing to match against, so it's the hardest case.

**Warm** **[used]**
The opposite: plenty of history to work with.

**Head vs tail** **[used]**
Head = popular items. Tail = rarely-touched items. Most items are tail.
Systems usually look good on head and bad on tail.

---

## 9. Splitting the data, and cheating

**Temporal split** **[used]**
Dividing your data by *time*: earliest chunk to build on, middle to tune with, latest to test on.

**Random split** **[forbidden]**
Dividing rows randomly. **Banned in this assignment**, because it lets you learn from the future
to predict the past. That inflates your score and means nothing.

**Train / validation / test** **[used]**
Three chunks. *Train* = build on it. *Validation* = tune your choices on it.
*Test* = your final honest score — you look at it once, at the end.

**Leakage** **[used]**
Using information you couldn't possibly have had at the time. Cheating, usually by accident.

**Future-click leakage** **[used]**
The specific version here: using a click that happened *after* the moment you're predicting.

**Behaviour-window boundary** **[used]**
The cut-off line. History must come from before it, predictions from after it.

**Serving time** **[used]**
The moment a real system would have to make this recommendation, live.
If a piece of information doesn't exist yet at that moment, you're not allowed to use it.

**Serving-unavailable feature** **[used]**
Data that only exists later. Example: an article's total lifetime view count — that's only known
after the fact. Using it inflates your score dishonestly. The brief demands you report your
numbers both with and without such features. Ours: it was worth +0.041 AUC, more than our entire
meaning-matching method gained.

**Anti-gaming** **[used]**
The brief's rules to stop you inflating your numbers, accidentally or otherwise.

**Ablation** **[named]**
Removing one piece and re-measuring, to prove that piece actually mattered.

---

## 10. Being sure your numbers are real

**Bootstrap** **[used]**
A way to find out how much your score would wobble if you'd happened to collect slightly
different data. You re-draw your data at random (with repeats allowed) many times — we did 1,000 —
and watch how much the answer moves.

**Confidence interval (CI)** **[used]**
The resulting range. "0.64, somewhere between 0.63 and 0.65."

**Paired bootstrap** **[used]**
Comparing two methods on the *same* re-drawn data each time. Fairer, because both methods face
identical luck.

**"the CI excludes zero"** **[used]**
Means an improvement is real rather than noise. If the range of the *difference* between two
methods includes zero, they might genuinely be equally good and you can't claim a win.

---

## 11. Admin words

**Leaderboard** **[used]** — a public ranking of everyone's submissions.
**Codabench** **[used]** — the website hosting the two leaderboards you must submit to.
**Design note** **[used]** — the report you hand in, 4 pages maximum.
**10× scale** **[used]** — "what would break if this got ten times bigger?"
**Viva** — the live conversation where you explain and modify your own code.

---

## 12. Tooling words — NOT from your course

You don't need these for the assignment. Listed only because they've come up.

**ADR — Architecture Decision Record** **[tooling]**
A short note recording why a technical choice was made. It came from a plugin, not your course.

**Parquet** **[tooling]** — a file format for tables. Smaller and much faster than CSV.
**Polars** **[tooling]** — the library we use to handle tables. Like pandas, but faster and lighter.
**Streaming** **[tooling]** — processing data in chunks rather than loading it all at once.
**OOM (Out Of Memory)** **[tooling]** — the program asked for more memory than existed and was killed.
**RSS** **[tooling]** — how much memory a program is actually using right now.
**SLURM** **[tooling]** — the job scheduler on your university GPU cluster.

# Step 6 + scale-up: the semantic axis, score fusion, and EB-NeRD small

## Context

You asked whether to chase better results or finish step 6. Measured on the current data, they are
the same thing — step 6 is the largest accuracy lever left inside Component-1:

| signal | EB-NeRD val | MIND val |
|---|---|---|
| BM25 (built) | 0.527 | 0.580 |
| **Contrastive embeddings** | **0.560** | not yet built |
| Train-click popularity | 0.459 | 0.502 |
| Article freshness | 0.510 | — |

Two findings shaped this plan. Embeddings beat BM25 by **+0.032** on EB-NeRD, so the semantic axis
is worth building next on accuracy grounds alone. And **simple behavioural features are not a
shortcut** — popularity scores *below* random on EB-NeRD because the candidate pool is already
popularity-filtered, so real behavioural gains need a learned re-ranker, which `problem.md` assigns
to Component-2.

Confirmed scope: stay inside C1 (no re-ranker — that is your partner's half and the ownership matrix
depends on it), and scale EB-NeRD demo → small immediately after step 6.

Honest expectation: this lands EB-NeRD around 0.56-0.58 and MIND around 0.60-0.62. It will not be
leaderboard-competitive, and it does not need to be — `problem.md` states grading is never on
leaderboard rank, and C1's rubric weight sits in the pipeline, the temporal evaluation, and the
two-stage system covering all three axes.

## Step 6a — `retrieval/embeddings.py`

Mirror `retrieval/bm25.py` deliberately: same CLI, same query-dedup pass, same output shape. The two
scorers should differ only in how a score is produced, so they are directly comparable and the
design is one idea rather than two.

- **EB-NeRD**: use the provided 768-d `contrastive_vector.parquet` — already downloaded, covers all
  11,777 demo articles and all 125,541 EB-NeRD articles, so it covers `small` too with no refetch.
- **MIND**: no provided embeddings. Encode `title + abstract` for the 65,238-article union with
  `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (ungated, verified reachable) on CPU, and **cache to
  `data/processed/mind_small/embeddings.parquet`** so it runs once, not once per split.
- **User vector**: mean of the last `HISTORY_LEN` history article vectors, L2-normalised. Reuse the
  existing `HISTORY_LEN = 30`; measured better than 5 on EB-NeRD (0.5596 vs 0.5505).
- **Re-rank track**: cosine against each candidate.
- **Retrieval track**: FAISS `IndexFlatIP` over normalised vectors → top-K, then the same
  `published_time <= impression_time` filter as BM25. Flat is exact and trivial at 11k-65k vectors;
  IVF/PQ belongs in the design note as the 10× scaling argument, not in the code now.
- Cold-start users get a zero vector and empty retrieval, matching the BM25 convention already in
  `score_split`.

Outputs, mirroring BM25's naming: `emb_<split>.parquet`, `retrieval_emb_<split>.parquet`.

## Step 6b — `retrieval/fuse.py`

BM25 and cosine are on different scales, so combine them per impression, not globally:

- z-normalise each score **within the candidate pool**, then `score = α·emb + (1-α)·bm25`.
- **Tune α on val only, apply to test.** This is the temporal-hygiene point that makes the fusion
  defensible; tuning on test would silently invalidate the reported number.
- Output `fused_<split>.parquet` in the same shape as the other two.

Expected to add a little over the better single signal — lexical and semantic errors are partly
uncorrelated. If it does not, that is a reportable result, not a failure to hide.

## Step 6c — scale EB-NeRD demo → small

`ebnerd_small.zip` is 84 MB and verified fetchable; `pipeline/download.py` already knows the bundle.

- **Do not assume small shares demo's timestamps.** Inspect its actual `impression_time` ranges
  first, then derive cutoffs the same way NOTES.md justifies for demo: adopt the provided
  train/validation boundary as `test_start`, carve `val_start` out of the earlier block by time.
- Add an `ebnerd_small` entry to `configs/datasets.yaml` (same keys, including
  `stopwords_file: configs/stopwords_da.txt`).
- Re-run `split → bm25 → embeddings → fuse`. No new code should be needed — if any is, that is a
  defect in the config-driven design worth fixing rather than patching around.

Watch RAM (15 GB total, ~2 GB free). If `split.py` strains, switch its reads to
`pl.scan_parquet` — the schema already supports it.

## Files

- new: `retrieval/embeddings.py`, `retrieval/fuse.py`
- edit: `configs/datasets.yaml` (MIND `model:`, new `ebnerd_small` block)
- edit: `NOTES.md` (results table, α, small's cutoffs and their justification)
- reuse: `document_text()` and the dedup/group pattern in `retrieval/bm25.py`; the loader/config
  pattern in `pipeline/split.py`

## Verification

- `python -m retrieval.embeddings` then `python -m retrieval.fuse` complete on both datasets.
- AUC/MRR/recall@200 reported per dataset × split for bm25 / emb / fused side by side.
  **Success = emb > bm25 on EB-NeRD** (predicted 0.560 vs 0.527 on val); fused ≥ best single.
- MIND embedding cache is written once — a second run must not re-encode.
- Byte-identical outputs on re-run, as verified for `split.py` and `bm25.py`.
- `ebnerd_small` passes every existing assertion in `check_integrity` unchanged.
- α is chosen on val; grep the code to confirm test scores never enter the tuning loop.

## Caveat to carry into step 7

Every number above is a point estimate from ad-hoc scripts. Until the eval harness exists with
bootstrap CIs, "+0.032" is suggestive, not established — differences this small on a 1,590-user
sample may not survive a confidence interval. That is precisely why step 7 follows immediately, and
why scaling to `small` matters: more impressions means tighter intervals.

1	"""Download and extract the raw EB-NeRD and MIND bundles.
2	
3	Idempotent: a bundle is skipped if its extract directory already holds a .done marker,
4	so re-running costs nothing.
5	
6	    python -m pipeline.download
7	    python -m pipeline.download ebnerd_small
8	"""
9	
10	import argparse
11	import shutil
12	import sys
13	import urllib.request
14	import zipfile
15	from pathlib import Path
16	
17	DATA = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data"
18	RAW = DATA / "raw"
19	INTERIM = DATA / "interim"
20	
21	EBNERD_BASE = "https://ebnerd-dataset.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com"
22	EBNERD_BUNDLES = ("ebnerd_demo", "ebnerd_small", "ebnerd_testset", "articles_large_only")
23	# Article embeddings ship separately from the impression bundles, under an artifacts/ prefix,
24	# and each one covers the full article set (so they apply to demo as well as large).
25	EBNERD_ARTIFACTS = (
26	    "Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector",
27	    "Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec",
28	    "Ekstra_Bladet_image_embeddings",
29	    "FacebookAI_xlm_roberta_base",
30	    "google_bert_base_multilingual_cased",
31	)
32	
33	MIND_REPO = "yjw1029/MIND"
34	MIND_BUNDLES = (
35	    "MINDsmall_train",
36	    "MINDsmall_dev",
37	    "MINDlarge_train",
38	    "MINDlarge_dev",
39	    "MINDlarge_test",
40	)
41	MIND_GATE_URL = f"https://huggingface.co/datasets/{MIND_REPO}"
42	
43	DEFAULT_BUNDLES = (
44	    "ebnerd_demo",
45	    "Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector",
46	    "MINDsmall_train",
47	    "MINDsmall_dev",
48	)
49	
50	
51	def _fetch_ebnerd(name: str) -> Path:
52	    dest = RAW / "ebnerd" / f"{name}.zip"
53	    if dest.exists():
54	        return dest
55	    dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
56	    prefix = "artifacts/" if name in EBNERD_ARTIFACTS else ""
57	    url = f"{EBNERD_BASE}/{prefix}{name}.zip"
58	    print(f"  downloading {url}")
59	    tmp = dest.with_suffix(".zip.part")
60	    with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response, open(tmp, "wb") as fh:
61	        shutil.copyfileobj(response, fh)
62	    tmp.rename(dest)
63	    return dest
64	
65	
66	def _fetch_mind(name: str) -> Path:
67	    from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
68	    from huggingface_hub.errors import GatedRepoError, HfHubHTTPError
69	
70	    print(f"  downloading {MIND_REPO}/{name}.zip")
71	    try:
72	        return Path(
73	            hf_hub_download(
74	                repo_id=MIND_REPO,
75	                repo_type="dataset",
76	                filename=f"{name}.zip",
77	                cache_dir=RAW / "mind",
78	            )
79	        )
80	    except (GatedRepoError, HfHubHTTPError) as exc:
81	        raise SystemExit(
82	            f"Could not fetch {name}.zip from the gated repo {MIND_REPO}.\n"
83	            f"Log in with `huggingface-cli login`, then open {MIND_GATE_URL} and click\n"
84	            f'"Agree and access repository" — access is granted automatically.\n'
85	            f"Original error: {exc}"
86	        ) from exc
87	
88	
89	def _extract(archive: Path, dest: Path) -> None:
90	    dest.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
91	    with zipfile.ZipFile(archive) as zf:
92	        zf.extractall(dest)
93	    (dest / ".done").touch()
94	
95	
96	def fetch(name: str, force: bool = False) -> None:
97	    dest = INTERIM / name
98	    if (dest / ".done").exists() and not force:
99	        print(f"{name}: already extracted, skipping")
100	        return
101	
102	    print(f"{name}:")
103	    if name in EBNERD_BUNDLES or name in EBNERD_ARTIFACTS:
104	        archive = _fetch_ebnerd(name)
105	    elif name in MIND_BUNDLES:
106	        archive = _fetch_mind(name)
107	    else:
108	        raise SystemExit(f"unknown bundle {name!r}")
109	
110	    print(f"  extracting to {dest}")
111	    _extract(archive, dest)
112	
113	
114	def main() -> None:
115	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
116	    parser.add_argument("bundles", nargs="*", default=list(DEFAULT_BUNDLES))
117	    parser.add_argument("--force", action="store_true", help="re-extract even if done")
118	    args = parser.parse_args()
119	
120	    for name in args.bundles:
121	        fetch(name, force=args.force)
122	
123	
124	if __name__ == "__main__":
125	    sys.exit(main())

"""Download and extract the raw EB-NeRD and MIND bundles.

Idempotent: a bundle is skipped if its extract directory already holds a .done marker,
so re-running costs nothing.

    python -m pipeline.download
    python -m pipeline.download ebnerd_small
"""

import argparse
import shutil
import sys
import urllib.request
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

DATA = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data"
RAW = DATA / "raw"
INTERIM = DATA / "interim"

EBNERD_BASE = "https://ebnerd-dataset.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com"
EBNERD_BUNDLES = ("ebnerd_demo", "ebnerd_small", "ebnerd_testset", "articles_large_only")
# Article embeddings ship separately from the impression bundles, under an artifacts/ prefix,
# and each one covers the full article set (so they apply to demo as well as large).
EBNERD_ARTIFACTS = (
    "Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector",
    "Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec",
    "Ekstra_Bladet_image_embeddings",
    "FacebookAI_xlm_roberta_base",
    "google_bert_base_multilingual_cased",
)

MIND_REPO = "yjw1029/MIND"
MIND_BUNDLES = (
    "MINDsmall_train",
    "MINDsmall_dev",
    "MINDlarge_train",
    "MINDlarge_dev",
    "MINDlarge_test",
)
MIND_GATE_URL = f"https://huggingface.co/datasets/{MIND_REPO}"

DEFAULT_BUNDLES = (
    "ebnerd_demo",
    "Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector",
    "MINDsmall_train",
    "MINDsmall_dev",
)


def _fetch_ebnerd(name: str) -> Path:
    dest = RAW / "ebnerd" / f"{name}.zip"
    if dest.exists():
        return dest
    dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    prefix = "artifacts/" if name in EBNERD_ARTIFACTS else ""
    url = f"{EBNERD_BASE}/{prefix}{name}.zip"
    print(f"  downloading {url}")
    tmp = dest.with_suffix(".zip.part")
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response, open(tmp, "wb") as fh:
        shutil.copyfileobj(response, fh)
    tmp.rename(dest)
    return dest


def _fetch_mind(name: str) -> Path:
    from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
    from huggingface_hub.errors import GatedRepoError, HfHubHTTPError

    print(f"  downloading {MIND_REPO}/{name}.zip")
    try:
        return Path(
            hf_hub_download(
                repo_id=MIND_REPO,
                repo_type="dataset",
                filename=f"{name}.zip",
                cache_dir=RAW / "mind",
            )
        )
    except (GatedRepoError, HfHubHTTPError) as exc:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"Could not fetch {name}.zip from the gated repo {MIND_REPO}.\n"
            f"Log in with `huggingface-cli login`, then open {MIND_GATE_URL} and click\n"
            f'"Agree and access repository" — access is granted automatically.\n'
            f"Original error: {exc}"
        ) from exc


def _extract(archive: Path, dest: Path) -> None:
    dest.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with zipfile.ZipFile(archive) as zf:
        zf.extractall(dest)
    (dest / ".done").touch()


def fetch(name: str, force: bool = False) -> None:
    dest = INTERIM / name
    if (dest / ".done").exists() and not force:
        print(f"{name}: already extracted, skipping")
        return

    print(f"{name}:")
    if name in EBNERD_BUNDLES or name in EBNERD_ARTIFACTS:
        archive = _fetch_ebnerd(name)
    elif name in MIND_BUNDLES:
        archive = _fetch_mind(name)
    else:
        raise SystemExit(f"unknown bundle {name!r}")

    print(f"  extracting to {dest}")
    _extract(archive, dest)


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("bundles", nargs="*", default=list(DEFAULT_BUNDLES))
    parser.add_argument("--force", action="store_true", help="re-extract even if done")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    for name in args.bundles:
        fetch(name, force=args.force)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

content.text:
Cleaned up and all 19 tests still pass. Here's what happened and what's where.

## What I removed (≈1 GB)

| removed | size | why it was safe |
|---|---|---|
| `submissions/predictions.txt` | 703 MB | Byte-for-byte identical to the file inside `ebnerd_predictions.zip` — I checked the checksums matched before deleting, not just the sizes |
| `submissions/prediction.txt` | 291 MB | Same, for `mind_prediction.zip` |
| 4 × `__pycache__/` | small | Python's own speed cache. Rebuilds itself |
| `.pytest_cache/` | small | Same, for the test runner |

Nothing else was redundant. Every remaining file is either something you hand in, something the code needs, or a note you'll want before the viva.

## The directory, explained

```
ass-1/
├── Assignment1_v1.pdf      ← the real brief (the PDF beats problem.md)
├── problem.md              ← the earlier informal version. Kept for reference
├── SPEC.md                 ← my build plan, written before any code
│
├── DESIGN_NOTE.md          ← ★ THE THING YOU HAND IN. 12 sections
├── design_note_c1.pdf      ← that file, as a 4-page PDF
├── build_design_note.sh    ← turns the .md into the .pdf, warns if over 4 pages
│
├── NOTES.md                ← lab diary: every decision, every bug, why
├── GLOSSARY.md             ← the plain-English terms list from yesterday
├── README.md               ← how to run it
├── CLAUDE.md               ← project rules
├── Makefile                ← shortcuts: make test, make submissions
│
├── configs/
│   ├── datasets.yaml       ← the 3 datasets, their date cut-offs, settings
│   └── stopwords_da.txt    ← the Danish "the/and/is" list I had to write myself
│
├── pipeline/               ← STAGE 1: get and prepare the data
│   ├── download.py         ← fetch + unzip the datasets
│   ├── split.py            ← cut the data by time into train/val/test
│   └── submit.py           ← build the two Codabench zips
│
├── retrieval/              ← STAGE 2: the actual recommending
│   ├── bm25.py             ← word matching
│   ├── embeddings.py       ← meaning matching
│   └── fuse.py             ← blend the two
│
├── eval/                   ← STAGE 3: measuring how good it is
│   ├── metrics.py          ← AUC, MRR, nDCG, recall@K
│   ├── bootstrap.py        ← confidence intervals
│   ├── slicing.py          ← scores for subgroups (cold users, tail articles)
│   ├── beyond_accuracy.py  ← diversity, novelty, coverage
│   └── run.py              ← runs all of the above, writes results/
│
├── tests/test_leakage.py   ← 19 checks that you aren't cheating with the future
├── results/                ← 12 score reports (3 datasets × val/test × md+json)
├── submissions/            ← the 2 zips to upload to Codabench
│
├── data/       (8.7 GB)    ← not in git
│   ├── raw/       downloaded zips
│   ├── interim/   unzipped originals
│   └── processed/ the cleaned, time-split tables the code reads
└── .venv/      (1.7 GB)    ← installed Python libraries. Not in git
```

The shape is deliberately **three stages in a row**: `pipeline` prepares → `retrieval` recommends → `eval` measures. Each folder does one job, and `configs/datasets.yaml` is the only place dataset-specific settings live. That's the answer if they ask "why is it laid out this way" in the viva.

It's about 2,100 lines of code total — small enough that you can read all of it in a sitting.

## Two bigger deletions I did *not* do

Both are real duplication, but both cost real time to undo, so it's your call:

1. **`data/raw/ebnerd/*.zip` — 2.0 GB.** Already unpacked into `interim/`, and I confirmed the code never reads the zips again. But `ebnerd_testset.zip` alone is 1.6 GB to re-download.
2. **The leaderboard-only data — 3.9 GB.** (`interim/ebnerd_testset`, `interim/MINDlarge_test`, and two cache files in `processed/`.) These exist purely to build the two submission zips, which are built and validated.

My recommendation: **hold both until your Codabench upload actually succeeds.** If the upload fails in a way that needs a different file format, you'd have to re-fetch 2.2 GB. You've got 136 GB free, so there's no pressure. Once a submission is accepted, say the word and I'll clear all 5.9 GB.

Yes — checked line by line, and they match exactly.

## The four links the PDF gives

| PDF says | `download.py` builds | |
|---|---|---|
| `…amazonaws.com/ebnerd_demo.zip` | identical | ✅ |
| `…amazonaws.com/ebnerd_small.zip` | identical | ✅ |
| `…amazonaws.com/artifacts/Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec.zip` | identical | ✅ |
| `…amazonaws.com/artifacts/google_bert_base_multilingual_cased.zip` | identical | ✅ |
| `huggingface.co/datasets/yjw1029/MIND/…/MINDsmall_train.zip` | identical | ✅ |
| `huggingface.co/datasets/yjw1029/MIND/…/MINDsmall_dev.zip` | identical | ✅ |

Same S3 bucket, same HuggingFace repository, same file names. [pipeline/download.py:21](pipeline/download.py#L21) holds the EB-NeRD address and [pipeline/download.py:33](pipeline/download.py#L33) the MIND one.

One small difference in *how*, not *where*: for MIND the PDF uses `wget`, we use the HuggingFace library. It fetches that exact same address — it just also caches the file and gives you a readable message if you haven't clicked "Agree and access repository" yet, instead of a bare HTTP error.

## Two things we download that the PDF doesn't list

Both are deliberate. Neither is a different dataset — same bucket, same repo.

**1. `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector.zip`** — this is the one worth knowing about.

The PDF offers pre-trained embeddings as **optional** and names two: `word2vec` and `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased`. We used a third one from the same official folder — `contrastive_vector` — because Ekstra Bladet trained it specifically on their own news, so it fits the Danish articles better than a general-purpose model.

That's a defensible choice, but it's **not the two the PDF names**. This is the gap I flagged earlier: the honest version is to download the other encoders too (they're all pre-computed, no GPU needed, ~857 MB) and report a side-by-side comparison. That turns "I picked one" into "I tested four and here's why this one won" — which is exactly what a marker wants to see, and it directly answers the likely viva question *"why that embedding?"*

**2. `ebnerd_testset.zip` and `MINDlarge_test.zip`** — the leaderboard test sets.

The PDF *requires* you to submit to both Codabench competitions (Q5) but doesn't give links for the files you'd submit predictions on. These are the files those competitions actually score. Same bucket, same repo, following the same naming pattern.

So: nothing came from an unofficial source, and nothing substituted for what was asked.

Want me to run the four-encoder comparison? It's a download plus a re-run — no GPU, no new code — and it fills the one real gap between your setup and the brief's wording.

**`FacebookAI_xlm_roberta_base`** — that's the fourth.

It's a fourth text encoder sitting in the same official EB-NeRD artifacts folder, alongside the two the PDF names. The brief doesn't mention it, but Ekstra Bladet published it as part of the same set.

Why it belongs in the comparison: it's a multilingual model like `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased`, but a stronger and more recent one, and it handles Danish noticeably better than BERT-multilingual does. So the four make a clean ladder:

| encoder | what it is |
|---|---|
| `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` | oldest and simplest — one fixed vector per word |
| `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` | reads whole sentences, trained on many languages |
| `FacebookAI_xlm_roberta_base` | same idea, newer and better at Danish |
| `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector` | trained by the newspaper on their own articles — the one we used |

That's the story the comparison would tell: general-purpose → multilingual → better multilingual → purpose-built. If our choice really is the right one, its score should sit at the top of that ladder. If it doesn't, that's a finding worth reporting too.

I checked all four are live on the S3 bucket right now. The three we don't have come to **818 MB** total (133 + 344 + 341).

There's a fifth file in that folder, `Ekstra_Bladet_image_embeddings` — vectors for article *photographs*, not text. Not comparable to the others, so I left it out.

content.content:
1	"""Semantic counterpart to retrieval/bm25.py — same two tracks, same output shape.
2	
3	Deliberately mirrors bm25.py: same CLI, same query-deduplication pass, same file naming.
4	Only the scorer differs, so the lexical and semantic axes stay directly comparable.
5	
6	  re-rank    cosine between the user vector and each candidate in the given pool
7	  retrieval  FAISS inner-product search over the whole corpus for the top-K
8	
9	The user vector is the mean of the L2-normalised vectors of their last HISTORY_LEN clicked
10	articles. History is guaranteed strictly earlier than the impression by pipeline.split.
11	
12	Article vectors come from whichever source the dataset has:
13	  EB-NeRD  the organisers' 768-d contrastive vectors (config `embeddings`)
14	  MIND     encoded here with a sentence-transformers model (config `model`) and cached
15	           to data/processed/<dataset>/embeddings.parquet, so encoding happens once
16	
17	    python -m retrieval.embeddings
18	    python -m retrieval.embeddings mind_small --splits test
19	
20	Writes, per dataset and split:
21	    emb_<split>.parquet            impression_id, emb        aligned to `candidates`
22	    retrieval_emb_<split>.parquet  impression_id, retrieved  top-K ids, best first
23	"""
24	
25	import argparse
26	from collections import defaultdict
27	from pathlib import Path
28	
29	import faiss
30	import numpy as np
31	import polars as pl
32	import yaml
33	from tqdm import tqdm
34	
35	from retrieval.bm25 import HISTORY_LEN, OVERFETCH, TOP_K
36	
37	ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
38	CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
39	PROC = ROOT / "data/processed"
40	
41	SEARCH_BATCH = 4096
42	
43	
44	def _encode_corpus(articles: pl.DataFrame, model_name: str) -> np.ndarray:
45	    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
46	
47	    texts = (
48	        articles.select(
49	            pl.concat_str(
50	                [pl.col("title").fill_null(""), pl.col("abstract").fill_null("")],
51	                separator=" ",
52	            )
53	        )
54	        .to_series()
55	        .to_list()
56	    )
57	    print(f"  encoding {len(texts):,} articles with {model_name} (CPU)")
58	    model = SentenceTransformer(model_name, device="cpu")
59	    return model.encode(
60	        texts, batch_size=256, convert_to_numpy=True, show_progress_bar=True
61	    ).astype(np.float32)
62	
63	
64	def _unnest(column: pl.Series, rows: int) -> np.ndarray:
65	    """A List(Float) column as a dense (rows, dim) float32 array.
66	
67	    Deliberately not `np.vstack(column.to_list())`: that boxes every scalar into a Python
68	    float on the way through and peaks at 5.8 GB to build a 385 MB array (measured on
69	    EB-NeRD's 125,541 x 768 contrastive vectors).
70	    """
71	    return column.explode().to_numpy().astype(np.float32).reshape(rows, len(column[0]))
72	
73	
74	def load_vectors(name: str, cfg: dict, articles: pl.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
75	    """Article vectors, L2-normalised, in the same row order as `articles`."""
76	    if cfg.get("embeddings"):
77	        wanted = articles["article_id"].to_list()
78	        table = (
79	            pl.scan_parquet(ROOT / cfg["embeddings"])
80	            .with_columns(pl.col("article_id").cast(pl.String))
81	            .filter(pl.col("article_id").is_in(wanted))
82	            .collect()
83	        )
84	        column = next(c for c in table.columns if c != "article_id")
85	        found = dict(zip(table["article_id"], range(table.height)))
86	        missing = [a for a in wanted if a not in found]
87	        assert not missing, f"{len(missing)} articles have no provided embedding"
88	        raw = _unnest(table[column], table.height)
89	        vectors = raw[[found[a] for a in wanted]]
90	        print(f"  provided embeddings: {vectors.shape[0]:,} x {vectors.shape[1]}")
91	    else:
92	        cache = PROC / name / "embeddings.parquet"
93	        if cache.exists():
94	            table = pl.read_parquet(cache)
95	            assert table["article_id"].to_list() == articles["article_id"].to_list(), (
96	                "cached embeddings do not match the current corpus; delete "
97	                f"{cache} to re-encode"
98	            )
99	            vectors = _unnest(table["vector"], table.height)
100	            print(f"  cached embeddings: {vectors.shape[0]:,} x {vectors.shape[1]}")
101	        else:
102	            vectors = _encode_corpus(articles, cfg["model"])
103	            pl.DataFrame({
104	                "article_id": articles["article_id"],
105	                "vector": [v.tolist() for v in vectors],
106	            }).write_parquet(cache)
107	            print(f"  encoded and cached to {cache}")
108	
109	    return vectors / (np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)
110	
111	
112	def score_split(impressions, articles, vectors, position, published):
113	    """One pass over distinct histories, filling both tracks."""
114	    histories = [tuple(h[-HISTORY_LEN:]) for h in impressions["history"].to_list()]
115

"""Semantic counterpart to retrieval/bm25.py — same two tracks, same output shape.

Deliberately mirrors bm25.py: same CLI, same query-deduplication pass, same file naming.
Only the scorer differs, so the lexical and semantic axes stay directly comparable.

  re-rank    cosine between the user vector and each candidate in the given pool
  retrieval  FAISS inner-product search over the whole corpus for the top-K

The user vector is the mean of the L2-normalised vectors of their last HISTORY_LEN clicked
articles. History is guaranteed strictly earlier than the impression by pipeline.split.

Article vectors come from whichever source the dataset has:
  EB-NeRD  the organisers' 768-d contrastive vectors (config `embeddings`)
  MIND     encoded here with a sentence-transformers model (config `model`) and cached
           to data/processed/<dataset>/embeddings.parquet, so encoding happens once

    python -m retrieval.embeddings
    python -m retrieval.embeddings mind_small --splits test

Writes, per dataset and split:
    emb_<split>.parquet            impression_id, emb        aligned to `candidates`
    retrieval_emb_<split>.parquet  impression_id, retrieved  top-K ids, best first
"""

import argparse
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import faiss
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml
from tqdm import tqdm

from retrieval.bm25 import HISTORY_LEN, OVERFETCH, TOP_K

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
PROC = ROOT / "data/processed"

SEARCH_BATCH = 4096


def _encode_corpus(articles: pl.DataFrame, model_name: str) -> np.ndarray:
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

    texts = (
        articles.select(
            pl.concat_str(
                [pl.col("title").fill_null(""), pl.col("abstract").fill_null("")],
                separator=" ",
            )
        )
        .to_series()
        .to_list()
    )
    print(f"  encoding {len(texts):,} articles with {model_name} (CPU)")
    model = SentenceTransformer(model_name, device="cpu")
    return model.encode(
        texts, batch_size=256, convert_to_numpy=True, show_progress_bar=True
    ).astype(np.float32)


def _unnest(column: pl.Series, rows: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """A List(Float) column as a dense (rows, dim) float32 array.

    Deliberately not `np.vstack(column.to_list())`: that boxes every scalar into a Python
    float on the way through and peaks at 5.8 GB to build a 385 MB array (measured on
    EB-NeRD's 125,541 x 768 contrastive vectors).
    """
    return column.explode().to_numpy().astype(np.float32).reshape(rows, len(column[0]))


def load_vectors(name: str, cfg: dict, articles: pl.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
    """Article vectors, L2-normalised, in the same row order as `articles`."""
    if cfg.get("embeddings"):
        wanted = articles["article_id"].to_list()
        table = (
            pl.scan_parquet(ROOT / cfg["embeddings"])
            .with_columns(pl.col("article_id").cast(pl.String))
            .filter(pl.col("article_id").is_in(wanted))
            .collect()
        )
        column = next(c for c in table.columns if c != "article_id")
        found = dict(zip(table["article_id"], range(table.height)))
        missing = [a for a in wanted if a not in found]
        assert not missing, f"{len(missing)} articles have no provided embedding"
        raw = _unnest(table[column], table.height)
        vectors = raw[[found[a] for a in wanted]]
        print(f"  provided embeddings: {vectors.shape[0]:,} x {vectors.shape[1]}")
    else:
        cache = PROC / name / "embeddings.parquet"
        if cache.exists():
            table = pl.read_parquet(cache)
            assert table["article_id"].to_list() == articles["article_id"].to_list(), (
                "cached embeddings do not match the current corpus; delete "
                f"{cache} to re-encode"
            )
            vectors = _unnest(table["vector"], table.height)
            print(f"  cached embeddings: {vectors.shape[0]:,} x {vectors.shape[1]}")
        else:
            vectors = _encode_corpus(articles, cfg["model"])
            pl.DataFrame({
                "article_id": articles["article_id"],
                "vector": [v.tolist() for v in vectors],
            }).write_parquet(cache)
            print(f"  encoded and cached to {cache}")

    return vectors / (np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)


def score_split(impressions, articles, vectors, position, published):
    """One pass over distinct histories, filling both tracks."""
    histories = [tuple(h[-HISTORY_LEN:]) for h in impressions["history"].to_list()]

    order: dict[tuple, int] = {}
    per_impression = []
    for h in histories:
        per_impression.append(order.setdefault(h, len(order)))
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = defaultdict(list)
    for row, q_id in enumerate(per_impression):
        groups[q_id].append(row)
    print(f"    {len(order):,} distinct histories for {impressions.height:,} impressions")

    # Mean of the history vectors, renormalised. Cold start stays all-zero, which scores
    # every candidate 0 rather than inventing a ranking.
    users = np.zeros((len(order), vectors.shape[1]), dtype=np.float32)
    for history, q_id in order.items():
        rows = [position[a] for a in history if a in position]
        if rows:
            users[q_id] = vectors[rows].mean(axis=0)
    users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9

    index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(vectors.shape[1])
    index.add(vectors)
    n_fetch = min(TOP_K * OVERFETCH, vectors.shape[0])
    top = np.empty((len(order), n_fetch), dtype=np.int64)
    for start in tqdm(range(0, len(order), SEARCH_BATCH), desc="    searching", leave=False):
        chunk = users[start:start + SEARCH_BATCH]
        top[start:start + len(chunk)] = index.search(chunk, n_fetch)[1]

    candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
    timestamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
    article_ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy()
    cand_scores: list = [None] * impressions.height
    retrieved: list = [None] * impressions.height

    for q_id, rows in groups.items():
        user = users[q_id]
        cold = not user.any()
        for row in rows:
            cand_scores[row] = (vectors[[position[a] for a in candidates[row]]] @ user).astype(np.float32)
            if cold:
                retrieved[row] = []
                continue
            hits = top[q_id]
            if published is not None:
                hits = hits[published[hits] <= np.datetime64(timestamps[row])]
            retrieved[row] = article_ids[hits[:TOP_K]].tolist()

    return cand_scores, retrieved


def run(name: str, cfg: dict, splits: list[str]) -> None:
    print(f"\n{name}")
    articles = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / "articles.parquet")
    vectors = load_vectors(name, cfg, articles)

    position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
    published = None
    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
        published = articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
    else:
        print("  note: no publication dates; retrieval cannot filter unpublished articles")

    for split in splits:
        impressions = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / f"impressions_{split}.parquet")
        print(f"  {split}: {impressions.height:,} impressions")
        cand_scores, retrieved = score_split(
            impressions, articles, vectors, position, published
        )

        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "emb": [s.tolist() for s in cand_scores],
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"emb_{split}.parquet")
        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "retrieved": retrieved,
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"retrieval_emb_{split}.parquet")

        clicked = impressions["clicked"].to_list()
        hit = sum(bool(set(c) & set(r)) for c, r in zip(clicked, retrieved) if c)
        print(f"    recall@{TOP_K} (full-corpus retrieval): {hit / impressions.height:.4f}")


def main() -> None:
    config = yaml.safe_load(CONFIG.read_text())
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", default=list(config))
    parser.add_argument("--splits", nargs="+", default=["train", "val", "test"])
    args = parser.parse_args()

    for name in args.datasets:
        run(name, config[name], args.splits)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
