# IRE Assignment-1, Component-1 — lexical & semantic retrieval

Two-stage news recommendation on **EB-NeRD** (Danish, Ekstra Bladet) and **MIND** (English,
Microsoft), with a temporal data pipeline, BM25 and embedding candidate generation, and an
offline evaluation harness with bootstrap confidence intervals.

See `NOTES.md` for the measured data facts and every decision's justification, `DESIGN_NOTE.md`
for the write-up, and `results/` for the generated metric reports.

## Run it

```bash
make venv      # once: Python 3.11 venv + dependencies
make all       # download -> split -> retrieve -> evaluate
```

`make all` is idempotent: re-running skips completed downloads and rewrites the same bytes.
Individual stages: `make download`, `make split`, `make retrieve`, `make results`.
`make test` runs the anti-leakage checks against the built artifacts in seconds.

`make submissions` builds the two Codabench leaderboard files. It is deliberately outside
`make all`: the competitions score their own held-out test sets — EB-NeRD 13.5M impressions,
MIND-large 2.4M — not the temporal splits this repo evaluates on, so it downloads ~2.2 GB more
and takes ~13 min for EB-NeRD plus a one-off MIND encode.

**One manual step.** MIND is gated. The URL in every tutorial
(`mind201910small.blob.core.windows.net`) is dead — "Public access is not permitted on this
storage account" — and `msnews.github.io` now redirects to a HuggingFace mirror. Before the
first run, log in with `huggingface-cli login`, then open
<https://huggingface.co/datasets/yjw1029/MIND> and click *"Agree and access repository"*.
Access is automatic. EB-NeRD needs no auth.

## Layout

```
configs/datasets.yaml     split cutoffs, language, stopwords, embedding source — per dataset
configs/stopwords_da.txt  Danish stopwords (bm25s ships none; measured worth +0.020 AUC)
pipeline/download.py      fetch + extract, idempotent
pipeline/split.py         temporal split -> normalised schema, with integrity assertions
pipeline/submit.py        streaming scorer for the two Codabench leaderboards
retrieval/bm25.py         lexical scoring: re-rank track + full-corpus retrieval track
retrieval/embeddings.py   semantic scoring: same two tracks, same output shape
retrieval/fuse.py         per-pool z-normalised blend; alpha tuned on val only
eval/                     metrics, beyond-accuracy, slicing, bootstrap, runner
tests/test_leakage.py     no-future-click assertions against the built artifacts
results/                  generated reports (markdown + json)
```

## What it produces

`data/processed/<dataset>/` holds one schema for both datasets, so every downstream stage has a
single code path:

```
impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet
    impression_id, user_id, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[],
    history[], history_timestamps[]
articles.parquet
    article_id, title, abstract, body, category, entities, published_time,
    total_inviews, total_pageviews, total_read_time     <- serving-unavailable, eval only
```

Then per split: `bm25_*`, `emb_*`, `fused_*` (scores aligned to `candidates`) and
`retrieval_*`, `retrieval_emb_*` (full-corpus top-200).

## Correctness guarantees

`pipeline/split.py` asserts on every build, failing rather than warning:

- `train < val < test` strictly, by impression timestamp
- every history click strictly precedes its impression (per-item, EB-NeRD)
- `clicked` is a subset of `candidates`
- every candidate resolves to an article; no empty ids

Where a check is impossible it says so instead of passing vacuously — MIND's history carries no
per-item timestamps, so the harness reports that the guarantee there is structural rather than
verified. Outputs are byte-identical across runs.

`make test` re-checks the same properties from outside, reading only `data/processed/`. That is a
stronger claim than the build-time assertions: the build asserts what it *intended* to write, the
tests assert what is *actually on disk* and what every downstream stage therefore reads. One test
also fails if any module outside `eval/run.py` so much as mentions a serving-unavailable column.

Good questions — one of them found a real gap. Answering each from the actual data.

## 1. What format are the datasets in?

They arrive in **completely different formats**, which is why the pipeline has two readers and one output shape.

**EB-NeRD (Danish) — Parquet files**, already structured:

| file | rows (demo) | what it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `articles.parquet` | 11,777 | 21 columns — title, subtitle, body, category, `ner_clusters`, published time, view counts… |
| `train/behaviors.parquet` | 24,724 | 17 columns — one row per impression: what was shown, what was clicked, when, device, age, gender… |
| `train/history.parquet` | 1,590 | one row **per user**, with their whole click history as a list |

**MIND (English) — TSV files** (tab-separated text), much rawer:

| file | columns |
|---|---|
| `news.tsv` | 8, no header — id, category, subcategory, title, abstract, url, title entities, abstract entities |
| `behaviors.tsv` | 5, no header — id, user, time, history, **impressions with `-0`/`-1` glued onto each article id** |

That last bit is the awkward part: MIND writes `N12345-1 N67890-0` in a single text column, so "what was shown" and "what was clicked" have to be pulled apart by string surgery. EB-NeRD gives you two clean list columns instead.

Both get normalised into one shape, so nothing downstream needs to know which dataset it's looking at.

## 2. What are the temporal splits?

Both datasets ship their own train/test boundary, so I **adopted theirs** rather than inventing one, then carved validation out of the earlier block by time.

| dataset | split | impressions | date range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EB-NeRD demo** | train | 17,852 | 18 May 07:00 → 23 May 06:58 |
| | val | 6,872 | 23 May 07:01 → 25 May 06:59 |
| | test | 25,356 | 25 May 07:00 → 1 Jun 06:59 |
| **EB-NeRD small** | train | 168,522 | 18 May 07:00 → 23 May 06:59 |
| | val | 64,365 | 23 May 07:00 → 25 May 06:59 |
| | test | 244,647 | 25 May 07:00 → 1 Jun 06:59 |
| **MIND-small** | train | 95,071 | 9 Nov 00:00 → 12 Nov 23:59 |
| | val | 61,894 | 13 Nov 00:01 → 14 Nov 23:59 |
| | test | 73,152 | 15 Nov 00:00 → 15 Nov 23:58 |

Two things to have ready for the viva:

- **EB-NeRD's day boundary is 07:00, not midnight.** You only find that by looking at the data. Splitting at midnight would have cut through the middle of their collection days.
- **No overlap anywhere.** Train ends 06:58, val starts 07:01. There's a test in `make test` that fails the build if that ever stops being true.

## 3. Did you use the entire datasets?

**Yes — 100% of every row, on all three.** I checked rather than assumed:

| | raw rows | processed rows | kept |
|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD demo | 50,080 | 50,080 | **100%** |
| EB-NeRD small | 477,534 | 477,534 | **100%** |
| MIND-small | 230,117 | 230,117 | **100%** |

Nothing sampled, nothing dropped. What you're *not* using is EB-NeRD **large** and MIND **large** as training data — those only appear as the leaderboard's hidden test sets, which is exactly what the PDF asks for.

## 4. What's a "feature store", and did we build one?

Despite the grand name, it just means: **one tidy place where every fact about an article and every fact about a user lives**, so no later stage has to go back and re-parse raw files.

The PDF asks for specific things. Here's the honest scorecard:

| asked for | have it? | where |
|---|---|---|
| title | ✅ | `articles.parquet` |
| abstract | ✅ | `articles.parquet` |
| body | ✅ | `articles.parquet` |
| category | ✅ | `articles.parquet` |
| entities | ✅ | `articles.parquet` (74% / 87% non-empty) |
| embeddings | ✅ | separate file, referenced from config |
| click history | ✅ | `impressions_*.parquet` |
| **recency** | ⚠️ **derivable, not stored** | computed from `history_timestamps` |

**That last row is a real gap and you should know about it.** I store `history_timestamps` — the exact time of every past click — so recency is one subtraction away (`impression time − last click time`). But there's no column literally called `recency`.

My reasoning was that storing a number you can derive in one line invites the two copies drifting apart. But the brief lists it explicitly, and in a viva "show me the recency feature" is a fair question. **Want me to materialise it?** It's a small change to `split.py` and a rebuild.

## 5. The "single script" question — you half-caught something

You read it right that it matters, but the requirement is narrower than you think. The exact wording:

> **One-command rebuild** — a single script (e.g., `make data` or `python build_pipeline.py`) that rebuilds everything from raw files

The requirement is **one command**, and `make data` is *the PDF's own example*. So a Makefile target is precisely what they're asking for — not one giant Python file.

What we have: `make all` runs the whole thing from raw archives to final metrics. The separate modules are just organisation behind that one entry point, which is better than a 600-line script — and matters for you, since the viva asks you to *modify* the code.

**But your instinct caught something worth fixing.** `make all` went all the way through to evaluation, while Q1 asks specifically for "raw files to a ready-to-use feature store". So I've added the exact target the PDF names:

```
make data    →  download  →  split        (Q1's deliverable, stops at the feature store)
make all     →  download  →  split  →  bm25  →  embeddings  →  fuse  →  evaluate
```

Also: **`submit.py` isn't part of the pipeline at all.** It only builds the Codabench leaderboard files, and it's deliberately outside `make all` because it scores the competitions' hidden test sets, not your splits. So you were right to set it aside — it doesn't count against the one-command rule.

"""Temporal train/val/test split into one normalized schema for both datasets.

EB-NeRD and MIND describe the same thing in different shapes. Everything downstream
(BM25, embeddings, eval) reads the normalized output, so it has exactly one code path.

    data/processed/<dataset>/impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet
        impression_id       Int64
        user_id             String
        timestamp           Datetime         impression time
        candidates          List(String)     the pool shown, article ids
        clicked             List(String)     subset of candidates that was clicked
        history             List(String)     this user's prior clicks, strictly earlier
        history_timestamps  List(Datetime)   EB-NeRD only; null for MIND (see NOTES.md)

    data/processed/<dataset>/articles.parquet
        article_id  String
        title       String
        abstract    String     EB-NeRD subtitle / MIND abstract
        body        String     EB-NeRD only; MIND-small ships no body text
        category    String
        entities    List(String)  named-entity surface forms (EB-NeRD ner_clusters /
                                  MIND title+abstract entity Labels)
        published_time Datetime   EB-NeRD only; MIND news.tsv carries no date

Article ids are strings in both datasets so the two share a schema; EB-NeRD's integer
ids are cast on the way in.

    python -m pipeline.split                # both datasets
    python -m pipeline.split ebnerd_demo
"""

import argparse
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl
import yaml

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
OUT = ROOT / "data/processed"

MIND_BEHAVIORS = ["impression_id", "user_id", "time", "history", "impressions"]
MIND_NEWS = ["article_id", "category", "subcategory", "title", "abstract", "url",
             "title_entities", "abstract_entities"]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------- EB-NeRD

def _ebnerd_block(root: Path) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """One provided block (train or validation) -> normalized impressions."""
    behaviors = pl.read_parquet(root / "behaviors.parquet")
    history = pl.read_parquet(root / "history.parquet")

    ids = pl.element().cast(pl.String)
    return (
        behaviors.join(history, on="user_id", how="left")
        .select(
            pl.col("impression_id").cast(pl.Int64),
            pl.col("user_id").cast(pl.String),
            pl.col("impression_time").alias("timestamp"),
            pl.col("article_ids_inview").list.eval(ids).alias("candidates"),
            pl.col("article_ids_clicked").list.eval(ids).alias("clicked"),
            pl.col("article_id_fixed").list.eval(ids).alias("history"),
            pl.col("impression_time_fixed").alias("history_timestamps"),
        )
    )


def load_ebnerd(cfg: dict) -> tuple[pl.DataFrame, pl.DataFrame, pl.DataFrame]:
    early = _ebnerd_block(ROOT / cfg["early_root"])
    test = _ebnerd_block(ROOT / cfg["test_root"])
    articles = pl.read_parquet(ROOT / cfg["articles"]).select(
        pl.col("article_id").cast(pl.String),
        pl.col("title"),
        pl.col("subtitle").alias("abstract"),
        pl.col("body"),
        pl.col("category_str").alias("category"),
        # Named-entity surface forms. EB-NeRD ships them pre-extracted (86% of articles);
        # MIND ships JSON that _mind_news parses to the same List(String) shape.
        pl.col("ner_clusters").alias("entities"),
        pl.col("published_time"),
        # Lifetime aggregates computed over the whole collection period, so they embed the
        # future and are not available at serving time. Carried only so the harness can
        # report metrics with and without them (an organiser requirement); no scorer that
        # claims to be servable may read these.
        pl.col("total_inviews"),
        pl.col("total_pageviews"),
        pl.col("total_read_time"),
    )
    return early, test, articles


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------ MIND

def _mind_block(root: Path) -> pl.DataFrame:
    behaviors = pl.read_csv(
        root / "behaviors.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False,
        new_columns=MIND_BEHAVIORS, quote_char=None,
    ).with_row_index("row")

    # "N55689-1 N35729-0" -> candidates + the clicked subset
    pairs = (
        behaviors.select("row", pl.col("impressions").str.split(" ").alias("pair"))
        .explode("pair")
        .with_columns(
            pl.col("pair").str.split("-").list.first().alias("article_id"),
            (pl.col("pair").str.split("-").list.last() == "1").alias("was_clicked"),
        )
    )
    labelled = pairs.group_by("row").agg(
        pl.col("article_id").alias("candidates"),
        pl.col("article_id").filter(pl.col("was_clicked")).alias("clicked"),
    )

    return (
        behaviors.join(labelled, on="row", how="left")
        .select(
            pl.col("impression_id").cast(pl.Int64),
            pl.col("user_id").cast(pl.String),
            pl.col("time").str.strptime(pl.Datetime, "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p").alias("timestamp"),
            pl.col("candidates"),
            pl.col("clicked"),
            # A user with no prior clicks is a cold start, not a missing value — but
            # "".split(" ") is [""], not [], so drop the empty token or every cold-start
            # user gets a phantom one-item history and lands in the wrong eval slice.
            pl.col("history").fill_null("").str.split(" ")
            .list.eval(pl.element().filter(pl.element() != "")).alias("history"),
            pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.List(pl.Datetime)).alias("history_timestamps"),
        )
    )


def _entity_labels(column: str) -> pl.Expr:
    """MIND ships entities as a JSON array per field; we keep the surface labels.

    `json_decode` needs the shape up front, and we only want one field of it, so the
    struct is declared with just `Label` — the rest of each record is discarded.
    """
    dtype = pl.List(pl.Struct({"Label": pl.String}))
    return (
        pl.col(column).fill_null("[]").str.json_decode(dtype)
        .list.eval(pl.element().struct.field("Label"))
    )


def _mind_news(root: Path) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return pl.read_csv(
        root / "news.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False,
        new_columns=MIND_NEWS, quote_char=None,
    ).select(
        "article_id", "title", "abstract",
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.String).alias("body"),
        "category",
        # Title and abstract entities are one pool; duplicates across the two are
        # the same entity mentioned twice, not two entities.
        pl.concat_list(_entity_labels("title_entities"),
                       _entity_labels("abstract_entities"))
        # maintain_order, or the deduplication is hash-ordered and the file stops
        # being byte-identical between runs.
        .list.unique(maintain_order=True).alias("entities"),
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Datetime).alias("published_time"),
        # MIND ships no lifetime aggregates; kept for schema parity with EB-NeRD.
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Int32).alias("total_inviews"),
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Int32).alias("total_pageviews"),
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Float32).alias("total_read_time"),
    )


def load_mind(cfg: dict) -> tuple[pl.DataFrame, pl.DataFrame, pl.DataFrame]:
    early_root, test_root = ROOT / cfg["early_root"], ROOT / cfg["test_root"]
    early = _mind_block(early_root)
    test = _mind_block(test_root)
    # The two splits ship different news files; 13,956 articles appear only in dev.
    # Indexing either alone leaves part of the test corpus unreachable.
    articles = pl.concat([_mind_news(early_root), _mind_news(test_root)]).unique(
        subset="article_id", keep="first"
    )
    return early, test, articles


LOADERS = {"ebnerd": load_ebnerd, "mind": load_mind}


# ------------------------------------------------------------------- integrity

def check_integrity(splits: dict[str, pl.DataFrame], articles: pl.DataFrame) -> None:
    """Fail loudly on anything that would let future information into a split."""
    train, val, test = splits["train"], splits["val"], splits["test"]

    # 1. strict temporal ordering
    bounds = {k: (v["timestamp"].min(), v["timestamp"].max()) for k, v in splits.items()}
    assert bounds["train"][1] < bounds["val"][0], "train overlaps val"
    assert bounds["val"][1] < bounds["test"][0], "val overlaps test"
    print("  [ok] train < val < test, strictly")

    # 2. no future clicks in history
    if train["history_timestamps"].dtype != pl.Null and train["history_timestamps"].null_count() < train.height:
        for name, df in splits.items():
            late = df.filter(
                pl.col("history_timestamps").list.max() >= pl.col("timestamp")
            ).height
            assert late == 0, f"{name}: {late} impressions have history at/after impression time"
        print("  [ok] every history click strictly precedes its impression (per-item)")
    else:
        print("  [--] history carries no timestamps; per-item leakage check not possible.")
        print("       Guarantee is structural only (history precedes the log period).")

    # 3. labels must be drawn from the pool shown
    for name, df in splits.items():
        bad = df.filter(
            pl.col("clicked").list.set_difference(pl.col("candidates")).list.len() > 0
        ).height
        assert bad == 0, f"{name}: {bad} impressions clicked outside the candidate pool"
    print("  [ok] clicked is a subset of candidates")

    # 4. candidates must exist in the corpus, and no id may be the empty string —
    #    an empty token is how a cold-start history silently turns into a 1-item one.
    known = set(articles["article_id"])
    for name, df in splits.items():
        for col in ("candidates", "clicked", "history"):
            ids = set(df[col].explode().drop_nulls())
            assert "" not in ids, f"{name}.{col}: contains an empty article id"
            if col == "candidates":
                assert not (ids - known), (
                    f"{name}: {len(ids - known)} candidates absent from articles.parquet"
                )
    print("  [ok] every candidate resolves to an article; no empty ids")

    # 5. articles published after a split's start cannot be retrieved for it.
    #    Only reportable where the corpus carries a date (EB-NeRD).
    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
        future = articles.filter(pl.col("published_time") > bounds["test"][1]).height
        print(f"  [!!] {future} articles published after the test window ends "
              f"({bounds['test'][1]}).")
        print("       Full-corpus retrieval must filter published_time <= impression_time.")
    else:
        print("  [--] corpus has no publication dates; the published-after-impression")
        print("       filter cannot be applied for this dataset.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------- driver

def build(name: str, cfg: dict) -> None:
    print(f"\n{name}")
    early, test, articles = LOADERS[cfg["loader"]](cfg)

    val_start = datetime.fromisoformat(cfg["val_start"])
    test_start = datetime.fromisoformat(cfg["test_start"])

    splits = {
        "train": early.filter(pl.col("timestamp") < val_start),
        "val": early.filter(pl.col("timestamp") >= val_start),
        "test": test,
    }
    assert splits["test"]["timestamp"].min() >= test_start, (
        f"test block starts before its declared test_start {test_start}"
    )

    check_integrity(splits, articles)

    out = OUT / name
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    # Sort on a unique key before writing. `unique()` is hash-based and row order after it
    # varies run to run, which would make the pipeline non-reproducible byte-for-byte.
    articles.sort("article_id").write_parquet(out / "articles.parquet")
    total = sum(df.height for df in splits.values())
    for split, df in splits.items():
        (df.sort(["timestamp", "impression_id"])
           .write_parquet(out / f"impressions_{split}.parquet"))
        print(f"  {split:<5} {df.height:>7,} ({df.height / total:5.1%})  "
              f"{df['timestamp'].min()} -> {df['timestamp'].max()}")
    print(f"  articles {articles.height:,} -> {out}")


def main() -> None:
    config = yaml.safe_load(CONFIG.read_text())
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", default=list(config))
    args = parser.parse_args()

    for name in args.datasets:
        build(name, config[name])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Repaired and verified.

## The corruption is gone

`ebnerd_small/impressions_test.parquet` is back — 244,647 rows, readable, and all integrity checks pass including the new one:

```
[ok] train < val < test, strictly
[ok] every history click strictly precedes its impression (per-item)
[ok] recency_seconds is strictly positive wherever it is defined
[ok] clicked is a subset of candidates
[ok] every candidate resolves to an article; no empty ids
```

I checked all nine split files against the snapshot I took beforehand: **row counts and impression ordering are identical, `recency_seconds` is the only column added, nothing removed.** So `bm25_*`, `emb_*`, `fused_*` and both submission zips are still valid — no recomputation needed.

**`make test`: 19/19 pass.**

## One thing you should know before the viva

The values have a structure that isn't about user behaviour:

| split | impressions start | recency min | median | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| train | 18 May 07:00 | **0.00 d** | 2.96 d | 24.18 d |
| val | 23 May 07:00 | **5.00 d** | 6.48 d | 26.25 d |
| test | 25 May 07:00 | **0.00 d** | 4.13 d | 26.93 d |

Look at **val: the minimum is exactly 5.00 days.** That's not a coincidence — it's precisely the gap between when the history window ends (18 May) and when val begins (23 May).

The reason: EB-NeRD doesn't give you a live click stream. It ships a **fixed history block per split**, whose window ends where that split's impressions begin. So for validation, *nobody* has a click more recent than 18 May, because the file simply doesn't contain one.

Train and test start at 0.00 d because each has its own history block ending right at its start.

**What this means:** the feature is correct and leak-free, but on validation it's measuring "how far into the split are we" more than "how recently did this person read something". It would carry much more signal in a real system with a continuous stream. That's a fair thing to say out loud if asked — it's a property of how the dataset is packaged, not a flaw in the pipeline.

MIND is `null` throughout, as expected — that dataset ships no per-item history times at all.

## My mistake, and the fix for it

The corruption happened because `split.py` writes parquet directly to its final path, so being killed mid-write destroys a good file. That's a real fragility, not bad luck. Want me to make the writes atomic — write to a temp file, then rename into place? It's a small change and it makes an interrupted run harmless instead of destructive.

"""BM25 over article text, on the two tracks the assignment asks for.

  re-rank    score the candidate pool the log already shows for an impression.
             Comparable to the leaderboards, which rank within the given pool.
  retrieval  ignore the pool and pull the top-K from the whole corpus.
             This is the "candidate generation to a few hundred" half of the spec.

The query for both is the user's recent click history: the titles of their last
HISTORY_LEN clicked articles, concatenated. History is already guaranteed strictly
earlier than the impression by pipeline.split, so the query cannot leak.

Both tracks come out of a single scoring pass. Queries are deduplicated first — history
is constant per user within a split, so the ~230k MIND impressions collapse to far fewer
distinct queries, and BM25 runs once per distinct query rather than once per impression.

    python -m retrieval.bm25                       # both datasets, all splits
    python -m retrieval.bm25 ebnerd_demo --fields title

Writes, per dataset and split:
    bm25_<split>.parquet       impression_id, bm25        aligned to `candidates`
    retrieval_<split>.parquet  impression_id, retrieved   top-K ids, best first
"""

import argparse
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import bm25s
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import Stemmer
import yaml
from tqdm import tqdm

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
PROC = ROOT / "data/processed"

HISTORY_LEN = 30   # most recent clicks forming the query; news interest decays fast
TOP_K = 200        # "a few hundred candidates"
OVERFETCH = 3      # fetch TOP_K*OVERFETCH before the publication-date filter thins it

FIELDS = {
    "title": ("title",),
    "title_abstract": ("title", "abstract"),
    "title_abstract_body": ("title", "abstract", "body"),
}


def document_text(articles: pl.DataFrame, fields: tuple[str, ...]) -> list[str]:
    present = [f for f in fields if articles[f].null_count() < articles.height]
    missing = set(fields) - set(present)
    if missing:
        print(f"  note: {'/'.join(sorted(missing))} is empty for this dataset, skipping")
    return (
        articles.select(
            pl.concat_str([pl.col(f).fill_null("") for f in present], separator=" ")
        )
        .to_series()
        .to_list()
    )


def stopwords_for(cfg: dict):
    """bm25s ships lists for some languages only; others come from configs/."""
    if cfg.get("stopwords_file"):
        lines = (ROOT / cfg["stopwords_file"]).read_text().splitlines()
        return [w for w in (ln.strip() for ln in lines) if w and not w.startswith("#")]
    return cfg.get("stopwords")


def build_index(articles: pl.DataFrame, cfg: dict, fields: tuple[str, ...]):
    stemmer = Stemmer.Stemmer(cfg["language"])
    texts = document_text(articles, fields)
    tokens = bm25s.tokenize(
        texts, stopwords=stopwords_for(cfg), stemmer=stemmer, show_progress=False
    )
    index = bm25s.BM25()
    index.index(tokens, show_progress=False)
    return index, stemmer


def build_queries(impressions: pl.DataFrame, title_of: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    """Last HISTORY_LEN clicked titles per impression. Empty for cold-start users."""
    return [
        " ".join(title_of.get(a, "") for a in hist[-HISTORY_LEN:])
        for hist in impressions["history"].to_list()
    ]


def score_split(index, stemmer, cfg, impressions, articles, position, published):
    """One pass over distinct queries, filling both tracks."""
    queries = build_queries(impressions, dict(zip(articles["article_id"], articles["title"])))

    order: dict[str, int] = {}
    per_impression = []
    for q in queries:
        per_impression.append(order.setdefault(q, len(order)))
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = defaultdict(list)
    for row, q_id in enumerate(per_impression):
        groups[q_id].append(row)
    print(f"    {len(order):,} distinct queries for {impressions.height:,} impressions")

    tokenized = bm25s.tokenize(
        list(order), stopwords=stopwords_for(cfg), stemmer=stemmer,
        return_ids=False, show_progress=False,
    )

    candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
    timestamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
    article_ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy()
    n_fetch = min(TOP_K * OVERFETCH, len(article_ids))

    cand_scores: list = [None] * impressions.height
    retrieved: list = [None] * impressions.height

    for q_id, tokens in enumerate(tqdm(tokenized, desc="    scoring", unit="q", leave=False)):
        rows = groups[q_id]
        if not tokens:
            # Cold start: no history, so BM25 has no query. Zero scores and an empty
            # retrieval, rather than an arbitrary ranking that would look like a result.
            for row in rows:
                cand_scores[row] = np.zeros(len(candidates[row]), dtype=np.float32)
                retrieved[row] = []
            continue

        scores = index.get_scores(tokens)
        top = np.argpartition(-scores, n_fetch - 1)[:n_fetch]
        top = top[np.argsort(-scores[top])]

        for row in rows:
            cand_scores[row] = scores[[position[a] for a in candidates[row]]].astype(np.float32)
            hits = top
            if published is not None:
                # An article published after the impression could not have been shown.
                hits = hits[published[hits] <= np.datetime64(timestamps[row])]
            retrieved[row] = article_ids[hits[:TOP_K]].tolist()

    return cand_scores, retrieved


def run(name: str, cfg: dict, fields: tuple[str, ...], splits: list[str]) -> None:
    print(f"\n{name}  fields={'+'.join(fields)}")
    articles = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / "articles.parquet")
    index, stemmer = build_index(articles, cfg, fields)
    print(f"  indexed {articles.height:,} articles")

    position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
    published = None
    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
        published = articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
    else:
        print("  note: no publication dates; retrieval cannot filter unpublished articles")

    for split in splits:
        impressions = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / f"impressions_{split}.parquet")
        print(f"  {split}: {impressions.height:,} impressions")
        cand_scores, retrieved = score_split(
            index, stemmer, cfg, impressions, articles, position, published
        )

        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "bm25": [s.tolist() for s in cand_scores],
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"bm25_{split}.parquet")
        pl.DataFrame({

content.text:
An **inverted index** is the data structure that makes word search fast. And yes, you have one — built at [retrieval/bm25.py:79](retrieval/bm25.py#L79).

## The idea

Think of the index at the back of a textbook. It doesn't say *"page 42 contains: photosynthesis, chlorophyll, sunlight…"*. It says the opposite:

> **photosynthesis** … 42, 87, 91

That's *inverted*. The natural direction is **document → words**. Flipping it to **word → documents** is what makes it "inverted".

## Why bother

Say someone's history gives you the query *"Denmark football"*. Without an index, you'd read all 20,738 articles and check each one — every single search.

With an inverted index you look up two words and get two short lists of article numbers. You only ever touch articles that actually contain your words. Most articles contain neither, and you never load them at all.

## What's actually inside yours

Here's a real three-article index I built from your code:

```
doc 0: Denmark wins the football match
doc 1: The football team travels to Denmark
doc 2: New recipe for rye bread
```

```
footbal  -> doc0(0.18), doc1(0.18)
denmark  -> doc0(0.18), doc1(0.18)
match    -> doc0(0.38)
win      -> doc0(0.38)
team     -> doc1(0.38)
travel   -> doc1(0.38)
rye      -> doc2(0.43)
recip    -> doc2(0.43)
bread    -> doc2(0.43)
```

Three details worth noticing, because they're all decisions in your pipeline:

- **"the", "to", "for", "new" are missing.** Those are stopwords, thrown away — they'd match everything and mean nothing. This is where the Danish bug came from.
- **"football" is stored as `footbal`, "recipe" as `recip`.** That's the stemmer chopping words to a root so *travel/travels/travelling* all match.
- **The numbers aren't counts, they're BM25 weights.** `rye` scores 0.43 while `denmark` scores 0.18 — because `rye` appears in one article and `denmark` in two, so `rye` is more informative. Rare words are worth more. The weights are computed once, at build time, so searching is just lookup and addition.

## The size of yours

| dataset | articles | distinct words | word→document entries |
|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD small | 20,738 | 30,387 | 297,145 |
| MIND-small | 65,238 | 44,263 | 1,783,811 |

That right-hand column is the index. **1.78 million entries for MIND** — each one saying "this word appears in that article, with this weight".

## Does this satisfy Q2.1?

Yes. Q2.1 asks you to *"build an inverted index over article text (title + abstract)"*, and that's exactly what `bm25s` does when `index.index(tokens)` runs — over `title + abstract`, which is the default `--fields title_abstract`.

One honesty point for your viva, since it's a fair question: **you didn't hand-write the index, the library did.** That's the normal and correct choice — but be ready to say what it's doing, which is what's above. The three things you *did* decide are the stopword list, the stemmer, and which fields go in — and those are the decisions that actually moved the score.

content.text:
Two separate questions, and the answers point in opposite directions.

## Did the assignment ask for stemming?

**No.** I grepped the whole PDF — it never mentions stemming, lemmatising, tokenising, stopwords, or preprocessing at all. Q2 says only:

> 1. Build an inverted index over article text (title + abstract)
> 2. …construct a query… 3. Retrieve top-K… 4. Report recall@K

So every text-normalisation decision in your repo is **yours**, not theirs. That's worth knowing: in a viva, "why did you stem?" is a fair question and "the assignment said so" isn't an available answer.

## Does BM25 need stemming?

**No.** BM25 is just a scoring formula — it counts how often your query words appear in a document, adjusted for word rarity and document length. It doesn't care where the words came from. You could feed it raw untouched text and it would run fine.

Stemming is a completely separate step that happens *before* BM25 sees anything. It exists to fix one problem: **BM25 matches strings exactly.** Without it, a query containing `fodbolden` ("the football") would not match an article saying `fodbold` ("football") — they're different strings, so the score is zero. Stemming chops both to `fodbold` so they match.

Here's your actual Danish stemmer:

```
fodbold      -> fodbold
fodbolden    -> fodbold     ← now these two match
regeringen   -> regering
regeringens  -> regering    ← "the government" / "the government's"
huset        -> hus
huse         -> hus
løber       -> løb          ← "runs" -> "run"
```

## So why not lemmatise?

Genuinely the better technique, and you're right to ask. The difference:

- **Stemming** hacks endings off by rule. Crude, fast, no dictionary. It produces non-words — look at `bedre` → `bedr`, which isn't Danish.
- **Lemmatising** looks the word up and returns its real dictionary form. `bedre` → `god` ("better" → "good"), `løber` → `løbe`. It knows `went` and `go` are the same verb; a stemmer never will.

Three reasons it isn't here, in order of how much they actually mattered:

**1. Availability — the real blocker.** Your stemmer covers **36 languages including Danish**, from one tiny dependency. Lemmatising needs a language-specific dictionary plus grammar tagging. For English that's easy. For Danish it's a much thinner field, and you'd be adding a heavy dependency to serve one dataset. Nothing lemmatisation-capable is installed in your environment at all.

**2. It matters less than you'd expect for retrieval.** Stemming's crudeness is partly a *feature* here. `bedr` isn't a word, but it doesn't need to be — it just needs *query* and *document* to be mangled the same way, and they are. Both sides go through the identical function, so the wrongness cancels. Search engines have used stemming for decades for exactly this reason. Lemmatising helps most when you need the actual word back; retrieval never does.

**3. Cost.** Stemming is a few string rules per word. Lemmatising typically means running a model over all 86,000 articles.

## Where this genuinely costs you

One place, and it's visible in the output above:

```
fodbold      -> fodbold
fodboldkamp  -> fodboldkamp     ← stays separate
```

`fodboldkamp` is "football match" — Danish glues words together into compounds. A rule-based stemmer can't split those, so `fodboldkamp` never matches a query for `fodbold`. **Danish is far more compound-heavy than English**, so this hurts EB-NeRD more than MIND, and it's part of why the Danish lexical scores are weak. A proper Danish tool with compound splitting would help here — more than lemmatising would.

## The honest bit

**I chose stemming without measuring the alternative.** The reasoning above is sound, but it's reasoning, not evidence — and the assignment marks "ablation rigour".

If you want it to be evidence, the cheap version is a three-way comparison on validation: no normalisation at all / stemming (current) / stemming plus compound splitting. The first is free and would tell you how much stemming is buying you — which is the number you'd actually want when someone asks "why did you stem?"

Want me to run that?

38

40	    ideal = float((best * (1.0 / np.log2(np.arange(2, len(best) + 2)))).sum())

"""Ranking metrics, computed per impression so the harness can slice and bootstrap them.

Every function takes the scores for one impression's candidate pool and a boolean label
array, and returns one number. Aggregation, slicing and confidence intervals all happen on
the resulting per-impression vector — that is what makes bootstrapping possible at all.

Impressions where every candidate is clicked, or none is, carry no ranking information;
`per_impression` skips them and reports how many it dropped.
"""

import numpy as np
import polars as pl


def ranks_of(scores: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """1-based rank of each candidate, best first. Ties broken by position, deterministic."""
    order = np.argsort(-scores, kind="stable")
    ranks = np.empty(len(scores), dtype=np.float64)
    ranks[order] = np.arange(1, len(scores) + 1)
    return ranks


def auc(scores: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Probability a clicked candidate outranks an unclicked one, within this impression."""
    ranks = ranks_of(scores)
    return float((ranks[~labels][None, :] > ranks[labels][:, None]).mean())


def mrr(scores: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(1.0 / ranks_of(scores)[labels].min())


def ndcg(scores: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray, k: int) -> float:
    gains = labels.astype(np.float64)
    top = np.argsort(-scores, kind="stable")[:k]
    discount = 1.0 / np.log2(np.arange(2, len(top) + 2))
    actual = float((gains[top] * discount).sum())

    best = np.sort(gains)[::-1][:k]
    ideal = float((best * (1.0 / np.log2(np.arange(2, len(best) + 2)))).sum())
    return actual / ideal if ideal > 0 else 0.0


METRICS = {
    "auc": auc,
    "mrr": mrr,
    "ndcg@5": lambda s, y: ndcg(s, y, 5),
    "ndcg@10": lambda s, y: ndcg(s, y, 10),
}


def per_impression(scores: list, labels: list) -> tuple[dict[str, np.ndarray], np.ndarray]:
    """Per-impression value of every metric, plus the mask of impressions kept."""
    keep = np.array([y.any() and not y.all() for y in labels])
    out = {}
    for name, fn in METRICS.items():
        out[name] = np.array(
            [fn(s, y) for s, y, ok in zip(scores, labels, keep) if ok], dtype=np.float64
        )
    return out, keep


def recall_at_k(retrieved: pl.Series, clicked: pl.Series, ks: tuple[int, ...],
                keep: np.ndarray) -> dict[int, np.ndarray]:

    its top K, averaged over impressions — the definition the brief asks for ("how many
    ground-truth clicked articles appear in the top-K candidates").

    retriever that cannot serve a user has failed for that user, and excluding them would
    quietly report the recall of only the users we could handle.

    Stays in Polars deliberately. Materialising these lists in Python costs ~5 GB per
    system at ebnerd_small (245k impressions x 200 ids) and OOMs a 15 GB machine; the
    set intersection runs in Rust and only the one float per impression crosses back.

    truth_size = pl.col("clicked").list.len()
    return {
        k: rows.select(
            pl.col("retrieved").list.head(k)
            .list.set_intersection(pl.col("clicked"))
            .list.len() / truth_size
        ).to_series().to_numpy().astype(np.float64)
        for k in ks
    }

"""Bootstrap confidence intervals over per-impression metric values.

Resampling is over impressions, which is the unit that is (approximately) independent
here — resampling candidates within an impression would understate the variance badly.

`paired` reuses the *same* resampled indices for both systems. That is the whole point: two
systems evaluated on the same impressions have correlated errors, so an unpaired comparison
of two independent intervals is far too conservative and will hide real differences.
"""

import numpy as np

RESAMPLES = 1000
SEED = 0


# Resampling 1000 x 73k impressions at once would allocate ~585 MB; draw in chunks instead.
CHUNK = 50


def _resample_means(arrays: tuple[np.ndarray, ...], resamples: int, seed: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, ...]:
    """Chunked resampling. All arrays share each draw, which is what makes it paired."""
    n = len(arrays[0])
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = [np.empty(resamples) for _ in arrays]
    for start in range(0, resamples, CHUNK):
        size = min(CHUNK, resamples - start)
        idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(size, n))
        for values, dest in zip(arrays, out):
            dest[start:start + size] = values[idx].mean(axis=1)
    return tuple(out)


def ci(values: np.ndarray, resamples: int = RESAMPLES, seed: int = SEED, level: float = 95.0):
    """(mean, low, high) for one system."""
    (means,) = _resample_means((values,), resamples, seed)
    tail = (100.0 - level) / 2.0
    return float(values.mean()), float(np.percentile(means, tail)), float(np.percentile(means, 100 - tail))


def paired(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, resamples: int = RESAMPLES, seed: int = SEED,
           level: float = 95.0):
    """(mean difference a-b, low, high, excludes_zero) on shared resamples."""
    assert len(a) == len(b), "paired bootstrap needs the same impressions on both sides"
    means_a, means_b = _resample_means((a, b), resamples, seed)
    diffs = means_a - means_b
    tail = (100.0 - level) / 2.0
    low, high = float(np.percentile(diffs, tail)), float(np.percentile(diffs, 100 - tail))
    return float((a - b).mean()), low, high, bool(low > 0 or high < 0)


def fmt(mean: float, lo: float, hi: float) -> str:
    return f"{mean:.4f} [{lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f}]"

"""Does text normalisation earn its place? Three variants, val only, one thing changed at a time.

    none        tokenise + stopwords, no stemmer at all
    stem        + Snowball stemmer                          <- what ships today
    stem_split  + greedy compound splitting before stemming

Everything else is held fixed: same articles, same queries, same stopword list, same BM25,
same metric code as eval/. So any difference is attributable to the normalisation step.

Compound splitting is built from the corpus itself rather than a dictionary: a word is split
when it decomposes into two words the corpus already uses often on their own. Both parts are
emitted *alongside* the original, so a split that is wrong can only add noise, never destroy
an exact match that would otherwise have fired. Danish glues nouns together (`fodboldkamp` =
`fodbold` + `kamp`) and a rule-based stemmer cannot undo that; this is the cheap approximation
of a proper decompounder.
"""
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter

import bm25s
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import Stemmer
import yaml

sys.path.insert(0, "/home/neemon/Desktop/semesters/sem-5/ire/assignments/ass-1")
from eval import bootstrap, metrics                                    # noqa: E402
from retrieval.bm25 import (HISTORY_LEN, OVERFETCH, TOP_K, ROOT, PROC,  # noqa: E402
                            document_text, stopwords_for, FIELDS)

WORD = re.compile(r"[^\W\d_]+", re.UNICODE)
MIN_PART = 4      # a compound part shorter than this is usually an inflection, not a word
MIN_COUNT = 20    # and it must be a word the corpus genuinely uses on its own


def compound_vocab(texts: list[str]) -> set[str]:
    counts = Counter(w.lower() for t in texts for w in WORD.findall(t))
    return {w for w, c in counts.items() if c >= MIN_COUNT and len(w) >= MIN_PART}


def split_compounds(texts: list[str], vocab: set[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Emit `fodboldkamp fodbold kamp` in place of `fodboldkamp`, when both parts are known."""
    cache: dict[str, str] = {}

    def expand(word: str) -> str:
        low = word.lower()
        if low in cache:
            return cache[low]
        out = word
        if len(low) >= 2 * MIN_PART and low not in vocab:
            for i in range(MIN_PART, len(low) - MIN_PART + 1):
                head, tail = low[:i], low[i:]
                if head in vocab and tail in vocab:
                    out = f"{word} {head} {tail}"
                    break
        cache[low] = out
        return out

    return [" ".join(expand(w) for w in WORD.findall(t)) for t in texts]


def prepare(texts: list[str], mode: str, vocab):
    return split_compounds(texts, vocab) if mode == "stem_split" else texts


def run(dataset: str, mode: str, cfg: dict) -> dict:
    articles = pl.read_parquet(PROC / dataset / "articles.parquet")
    impressions = pl.read_parquet(PROC / dataset / "impressions_val.parquet")

    doc_text = document_text(articles, FIELDS["title_abstract"])
    vocab = compound_vocab(doc_text) if mode == "stem_split" else None
    stemmer = None if mode == "none" else Stemmer.Stemmer(cfg["language"])
    stops = stopwords_for(cfg)

                         stemmer=stemmer, show_progress=False)
    index = bm25s.BM25()
    index.index(tok, show_progress=False)

    title_of = dict(zip(articles["article_id"], articles["title"]))
    queries = [" ".join(title_of.get(a, "") for a in h[-HISTORY_LEN:])
               for h in impressions["history"].to_list()]

    order, per_row = {}, []
    for q in queries:
        per_row.append(order.setdefault(q, len(order)))
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = {}
    for row, q_id in enumerate(per_row):
        groups.setdefault(q_id, []).append(row)

    q_tokens = bm25s.tokenize(prepare(list(order), mode, vocab), stopwords=stops,
                              stemmer=stemmer, return_ids=False, show_progress=False)

    article_ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy()
    published = (articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
                 if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height else None)
    n_fetch = min(TOP_K * OVERFETCH, len(article_ids))

    cand = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
    stamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
    scores_out: list = [None] * impressions.height
    retrieved: list = [None] * impressions.height

    for q_id, tokens in enumerate(q_tokens):
        rows = groups[q_id]

                scores_out[row] = np.zeros(len(cand[row]), dtype=np.float32)
                retrieved[row] = []
            continue
        s = index.get_scores(tokens)
        top = np.argpartition(-s, n_fetch - 1)[:n_fetch]
        top = top[np.argsort(-s[top])]
        for row in rows:
            scores_out[row] = s[[position[a] for a in cand[row]]].astype(np.float32)

    results: dict = {}
    for dataset in ["ebnerd_small", "mind_small"]:

        for mode in ["none", "stem", "stem_split"]:
            print(f"{dataset} / {mode} ...", flush=True)

    for dataset, bymode in results.items():
        print(f"\n=== {dataset} (val) ===")
        print(f"{'variant':<12}{'vocab':>9}  {'AUC':<26}{'recall@200'}")
        for mode, r in bymode.items():
            a = bootstrap.ci(r["auc"])
            k = bootstrap.ci(r["recall@200"])
            print(f"{mode:<12}{r['vocab']:>9,}  {bootstrap.fmt(*a):<26}{bootstrap.fmt(*k)}")
        print("  paired differences (AUC):")
        for a, b in [("stem", "none"), ("stem_split", "stem")]:
            d, lo, hi, sig = bootstrap.paired(bymode[a]["auc"], bymode[b]["auc"])
            print(f"    {a} - {b:<12} {d:+.4f} [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]  "
                  f"{'significant' if sig else 'includes zero'}")

"""Does text normalisation earn its place? Three variants, val only, one thing changed at a time.

    none        tokenise + stopwords, no stemmer at all
    stem        + Snowball stemmer                          <- what ships today
    stem_split  + greedy compound splitting before stemming

Everything else is held fixed: same articles, same queries, same stopword list, same BM25,
same metric code as eval/. So any difference is attributable to the normalisation step.

Compound splitting is built from the corpus itself rather than a dictionary: a word is split
when it decomposes into two words the corpus already uses often on their own. Both parts are
emitted *alongside* the original, so a split that is wrong can only add noise, never destroy
an exact match that would otherwise have fired. Danish glues nouns together (`fodboldkamp` =
`fodbold` + `kamp`) and a rule-based stemmer cannot undo that; this is the cheap approximation
of a proper decompounder.
"""
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter

import bm25s
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import Stemmer
import yaml

sys.path.insert(0, "/home/neemon/Desktop/semesters/sem-5/ire/assignments/ass-1")
from eval import bootstrap, metrics                                    # noqa: E402
from retrieval.bm25 import (HISTORY_LEN, OVERFETCH, TOP_K, ROOT, PROC,  # noqa: E402
                            document_text, stopwords_for, FIELDS)

WORD = re.compile(r"[^\W\d_]+", re.UNICODE)
MIN_PART = 3      # a compound part shorter than this is usually an inflection, not a word
MIN_COUNT = 10    # and it must be a word the corpus genuinely uses on its own
SPLITS = Counter()  # how often the splitter actually fired, so "no effect" is distinguishable
                    # from "never triggered"


def compound_vocab(texts: list[str]) -> set[str]:
    counts = Counter(w.lower() for t in texts for w in WORD.findall(t))
    return {w for w, c in counts.items() if c >= MIN_COUNT and len(w) >= MIN_PART}


def split_compounds(texts: list[str], vocab: set[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Emit `fodboldkamp fodbold kamp` in place of `fodboldkamp`, when both parts are known."""
    cache: dict[str, str] = {}

    def expand(word: str) -> str:
        low = word.lower()
        if low in cache:
            return cache[low]
        out = word
        # No `low not in vocab` guard: a compound common enough to be its own vocabulary
        # entry still benefits from having its parts indexed. Parts are added, never
        # substituted, so the original exact match always survives.
        if len(low) >= 2 * MIN_PART:
            for i in range(MIN_PART, len(low) - MIN_PART + 1):
                head, tail = low[:i], low[i:]
                if head in vocab and tail in vocab:
                    out = f"{word} {head} {tail}"
                    SPLITS["fired"] += 1
                    break
        SPLITS["seen"] += 1
        cache[low] = out
        return out

    return [" ".join(expand(w) for w in WORD.findall(t)) for t in texts]


def prepare(texts: list[str], mode: str, vocab):
    return split_compounds(texts, vocab) if mode == "stem_split" else texts


def run(dataset: str, mode: str, cfg: dict) -> dict:
    articles = pl.read_parquet(PROC / dataset / "articles.parquet")
    impressions = pl.read_parquet(PROC / dataset / "impressions_val.parquet")

    doc_text = document_text(articles, FIELDS["title_abstract"])
    vocab = compound_vocab(doc_text) if mode == "stem_split" else None
    stemmer = None if mode == "none" else Stemmer.Stemmer(cfg["language"])
    stops = stopwords_for(cfg)

    tok = bm25s.tokenize(prepare(doc_text, mode, vocab), stopwords=stops,
                         stemmer=stemmer, show_progress=False)
    index = bm25s.BM25()
    index.index(tok, show_progress=False)

    title_of = dict(zip(articles["article_id"], articles["title"]))
    queries = [" ".join(title_of.get(a, "") for a in h[-HISTORY_LEN:])
               for h in impressions["history"].to_list()]

    order, per_row = {}, []
    for q in queries:
        per_row.append(order.setdefault(q, len(order)))
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = {}
    for row, q_id in enumerate(per_row):
        groups.setdefault(q_id, []).append(row)

    q_tokens = bm25s.tokenize(prepare(list(order), mode, vocab), stopwords=stops,
                              stemmer=stemmer, return_ids=False, show_progress=False)

    position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
    article_ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy()
    published = (articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
                 if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height else None)
    n_fetch = min(TOP_K * OVERFETCH, len(article_ids))

    cand = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
    stamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
    scores_out: list = [None] * impressions.height
    retrieved: list = [None] * impressions.height

    for q_id, tokens in enumerate(q_tokens):
        rows = groups[q_id]
        if not tokens:
            for row in rows:
                scores_out[row] = np.zeros(len(cand[row]), dtype=np.float32)
                retrieved[row] = []
            continue
        s = index.get_scores(tokens)
        top = np.argpartition(-s, n_fetch - 1)[:n_fetch]
        top = top[np.argsort(-s[top])]
        for row in rows:
            scores_out[row] = s[[position[a] for a in cand[row]]].astype(np.float32)
            hits = top if published is None else top[published[top] <= np.datetime64(stamps[row])]
            retrieved[row] = article_ids[hits[:TOP_K]].tolist()

    clicked = impressions["clicked"].to_list()
    labels = [np.fromiter((c in set(cl) for c in cs), dtype=bool, count=len(cs))
              for cs, cl in zip(cand, clicked)]
    vals, keep = metrics.per_impression(scores_out, labels)
    rec = metrics.recall_at_k(pl.Series(retrieved), impressions["clicked"], (200,), keep)
    fired = f"{SPLITS['fired']:,}/{SPLITS['seen']:,}" if mode == "stem_split" else "-"
    return {"auc": vals["auc"], "recall@200": rec[200], "vocab": len(tok.vocab), "split": fired}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    config = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml").read_text())
    results: dict = {}
    for dataset in ["ebnerd_small", "mind_small"]:
        results[dataset] = {}
        for mode in ["none", "stem", "stem_split"]:
            print(f"{dataset} / {mode} ...", flush=True)
            SPLITS.clear()
            results[dataset][mode] = run(dataset, mode, config[dataset])

    for dataset, bymode in results.items():
        print(f"\n=== {dataset} (val) ===")
        print(f"{'variant':<12}{'vocab':>9}{'splits fired':>16}  {'AUC':<26}{'recall@200'}")
        for mode, r in bymode.items():
            a = bootstrap.ci(r["auc"])
            k = bootstrap.ci(r["recall@200"])
            print(f"{mode:<12}{r['vocab']:>9,}{r['split']:>16}  "
                  f"{bootstrap.fmt(*a):<26}{bootstrap.fmt(*k)}")
        print("  paired differences (AUC):")
        for a, b in [("stem", "none"), ("stem_split", "stem")]:
            d, lo, hi, sig = bootstrap.paired(bymode[a]["auc"], bymode[b]["auc"])
            print(f"    {a} - {b:<12} {d:+.4f} [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]  "
                  f"{'significant' if sig else 'includes zero'}")

## Does text normalisation earn its place? (stemming ablation)

The assignment specifies nothing about tokenisation, stemming or stopwords — grep the PDF and
those words do not appear. So stemming was my choice, and until now an untested one. Three
variants on **val**, one thing changed at a time, everything else held fixed (same articles,
same queries, same stopword list, same BM25, same metric code as `eval/`):

| dataset | variant | vocab | AUC | recall@200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ebnerd_small | none | 43,451 | 0.5202 [0.5176, 0.5226] | **0.0234** [0.0222, 0.0246] |
| | **stem** (ships) | 30,388 | **0.5205** [0.5177, 0.5230] | 0.0214 [0.0202, 0.0225] |
| | stem+split | 29,770 | 0.5165 [0.5137, 0.5192] | 0.0219 [0.0208, 0.0230] |
| mind_small | none | 60,914 | 0.5782 [0.5756, 0.5807] | **0.0384** [0.0370, 0.0397] |
| | **stem** (ships) | 44,264 | **0.5801** [0.5775, 0.5827] | 0.0361 [0.0347, 0.0373] |
| | stem+split | 41,650 | 0.5788 [0.5763, 0.5812] | 0.0323 [0.0310, 0.0335] |

Paired, `stem - none`:

| dataset | AUC | recall@200 |
|---|---|---|
| ebnerd_small | +0.0003 [-0.0014, +0.0019] **includes zero** | **-0.0020** [-0.0030, -0.0011] |
| mind_small | **+0.0019** [+0.0007, +0.0029] | **-0.0023** [-0.0031, -0.0015] |

**Stemming does not do what I assumed.** It helps re-ranking on English only, does nothing
measurable on Danish, and **significantly hurts full-corpus retrieval on both**. I had written
that stemming was the obvious standard choice; on the retrieval track that was wrong, and the
ablation is what caught it.

The mechanism is consistent across both datasets: stemming collapses distinct words into one
bucket, trading precision for recall of morphological variants. Ordering 8 candidates the log
already filtered, that trade pays on English. Picking 200 out of 20,738, the extra spurious
matches cost more than the variant-matching gains — the query is 30 concatenated titles and
already noisy, so making the index *less* discriminative is the wrong direction.

**Compound splitting was my idea, tested, and rejected.** Danish glues nouns together
(`fodboldkamp` = `fodbold` + `kamp`) and a rule-based stemmer cannot undo it, so I built a
greedy splitter from the corpus's own vocabulary, emitting parts alongside the original so a
wrong split could only add noise. It fired on 15% of tokens (7,451/50,328 Danish,
10,972/80,239 English) — so "no effect" is ruled out — and made things **worse**: -0.0040 AUC
on EB-NeRD and -0.0013 AUC / -0.0038 recall on MIND, all significant. Corpus-vocabulary
splitting produces too many false compounds; a real decompounder needs a proper Danish
lexicon, not word statistics. Recorded because a rejected idea with numbers is worth more
than an untried one.

**Kept stemming anyway**, deliberately: it is the right call for the reported headline metric
on MIND and neutral on EB-NeRD, and the effect sizes here (0.002-0.004 AUC) are an order of
magnitude below the encoder choice (0.04) and the serving-unavailable popularity feature
(0.05). Dropping it for Danish only is defensible on this evidence — per-language stopword
lists already exist, so per-language stemming would not strain the config — but it would buy
~0.002 recall and cost a full re-run of every EB-NeRD artifact and the leaderboard file.
Reproduce with `scratchpad/text_ablation.py`.
EOF

**The finding that mattered.** EB-NeRD first scored AUC **0.5035** — random. Rather than report
that, I tested whether it was my bug: an **oracle test** (query = the clicked article's own title)
ranked it #1 in 300/300 impressions at AUC 0.9990, proving alignment was correct, and a
history-length sweep was flat, ruling out query dilution. MIND meanwhile worked at 0.58, and that
asymmetry pointed at the cause — **bm25s ships no Danish stopword list**, so thirty concatenated
Danish titles were mostly function words. Adding the Snowball list moved EB-NeRD to **0.5232**. A
missing stopword list is silent: it degrades ranking without ever erroring.

content.text:
Back to 4 pages. Here's what the ablation found — and it contradicts what I told you earlier.

## The results (validation, paired comparisons)

| dataset | variant | vocabulary | AUC | recall@200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EB-NeRD** | no stemming | 43,451 | 0.5202 | **0.0234** |
| | **stemming** (ships) | 30,388 | **0.5205** | 0.0214 |
| | stem + compound split | 29,770 | 0.5165 | 0.0219 |
| **MIND** | no stemming | 60,914 | 0.5782 | **0.0384** |
| | **stemming** (ships) | 44,264 | **0.5801** | 0.0361 |
| | stem + compound split | 41,650 | 0.5788 | 0.0323 |

`stemming − none`, paired:

| dataset | AUC | recall@200 |
|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD | +0.0003 [−0.0014, +0.0019] — **includes zero** | **−0.0020** [−0.0030, −0.0011] |
| MIND | **+0.0019** [+0.0007, +0.0029] | **−0.0023** [−0.0031, −0.0015] |

## What this means

**Stemming does not do what I said it did.** I told you it was the obvious standard choice. On the re-ranking metric that holds for English and is *nothing at all* on Danish. On the retrieval metric — the one Q2.4 actually asks you to report — **it makes things significantly worse on both datasets.** My reasoning was wrong on that half, and only measuring caught it.

The mechanism is consistent, and it's a good viva answer: stemming **trades precision for variant-matching.** Merging `fodbold`/`fodbolden` into one bucket helps you match word forms, but it also makes the index blunter — more things look alike.

Which way that trade lands depends on the job:

- **Ordering ~8 candidates** the log already filtered → the extra matches help. Stemming wins.
- **Picking 200 out of 20,738** with a query that's 30 concatenated titles glued together → that query is already noisy, and making the index *less* discriminating is the wrong direction. Stemming loses.

Same setting, opposite verdicts, depending on which of your two tracks you're looking at.

## The compound splitter failed

My idea, so worth being blunt: it made things **worse** everywhere. −0.0040 AUC on Danish, −0.0013 AUC and −0.0038 recall on English, all significant.

And I can rule out "it never triggered" — I counted, and it fired on **15% of tokens** (7,451 of 50,328 Danish; 10,972 of 80,239 English). It ran plenty; it was just wrong too often. Splitting words using nothing but the corpus's own word statistics invents compounds that aren't real, and the false splits cost more than the true ones earn. A proper Danish decompounder needs an actual lexicon.

## What I did and didn't change

**I kept stemming**, and documented why rather than quietly switching:

- It's the right call for AUC, which is the headline metric, on MIND
- It's neutral on EB-NeRD
- The effect sizes here (0.002–0.004) are **ten times smaller** than the encoder choice (0.04) or the serving-unavailable popularity feature (0.05)

Dropping it for Danish only is defensible on this evidence — you already have per-language stopword lists, so per-language stemming wouldn't strain the config. It would buy roughly 0.002 recall and cost a full re-run of every EB-NeRD artifact plus the leaderboard file. Say the word if you want it.

Written up in `NOTES.md` in full, and compressed into §3 of the design note — a rejected idea with numbers attached is worth more to the "ablation rigour" mark than an untried one. Reproduce with `scratchpad/text_ablation.py`.

content.text:
**Keep it.** Here are the percentages first, because they're the reason it's not obvious.

## How much worse, in percent

| dataset | metric | without stemming | with stemming | relative change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD | AUC | 0.5202 | 0.5205 | **+0.1%** |
| EB-NeRD | recall@200 | 0.0234 | 0.0214 | **−8.5%** |
| MIND | AUC | 0.5782 | 0.5801 | **+0.3%** |
| MIND | recall@200 | 0.0384 | 0.0361 | **−6.0%** |

So stemming costs you **6–9% of your recall** and buys **0.1–0.3% of AUC**. Stated that way it looks like an obvious loss.

## Why the percentages mislead here

Those two columns aren't measured on comparable scales, and this is the bit worth understanding:

**AUC starts at 0.5, not 0.** A coin flip already scores 0.5, so the *whole* useful range is what sits above it. Your EB-NeRD score of 0.5205 means "0.0205 better than random" — and against that, +0.0003 is **+1.5%** of the signal you actually have. On MIND it's **+2.4%**. Not the 0.1% and 0.3% the naive percentage suggests.

**Recall genuinely starts at 0**, so its −8.5% is honest. But the absolute numbers are 0.0234 vs 0.0214 — you're arguing over 2 clicked articles per thousand.

Percentages of tiny numbers are loud. Both effects are small.

## The actual recommendation: keep stemming

Three reasons, in order of weight:

**1. AUC is your headline metric, everywhere.** Every table in the report, every slice, every paired comparison, both leaderboard submissions — all AUC. Dropping stemming costs a *statistically real* AUC loss on MIND and gains nothing on EB-NeRD. You'd be trading your main number for your secondary one.

**2. The recall gain doesn't change a single conclusion.** Your retrieval track is weak for a structural reason that dwarfs this: EB-NeRD's catalogue spans 1998–2023 while impressions are one week in May 2023, and nothing filters out stale articles. Recall goes 0.0214 → 0.0234. It's still ~2%. No sentence in your report would change.

**3. Scale.** This is 0.002–0.004 AUC. Your encoder choice was **0.04** and the serving-unavailable popularity feature was **0.05** — ten and twenty times larger. Spending a full pipeline re-run plus a leaderboard rebuild on the smallest lever you've measured is poor use of the time you have left before the 27th.

## What actually makes this worth marks

Not the choice — **the fact you measured it.** "I stemmed because everyone stems" is a weak viva answer. "I stemmed, measured it, found it helps ranking and hurts retrieval, and kept it because ranking is the reported metric" is a strong one. That's already in `NOTES.md` and §3 of the design note.

## The one option I'd flag but not take

The finding logically implies: **stem for re-ranking, don't stem for retrieval** — two indexes, each tuned to its job. It's the technically correct answer and would take both wins.

I'd skip it. It roughly doubles index build time, adds a subtlety you'd have to defend live, and buys 0.002 recall. Given the assignment explicitly grades code you can explain and modify on the spot, that's a bad trade. But it's a genuinely good thing to *say* in the viva — "here's what the result implies, here's why I judged it not worth the complexity" shows you understood your own measurement.

content.text:
Fetched both live leaderboards. Short answer: **no, you're not uniquely near-random on EB-NeRD — about a third of teams are down there with you.** MIND is a different story.

## EB-NeRD (RecSys 2024) — 156 teams

| | AUC |
|---|---|
| Best (sugawarya) | 0.8922 |
| Median team | 0.6382 |
| Worst team | 0.4397 — **below random** |
| **Teams scoring under 0.55** | **51 of 156 — a third of the field** |

Your ~0.51 would land around **rank 122–126 of 156**, beating roughly 30 teams.

So low, yes — bottom third. But "the only one near random"? Not remotely. Fifty-one teams are under 0.55, and the bottom of the board is *worse than a coin flip*, which means people submitted systems with an actively inverted signal. This is a known-hard dataset.

## MIND — 35 teams

| | AUC |
|---|---|
| Best (zetik) | 0.7326 |
| Median team | 0.7048 |
| Worst team | 0.4794 |
| Teams under 0.55 | **1 of 35** |

Your 0.634 would sit around **rank 32 of 35**. Bottom of the pack — but this board is *tight*: almost everyone is clustered between 0.70 and 0.73, so 0.634 is behind but plainly a working system, not noise.

## The comparison isn't fair, in your favour

Two things make those top numbers not the right yardstick:

**1. They're trained models; yours isn't.** The RecSys 2024 winners were large ensembles of trained neural recommenders using behavioural signals. Yours is entirely unsupervised — no training anywhere in Component-1 — and **deliberately excludes the behavioural axis**, because that's Component-2's job. You are missing, by design, the single most predictive family of features in news recommendation.

**2. You're submitting your weakest system.** Your EB-NeRD entry is embeddings-only (0.5036), because BM25 can't scale to 13.5M impressions. Your best offline system is fused at 0.5131. Neither is what you'd submit if the leaderboard were the goal.

Also worth remembering: the leaderboard scores a **different, much larger test set** than your splits, so your 0.51 is indicative, not a prediction.

## The honest read

**MIND is your real result.** 0.635 from a content-only, untrained system, against a field clustered at 0.70–0.73 from trained models — that's a respectable showing for what it is, and your design note already says so.

**EB-NeRD's 0.51 is genuinely poor**, and your note gives the structural reason: candidate pools of ~8–9 articles drawn from a tight recency window, where every option is already plausible and topically close. There's very little for pure content matching to separate. The leaderboard supports that reading — a third of all teams are under 0.55 on this dataset while only 1 of 35 is on MIND.

One thing this does change: your design note says EB-NeRD "tops out at 0.5131" without context. Want me to add a line citing the leaderboard distribution — that 51/156 teams score under 0.55 — so the marker sees your weak Danish number is a property of the task, not a broken pipeline? It's one sentence and it's now backed by real data.

content.text:
Here are the BM25 recall@K numbers — Q2.4's deliverable — with 95% bootstrap intervals, from `results/`:

## BM25, full-corpus retrieval

| dataset | split | recall@50 | recall@100 | recall@200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EB-NeRD demo** | val | 0.0114 [0.0090, 0.0138] | 0.0217 [0.0185, 0.0250] | 0.0434 [0.0386, 0.0479] |
| | **test** | **0.0108** [0.0095, 0.0122] | **0.0216** [0.0199, 0.0234] | **0.0390** [0.0368, 0.0413] |
| **EB-NeRD small** | val | 0.0052 [0.0047, 0.0058] | 0.0110 [0.0101, 0.0118] | 0.0214 [0.0202, 0.0225] |
| | **test** | **0.0072** [0.0069, 0.0075] | **0.0133** [0.0128, 0.0138] | **0.0247** [0.0241, 0.0253] |
| **MIND-small** | val | 0.0145 [0.0136, 0.0154] | 0.0237 [0.0227, 0.0249] | 0.0361 [0.0347, 0.0373] |
| | **test** | **0.0060** [0.0056, 0.0065] | **0.0124** [0.0117, 0.0132] | **0.0220** [0.0210, 0.0230] |

## What these mean

Recall here is: **of the articles a person actually clicked, what fraction did BM25 pull into its top K — searching the entire catalogue**, not the short list the log already showed them.

So `recall@200 = 0.0247` means: out of the whole 20,738-article corpus, BM25's 200 best guesses contained about **2.5%** of what that person really clicked.

Doubling K roughly doubles recall (50 → 100 → 200 gives ~0.007 → 0.013 → 0.025). That's close to what random selection would do, and it's the honest signal that BM25 isn't finding a concentrated pocket of good candidates — it's mostly widening the net.

## Two things to be ready for

**1. These are low, and the reason is structural, not a bug.** EB-NeRD's catalogue spans 1998–2023 while every impression is from one week in May 2023. The only date filter is `published_time <= impression_time`, which removes *future* articles but not *ancient* ones — so BM25 happily retrieves a well-matching article from 2007 that nobody would ever be shown. A recency window on the retrievable corpus is the obvious fix, and it belongs with the behavioural work in Component-2.

**2. BM25 beats embeddings on EB-NeRD at every K** — and by a wide margin (0.0247 vs 0.0165 at K=200 on small, roughly 50% better). On MIND it flips: embeddings win at every K on test (0.0239 vs 0.0220). Same code, same K, opposite verdicts. That's the §5 finding in your design note, and it's the reason there's no dataset-wide answer to "which retriever is better".

Also note MIND's val-to-test drop (0.0361 → 0.0220). MIND test is a single day with 50,000 users, many unseen — a harder, colder slice than validation.

content.text: By embeddings vs BM25 do you mean semantic vs lexical?

Yes — exactly that. Same distinction, different naming level.

| the axis | the method we used | the column in results |
|---|---|---|
| **lexical** — matching *words* | BM25 | `bm25` |
| **semantic** — matching *meaning* | word2vec vectors + cosine | `emb` |
| both, blended | z-normalise each, mix with alpha | `fused` |

So when I said "BM25 beats embeddings on EB-NeRD at every K", that's the same sentence as "the lexical axis beats the semantic axis on Danish retrieval".

## Why both names exist

They sit at different levels, and it's worth keeping them apart:

- **Lexical / semantic** are the *ideas* — the two kinds of clue. That's the assignment's vocabulary ("all three modelling axes"), and it's what a marker asks about.
- **BM25 / embeddings** are the *specific things we built* to chase those ideas. Swappable. You could do lexical with TF-IDF instead of BM25, or semantic with BERT instead of word2vec — the axis wouldn't change, only the implementation.

That distinction actually matters for your results. When multilingual BERT scored below random, **the semantic axis didn't fail — that one implementation of it did.** Swapping to word2vec, same axis, took it from 0.4857 to 0.5098. If you'd conflated the two you'd have concluded "meaning-matching doesn't work on Danish", which isn't what the evidence says.

## Careful with one thing

They aren't perfectly interchangeable in casual use. In the wider field, "semantic search" usually implies *dense vectors* specifically — but you can chase meaning lexically too, for example by expanding a query with synonyms before running BM25. So:

- **lexical → BM25** is a choice we made, not a definition
- **semantic → embeddings** is likewise a choice

In your repo they happen to map one-to-one, so treating them as synonyms is safe here. Just don't say "semantic means embeddings" in the viva — say "we implemented the semantic axis with embeddings", which is both true and shows you know they're separable.

The third axis, **behavioural** — what's popular, what's fresh, what people clicked lately — has no column in your results because it's Component-2. The one probe you did run is in §8: train-click popularity scored *below* random on EB-NeRD.

content.text:
Your intuition is correct — and the data shows exactly *when* it holds. Look at `emb − bm25` across all four encoders we've measured:

| dataset | encoder | emb − bm25 (AUC) | winner |
|---|---|---|---|
| MIND | **MiniLM** | **+0.0693** [+0.0668, +0.0718] | embeddings, hugely |
| EB-NeRD | **contrastive_vector** | **+0.0301** [+0.0269, +0.0336] | embeddings |
| EB-NeRD | **word2vec** (ships) | **−0.0107** [−0.0140, −0.0071] | BM25 |
| EB-NeRD | **multilingual BERT** | **−0.0348** [−0.0383, −0.0310] | BM25, badly |

Embeddings beat BM25 in two of four cases and lose in two. It isn't the *idea* that fails — it's **two specific encoders**.

## What separates the winners from the losers

One property, and it's the whole answer:

**Was the model trained so that "close together" means "about the same topic"?**

- **MiniLM** — a sentence-transformer trained on *pairs of similar sentences*, for the express purpose of making cosine similarity meaningful. Fit for purpose. Wins by 0.069.
- **contrastive_vector** — trained by Ekstra Bladet on their own articles, with a contrastive objective, which is literally "pull related articles together, push unrelated ones apart". Fit for purpose. Wins by 0.030.
- **word2vec** — trained in 2013 to predict neighbouring *words*. Nobody ever asked it to make document similarity work; we average word vectors and hope. Loses.
- **multilingual BERT** — trained to fill in blanked-out words. Its raw sentence vectors are famously bad at similarity. Loses, and scores below random.

The first two were *built* for this job. The last two are being asked to do a job they were never trained for.

## So why does your repo ship a losing one?

Because you told me to — and for a good reason. `contrastive_vector` is the one that beats BM25 on Danish, but **the assignment doesn't name it.** It names word2vec and multilingual BERT. You chose fidelity to the brief over the better number, and I agree with that call.

The cost is exactly this: **that decision is what flipped EB-NeRD from "embeddings win" to "BM25 wins".** It's recorded in `NOTES.md` rather than hidden, and it's a strong viva answer — you know precisely what the choice cost and why you made it.

## The wider point worth knowing

"Embeddings beat BM25" is true of *trained retrievers* fine-tuned on the task. It is **not** reliably true of off-the-shelf embeddings used as-is.

BM25 is a notoriously strong baseline — there's a well-known pattern of neural retrieval papers claiming to beat it and turning out to have compared against a badly-tuned version. Your own project shows the same thing from the other side: your biggest single win all term wasn't a fancier model, it was **adding the missing Danish stopword list**, which moved BM25 from 0.5035 (random) to 0.5232.

Two more reasons your embeddings are handicapped here, both fixable in Component-2:

- **Mean-pooling flattens the user.** You average up to 30 article vectors into one. Someone who reads football *and* politics becomes a single point between the two, matching neither well. BM25 keeps all 30 titles' words distinct and can fire on any of them.
- **No training anywhere.** Component-1 is entirely unsupervised. The systems on those leaderboards at 0.73 and 0.89 learned from clicks. Yours never sees a label.
