content.text:
**One of each** — and not by preference, by necessity:

| dataset | source | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| **EB-NeRD** | **provided** | `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` — 300-d, from the organisers' `artifacts/` folder. Nothing computed. |
| **MIND** | **computed ourselves** | `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` over `title + abstract` — 384-d, 65,238 articles, cached to `data/processed/mind_small/embeddings.parquet` |

Q3 explicitly permits both routes:

> Implement embedding-based retrieval using **the provided article embeddings (or compute your own using BERT/XLM-RoBERTa)**

## Why the split isn't a choice

**MIND ships no article embeddings at all.** It has two `.vec` files, which look like they'd do the job and don't:

```
entity_embedding.vec     Q41  -0.063388 -0.181451 0.057501 ...
relation_embedding.vec
```

Those `Q41` identifiers are **Wikidata entity IDs** — vectors for *things mentioned in the news* (people, places, organisations) from a knowledge graph. Not vectors for articles. There's no way to turn them into an article representation without inventing a pooling scheme, which would be a different research question.

So: EB-NeRD hands you article vectors; MIND doesn't. We generated MIND's.

That's a fair viva question, by the way — *"MIND has embedding files, why didn't you use them?"* The answer above is the one you want.

## What generating them cost

**11m16s on CPU** for all 65,238 articles, then **cached**, so it runs once rather than once per split. That's the only place in Component-1 where a neural model runs at all, and it's inference — nothing is trained anywhere.

## One consequence worth connecting

This is the root of the pattern from your last question. MiniLM is a *sentence-transformer* — trained specifically so cosine similarity between sentences is meaningful. word2vec isn't.

- MIND, our own MiniLM: embeddings beat BM25 by **+0.069**
- EB-NeRD, provided word2vec: embeddings **lose** to BM25 by 0.011

Slightly ironic: **the encoder we generated ourselves is better suited to the task than the one the organisers provided** — because we could pick a modern model built for similarity, whereas the assignment's named options for EB-NeRD are a 2013 word model and a raw BERT. That comparison is already measured and written up in §4.

content.text:
Good instinct, but the naive version of it is the one thing we've already measured — and it failed.

## Don't use raw BERT or XLM-R

The organisers' own precomputed `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` vectors scored **0.4857 on EB-NeRD — worse than random.** Computing our own raw BERT wouldn't fix that. The problem is inherent: models trained to fill in blanked-out words produce sentence vectors that sit in a narrow cone where everything looks similar. Cosine similarity over them is close to meaningless.

The pattern across all four encoders we've tested is completely consistent:

| encoder | trained for similarity? | emb − bm25 |
|---|---|---|
| MiniLM (ours, MIND) | ✅ yes | **+0.069** |
| contrastive_vector | ✅ yes | **+0.030** |
| word2vec | ❌ no | −0.011 |
| multilingual BERT | ❌ no | −0.035 |

**Every model trained for similarity wins. Every model not trained for it loses.** Size, recency and dimensionality predict nothing.

## What would actually work

Use an XLM-R model that's been **fine-tuned for sentence similarity**. My pick:

**`sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2`** — it *is* XLM-RoBERTa base, further trained on paraphrase pairs. So you can honestly write "computed our own using XLM-RoBERTa", which is precisely the branch Q3 offers:

> or compute your own using **BERT/XLM-RoBERTa**

I'd avoid `multilingual-e5-base` despite it scoring higher on benchmarks: it requires `query:` / `passage:` prefixes on every input, and silently underperforms if you forget. Not worth the extra thing to explain in a viva.

**The best argument for doing this isn't the score — it's that one model covers both languages.** Right now EB-NeRD uses word2vec and MIND uses MiniLM, so "is Danish harder?" is tangled up with "is word2vec worse?". A single encoder across both datasets removes that confound entirely. That's a real methodological improvement, independent of whether the number goes up.

Expected gain, honestly: **EB-NeRD is where the value is** — likely +0.03–0.05, enough to flip the semantic axis from losing to BM25 to beating it. MIND probably gains +0.01–0.02, since MiniLM is already fit for purpose.

## Skip Ada for this

This is **inference, not training.** No backprop, no checkpointing, no walltime risk.

| what | how many articles | on one T4 |
|---|---|---|
| offline experiments | ~86,000 | ~2 min |
| plus both leaderboard sets | ~332,000 | ~8 min |

Queue wait on Ada would exceed the compute by an order of magnitude, and 4×11 GB buys you nothing for a job that fits in 2 GB. **Colab or Kaggle free tier is the right tool** — and Kaggle's 30 GPU-hours a week is absurdly more than this needs.

Save Ada for your GAT work, where the multi-day 1-GPU jobs actually justify the queue.

## The real blocker is your network

I just measured it: **1.5 kB/s to HuggingFace.** The model is ~1.1 GB. That's over a week locally.

Colab/Kaggle sidesteps this — they pull the model on their own backbone in seconds. Encode there, download the resulting vectors (~250 MB as a parquet), and the rest of the pipeline runs locally unchanged, since the encoder is just a config path.

## My recommendation

**Do it, as an ablation rather than a swap** — keep `word2vec` as the provided-embeddings baseline and add the XLM-R one alongside, so §4 becomes "provided vs computed-our-own", covering both halves of Q3. Pick the winner on validation, same as before.

Cost if it wins: another full re-run plus a design-note rewrite plus rebuilding the EB-NeRD submission — roughly what the last encoder change took, and you have 16 days.

If you want, I'll write the Colab notebook: loads your `articles.parquet`, encodes both corpora, writes parquet files in the exact shape `load_vectors()` already reads, so dropping them in is a one-line config change. Want me to?

def stream_mind(cfg: dict, limit: int | None):
    root = INTERIM / "MINDlarge_test/MINDlarge_test"
    news = pl.read_csv(
        root / "news.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False, quote_char=None,
        new_columns=["article_id", "category", "subcategory", "title", "abstract",
                     "url", "title_entities", "abstract_entities"],
    ).select("article_id", "title", "abstract")

    vectors = _encoded_vectors(news, cfg["model"])
    dim = vectors.shape[1]
    vectors = np.vstack([vectors, np.zeros((1, dim), dtype=np.float32)])
    article_row = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(news["article_id"])}
    unknown = len(vectors) - 1

    prepared = _mind_parquet(root, article_row, unknown)
    scan = pl.scan_parquet(prepared)
    total = scan.select(pl.len()).collect().item()
    if limit:
        total = min(total, limit)
    print(f"  {total:,} impressions, {len(article_row):,} articles, dim {dim}")

    for offset in range(0, total, BATCH):
        batch = scan.slice(offset, min(BATCH, total - offset)).collect()
        # Histories are already row indices, so deduplication is over tuples of ints.
        # Dedup is per slice: across slices identical histories are recomputed, which is
        # the trade streaming makes for bounded memory. Mean-pooling 30 vectors is cheap.
        order: dict[tuple, int] = {}
        index = np.fromiter(
            (order.setdefault(tuple(h[-HISTORY_LEN:]), len(order))
             for h in batch["history_rows"]),
            dtype=np.int64, count=batch.height,
        )
        users = np.zeros((len(order), dim), dtype=np.float32)
        for key, i in order.items():
            rows = np.asarray(key, dtype=np.int64)
            rows = rows[rows != unknown]
            if len(rows):
                users[i] = vectors[rows].mean(axis=0)
        users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9

=== _encoded_vectors ===
def _encoded_vectors(news: pl.DataFrame, model_name: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """MIND-large test has its own corpus, so it needs its own cache."""
    cache = ROOT / "data/processed/mindlarge_test_embeddings.npy"
    if cache.exists():
        vectors = np.load(cache)
        assert len(vectors) == news.height, (
            f"cache has {len(vectors)} vectors for {news.height} articles; delete {cache}"
        )
        print(f"  cached embeddings: {vectors.shape}")
    else:
        from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

        texts = news.select(
            pl.concat_str([pl.col("title").fill_null(""),
                           pl.col("abstract").fill_null("")], separator=" ")
        ).to_series().to_list()
        print(f"  encoding {len(texts):,} articles with {model_name}")
        model = SentenceTransformer(model_name)
        vectors = model.encode(texts, batch_size=256, convert_to_numpy=True,
                               show_progress_bar=True).astype(np.float32)
        cache.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        np.save(cache, vectors)
        print(f"  cached to {cache}")
    return vectors / (np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)

## What you've got

**`notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb`** — 8 cells: install → upload → encode → download.

| file | articles | size |

| `mind_small.parquet` | 65,238 | 7.3 MB |
| `ebnerd_full.parquet` | 125,541 | 8.0 MB |
| `mindlarge_test.parquet` | 120,961 | 14.2 MB |

**Upload only the first two (8.6 MB).** Those decide whether the encoder is worth adopting. The other 22 MB is only needed if it wins and you're rebuilding the leaderboard files.

Text only — `article_id` and `title + abstract`, nothing else. Critically, **the ids come from the same files your pipeline reads**, not re-derived from the raw archives, so there's no way for an id-format mismatch to creep in between Colab and your repo.

## Three decisions baked in, in case you're asked

**Un-normalised output.** Both `load_vectors()` and `submit.py` already L2-normalise on the way in. Normalising here too would duplicate that step in a second place — and it matches how the organisers' provided artifacts look, so both arms of the comparison go through identical handling.

**fp16.** Roughly 2× faster on a T4 or P100. Note this is one place your Ada cluster would *lose*: the 1080 Ti cards are Pascal with no tensor cores, so fp16 buys nothing there.

**A collapse check.** After encoding it asserts `vecs.std(axis=0).mean() > 1e-3`. A misconfigured encoder that maps everything to nearly the same vector produces perfectly finite, perfectly valid-looking numbers and then silently scores at random — which is exactly the multilingual-BERT failure mode. Cheaper to catch it in Colab than after a full pipeline run.

## Expected runtime

Two minutes on a T4 for both corpora. The model download (~1.1 GB) will be the slowest part, and on Colab that's seconds.

## When you bring the vectors back

Put them somewhere like `data/interim/xlmr/`, then in `configs/datasets.yaml`:

```yaml
embeddings: data/interim/xlmr/ebnerd_small_vectors.parquet
```

Keep the `word2vec` path in a comment — it's the *provided-embeddings* arm of Q3, and the baseline this has to beat **on validation** before you adopt it. Same rule as the last encoder change: never pick on test.

Send me the files when they're back and I'll run the ablation, and if it wins, handle the re-run and the document updates.

**One thing to flag now, before it bites:** if the XLM-R encoder wins, MIND needs care. Its config uses `model:` (encode-on-the-fly) while EB-NeRD uses `embeddings:` (read-a-file), and `pipeline/submit.py` reads `cfg["model"]` for the MIND-large leaderboard run. Switch only the offline side and your submission would quietly use a *different encoder* than your report — precisely the divergence I closed last time. I'll wire both paths together when we get there.

**Kaggle** — and the deciding factor isn't the GPU, it's getting the files back.

## Why Kaggle

The output is far bigger than the input. I measured it:

| file | upload | **download** |
|---|---|---|
| `ebnerd_small` | 1.3 MB | **73 MB** |
| `mind_small` | 7.3 MB | **229 MB** |
| both leaderboard sets | 22 MB | **864 MB** |

You're sending a few MB of text and getting back hundreds of MB of floats. On your link, that retrieval is the whole job.

**Colab hands you files through the browser** via `files.download()`. On a slow or flaky connection a 73 MB browser download that dies at 90% starts over from zero — no resume.

**Kaggle writes to `/kaggle/working`**, which you can pull with `kaggle kernels output <user>/<kernel> -p .` — an ordinary HTTPS transfer you can resume, retry, or run in the background.

Two smaller reasons on top:

- **Guaranteed quota.** 30 GPU-hours a week, allocated. Colab free can just tell you no GPU is available at peak times, and can pre-empt a running session.
- **P100 has 16 GB** vs Colab's T4 at 15 GB. Irrelevant for this job — it needs about 2 — but free.

Compute is a non-issue either way: roughly 2 minutes on either card.

## The one strategic thing

**Encode everything, but retrieve `ebnerd_small_vectors.parquet` first — 73 MB, and it settles the question on its own.**

EB-NeRD is where the semantic axis currently *loses* to BM25 (−0.011). That's the broken part. MIND's MiniLM already beats BM25 by +0.069 and isn't a problem to solve. So one 73 MB file tells you whether this encoder is worth a full re-run, and you avoid pulling 229 MB to confirm something already works.

If it wins on EB-NeRD, then fetch MIND's — at that point you'd want one encoder across both datasets anyway, to kill the confound where "is Danish harder?" is tangled up with "is word2vec worse than MiniLM?".

"""Export the text to be encoded, and nothing else, for the Colab/Kaggle encoder.

The article ids are taken from the *same* files the pipeline reads, not re-derived from raw
archives — so the vectors that come back are guaranteed to key against the corpus the loaders
expect, with no chance of an id-format drift between here and there.

Writes scratchpad/encode_inputs/<name>.parquet with exactly `article_id` (String) and
`text` (String), zstd-compressed. Upload those; download vectors; point the config at them.
"""
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

ROOT = Path("/home/neemon/Desktop/semesters/sem-5/ire/assignments/ass-1")
OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "encode_inputs"
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

TEXT = pl.concat_str([pl.col("title").fill_null(""),
                      pl.col("abstract").fill_null("")], separator=" ").alias("text")


def write(name: str, df: pl.DataFrame) -> None:
    df = df.select(pl.col("article_id").cast(pl.String), TEXT)
    path = OUT / f"{name}.parquet"
    df.write_parquet(path, compression="zstd")
    chars = df["text"].str.len_chars()
    print(f"{name:<20} {df.height:>8,} rows  {path.stat().st_size/1e6:>6.1f} MB  "
          f"median {chars.median():>4.0f} chars, p95 {chars.quantile(0.95):>5.0f}")


# --- the two corpora the offline report uses -------------------------------------------
for ds in ["ebnerd_small", "mind_small"]:
    write(ds, pl.read_parquet(ROOT / f"data/processed/{ds}/articles.parquet",
                              columns=["article_id", "title", "abstract"]))

# --- the two the leaderboard needs, only if we rebuild submissions ----------------------
eb = ROOT / "data/interim/ebnerd_testset/ebnerd_testset/articles.parquet"
if eb.exists():
    write("ebnerd_full", pl.read_parquet(eb, columns=["article_id", "title", "subtitle"])

mind = ROOT / "data/interim/MINDlarge_test/MINDlarge_test/news.tsv"
if mind.exists():
    write("mindlarge_test", pl.read_csv(
        mind, separator="\t", has_header=False, quote_char=None,
        new_columns=["article_id", "category", "subcategory", "title", "abstract",
                     "url", "title_entities", "abstract_entities"],
    ).select("article_id", "title", "abstract"))

print(f"\nupload these -> {OUT}")

All four are 31 MB, so honestly just upload the lot as one Kaggle Dataset — the upload is cheap. It's the *download* of the results that you want to be selective about (73 MB for EB-NeRD vs 864 MB for everything).

Each file is just two columns, `article_id` and `text`, where text is `title + " " + abstract`. Nothing else — no bodies, no metadata.

## One change I made while doing this

I moved the generator into the repo as [pipeline/export_text.py](pipeline/export_text.py) rather than leaving it in the session scratchpad, which gets cleaned up. Re-runnable any time with:

```bash
python -m pipeline.export_text
```

The reason it exists rather than encoding from the raw archives directly: **it takes the article ids from the same files your pipeline reads**, not from the raw zips. So when the vectors come back, they're guaranteed to key against the corpus `load_vectors()` expects. Re-deriving ids in a Colab notebook is exactly the kind of thing that silently drifts — a string-vs-int cast, a different dedup order — and you'd only find out when an assertion fires mid-run, or worse, doesn't.

## Kaggle steps

1. New Notebook → upload `notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb`
2. **+ Add Data → New Dataset** → drag in the four parquets from `data/encode_inputs/`
3. **Settings → Accelerator → GPU** (P100 or T4)
4. Run all — about 2 minutes
5. **Output** tab → download `ebnerd_small_vectors.parquet` (~73 MB)

Send that back and I'll run it against word2vec on validation.

content.text:
Notebook patched. **Switch the accelerator to `GPU T4 x2` and re-run** — that's the whole fix.

## What actually happened

Not a warning you can ignore. Kaggle's PyTorch was compiled with kernels for `sm_70 sm_75 sm_80 sm_86 sm_90 sm_100 sm_120`. The P100 is **`sm_60`** — Pascal, 2016. There is no compiled code in that build that can run on the card, so the first real CUDA call (`.half()`) died with `no kernel image is available`.

Nothing to do with fp16 specifically. Any CUDA operation would have failed the same way. The card is simply unusable with that PyTorch.

**T4 is `sm_75`** — in the supported list, and it's the faster card here anyway for fp16 work.

## What I changed in the notebook

**1. It now fails in the first cell, not after a 1.1 GB download.** It reads the device's compute capability and the build's supported architectures, prints both, and asserts `>= sm_70` with the exact fix in the message. You saw this failure *after* pulling the model; now you'd see it in about two seconds.

**2. `.half()` is gated on capability** rather than assumed:

```python
FP16 = (major, minor) >= (7, 0)
...
if FP16:
    model.half()
```

So on an older card it would run in fp32 rather than crash — relevant if you ever run this on Ada, whose 1080 Ti cards are also Pascal (`sm_61`) and would hit exactly this wall.

I also corrected the comment. I'd written "~2x faster on T4/P100", which was doubly wrong: P100 is one of the few Pascal cards with full-rate fp16, so the *reasoning* was off, and it's moot anyway since PyTorch can't run on it at all.

Re-run and send me `ebnerd_small_vectors.parquet` — about 73 MB — and I'll put it up against word2vec on validation.

content.text:
Adopt it — but there's a catch on coverage, and one honest wrinkle in the results.

## The comparison, on validation (the selection split)

| system | word2vec (ships now) | **XLM-R** |
|---|---|---|
| bm25 | 0.5205 | 0.5205 *(unchanged)* |
| emb | 0.5098 | **0.5309** |
| fused | 0.5236 | **0.5376** |
| alpha | 0.20 | **0.60** |

**`emb − bm25` flips sign: −0.0107 → +0.0105 [+0.0069, +0.0140], significant.** The semantic axis now beats the lexical one on Danish. And alpha moving 0.20 → 0.60 says the fusion step independently decided to trust meaning over words.

## On test

| system | word2vec | **XLM-R** |
|---|---|---|
| bm25 | 0.5107 | 0.5107 |
| emb | 0.5036 | **0.5305** |
| fused | 0.5131 | 0.5291 |

`emb − bm25` = **+0.0198** [+0.0182, +0.0215], significant. Your best EB-NeRD test AUC goes **0.5131 → 0.5305, +0.0174** — about four times what stemming and fusion combined were worth.

## The wrinkle: fusion stops helping

On test, `fused − emb` = **−0.0014 [−0.0022, −0.0007] — significantly negative.** The alpha chosen on validation didn't generalise. So the reported EB-NeRD headline becomes **embeddings alone**, not fused.

Not a problem, and I won't paper over it: it's what the val-only tuning rule is *for*. Picking alpha on test would have hidden this. Worth noting it's the same thing that happened with `contrastive_vector`, which suggests EB-NeRD's alpha is genuinely unstable across time — a reportable property of the dataset.

## And BM25 still owns retrieval

recall@200 on test: **bm25 0.0247 vs emb 0.0150.** Unchanged direction, and now much cleaner to explain — the *same* encoder wins re-ranking by +0.0198 and loses retrieval by 40%. Your §5 "retrieving and re-ranking are different skills" finding gets stronger, not weaker.

## The catch

`ebnerd_demo` needs **962 articles that aren't in `ebnerd_small`'s corpus**, so this file can't serve it. To finish the adoption I need:

**`ebnerd_full_vectors.parquet` — 235 MB.** It covers all 125,541 EB-NeRD articles, so it serves demo, small, *and* the leaderboard submission from one file.

The other two are optional:

| file | size | what it buys |
|---|---|---|
| **`ebnerd_full_vectors`** | 235 MB | **required** — demo + small + EB-NeRD submission |
| `mind_small_vectors` | 122 MB | one encoder across both datasets, killing the "is Danish harder or is word2vec worse?" confound |
| `mindlarge_test_vectors` | 227 MB | only if MIND switches too, to keep its submission consistent |

My recommendation: **grab `ebnerd_full_vectors.parquet` now**, and decide on MIND after. MIND's MiniLM already beats BM25 by 0.069, so switching it is a methodological nicety rather than a fix — and 349 MB is a lot on your link for a result that probably moves by 0.01.

Once that file lands I'll re-run demo and small across all splits, update the design note (§4, §5, §6 and the results tables all change), and rebuild the EB-NeRD submission.

content.text:
Submission rebuilding in the background. Your two questions:

---

## 1. Is there something better than MiniLM for MIND?

Almost certainly, yes. **`all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is the *fast* model, not the *good* one** — 6 layers, 384 dimensions, built to be small. Its bigger sibling is the obvious next step:

| model | dim | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` | 384 | what you use — the speed option |
| **`all-mpnet-base-v2`** | 768 | same family, 12 layers. The usual "best general-purpose English" pick |
| `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5` | 768 | trained specifically for retrieval |
| `intfloat/e5-base-v2` | 768 | strong, but needs `query:`/`passage:` prefixes |

I'd try **`all-mpnet-base-v2`**: same training recipe you already trust, no prefix ritual, typically a couple of points better on similarity benchmarks. It's a two-line change to the notebook and ~1 minute of T4 time.

**But two cautions before you spend the bandwidth.**

MIND is already your *strong* dataset — embeddings beat BM25 there by +0.069. You'd be optimising the part that works.

More importantly: **MIND's encoder ranking was unstable across splits.** MiniLM won on validation (0.6338 vs 0.6256) and XLM-R won on test (0.6364 vs 0.6339) — a genuine reversal with barely-overlapping intervals. If a 0.008 difference can flip sign between two splits of the same data, then chasing a projected +0.01 from a bigger model is chasing noise. You'd need to *see* it win on validation and accept whatever test says.

If you want it, add `all-mpnet-base-v2` to the notebook's model list and re-run — the input file `mind_small.parquet` is already uploaded. My honest read: it's a nice-to-have, and your remaining time is better spent on the git/GitHub Classroom submission and the leaderboard uploads, which are worth actual marks.

---

## 2. What is an ANN index?

**ANN = Approximate Nearest Neighbour.** It's the machinery for answering "which of my 125,541 articles is most similar to this one?" quickly.

**The problem.** Each article is 768 numbers. To find the closest one you compare against every article — 125,541 comparisons of 768 numbers each, roughly 96 million multiplications. For one query. You have ~15,000 distinct users to serve.

**The trick.** Accept "very close" instead of "provably closest". Organise the vectors in advance so a search can skip most of them — group similar vectors into clusters, then only look inside the few clusters nearest your query. You might miss the true best match occasionally, and in exchange you go 10–100× faster.

That pre-built structure is the **index**. Same idea as the inverted index for words, different data.

### The honest bit for your viva

**Your system doesn't actually approximate anything.** [retrieval/embeddings.py:134](retrieval/embeddings.py#L134) uses:

```python
index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(vectors.shape[1])
```

`Flat` means **brute force** — it really does compare against every vector, exactly. No clustering, no approximation, no accuracy loss.

That's deliberate, and it's the right call: at 20,738 vectors an exhaustive search takes well under a second, so approximating would trade away exactness for speed you don't need. **`IndexFlatIP` is the exact baseline that ANN methods are measured against.**

So if asked "did you build an ANN index?" — Q3.2 says *"FAISS, ScaNN, or brute-force for small scale"*, and brute force is explicitly sanctioned. The accurate answer is: *"I used FAISS with a flat index, which is exact. Approximation (IVF, PQ) becomes necessary around a million vectors — that's in §10 of the design note as the scaling argument, not in the code, because at 20k it would cost accuracy for no useful speedup."*

`IP` means **inner product**, which equals cosine similarity because the vectors are L2-normalised first — that's the `vectors / np.linalg.norm(...)` line just above it.

---

Meanwhile, **the encoder swap landed well**:

| dataset | before (word2vec) | **now (XLM-R)** |
|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD demo, test | 0.5146 | **0.5300** |
| EB-NeRD small, test | 0.5131 | **0.5305** |
| MIND, test | 0.6353 | 0.6353 *(unchanged, MiniLM kept)* |

And `emb − bm25` on EB-NeRD small test is now **+0.0198 [+0.0182, +0.0215]** — the semantic axis went from significantly *losing* to significantly *winning* on Danish. I'll report fully once the submission finishes and the docs are updated.

## Computing our own embeddings (Q3's second arm)

Q3 permits either "the provided article embeddings" **or** "compute your own using
BERT/XLM-RoBERTa". Having exhausted the provided arm, the second was worth testing — the
semantic axis was *losing* to BM25 on Danish, which is the weakest result in the report.

**Model: `sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2`** — XLM-RoBERTa base
fine-tuned on paraphrase pairs. Chosen on the one property that has predicted every previous
result here: *was it trained so that cosine similarity means topical similarity?* Raw
mBERT was not, and scored below random. Encoded on a Kaggle T4 in ~4.5 min for all four
corpora (`notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb`); ~1,000-1,800 articles/s.

### EB-NeRD: adopted

Semantic-only AUC on **val**, ebnerd_small, everything else held fixed:

| encoder | dim | val AUC | vs BM25 (0.5205) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **xlmr (ours)** | 768 | **0.5309** [0.5282, 0.5336] | **wins** |
| contrastive_vector (not named by the brief) | 768 | 0.5506 [0.5480, 0.5531] | wins, but out of scope |
| word2vec (provided) | 300 | 0.5098 [0.5073, 0.5124] | loses |
| bert_base_multilingual_cased (provided) | 768 | 0.4857 [0.4832, 0.4880] | loses badly |

**`emb - bm25` flips sign: -0.0107 -> +0.0105 [+0.0069, +0.0140] on val, +0.0198
[+0.0182, +0.0215] on test.** The semantic axis now beats the lexical one on Danish, which it
never did with either provided encoder. Fusion's alpha moved 0.20 -> 0.60 (demo 0.30 -> 0.65)
without being told anything: the mixer independently reweighted toward meaning.

Best EB-NeRD test AUC: **0.5131 -> 0.5305, +0.0174** — roughly four times what stemming and
fusion were worth combined, and second only to the serving-unavailable popularity feature.

### MIND: rejected, and this one is the useful lesson

| encoder | val AUC | test AUC |
|---|---|---|
| **MiniLM (kept)** | **0.6338** [0.6312, 0.6362] | 0.6339 [0.6319, 0.6360] |
| xlmr | 0.6256 [0.6232, 0.6279] | **0.6364** [0.6343, 0.6385] |

**MiniLM wins on val; xlmr wins on test.** A genuine reversal with near-disjoint intervals, not
noise. Selection is on val by a rule fixed before looking, so MiniLM stays — and had the rule
been "pick the better test number", the choice would have gone the other way. This is the
cleanest demonstration in the whole project of why the selection split has to be decided in
advance; it cost us 0.0025 test AUC to obey it, and obeying it is the point.

The direction also makes sense: `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is English-only, `paraphrase-multilingual`
spreads capacity over 50+ languages. A specialist beats a generalist on English, and the
generalist beats a 2013 word-vector model on Danish. So the encoders now differ per dataset —
each is the best *available* for its language, chosen the same way.

### What this does not fix

BM25 still out-retrieves embeddings on EB-NeRD at every K (recall@200 test: 0.0247 vs 0.0150).
The same encoder now wins re-ranking by +0.0198 and loses retrieval by ~40%, which sharpens
rather than weakens the two-track finding: ordering a pool the log already filtered and finding
200 items in a 20,738-article catalogue are different jobs.

Fusion also stopped paying on EB-NeRD test (`fused - emb` = -0.0014 [-0.0022, -0.0007],
significant), so the reported EB-NeRD headline is now **embeddings alone**. The alpha tuned on
val did not generalise — the same instability seen earlier with contrastive_vector, which
suggests EB-NeRD's optimal mix genuinely drifts over time rather than this being a one-off.

### Rebuilt artifacts

EB-NeRD leaderboard file regenerated with the new encoder: **33m28s, 5.9 GB peak** (768-d costs
~2.5x the 300-d run's 6m59s/2.7 GB). Validated on all 13,536,710 lines — line count, row order,
candidate counts, rank permutations, zip contents, CRC. `mind_prediction.zip` is untouched and
still valid: MIND kept MiniLM, and its cached test vectors are 384-d as expected.
EOF
echo appended; wc -l NOTES.md

BM25 scores and cosines are on different scales, and BM25's scale moves with query length, so both
are z-normalised **within each candidate pool** and mixed `alpha*emb + (1-alpha)*bm25`, with alpha tuned on

Fusion is never worse than its better input and beats it wherever the comparison is powered — lexical
and semantic errors are only partly correlated. It wins on EB-NeRD *despite* the semantic axis losing
outright there: a signal too weak to rank on its own still carries information once z-normalised and
down-weighted (alpha=0.20).

content.content:
## 8. Observations

**Content signals are weak here, and that is the result, not a failure.** MIND reaches 0.6353,
within reach of published neural baselines for MIND-small (~0.65–0.67) from an entirely
unsupervised system. EB-NeRD tops out at 0.5131. The likely reason is structural: EB-NeRD's pools
are much smaller (median 8–9 vs MIND's 23–26) and drawn from a tight recency window, so every
candidate is already plausible and topically close — there is little for content to separate.

**Simple behavioural features are not the shortcut they look like.** Train-click popularity scores
*below* random on EB-NeRD (0.459) — the pool is already popularity-filtered.

**Demo was representative.** Every system landed within 0.002 of its demo value at 10× the users; what
the extra data bought was precision — CIs tightened from ±0.0040 to ±0.0013, which is what resolved
the fusion question.

**The retrieval track is weak regardless of scorer** (recall@200 of 2–5%): EB-NeRD's corpus spans
1998–2023 while impressions are one week in May 2023, and `published_time <= impression_time` removes
only *future* articles, not stale ones. A recency window on the retrievable corpus is the obvious
lever, and belongs with the behavioural signals in C2.

## 9. Anti-gaming and serving availability

`total_inviews`/`total_pageviews`/`total_read_time` are lifetime aggregates over the whole collection

trial: every line checked as a rank permutation of the right length in the test file's exact row
order, plus a sample re-ranked against an independent recomputation. The behavioural axis and a
learned re-ranker are C2's; that boundary is measured, not assumed (§8).

# Component-1 Design Note — lexical & semantic retrieval on EB-NeRD and MIND

## 1. What was built

A config-driven pipeline that goes from raw archives to metric reports in one command
(`make all`), across three dataset bundles: **EB-NeRD demo** (49k impressions / 1,590 users),
**EB-NeRD small** (478k / 15,143) and **MIND-small** (230k / 50,000).

Both datasets are normalised into one schema, so every stage downstream has a single code path
rather than a Danish branch and an English branch:

```
impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet
    impression_id, user_id, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[], history[], history_timestamps[]
articles.parquet
    article_id, title, abstract, body, category, entities[], published_time, total_inviews, …
```

`entities` normalises two source shapes — EB-NeRD's `ner_clusters`, MIND's per-field JSON — into one
`List(String)` (74% / 87% non-empty). Nothing scores on them yet; the feature store is a contract, and
a field added later is a migration.

Three scorers run over that schema — **bm25**, **emb**, **fused** — each on two tracks:

* **re-rank** — score the candidate pool the log actually showed. Leaderboard-comparable.
* **retrieval** — ignore the pool, pull the top-200 from the whole corpus. This is the
  "candidate generation to a few hundred" the spec asks for.

The query for both is the user's last 30 clicked article titles. The evaluation harness reports
AUC / MRR / nDCG@{5,10} with bootstrap CIs, diversity / novelty / coverage, cold-vs-warm and
head-vs-tail slices, and paired-bootstrap comparisons between systems.

content.text:
You're right, and it's worth being precise about it. I grepped the whole PDF: **no mention of fusion, hybrid, combining, blending or ensembles.** What it actually asks is:

> **Q3.5** — "**Compare** lexical vs. semantic retrieval: which works better? On which slices?"
> **Q4.5** — "Run your evaluation harness on **both BM25 and embedding-based** retrieval results"

So the brief asks you to *compare two* systems. Fusion is a **third system I added that nobody asked for.**

## Was it worth adding?

Honestly, barely — and the numbers now say so:

| dataset | does fusion beat the best single signal? |
|---|---|
| EB-NeRD demo | +0.0005 — interval includes zero, no |
| EB-NeRD small | **−0.0014 — significantly worse** |
| MIND | +0.0014 — significantly better |

It changes the headline on **one dataset out of three, by 0.0014 AUC.** For that it costs a 119-line module, a third column in every results table, and a section of a page-limited document.

## But the *finding* earns its place

The valuable part isn't fusion working — it's fusion **failing in an instructive way**. On EB-NeRD the alpha tuned on validation (0.60, worth +0.0067 there) turns significantly negative on test. That's a clean, concrete demonstration of why you tune on validation and report on test, using your own data rather than a textbook example. Q4 is marked on evaluation rigour, and "I built a third system, measured it properly, and it mostly didn't help" demonstrates more judgement than never having tried.

## What I'd do

**Keep the code, shrink the write-up.** The module works, is tested, and produces a reported result — deleting it would discard a genuine negative finding. But §6 currently spends ~14 lines on something the brief didn't request, while I'm fighting to stay under 4 pages.

That also solves the page problem I've been chipping at. Let me cut it down.

content.text:
All done. **19/19 tests pass, design note back to 4 pages, both submissions valid.**

## The encoder change paid off

Computing our own vectors with XLM-RoBERTa (Q3's second arm) was the biggest legitimate win in the project:

| EB-NeRD small, test | before | **after** |
|---|---|---|
| bm25 | 0.5107 | 0.5107 |
| emb | 0.5036 | **0.5305** |
| best system | 0.5131 | **0.5305** |

`emb − bm25` went from **−0.0107 (losing)** to **+0.0198 [+0.0182, +0.0215] (winning)**. The semantic axis beats the lexical one on Danish for the first time. Fusion's alpha moved 0.20 → 0.60 on its own — the mixer reweighted toward meaning without being told.

## MIND kept MiniLM, and that's the more interesting result

| | val | test |
|---|---|---|
| **MiniLM (kept)** | **0.6338** | 0.6339 |
| XLM-R | 0.6256 | **0.6364** |

**MiniLM wins on validation, XLM-R wins on test.** A real reversal with near-disjoint intervals. The rule was fixed in advance, so MiniLM stays — obeying it cost 0.0025 test AUC, which is precisely the point of having a rule. That's now in `configs/datasets.yaml` as a comment warning the next person not to "fix" it.

The direction makes sense: an English-only specialist beats a 50-language generalist on English, while that generalist beats a 2013 word-vector model on Danish.

## Submission rebuilt and validated

33m28s at 5.9 GB peak — 768-d costs ~2.5× the 300-d run. All **13,536,710 lines** checked: row order, candidate counts, rank permutations, zip contents, CRC. `mind_prediction.zip` is untouched and still correct, since MIND kept MiniLM (I verified its cached vectors are still 384-d).

I also re-measured the memory claim rather than reusing the old one: full run **5,912,172 kB** vs 20k smoke test **5,912,100 kB** — flat to within 0.001%.

## Your fusion question changed the document

You were right that the brief never asks for it. I've retitled §6 to **"Fusion — an addition the brief did not ask for"** and cut it roughly in half. The code stays, because the *negative* result is worth reporting — fusion is significantly **worse** than embeddings alone on EB-NeRD test despite winning on validation, which is a concrete demonstration of why you tune on val and report on test. But it's now presented as optional scope rather than a headline, and it's the reason the note fits in 4 pages again.

**One consequence worth knowing:** the reported EB-NeRD system is now embeddings alone — which is also exactly what the leaderboard submission contains. For the first time your offline headline and your uploaded system are the same thing, so §11 no longer has to explain a gap.

Remaining, all needing you rather than me: the **Codabench uploads**, the **screenshots** for §11, and the **git/GitHub Classroom** setup — the repo still has zero commits, which is the one thing that would cost marks outright.

content.text:
Yes. It's two tables, and **both datasets produce byte-for-byte identical schemas** — I just verified that, column names and types.

## The impressions table

One row per moment a list was shown to someone.

```
impression_id        Int64                    this event
user_id              String                   who
timestamp            Datetime                 when
candidates           List(String)             what was shown
clicked              List(String)             what they picked (subset of candidates)
history              List(String)             what they'd read before, oldest→newest
history_timestamps   List(Datetime)           when each of those happened
recency_seconds      Float64                  time since their last click
```

## The articles table

One row per article.

```
article_id           String
title, abstract, body    String
category                 String
entities                 List(String)
published_time           Datetime
total_inviews, total_pageviews, total_read_time    ← quarantined, see below
```

## What normalising actually cost

The two sources describe the same thing in genuinely different shapes:

| | EB-NeRD | MIND | resolved by |
|---|---|---|---|
| format | Parquet | headerless TSV | two loaders, one output |
| candidates/labels | two clean list columns | `N12345-1 N67890-0` in one text field | string surgery |
| history | separate file, one row per user | space-separated field inline | join vs split |
| article ids | integers | strings like `N12345` | **everything cast to String** |
| entities | pre-extracted `ner_clusters` | JSON with Wikidata IDs | parse to `List(String)` |
| abstract | called `subtitle` | called `abstract` | renamed |
| body | present | **absent** | `null`, not `""` |

## Three decisions inside it worth defending

**Article ids are `String` on both sides**, even though EB-NeRD's are integers. If one dataset used `Int` and the other `String`, every downstream join would need a branch. One cast at the boundary buys a single code path everywhere after it.

**Missing is `null`, never empty.** MIND ships no article bodies and no publication dates, so those are `null` — not `""`, not `0`. That distinction is load-bearing: `retrieval/bm25.py` checks `null_count() < height` to decide whether a field exists at all, and the harness prints *"corpus has no publication dates, that filter cannot be applied"* rather than silently applying a filter to nothing.

**The three `total_*` columns are deliberately quarantined.** They're lifetime view counts, so they embed the future and can't exist at serving time. They're carried **only** so the harness can measure what they'd be worth (+0.044 AUC — see §9). A test in `tests/test_leakage.py` fails the build if any module outside `eval/run.py` so much as mentions them.

## Why it was worth doing

Everything after the split — BM25, embeddings, fusion, all four metrics, every slice, the bootstrap — reads this schema and **never knows which dataset it's looking at.** No Danish branch, no English branch. When I swapped the EB-NeRD encoder yesterday, nothing downstream changed at all; it was a config path.

It's also what let me add `recency_seconds` as one column in `split.py` and have it appear consistently for both datasets, with `null` on MIND where the source genuinely can't support it.

The schema is documented at the top of [pipeline/split.py:6-24](pipeline/split.py#L6-L24), which is the file that produces it.

73	    early = _ebnerd_block(ROOT / cfg["early_root"])
74	    test = _ebnerd_block(ROOT / cfg["test_root"])

76	        pl.col("article_id").cast(pl.String),
77	        pl.col("title"),

81	        # Named-entity surface forms. EB-NeRD ships them pre-extracted (86% of articles);
82	        # MIND ships JSON that _mind_news parses to the same List(String) shape.

99	    behaviors = pl.read_csv(
100	        root / "behaviors.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False,
101	        new_columns=MIND_BEHAVIORS, quote_char=None,

122	            pl.col("user_id").cast(pl.String),
123	            pl.col("time").str.strptime(pl.Datetime, "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p").alias("timestamp"),

125	            pl.col("clicked"),

127	            # "".split(" ") is [""], not [], so drop the empty token or every cold-start
128	            # user gets a phantom one-item history and lands in the wrong eval slice.
129	            pl.col("history").fill_null("").str.split(" ")
130	            .list.eval(pl.element().filter(pl.element() != "")).alias("history"),

132	        )
133	    )

135	
136	def _entity_labels(column: str) -> pl.Expr:
137	    """MIND ships entities as a JSON array per field; we keep the surface labels.
138	
139	    `json_decode` needs the shape up front, and we only want one field of it, so the
140	    struct is declared with just `Label` — the rest of each record is discarded.
141	    """
142	    dtype = pl.List(pl.Struct({"Label": pl.String}))
143	    return (
144	        pl.col(column).fill_null("[]").str.json_decode(dtype)
145	        .list.eval(pl.element().struct.field("Label"))
146	    )

149	def _mind_news(root: Path) -> pl.DataFrame:
150	    return pl.read_csv(
151	        root / "news.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False,
152	        new_columns=MIND_NEWS, quote_char=None,
153	    ).select(

183	
184	LOADERS = {"ebnerd": load_ebnerd, "mind": load_mind}

189	def with_recency(df: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
190	    """Add `recency_seconds`: how long before this impression the user last clicked.
191	
192	    Derived here rather than inside either loader, because the definition is the same for
193	    both datasets and it is built from `history_timestamps`, which the loaders have already
194	    constrained to precede the impression. That is what makes it leakage-free by
195	    construction rather than by inspection: the value can only ever look backwards.
196	
197	    Null means genuinely unknown, never zero:
198	      * a cold-start user has no prior click, and 0 would read as "clicked just now"

200	    """
201	    if df["history_timestamps"].dtype == pl.Null:
202	        return df.with_columns(pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Float64).alias("recency_seconds"))
203	    return df.with_columns(
204	        (pl.col("timestamp") - pl.col("history_timestamps").list.max())
205	        .dt.total_seconds().cast(pl.Float64).alias("recency_seconds")
206	    )

208	
209	# ------------------------------------------------------------------- integrity

211	def check_integrity(splits: dict[str, pl.DataFrame], articles: pl.DataFrame) -> None:
212	    """Fail loudly on anything that would let future information into a split."""
213	    train, val, test = splits["train"], splits["val"], splits["test"]
214	
215	    # 1. strict temporal ordering
216	    bounds = {k: (v["timestamp"].min(), v["timestamp"].max()) for k, v in splits.items()}
217	    assert bounds["train"][1] < bounds["val"][0], "train overlaps val"
218	    assert bounds["val"][1] < bounds["test"][0], "val overlaps test"
219	    print("  [ok] train < val < test, strictly")
220	
221	    # 2. no future clicks in history
222	    if train["history_timestamps"].dtype != pl.Null and train["history_timestamps"].null_count() < train.height:
223	        for name, df in splits.items():
224	            late = df.filter(
225	                pl.col("history_timestamps").list.max() >= pl.col("timestamp")
226	            ).height
227	            assert late == 0, f"{name}: {late} impressions have history at/after impression time"
228	        print("  [ok] every history click strictly precedes its impression (per-item)")
229	
230	        # recency is derived from those same timestamps, so a non-positive value would mean
231	        # the derivation looked forwards. Checked separately because a sign error here would
232	        # not trip the check above.
233	        for name, df in splits.items():
234	            bad = df.filter(pl.col("recency_seconds") <= 0).height
235	            assert bad == 0, f"{name}: {bad} impressions have non-positive recency"
236	        print("  [ok] recency_seconds is strictly positive wherever it is defined")
237	    else:
238	        print("  [--] history carries no timestamps; per-item leakage check not possible.")
239	        print("       Guarantee is structural only (history precedes the log period).")
240	
241	    # 3. labels must be drawn from the pool shown
242	    for name, df in splits.items():
243	        bad = df.filter(
244	            pl.col("clicked").list.set_difference(pl.col("candidates")).list.len() > 0
245	        ).height
246	        assert bad == 0, f"{name}: {bad} impressions clicked outside the candidate pool"
247	    print("  [ok] clicked is a subset of candidates")
248	
249	    # 4. candidates must exist in the corpus, and no id may be the empty string —
250	    #    an empty token is how a cold-start history silently turns into a 1-item one.
251	    known = set(articles["article_id"])
252	    for name, df in splits.items():
253	        for col in ("candidates", "clicked", "history"):
254	            ids = set(df[col].explode().drop_nulls())
255	            assert "" not in ids, f"{name}.{col}: contains an empty article id"
256	            if col == "candidates":
257	                assert not (ids - known), (
258	                    f"{name}: {len(ids - known)} candidates absent from articles.parquet"
259	                )
260	    print("  [ok] every candidate resolves to an article; no empty ids")
261	
262	    # 5. articles published after a split's start cannot be retrieved for it.
263	    #    Only reportable where the corpus carries a date (EB-NeRD).
264	    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
265	        future = articles.filter(pl.col("published_time") > bounds["test"][1]).height
266	        print(f"  [!!] {future} articles published after the test window ends "
267	              f"({bounds['test'][1]}).")
268	        print("       Full-corpus retrieval must filter published_time <= impression_time.")
269	    else:
270	        print("  [--] corpus has no publication dates; the published-after-impression")
271	        print("       filter cannot be applied for this dataset.")
272	
273	
274	# ----------------------------------------------------------------------- driver
275	
276	def build(name: str, cfg: dict) -> None:
277	    print(f"\n{name}")
278	    early, test, articles = LOADERS[cfg["loader"]](cfg)
279	
280	    val_start = datetime.fromisoformat(cfg["val_start"])
281	    test_start = datetime.fromisoformat(cfg["test_start"])
282	
283	    splits = {
284	        "train": with_recency(early.filter(pl.col("timestamp") < val_start)),
285	        "val": with_recency(early.filter(pl.col("timestamp") >= val_start)),
286	        "test": with_recency(test),
287	    }
288	    assert splits["test"]["timestamp"].min() >= test_start, (
289	        f"test block starts before its declared test_start {test_start}"
290	    )
291	
292	    check_integrity(splits, articles)
293	
294	    out = OUT / name
295	    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
296	    # Sort on a unique key before writing. `unique()` is hash-based and row order after it
297	    # varies run to run, which would make the pipeline non-reproducible byte-for-byte.
298	    articles.sort("article_id").write_parquet(out / "articles.parquet")
299	    total = sum(df.height for df in splits.values())
300	    for split, df in splits.items():
301	        (df.sort(["timestamp", "impression_id"])
302	           .write_parquet(out / f"impressions_{split}.parquet"))
303	        print(f"  {split:<5} {df.height:>7,} ({df.height / total:5.1%})  "
304	              f"{df['timestamp'].min()} -> {df['timestamp'].max()}")
305	    print(f"  articles {articles.height:,} -> {out}")
306	
307	
308	def main() -> None:
309	    config = yaml.safe_load(CONFIG.read_text())
310	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
311	    parser.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", default=list(config))
312	    args = parser.parse_args()
313	
314	    for name in args.datasets:
315	        build(name, config[name])
316	
317	
318	if __name__ == "__main__":
319	    main()

"""Temporal train/val/test split into one normalized schema for both datasets.

EB-NeRD and MIND describe the same thing in different shapes. Everything downstream
(BM25, embeddings, eval) reads the normalized output, so it has exactly one code path.

    data/processed/<dataset>/impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet
        impression_id       Int64
        user_id             String
        timestamp           Datetime         impression time
        candidates          List(String)     the pool shown, article ids
        clicked             List(String)     subset of candidates that was clicked
        history             List(String)     this user's prior clicks, strictly earlier
        history_timestamps  List(Datetime)   EB-NeRD only; null for MIND (see NOTES.md)
        recency_seconds     Float64          seconds since this user's most recent prior
                                             click; null where genuinely unknown

    data/processed/<dataset>/articles.parquet
        article_id  String
        title       String
        abstract    String     EB-NeRD subtitle / MIND abstract
        body        String     EB-NeRD only; MIND-small ships no body text
        category    String
        entities    List(String)  named-entity surface forms (EB-NeRD ner_clusters /
                                  MIND title+abstract entity Labels)
        published_time Datetime   EB-NeRD only; MIND news.tsv carries no date

Article ids are strings in both datasets so the two share a schema; EB-NeRD's integer
ids are cast on the way in.

    python -m pipeline.split                # both datasets
    python -m pipeline.split ebnerd_demo
"""

import argparse
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl
import yaml

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
OUT = ROOT / "data/processed"

MIND_BEHAVIORS = ["impression_id", "user_id", "time", "history", "impressions"]
MIND_NEWS = ["article_id", "category", "subcategory", "title", "abstract", "url",
             "title_entities", "abstract_entities"]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------- EB-NeRD

def _ebnerd_block(root: Path) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """One provided block (train or validation) -> normalized impressions."""
    behaviors = pl.read_parquet(root / "behaviors.parquet")
    history = pl.read_parquet(root / "history.parquet")

    ids = pl.element().cast(pl.String)
    return (
        behaviors.join(history, on="user_id", how="left")
        .select(
            pl.col("impression_id").cast(pl.Int64),
            pl.col("user_id").cast(pl.String),
            pl.col("impression_time").alias("timestamp"),
            pl.col("article_ids_inview").list.eval(ids).alias("candidates"),
            pl.col("article_ids_clicked").list.eval(ids).alias("clicked"),
            pl.col("article_id_fixed").list.eval(ids).alias("history"),
            pl.col("impression_time_fixed").alias("history_timestamps"),
        )
    )


def load_ebnerd(cfg: dict) -> tuple[pl.DataFrame, pl.DataFrame, pl.DataFrame]:
    early = _ebnerd_block(ROOT / cfg["early_root"])
    test = _ebnerd_block(ROOT / cfg["test_root"])
    articles = pl.read_parquet(ROOT / cfg["articles"]).select(
        pl.col("article_id").cast(pl.String),
        pl.col("title"),
        pl.col("subtitle").alias("abstract"),
        pl.col("body"),
        pl.col("category_str").alias("category"),
        # Named-entity surface forms. EB-NeRD ships them pre-extracted (86% of articles);
        # MIND ships JSON that _mind_news parses to the same List(String) shape.
        pl.col("ner_clusters").alias("entities"),
        pl.col("published_time"),
        # Lifetime aggregates computed over the whole collection period, so they embed the
        # future and are not available at serving time. Carried only so the harness can
        # report metrics with and without them (an organiser requirement); no scorer that
        # claims to be servable may read these.
        pl.col("total_inviews"),
        pl.col("total_pageviews"),
        pl.col("total_read_time"),
    )
    return early, test, articles


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------ MIND

def _mind_block(root: Path) -> pl.DataFrame:
    behaviors = pl.read_csv(
        root / "behaviors.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False,
        new_columns=MIND_BEHAVIORS, quote_char=None,
    ).with_row_index("row")

    # "N55689-1 N35729-0" -> candidates + the clicked subset
    pairs = (
        behaviors.select("row", pl.col("impressions").str.split(" ").alias("pair"))
        .explode("pair")
        .with_columns(
            pl.col("pair").str.split("-").list.first().alias("article_id"),
            (pl.col("pair").str.split("-").list.last() == "1").alias("was_clicked"),
        )
    )
    labelled = pairs.group_by("row").agg(
        pl.col("article_id").alias("candidates"),
        pl.col("article_id").filter(pl.col("was_clicked")).alias("clicked"),
    )

    return (
        behaviors.join(labelled, on="row", how="left")
        .select(
            pl.col("impression_id").cast(pl.Int64),
            pl.col("user_id").cast(pl.String),
            pl.col("time").str.strptime(pl.Datetime, "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p").alias("timestamp"),
            pl.col("candidates"),
            pl.col("clicked"),
            # A user with no prior clicks is a cold start, not a missing value — but
            # "".split(" ") is [""], not [], so drop the empty token or every cold-start
            # user gets a phantom one-item history and lands in the wrong eval slice.
            pl.col("history").fill_null("").str.split(" ")
            .list.eval(pl.element().filter(pl.element() != "")).alias("history"),
            pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.List(pl.Datetime)).alias("history_timestamps"),
        )
    )


def _entity_labels(column: str) -> pl.Expr:
    """MIND ships entities as a JSON array per field; we keep the surface labels.

    `json_decode` needs the shape up front, and we only want one field of it, so the
    struct is declared with just `Label` — the rest of each record is discarded.
    """
    dtype = pl.List(pl.Struct({"Label": pl.String}))
    return (
        pl.col(column).fill_null("[]").str.json_decode(dtype)
        .list.eval(pl.element().struct.field("Label"))
    )


def _mind_news(root: Path) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return pl.read_csv(
        root / "news.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False,
        new_columns=MIND_NEWS, quote_char=None,
    ).select(
        "article_id", "title", "abstract",
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.String).alias("body"),
        "category",
        # Title and abstract entities are one pool; duplicates across the two are
        # the same entity mentioned twice, not two entities.
        pl.concat_list(_entity_labels("title_entities"),
                       _entity_labels("abstract_entities"))
        # maintain_order, or the deduplication is hash-ordered and the file stops
        # being byte-identical between runs.
        .list.unique(maintain_order=True).alias("entities"),
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Datetime).alias("published_time"),
        # MIND ships no lifetime aggregates; kept for schema parity with EB-NeRD.
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Int32).alias("total_inviews"),
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Int32).alias("total_pageviews"),
        pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Float32).alias("total_read_time"),
    )


def load_mind(cfg: dict) -> tuple[pl.DataFrame, pl.DataFrame, pl.DataFrame]:
    early_root, test_root = ROOT / cfg["early_root"], ROOT / cfg["test_root"]
    early = _mind_block(early_root)
    test = _mind_block(test_root)
    # The two splits ship different news files; 13,956 articles appear only in dev.
    # Indexing either alone leaves part of the test corpus unreachable.
    articles = pl.concat([_mind_news(early_root), _mind_news(test_root)]).unique(
        subset="article_id", keep="first"
    )
    return early, test, articles


LOADERS = {"ebnerd": load_ebnerd, "mind": load_mind}


# ------------------------------------------------------------------- user features

def with_recency(df: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Add `recency_seconds`: how long before this impression the user last clicked.

    Derived here rather than inside either loader, because the definition is the same for
    both datasets and it is built from `history_timestamps`, which the loaders have already
    constrained to precede the impression. That is what makes it leakage-free by
    construction rather than by inspection: the value can only ever look backwards.

    Null means genuinely unknown, never zero:
      * a cold-start user has no prior click, and 0 would read as "clicked just now"
      * MIND ships no per-item history times at all, so no impression there can have one
    """
    if df["history_timestamps"].dtype == pl.Null:
        return df.with_columns(pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.Float64).alias("recency_seconds"))
    return df.with_columns(
        (pl.col("timestamp") - pl.col("history_timestamps").list.max())
        .dt.total_seconds().cast(pl.Float64).alias("recency_seconds")
    )


# ------------------------------------------------------------------- integrity

def check_integrity(splits: dict[str, pl.DataFrame], articles: pl.DataFrame) -> None:
    """Fail loudly on anything that would let future information into a split."""
    train, val, test = splits["train"], splits["val"], splits["test"]

    # 1. strict temporal ordering
    bounds = {k: (v["timestamp"].min(), v["timestamp"].max()) for k, v in splits.items()}
    assert bounds["train"][1] < bounds["val"][0], "train overlaps val"
    assert bounds["val"][1] < bounds["test"][0], "val overlaps test"
    print("  [ok] train < val < test, strictly")

    # 2. no future clicks in history
    if train["history_timestamps"].dtype != pl.Null and train["history_timestamps"].null_count() < train.height:
        for name, df in splits.items():
            late = df.filter(
                pl.col("history_timestamps").list.max() >= pl.col("timestamp")
            ).height
            assert late == 0, f"{name}: {late} impressions have history at/after impression time"
        print("  [ok] every history click strictly precedes its impression (per-item)")

        # recency is derived from those same timestamps, so a non-positive value would mean
        # the derivation looked forwards. Checked separately because a sign error here would
        # not trip the check above.
        for name, df in splits.items():
            bad = df.filter(pl.col("recency_seconds") <= 0).height
            assert bad == 0, f"{name}: {bad} impressions have non-positive recency"
        print("  [ok] recency_seconds is strictly positive wherever it is defined")
    else:
        print("  [--] history carries no timestamps; per-item leakage check not possible.")
        print("       Guarantee is structural only (history precedes the log period).")

    # 3. labels must be drawn from the pool shown
    for name, df in splits.items():
        bad = df.filter(
            pl.col("clicked").list.set_difference(pl.col("candidates")).list.len() > 0
        ).height
        assert bad == 0, f"{name}: {bad} impressions clicked outside the candidate pool"
    print("  [ok] clicked is a subset of candidates")

    # 4. candidates must exist in the corpus, and no id may be the empty string —
    #    an empty token is how a cold-start history silently turns into a 1-item one.
    known = set(articles["article_id"])
    for name, df in splits.items():
        for col in ("candidates", "clicked", "history"):
            ids = set(df[col].explode().drop_nulls())
            assert "" not in ids, f"{name}.{col}: contains an empty article id"
            if col == "candidates":
                assert not (ids - known), (
                    f"{name}: {len(ids - known)} candidates absent from articles.parquet"
                )
    print("  [ok] every candidate resolves to an article; no empty ids")

    # 5. articles published after a split's start cannot be retrieved for it.
    #    Only reportable where the corpus carries a date (EB-NeRD).
    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
        future = articles.filter(pl.col("published_time") > bounds["test"][1]).height
        print(f"  [!!] {future} articles published after the test window ends "
              f"({bounds['test'][1]}).")
        print("       Full-corpus retrieval must filter published_time <= impression_time.")
    else:
        print("  [--] corpus has no publication dates; the published-after-impression")
        print("       filter cannot be applied for this dataset.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------- driver

def build(name: str, cfg: dict) -> None:
    print(f"\n{name}")
    early, test, articles = LOADERS[cfg["loader"]](cfg)

    val_start = datetime.fromisoformat(cfg["val_start"])
    test_start = datetime.fromisoformat(cfg["test_start"])

    splits = {
        "train": with_recency(early.filter(pl.col("timestamp") < val_start)),
        "val": with_recency(early.filter(pl.col("timestamp") >= val_start)),
        "test": with_recency(test),
    }
    assert splits["test"]["timestamp"].min() >= test_start, (
        f"test block starts before its declared test_start {test_start}"
    )

    check_integrity(splits, articles)

    out = OUT / name
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    # Sort on a unique key before writing. `unique()` is hash-based and row order after it
    # varies run to run, which would make the pipeline non-reproducible byte-for-byte.
    articles.sort("article_id").write_parquet(out / "articles.parquet")
    total = sum(df.height for df in splits.values())
    for split, df in splits.items():
        (df.sort(["timestamp", "impression_id"])
           .write_parquet(out / f"impressions_{split}.parquet"))
        print(f"  {split:<5} {df.height:>7,} ({df.height / total:5.1%})  "
              f"{df['timestamp'].min()} -> {df['timestamp'].max()}")
    print(f"  articles {articles.height:,} -> {out}")


def main() -> None:
    config = yaml.safe_load(CONFIG.read_text())
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", default=list(config))
    args = parser.parse_args()

    for name in args.datasets:
        build(name, config[name])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""BM25 over article text, on the two tracks the assignment asks for.

  re-rank    score the candidate pool the log already shows for an impression.
             Comparable to the leaderboards, which rank within the given pool.
  retrieval  ignore the pool and pull the top-K from the whole corpus.
             This is the "candidate generation to a few hundred" half of the spec.

The query for both is the user's recent click history: the titles of their last
HISTORY_LEN clicked articles, concatenated. History is already guaranteed strictly
earlier than the impression by pipeline.split, so the query cannot leak.

Both tracks come out of a single scoring pass. Queries are deduplicated first — history
is constant per user within a split, so the ~230k MIND impressions collapse to far fewer
distinct queries, and BM25 runs once per distinct query rather than once per impression.

    python -m retrieval.bm25                       # both datasets, all splits
    python -m retrieval.bm25 ebnerd_demo --fields title

Writes, per dataset and split:
    bm25_<split>.parquet       impression_id, bm25        aligned to `candidates`
    retrieval_<split>.parquet  impression_id, retrieved   top-K ids, best first
"""

import argparse
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import bm25s
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import Stemmer
import yaml
from tqdm import tqdm

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
PROC = ROOT / "data/processed"

HISTORY_LEN = 30   # most recent clicks forming the query; news interest decays fast
TOP_K = 200        # "a few hundred candidates"
OVERFETCH = 3      # fetch TOP_K*OVERFETCH before the publication-date filter thins it

FIELDS = {
    "title": ("title",),
    "title_abstract": ("title", "abstract"),
    "title_abstract_body": ("title", "abstract", "body"),
}


def document_text(articles: pl.DataFrame, fields: tuple[str, ...]) -> list[str]:
    present = [f for f in fields if articles[f].null_count() < articles.height]
    missing = set(fields) - set(present)
    if missing:
        print(f"  note: {'/'.join(sorted(missing))} is empty for this dataset, skipping")
    return (
        articles.select(
            pl.concat_str([pl.col(f).fill_null("") for f in present], separator=" ")
        )
        .to_series()
        .to_list()
    )


def stopwords_for(cfg: dict):
    """bm25s ships lists for some languages only; others come from configs/."""
    if cfg.get("stopwords_file"):
        lines = (ROOT / cfg["stopwords_file"]).read_text().splitlines()
        return [w for w in (ln.strip() for ln in lines) if w and not w.startswith("#")]
    return cfg.get("stopwords")


def build_index(articles: pl.DataFrame, cfg: dict, fields: tuple[str, ...]):
    stemmer = Stemmer.Stemmer(cfg["language"])
    texts = document_text(articles, fields)
    tokens = bm25s.tokenize(
        texts, stopwords=stopwords_for(cfg), stemmer=stemmer, show_progress=False
    )
    index = bm25s.BM25()
    index.index(tokens, show_progress=False)
    return index, stemmer


def build_queries(impressions: pl.DataFrame, title_of: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    """Last HISTORY_LEN clicked titles per impression. Empty for cold-start users."""
    return [
        " ".join(title_of.get(a, "") for a in hist[-HISTORY_LEN:])
        for hist in impressions["history"].to_list()
    ]


def score_split(index, stemmer, cfg, impressions, articles, position, published):
    """One pass over distinct queries, filling both tracks."""
    queries = build_queries(impressions, dict(zip(articles["article_id"], articles["title"])))

    order: dict[str, int] = {}
    per_impression = []
    for q in queries:
        per_impression.append(order.setdefault(q, len(order)))
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = defaultdict(list)
    for row, q_id in enumerate(per_impression):
        groups[q_id].append(row)
    print(f"    {len(order):,} distinct queries for {impressions.height:,} impressions")

    tokenized = bm25s.tokenize(
        list(order), stopwords=stopwords_for(cfg), stemmer=stemmer,
        return_ids=False, show_progress=False,
    )

    candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
    timestamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
    article_ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy()
    n_fetch = min(TOP_K * OVERFETCH, len(article_ids))

    cand_scores: list = [None] * impressions.height
    retrieved: list = [None] * impressions.height

    for q_id, tokens in enumerate(tqdm(tokenized, desc="    scoring", unit="q", leave=False)):
        rows = groups[q_id]
        if not tokens:
            # Cold start: no history, so BM25 has no query. Zero scores and an empty
            # retrieval, rather than an arbitrary ranking that would look like a result.
            for row in rows:
                cand_scores[row] = np.zeros(len(candidates[row]), dtype=np.float32)
                retrieved[row] = []
            continue

        scores = index.get_scores(tokens)
        top = np.argpartition(-scores, n_fetch - 1)[:n_fetch]
        top = top[np.argsort(-scores[top])]

        for row in rows:
            cand_scores[row] = scores[[position[a] for a in candidates[row]]].astype(np.float32)
            hits = top
            if published is not None:
                # An article published after the impression could not have been shown.
                hits = hits[published[hits] <= np.datetime64(timestamps[row])]
            retrieved[row] = article_ids[hits[:TOP_K]].tolist()

    return cand_scores, retrieved


def run(name: str, cfg: dict, fields: tuple[str, ...], splits: list[str]) -> None:
    print(f"\n{name}  fields={'+'.join(fields)}")
    articles = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / "articles.parquet")
    index, stemmer = build_index(articles, cfg, fields)
    print(f"  indexed {articles.height:,} articles")

    position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
    published = None
    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
        published = articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
    else:
        print("  note: no publication dates; retrieval cannot filter unpublished articles")

    for split in splits:
        impressions = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / f"impressions_{split}.parquet")
        print(f"  {split}: {impressions.height:,} impressions")
        cand_scores, retrieved = score_split(
            index, stemmer, cfg, impressions, articles, position, published
        )

        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "bm25": [s.tolist() for s in cand_scores],
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"bm25_{split}.parquet")
        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "retrieved": retrieved,
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"retrieval_{split}.parquet")

        # Recall@K here is a build-time sanity signal, not the reported metric.
        clicked = impressions["clicked"].to_list()
        hit = sum(
            bool(set(c) & set(r)) for c, r in zip(clicked, retrieved) if c
        )
        print(f"    recall@{TOP_K} (full-corpus retrieval): {hit / impressions.height:.4f}")


def main() -> None:
    config = yaml.safe_load(CONFIG.read_text())
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", default=list(config))
    parser.add_argument("--fields", choices=list(FIELDS), default="title_abstract")
    parser.add_argument("--splits", nargs="+", default=["train", "val", "test"])
    args = parser.parse_args()

    for name in args.datasets:
        run(name, config[name], FIELDS[args.fields], args.splits)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

67	    """A List(Float) column as a dense (rows, dim) float32 array.

70	    float on the way through and peaks at 5.8 GB to build a 385 MB array (measured on
