60	the behaviour-window boundary is given to us, cleanly, and is what the leakage test asserts.
61	
62	Coverage checks (all clean): history covers 1,590/1,590 and 1,562/1,562 users; 0 inview articles
63	and 0 history articles missing from `articles.parquet`. Train∩validation users = 1,217.
64	
65	Candidates per impression: mean 11.2, median 8, min 5, max 100. Distinct inview articles across
66	both splits: 3,729 (of 11,777 in the corpus).
67	
68	### Provided article embeddings
69	
70	The assignment names two, both 125,541 rows × 2 cols (`article_id Int32`, one `List(Float32)`):
71	
72	| artifact | file | dim |
73	|---|---|---|
74	| `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` | `document_vector.parquet` | 300 |
75	| `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` | `bert_base_multilingual_cased.parquet` | 768 |
76	
77	Both cover **all 11,777** demo and **all 20,738** `ebnerd_small` articles (0 missing either way), and
78	being full-corpus artifacts they serve every bundle with no re-download. Which of the two we use is
79	settled by measurement, not preference — see "Choosing the EB-NeRD encoder" below. This is the
80	semantic axis for EB-NeRD; nothing needs generating on that side. MIND has no equivalent and will need embeddings generated
81	(MiniLM on CPU over the 65,238-article union).
82	
83	## MIND-small
84	
85	English. `time` parses with `%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p`. Day boundary is midnight.
86	
87	`behaviors.tsv` — headerless, 5 cols: `impression_id, user_id, time, history, impressions`.
88	`history` is a space-separated list of news IDs **with no timestamps**. `impressions` is
89	space-separated `N12345-1` / `N12345-0` (clicked / not).
90	
91	`news.tsv` — headerless, 8 cols: `news_id, category, subcategory, title, abstract, url,
92	title_entities, abstract_entities` (entities are JSON strings with Wikidata IDs).
93	
94	| | behaviors | time range | users | news.tsv |
95	|---|---|---|---|---|
96	| train | 156,965 | 2019-11-09 00:00:19 → 2019-11-14 23:59:13 | 50,000 | 51,282 |
97	| dev | 73,152 | 2019-11-15 00:00:01 → 2019-11-15 23:58:03 | 50,000 | 42,416 |
98

100

102	Cold-start (null history): 3,238/156,965 train (2.1%), 2,214/73,152 dev (3.0%).
103	History length: median 19, mean 32.6, max 558.
104

106	dev-only. All dev candidates are covered by the union. **The retrieval index must be built over the
107	union**, or 21% of the corpus is unreachable at test time.
108	
109	Text coverage: title 100%; abstract 94.8% (48,616/51,282 train). 17 categories, 264 subcategories —
110	category is the natural grouping for the diversity metric.
111	
112	## Chosen temporal splits
113	
114	Rule: train < val < test strictly, by impression timestamp. We adopt each dataset's own provided
115	boundary as the train/test boundary rather than inventing one, and carve val out of the earlier
116	block by time.
117	
118	**EB-NeRD demo** (boundary 07:00)
119	
120	| split | window | source | history source |
121	|---|---|---|---|
122	| train | `[2023-05-18 07:00, 2023-05-23 07:00)` (5 d) | provided `train/` | `train/history.parquet` |
123	| val | `[2023-05-23 07:00, 2023-05-25 07:00)` (2 d) | provided `train/` | `train/history.parquet` |
124	| test | `[2023-05-25 07:00, 2023-06-01 07:00)` (7 d) | provided `validation/` | `validation/history.parquet` |
125	
126	**MIND-small** (boundary midnight)
127	
128	| split | window | source |
129	|---|---|---|
130	| train | `[2019-11-09 00:00, 2019-11-13 00:00)` (4 d) | provided `train` |
131	| val | `[2019-11-13 00:00, 2019-11-15 00:00)` (2 d) | provided `train` |
132	| test | `[2019-11-15 00:00, 2019-11-16 00:00)` (1 d) | provided `dev` |
133	
134	Realized counts (verified, ordering asserted):
135	
136	| dataset | train | val | test |
137	|---|---|---|---|
138	| EB-NeRD demo | 17,852 (35.6%), 1,476 u | 6,872 (13.7%), 1,110 u | 25,356 (50.6%), 1,562 u |
139	| MIND-small | 95,071 (41.3%), 40,148 u | 61,894 (26.9%), 31,664 u | 73,152 (31.8%), 50,000 u |
140	
141	EB-NeRD's test half being the largest block is a consequence of adopting the provided 7-day
142	`validation/` as test against a 5+2-day carve of `train/`. Kept deliberately: the test set is where
143	the bootstrap CIs are computed, and more test impressions means tighter intervals. The alternative
144	(train = all 7 provided train days, val/test = halves of provided validation) buys ~38% more
145	training data but makes test history up to 7 days stale by the end of the window; the current
146	arrangement keeps test history fresh at the test boundary.
147	
148	Known conservatism, recorded deliberately: EB-NeRD val impressions use the train history window,
149	which ends 2023-05-18 07:00 — so history is up to 5 days stale by the end of val. This is *safe*

# IRE Assignment-1, Component-1 — lexical & semantic retrieval

Two-stage news recommendation on **EB-NeRD** (Danish, Ekstra Bladet) and **MIND** (English,
Microsoft), with a temporal data pipeline, BM25 and embedding candidate generation, and an
offline evaluation harness with bootstrap confidence intervals.

See `NOTES.md` for the measured data facts and every decision's justification, `DESIGN_NOTE.md`
for the write-up, and `results/` for the generated metric reports.

## Run it

```bash
make venv      # once: Python 3.11 venv + dependencies
make data      # Q1 on its own: raw archives -> feature store
make all       # download -> split -> retrieve -> evaluate
```

`make all` is idempotent: re-running skips completed downloads and rewrites the same bytes.
Individual stages: `make download`, `make split`, `make retrieve`, `make results`.
`make test` runs the anti-leakage checks against the built artifacts in seconds.

`make submissions` builds the two Codabench leaderboard files. It is deliberately outside
`make all`: the competitions score their own held-out test sets — EB-NeRD 13.5M impressions,
MIND-large 2.4M — not the temporal splits this repo evaluates on, so it downloads ~2.2 GB more
and takes ~13 min for EB-NeRD plus a one-off MIND encode.

**One manual step.** MIND is gated. The URL in every tutorial
(`mind201910small.blob.core.windows.net`) is dead — "Public access is not permitted on this
storage account" — and `msnews.github.io` now redirects to a HuggingFace mirror. Before the
first run, log in with `huggingface-cli login`, then open
<https://huggingface.co/datasets/yjw1029/MIND> and click *"Agree and access repository"*.
Access is automatic. EB-NeRD needs no auth.

## Layout

```
configs/datasets.yaml     split cutoffs, language, stopwords, embedding source — per dataset
configs/stopwords_da.txt  Danish stopwords (bm25s ships none; measured worth +0.020 AUC)
pipeline/download.py      fetch + extract, idempotent
pipeline/split.py         temporal split -> normalised schema, with integrity assertions
pipeline/submit.py        streaming scorer for the two Codabench leaderboards
retrieval/bm25.py         lexical scoring: re-rank track + full-corpus retrieval track
retrieval/embeddings.py   semantic scoring: same two tracks, same output shape
retrieval/fuse.py         per-pool z-normalised blend; alpha tuned on val only
eval/                     metrics, beyond-accuracy, slicing, bootstrap, runner
tests/test_leakage.py     no-future-click assertions against the built artifacts
results/                  generated reports (markdown + json)
```

## What it produces

`data/processed/<dataset>/` holds one schema for both datasets, so every downstream stage has a
single code path:

```
impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet
    impression_id, user_id, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[],
    history[], history_timestamps[]
articles.parquet
    article_id, title, abstract, body, category, entities, published_time,
    total_inviews, total_pageviews, total_read_time     <- serving-unavailable, eval only
```

Then per split: `bm25_*`, `emb_*`, `fused_*` (scores aligned to `candidates`) and
`retrieval_*`, `retrieval_emb_*` (full-corpus top-200).

## Correctness guarantees

`pipeline/split.py` asserts on every build, failing rather than warning:

- `train < val < test` strictly, by impression timestamp
- every history click strictly precedes its impression (per-item, EB-NeRD)
- `clicked` is a subset of `candidates`
- every candidate resolves to an article; no empty ids

Where a check is impossible it says so instead of passing vacuously — MIND's history carries no
per-item timestamps, so the harness reports that the guarantee there is structural rather than
verified. Outputs are byte-identical across runs.

`make test` re-checks the same properties from outside, reading only `data/processed/`. That is a
stronger claim than the build-time assertions: the build asserts what it *intended* to write, the
tests assert what is *actually on disk* and what every downstream stage therefore reads. One test
also fails if any module outside `eval/run.py` so much as mentions a serving-unavailable column.

first run, log in with `huggingface-cli login`, then open
<https://huggingface.co/datasets/yjw1029/MIND> and click *"Agree and access repository"*.
Access is automatic. EB-NeRD needs no auth.

## Layout

```
configs/datasets.yaml     split cutoffs, language, stopwords, embedding source — per dataset
configs/stopwords_da.txt  Danish stopwords (bm25s ships none; measured worth +0.020 AUC)
pipeline/download.py      fetch + extract, idempotent
pipeline/split.py         temporal split -> normalised schema, with integrity assertions
pipeline/submit.py        streaming scorer for the two Codabench leaderboards
retrieval/bm25.py         lexical scoring: re-rank track + full-corpus retrieval track
retrieval/embeddings.py   semantic scoring: same two tracks, same output shape
retrieval/fuse.py         per-pool z-normalised blend; alpha tuned on val only
eval/                     metrics, beyond-accuracy, slicing, bootstrap, runner
tests/test_leakage.py     no-future-click assertions against the built artifacts
results/                  generated reports (markdown + json)
```

## What it produces

`data/processed/<dataset>/` holds one schema for both datasets, so every downstream stage has a
single code path:

```
impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet
    impression_id, user_id, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[],
    history[], history_timestamps[]
articles.parquet
    article_id, title, abstract, body, category, entities, published_time,
    total_inviews, total_pageviews, total_read_time     <- serving-unavailable, eval only
```

Then per split: `bm25_*`, `emb_*`, `fused_*` (scores aligned to `candidates`) and
`retrieval_*`, `retrieval_emb_*` (full-corpus top-200).

## Correctness guarantees

`pipeline/split.py` asserts on every build, failing rather than warning:

- `train < val < test` strictly, by impression timestamp
- every history click strictly precedes its impression (per-item, EB-NeRD)
- `clicked` is a subset of `candidates`
- every candidate resolves to an article; no empty ids

Where a check is impossible it says so instead of passing vacuously — MIND's history carries no
per-item timestamps, so the harness reports that the guarantee there is structural rather than
verified. Outputs are byte-identical across runs.

`make test` re-checks the same properties from outside, reading only `data/processed/`. That is a
stronger claim than the build-time assertions: the build asserts what it *intended* to write, the
tests assert what is *actually on disk* and what every downstream stage therefore reads. One test
also fails if any module outside `eval/run.py` so much as mentions a serving-unavailable column.

"""BM25 document-field ablation: title vs title+abstract vs title+abstract+body.

Answers "EB-NeRD ships body text, why aren't you indexing it?" with a measurement rather
than an assumption. Results are recorded in docs/NOTES.md under "Which article fields to
index (field ablation)".

Non-destructive by design: reuses retrieval.bm25's own functions but never writes to
data/processed, so the shipped artifacts and the reported results stay untouched. Verify
with `md5sum data/processed/ebnerd_small/bm25_val.parquet` before and after.

Only EB-NeRD carries a body, so the third variant is meaningful there alone; on MIND
`document_text` drops the all-null field automatically and prints a note.

    .venv/bin/python scratchpad/field_ablation.py            # ebnerd_small val
    .venv/bin/python scratchpad/field_ablation.py mind_small
"""
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from eval import bootstrap, metrics                         # noqa: E402
from retrieval.bm25 import TOP_K, build_index, score_split  # noqa: E402

DATASET = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "ebnerd_small"
# Selection would be on val in any case; test is never read here.
SPLIT = "val"
VARIANTS = {
    "title": ("title",),
    "title+abstract (ships)": ("title", "abstract"),
    "title+abstract+body": ("title", "abstract", "body"),
}

cfg = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml").read_text())[DATASET]
proc = ROOT / "data/processed" / DATASET
articles = pl.read_parquet(proc / "articles.parquet")
impressions = pl.read_parquet(proc / f"impressions_{SPLIT}.parquet")

print(f"{DATASET} {SPLIT}: {impressions.height:,} impressions, {articles.height:,} articles")
body_chars = articles["body"].str.len_chars()
print(f"body: {articles['body'].null_count():,} null, "
      f"median {body_chars.median() or 0:.0f} chars, p95 {body_chars.quantile(0.95) or 0:.0f}\n")

position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
published = (articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
             if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height else None)

labels = [
    np.fromiter((c in set(k) for c in cand), bool, len(cand))
    for cand, k in zip(impressions["candidates"].to_list(), impressions["clicked"].to_list())
]

results = {}
for name, fields in VARIANTS.items():
    print(f"--- {name} ---")
    t0 = time.time()
    # Everything except `fields` is held fixed, so any difference is attributable to the fields.
    index, stemmer = build_index(articles, cfg, fields)
    vocab = len(index.vocab_dict)
    cand_scores, retrieved = score_split(
        index, stemmer, cfg, impressions, articles, position, published
    )
    scores = [np.asarray(s, dtype=np.float64) for s in cand_scores]
    values, keep = metrics.per_impression(scores, labels)
    recall = metrics.recall_at_k(
        pl.Series("retrieved", retrieved), impressions["clicked"], (TOP_K,), keep
    )[TOP_K]
    results[name] = {"auc": values["auc"], "ndcg10": values["ndcg@10"], "recall": recall,
                     "vocab": vocab, "secs": time.time() - t0}
    print(f"    vocab {vocab:,}   {time.time() - t0:.0f}s\n")

print(f"\n{'variant':<24} {'vocab':>8}  {'AUC':<26} {'nDCG@10':<26} {f'recall@{TOP_K}':<26}")
print("-" * 116)
for name, r in results.items():
    cells = [bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(r[k])) for k in ("auc", "ndcg10", "recall")]
    print(f"{name:<24} {r['vocab']:>8,}  " + "  ".join(f"{c:<24}" for c in cells))

base = "title+abstract (ships)"
print(f"\npaired differences vs `{base}` (95% CI; significant if it excludes zero)")
print("-" * 116)
for name, r in results.items():
    if name == base:
        continue
    row = [name.ljust(24)]
    for key, label in (("auc", "AUC"), ("ndcg10", "nDCG@10"), ("recall", f"recall@{TOP_K}")):
        mean, lo, hi, sig = bootstrap.paired(r[key], results[base][key])
        row.append(f"{label} {mean:+.4f} [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}] {'SIG' if sig else '   '}")
    print("  ".join(row))

content.text:
**Yours are right, and the sizes aren't optional.** The line counts match the official test sets exactly:

| | your lines | official test set | match |
|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD | 13,536,710 | `ebnerd_testset`, 13,536,710 impressions | ✅ |
| MIND | 2,370,727 | MIND-large test, 2,370,727 impressions | ✅ |

Those competition figures came from the Codabench REST API submission specs, recorded in `NOTES.md`.

## Why the size is forced

The format requires one line per impression, containing a rank for *every* candidate in that impression:

```
6451339 [4,8,7,2,6,5,9,1,3]
```

EB-NeRD's test set has 205,925,868 candidate pairs. Each rank is 1-3 digits plus a comma, so you cannot express that in less than a few hundred MB of text:

| | uncompressed | zipped | bytes/line |
|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD | 703 MB | 230 MB | 51.9 |
| MIND | 291 MB | 107 MB | 122.9 |

There's no padding and no wasted space. It's ~52 bytes per impression for EB-NeRD, which is about as tight as that format gets.

## What your friend's sizes imply

Working backwards through the same compression ratios:

| | their zip | implies ~impressions | share of test set |
|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD | 1 MB | ~62,000 | **0.5%** |
| MIND | 300 KB | ~6,800 | **0.3%** |

So their files cover well under 1% of what the leaderboards score. The most likely causes, in order:

1. **They scored a local split instead of the competition test set.** This is the common trap, and EB-NeRD's own guidelines are blunt about it: *"Codabench is only evaluating ebnerd_testset (1.5GB)."* Running `submit` against `ebnerd_demo` or `mind_small` produces a plausible-looking file that the leaderboard can't use.
2. **A truncated run.** Streaming 13.5M impressions OOM-kills easily. That happened twice while building yours (`NOTES.md` records a partial file being mistaken for a complete one), and the partial output looks perfectly valid until you count lines.
3. A different competition phase, if MIND has one open besides Official Test.

## The check to send them

File size is a proxy; line count is the actual test. If they run:

```bash
unzip -p their_file.zip | wc -l
```

it has to print **13536710** for EB-NeRD and **2370727** for MIND. Anything else means the submission doesn't cover the evaluated set, and Codabench will either reject it or score it near zero for the missing impressions.

Worth asking whether they've actually had a score come back from the leaderboard. A submission missing 99.5% of impressions that still returned a normal-looking score would mean I'm wrong about how the scorer handles gaps, and that'd be worth knowing before you rely on your own numbers.

content.text:
Three separate EB-NeRD bundles, three jobs. The submission uses none of the two you named:

| bundle | size | scale | what it's for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ebnerd_demo` | 21.5 MB | 11,777 articles, 49,180 impressions, 1,590 users | **fast development iteration** |
| `ebnerd_small` | 84 MB | 20,738 articles, 477,534 impressions, 15,143 users | **the 10× scale-up check** |
| `ebnerd_testset` | 1.63 GB | 13,536,710 impressions | **Codabench submission only** |

[pipeline/submit.py:118](sem-5/ire/assignments/ass-1/pipeline/submit.py#L118) reads straight from `data/interim/ebnerd_testset/`, and MIND's from `MINDlarge_test/`. Your offline reports in `results/` never touch either.

## The trap in that code, which is exactly what your question caught

Line 303 looks like it says "submit demo":

```python
"ebnerd": (stream_ebnerd, "predictions.txt", "ebnerd_predictions.zip", "ebnerd_demo"),
```

**That fourth field is a config-lookup key, not a data source.** It's used only at line 315 to load a config block, and the only thing read out of that block is `cfg["embeddings"]` at line 178, the path to the article vectors. Since `ebnerd_demo` and `ebnerd_small` both point at the same `data/interim/xlmr/ebnerd_full_vectors.parquet` (config lines 25 and 41), the choice of key is arbitrary. Same story for MIND, where `"mind_small"` exists only to supply `cfg["model"]`.

The reason it's wired that way is a good one: it guarantees the leaderboard run uses the *same* encoder the offline report used, so the submitted system can't silently diverge from the reported one. But the naming makes it read like the opposite of what it does, and "why does your submission say demo?" is a very plausible viva question. It'd be worth a one-line comment or renaming the field to `encoder_cfg_key`.

## What demo and small are each actually for

**demo** is the development loop. Small enough that a full split + retrieve + evaluate cycle runs in seconds, so mistakes are cheap.

**small** exists for **statistical power**, and that's the interesting part. `NOTES.md` records that scaling up changed almost no point estimates: *"Every system lands within 0.002 of its demo value at 10x the users."* What it did change was interval width, ±0.0040 → ±0.0013 on AUC. That's what made the small negative fusion effect resolvable at all. At demo scale `fused − bm25` was +0.0020 [−0.0003, +0.0044], which includes zero and permits no claim; at small it became +0.0024 [+0.0017, +0.0030], which does.

So small's job isn't "more accurate numbers", it's "tighter error bars on the same numbers", and proving demo was representative in the first place. It also proved the config-driven design works: scaling up needed **no code change**, just a config block.

Want me to add that clarifying comment to `TARGETS` so the `"ebnerd_demo"` key can't be misread?

content.content:
--- cell 0 [markdown] ---
# Encode article text — Kaggle (or Colab) GPU

Produces the article vectors for the **semantic axis** (Q3, "compute your own using
BERT/XLM-RoBERTa") in exactly the shape `retrieval/embeddings.py` already reads, so wiring the
result in is a one-line config change and no code change.

**Model:** `sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2` — XLM-RoBERTa base,
further trained on paraphrase pairs so cosine similarity is meaningful. That last part is the
whole point: raw multilingual BERT scored **0.4857 AUC on EB-NeRD, worse than random**, because
models trained to fill in blanked-out words produce sentence vectors that all look alike. One
model covers Danish and English, which also removes a confound — until now EB-NeRD used word2vec
and MIND used MiniLM, so "is Danish harder?" was tangled up with "is word2vec worse?".

**Why not locally:** this is inference, a couple of minutes on any GPU. It runs here only because
the weights are ~1.1 GB and the local link to HuggingFace measured 1.5 kB/s.

**The output is much bigger than the input** — ~73 MB for `ebnerd_small`, ~229 MB for
`mind_small`. On a slow link, encode what you like but **retrieve `ebnerd_small` first**: EB-NeRD
is where the semantic axis currently loses to BM25, so that one file decides whether this is
worth adopting. MIND's MiniLM already beats BM25 by 0.069 and is not the problem.

Turn the GPU on first — Kaggle: *Settings -> Accelerator -> **GPU T4 x2***. Colab: *Runtime ->
Change runtime type -> GPU*.

**Not the P100.** Kaggle offers it, but its stock PyTorch has no kernels for Pascal (sm_60), so
every CUDA call fails with `no kernel image is available`. Only one of the two T4s is used.

--- cell 1 [code] ---
!pip -q install "sentence-transformers>=3.0" polars pyarrow
import torch

assert torch.cuda.is_available(), "No GPU. Kaggle: Settings -> Accelerator -> GPU T4 x2."
name = torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)
major, minor = torch.cuda.get_device_capability(0)
supported = torch.cuda.get_arch_list()
print(f"GPU: {name}  (compute capability sm_{major}{minor})")
print("this torch build has kernels for:", " ".join(supported))

# Kaggle still offers the P100, but its stock torch ships no sm_60 kernels, so every CUDA call
# dies with "no kernel image is available" - and only *after* the 1.1 GB model download. Fail
# here instead, with the fix.
assert (major, minor) >= (7, 0), (
    f"{name} is sm_{major}{minor}; this torch supports sm_70 and up. "
    "Switch Settings -> Accelerator to 'GPU T4 x2' and re-run."
)

# fp16 needs Volta or newer to be both correct and fast; gate the .half() on it rather than
# assuming.
FP16 = (major, minor) >= (7, 0)
print("fp16:", FP16)

--- cell 2 [markdown] ---
## 1. Point at the input files

**Kaggle** — upload `scratchpad/encode_inputs/*.parquet` as a Dataset (*+ Add Data -> New
Dataset*), and it appears under `/kaggle/input/<name>/`.

**Colab** — run `from google.colab import files; files.upload()` in a cell first; the files land
in the working directory.

--- cell 3 [code] ---
import glob, os
from pathlib import Path

ON_KAGGLE = Path("/kaggle/input").exists()
OUT_DIR = Path("/kaggle/working") if ON_KAGGLE else Path(".")
inputs = sorted(glob.glob("/kaggle/input/**/*.parquet", recursive=True)) if ON_KAGGLE \
         else sorted(p for p in glob.glob("*.parquet") if not p.endswith("_vectors.parquet"))

print("environment:", "Kaggle" if ON_KAGGLE else "Colab/local")
for p in inputs:
    print(f"  {os.path.getsize(p)/1e6:7.1f} MB  {p}")
assert inputs, "no input parquet found - attach the dataset (Kaggle) or upload (Colab)"

--- cell 4 [markdown] ---
## 2. Encode

Vectors are written **un-normalised**, matching the organisers' provided artifacts —
`load_vectors()` and `pipeline/submit.py` both L2-normalise on the way in, so doing it here would
put that step in two places and make the two arms of the comparison non-identical.

--- cell 5 [code] ---
import time
import numpy as np, polars as pl
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

MODEL = "sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2"
BATCH = 256

model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL, device="cuda")
if FP16:
    model.half()      # ~2x faster on Turing+. Skipped on older cards, where it is
                      # either unsupported or no faster (Pascal has no tensor cores).
print("dim:", model.get_sentence_embedding_dimension())

for path in inputs:
    name = Path(path).stem
    df = pl.read_parquet(path)
    assert df.columns == ["article_id", "text"], f"{path}: unexpected columns {df.columns}"

    t0 = time.time()
    vecs = model.encode(df["text"].to_list(), batch_size=BATCH, convert_to_numpy=True,
                        show_progress_bar=True).astype(np.float32)
    dt = time.time() - t0

    assert len(vecs) == df.height, "row count changed during encoding"
    assert np.isfinite(vecs).all(), "non-finite values in the output"
    # A collapsed encoder still emits perfectly finite numbers and then silently scores at
    # random - that is exactly the multilingual-BERT failure. Catch it here, not after a
    # full pipeline run.
    assert vecs.std(axis=0).mean() > 1e-3, "vectors barely vary - encoder likely misconfigured"

    out = OUT_DIR / f"{name}_vectors.parquet"
    pl.DataFrame({"article_id": df["article_id"],
                  "vector": [v.tolist() for v in vecs]}).write_parquet(out, compression="zstd")
    print(f"{name}: {df.height:,} x {vecs.shape[1]} in {dt/60:.1f} min "
          f"({df.height/dt:,.0f}/s) -> {out} ({out.stat().st_size/1e6:.0f} MB)")

--- cell 6 [markdown] ---
## 3. Retrieve the files

**Kaggle** — they are in `/kaggle/working`; grab them from the **Output** tab, or *Save Version*
and pull with `kaggle kernels output <user>/<kernel> -p .`, which is a plain resumable HTTPS
transfer. Prefer that on a bad link: a browser download that dies at 90% starts over.

**Colab** — `files.download()` below, which streams through the browser.

Then locally, in `configs/datasets.yaml`, point both EB-NeRD entries at the file:

```yaml
embeddings: data/interim/xlmr/ebnerd_small_vectors.parquet
```

Keep the `word2vec` line commented alongside — it is the *provided-embeddings* arm of Q3 and the
baseline this must beat **on val** before being adopted. Never pick on test.

--- cell 7 [code] ---
if not ON_KAGGLE:
    from google.colab import files
    for f in sorted(glob.glob("*_vectors.parquet")):
        files.download(f)
else:
    print("Kaggle: use the Output tab, or `kaggle kernels output <user>/<kernel> -p .`")
    for f in sorted(OUT_DIR.glob("*_vectors.parquet")):
        print(f"  {f.stat().st_size/1e6:7.0f} MB  {f}")

content.text:
**Model: `sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2`** — an XLM-RoBERTa base further fine-tuned on paraphrase pairs, 768 dimensions. Run on a **Kaggle T4** via [notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb](sem-5/ire/assignments/ass-1/notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb).

## Why that model specifically

The notebook states the reasoning, and it's the same principle that predicted every encoder result in the project: *"further trained on paraphrase pairs so cosine similarity is meaningful. That last part is the whole point: raw multilingual BERT scored 0.4857 AUC on EB-NeRD, worse than random, because models trained to fill in blanked-out words produce sentence vectors that all look alike."*

Paraphrase fine-tuning trains directly on "do these two texts mean the same thing", which is exactly what you then measure with cosine. Masked-language-model pretraining does not.

## Why Kaggle rather than locally

Two reasons: no GPU on this machine, and the weights are ~1.1 GB against a HuggingFace link that measured **1.5 kB/s** locally. It's pure inference, a couple of minutes on any GPU.

## The flow

```
pipeline/export_text.py   ->  data/encode_inputs/*.parquet   (article_id, text = title + abstract)
       upload as a Kaggle Dataset
notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb  ->  *_vectors.parquet       (fp16, batch 256)
       download via Output tab
data/interim/xlmr/ebnerd_full_vectors.parquet
       configs/datasets.yaml:25 points at it
```

`export_text.py` deliberately takes article IDs from the *same* processed files the pipeline reads, so the returned vectors can't key against a different corpus. And because one file covers all 125,541 EB-NeRD articles, it serves demo, small, and the leaderboard with no re-encoding.

Timing: ~4.5 min for all four corpora, 1,000-1,800 articles/s.

## Three details worth being able to explain

**The P100 guard.** Kaggle offers a P100, but its stock PyTorch ships no `sm_60` kernels, so every CUDA call dies with "no kernel image is available" — and only *after* the 1.1 GB model download. The notebook asserts compute capability ≥ 7.0 up front and tells you to switch to T4.

**The collapse guard**, which is the smart one:
```python
assert vecs.std(axis=0).mean() > 1e-3, "vectors barely vary - encoder likely misconfigured"
```
A collapsed encoder emits perfectly finite, perfectly valid-looking numbers and then silently scores at random. That is precisely the multilingual-BERT failure. This catches it in the notebook rather than after a full pipeline run.

**Vectors are written un-normalised**, matching the organisers' provided artifacts, because `load_vectors()` and `submit.py` both L2-normalise on the way in. Normalising in the notebook too would put that step in two places and make the provided-vs-own comparison non-identical.

## One inconsistency in the notebook

Cell 6 tells you to set `embeddings: data/interim/xlmr/ebnerd_small_vectors.parquet`, but the config actually uses `ebnerd_full_vectors.parquet` — the full 125,541-article export, which is the better choice since it also covers the leaderboard corpus. The notebook's instruction is stale. Want me to correct that line so the notebook matches what shipped?

Yes, it happened. The timestamps tell the story cleanly: exported at 00:25 on 11 Aug, first vectors back at **00:48**, the rest by **01:28** — matching the notebook's own advice to retrieve `ebnerd_small` first.

## What was uploaded

Not the datasets themselves. Four parquet files produced by `pipeline/export_text.py`, **~31 MB total**, each containing only two columns, `article_id` and `text` (title + abstract concatenated):

| file | rows | corpus |
|---|---|---|
| `ebnerd_small.parquet` | 20,738 | EB-NeRD small articles |
| `ebnerd_full.parquet` | 125,541 | EB-NeRD full corpus (testset) |
| `mind_small.parquet` | 65,238 | MIND-small train+dev union |
| `mindlarge_test.parquet` | 120,961 | MIND-large test articles |

No impressions, no behaviour logs, no user IDs. Just article text, because that's all the encoder needs.

## What came back

622 MB of vectors in `data/interim/xlmr/`. Note the output is ~20× the input, which is why the notebook warns about the download rather than the upload.

Only **one** of the four is actually used: `ebnerd_full_vectors.parquet`, which both EB-NeRD config entries point at. The other three are residue of the experiment:

- `ebnerd_small_vectors.parquet` — superseded, since the full file covers small too
- `mind_small_vectors.parquet` and `mindlarge_test_vectors.parquet` — the **rejected** MIND arm. XLM-R lost to MiniLM on MIND val (0.6256 vs 0.6338), so MIND kept MiniLM. These are the evidence for that ablation, not live artifacts.

That's ~450 MB of unused vectors on disk. Harmless, and arguably worth keeping as ablation evidence, but worth knowing they aren't wired into anything.

## One thing worth checking on your side

Both datasets are licensed research corpora: MIND ships under Microsoft Research License Terms and is gated (you had to accept terms to download it), and EB-NeRD has its own RecSys challenge terms. Uploading their article text to Kaggle put that licensed text on a third-party platform.

**If you created the Kaggle Dataset as private, this is a non-issue.** If it was created public, it's effectively redistributing gated corpus text, which the MSR terms likely don't permit. Worth a look at the dataset's visibility setting, and flipping it to private if it isn't. I'd rather flag it now than have it surface in a viva about data handling.

## Second stale line in that notebook

Cell 2 says to upload `scratchpad/encode_inputs/*.parquet`, but `export_text.py` writes to `data/encode_inputs/`. That's the second path in the notebook that doesn't match reality, along with the `ebnerd_small_vectors` vs `ebnerd_full_vectors` line I mentioned. Both landed **above** your offline numbers, which is worth noting because I predicted the opposite. Comparing like with like (you submitted `emb` on both):

**EB-NeRD** — rank 130

| | offline (`ebnerd_small` test) | leaderboard (`ebnerd_testset`) | diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| AUC | 0.5305 [0.5293, 0.5319] | **0.5336** | +0.0031 |
| MRR | 0.3365 | 0.3412 | +0.0047 |
| nDCG@5 | 0.3711 | 0.3779 | +0.0068 |
| nDCG@10 | 0.4518 | 0.4576 | +0.0058 |

**MIND** — rank 34

| | offline (`mind_small` test) | leaderboard (MIND-large test) | diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| AUC | 0.6339 [0.6319, 0.6360] | **0.646** | +0.0121 |
| MRR | 0.3486 | 0.316 | **−0.0326** |
| nDCG@5 | 0.3315 | 0.3405 | +0.0090 |
| nDCG@10 | 0.3911 | 0.3963 | +0.0052 |

## Three things worth saying about this

**Your offline harness is slightly conservative, not optimistic.** Seven of eight metrics came in higher on much larger, genuinely held-out sets. That's the good direction to be wrong in, and it's a real validation of the temporal split: a leaky evaluation typically produces offline numbers that *collapse* on held-out data. Yours didn't.

**I was wrong in `WALKTHROUGH.md` §13**, where I wrote "expect worse". Worth correcting before the viva, since an examiner may read it against the actual result.

**The MIND MRR drop is the one anomaly**, and I'd flag it as unexplained rather than guess confidently. AUC and both nDCGs rose while MRR fell 0.033. My honest hypothesis: MRR is the metric most sensitive to how multi-click impressions are handled. Yours takes `1/rank` of the *first* clicked article ([eval/metrics.py](sem-5/ire/assignments/ass-1/eval/metrics.py#L29)); if Codabench averages `1/rank` over *all* clicked articles, it scores systematically lower on multi-click impressions while leaving AUC and nDCG largely alone. That's testable but not from here.

## For the next submission

The honest situation: **for EB-NeRD you already submitted your best legitimate system.** `emb` beat `fused` offline, so there's no swap available.

Real levers, roughly by size:

1. **`fused` on MIND** (+0.0014 AUC offline, significant). Currently blocked: BM25's `get_scores` is ~10¹¹ operations at MIND-large scale. Needs a real inverted index with early termination, which is the §10 scaling story you already wrote.
2. **The popularity feature** is by far the biggest number available (+0.043 AUC on EB-NeRD, 0.5305 → 0.5731). The competition doesn't forbid it, since `total_inviews` ships in their own `articles.parquet`. But it's serving-unavailable, so if you submit it you must label it as the with-popularity system in the design note. The assignment wants both reported anyway, so this is legitimate as long as it's not passed off as the servable system.
3. **`contrastive_vector`** scored 0.5506 on `ebnerd_small` val against xlmr's 0.5309, the strongest EB-NeRD encoder you tested. You dropped it for assignment fidelity, which I'd stand by, but it's on the table if you decide the brief's encoder list isn't exhaustive.

Want me to fix the §13 prediction now, and add both scores to the design note's results section?

=== design note section 6 heading + opening ===
## 6. Fusion — an addition the brief did not ask for

Q3 asks only to *compare* lexical and semantic; this third system is mine. BM25 scores and cosines are on
different scales, and BM25's moves with query length, so both are z-normalised **within each candidate
pool** and mixed `alpha*emb + (1-alpha)*bm25`, alpha tuned on **val**, applied unchanged to test.

| test, AUC | bm25 | emb | fused | alpha | fused − emb |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD demo | 0.5125 | 0.5295 | **0.5300** | 0.65 | +0.0005 [−0.0013, +0.0026] — includes zero |
| EB-NeRD small | 0.5107 | **0.5305** | 0.5291 | 0.60 | **−0.0014** [−0.0022, −0.0007] — excludes zero |
| MIND-small | 0.5645 | 0.6339 | **0.6353** | 0.80 | +0.0014 [+0.0005, +0.0023] — excludes zero |

**It mostly does not pay, and that is the useful part.** On `ebnerd_small` fusion wins on val (0.5376 vs
0.5309) and is *significantly worse* on test — the alpha did not generalise, so **the reported EB-NeRD
system is embeddings alone**, and only MIND ships fused, for +0.0014. The harness is what caught it: on
val alone fusion looked a clear win on both datasets. The same instability appeared earlier under a
different encoder, so EB-NeRD's optimal mix genuinely drifts rather than this being a one-off.

1	# Walkthrough: what this system actually does, and why
2	
3	Written to be read start to finish, in plain English, assuming you know nothing.
4	`GLOSSARY.md` defines individual words; this explains how they fit together.
5	
6	Every number here comes from `NOTES.md` or `results/`. Nothing is invented.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 1. The task, in one sentence
11	
12	A person is shown a list of news articles. Some they click, most they don't.
13	**Your job: put that list in the right order, clicked ones at the top.**
14	
15	That's it. You are not choosing what to show. You are not writing headlines. You are given
16	a list somebody was actually shown, and you re-order it.
17	
18	## 2. The single most important thing to understand
19	
20	**Nothing in Component-1 is trained. There is no model with learned weights. There is no
21	loss function, no gradient descent, no epochs.**
22	
23	This is the thing you most need to be able to say out loud, because "what did you train on"
24	is the obvious viva question and the honest answer is "nothing, deliberately".
25	
26	When you asked "what do we train on, how do we train", the answer is that the question
27	doesn't apply yet. Component-1 is a **retrieval** system, not a **learning** system. It works
28	by measuring similarity:
29	
30	> "This person recently read articles A, B and C. Which of the candidates in front of me is
31	> most similar to A, B and C?"
32	
33	Similarity is computed two ways (word overlap, and meaning), and those are combined. No
34	training data is consumed to fit parameters, because there are no parameters to fit.
35	
36	Component-2 (the pair project) is where a trained re-ranker arrives. That's why the brief
37	splits them: C1 builds the measuring apparatus and the honest evaluation, C2 adds learning
38	on top.
39	
40	**Then what is the train split for?** Two things only, both of them bookkeeping rather than
41	learning:
42	
43	1. **Popularity counts** for the evaluation, so "is this a popular or an obscure article?"
44	   is decided using only the past (`eval/slicing.py`, `eval/beyond_accuracy.py`).
45	2. **A held-out region of time** that val and test must come after, which is what makes the
46	   temporal ordering meaningful at all.
47	
48	The one number that is actually *tuned* is the fusion weight `alpha`, a single value between
49	0 and 1, and it is tuned on **val**, not train. More on that in §9.
50	
51	---
52	
53	## 3. The atom of the data: an impression
54	
55	Everything is built from one record type. An **impression** is one moment:
56	
57	```
58	who:        user U73
59	when:       2023-05-24 08:14:02
60	shown:      [A991, A102, A448, A771, A053, A882, A310, A667]   <- candidates
61	clicked:    [A448]                                              <- the label
62	their past: [A031, A559, A004, ... ]                            <- click history
63	```
64	
65	Four parts, and each one has a job:
66	
67	- **candidates** are what you must order.
68	- **clicked** is the answer key. Usually exactly one article (EB-NeRD averages 1.01 clicks
69	  per impression, max 7).
70	- **history** is your only clue about this person. It is the *input* to your system.
71	- **timestamp** is what makes the whole assignment honest, because it lets you prove your
72	  history really came from before the moment you're predicting.
73	
74	`pipeline/split.py` converts both datasets into exactly this shape, so everything downstream
75	has one code path. That normalisation is why the same BM25 code runs on Danish and English
76	without knowing which it's looking at.
77	
78	---
79	
80	## 4. The two datasets, and how they differ
81	
82	Both are real logs from real news sites. They differ in ways that turn out to matter a lot.
83	
84	### EB-NeRD (Ekstra Bladet, Danish tabloid)
85	
86	Used at `demo` scale (11,777 articles, ~49k impressions, 1,590 users) and `small`
87	(20,738 articles, 477,534 impressions, 15,143 users).
88	
89	- Language: **Danish**
90	- Ships article **body text**, not just title and abstract
91	- Ships **publication dates**, which matter for the retrieval track (§7)
92	- Ships **pre-made article embeddings** (§8)
93	- Ships **lifetime view counts**, which are a leakage trap (§11)
94	- History has **per-item timestamps**, so you can check leakage click by click
95	- **No cold-start users at all.** Zero impressions with empty history. Median history is
96	  258 clicks. This bundle is a sample of *active* users.
97	- Candidate pools are **small**: mean 11.2, median 8
98	
99	### MIND (Microsoft News, English)
100	
101	Used at `small` scale: 65,238 articles (train and dev news files differ, so you must use
102	their union), 156,965 + 73,152 impressions, 50,000 users.
103	
104	- Language: **English**
105	- **No body text.** Title and abstract only (abstract present for 94.8%)
106	- **No publication dates**
107	- **No pre-made embeddings.** You generate them yourself
108	- History is a bare list of article IDs with **no timestamps**
109	- **Has real cold-start users**: 5,452 impressions with empty history
110	- Candidate pools are **larger**: mean 37.2, median 24, max 299
111	
112	### Why the differences matter
113	
114	These aren't trivia, they're the reason your results look the way they do:
115	
116	| difference | consequence |
117	|---|---|
118	| MIND has bigger, more varied pools | more room for a scorer to separate good from bad, so scores are higher there |
119	| EB-NeRD pools are small and topically tight | candidates are all plausible, little to distinguish, AUC hovers near 0.51 |
120	| MIND history has no timestamps | the per-click leakage assertion is *impossible* there; the guarantee is structural only |
121	| EB-NeRD has no cold-start users | the "cold vs warm" slice can't use "empty history" as its definition, so a bottom-decile cutoff is used on both |
122	| MIND has no publication dates | full-corpus retrieval can't filter out not-yet-published articles there |
123	
124	That last one and the timestamp one are the sort of thing a viva examiner loves, because the
125	honest answer is "I couldn't, and I said so rather than faking it".
126	
127	---
128	
129	## 5. The temporal split: what train, val and test are actually for
130	
131	**The rule: everything is divided by time. Never randomly.**
132	
133	Why: news recommendation predicts the future. If you shuffle rows randomly, some of your
134	"training" data is from *after* your "test" data, so you'd be using knowledge of the future
135	to predict the past. Your score would look great and mean nothing. A real system serving
136	live traffic has only the past.
137	
138	Both datasets already ship their own two blocks. Rather than invent boundaries, the split
139	adopts theirs and carves validation out of the earlier block:
140	
141	**EB-NeRD demo** (the day boundary in these logs is 07:00, not midnight):
142	
143	| split | window | comes from |
144	|---|---|---|
145	| train | 18 May 07:00 to 23 May 07:00 (5 days) | provided `train/` |
146	| val | 23 May 07:00 to 25 May 07:00 (2 days) | provided `train/` |
147	| test | 25 May 07:00 to 1 June 07:00 (7 days) | provided `validation/` |
148	
149	**MIND-small** (midnight boundary):
150	
151	| split | window | comes from |
152	|---|---|---|
153	| train | 9 Nov to 13 Nov (4 days) | provided `train` |
154	| val | 13 Nov to 15 Nov (2 days) | provided `train` |
155	| test | 15 Nov (1 day) | provided `dev` |
156

Walkthrough sent (§13 fixed, scores added to the design note). Contrastive vectors downloading in the background via parallel ranges. Now your three questions.

## 1. Fusion: no, the brief does not ask for it

Design note §6 is literally titled *"Fusion — an addition the brief did not ask for"*, and opens: **"Q3 asks only to *compare* lexical and semantic; this third system is mine."** I checked the PDF again just now and that holds.

So fusion is your own addition, and the honest finding is that **it mostly doesn't pay**: on `ebnerd_small` test `fused − emb` is −0.0014 with the CI excluding zero, so the reported EB-NeRD system is embeddings alone. Only MIND ships fused, for +0.0014. That's still worth keeping in the report, because a negative result you caught with your own harness is evidence the harness works.

## 2. Contrastive vector: adopt it, the numbers back you up

It wins on **both** val and test, so there's no selection-rule conflict:

| ebnerd_small, `emb` | val | test |
|---|---|---|
| xlmr (current) | 0.5309 | 0.5305 |
| **contrastive** | **0.5506** | **0.5397** |

But it **changes one of your findings**, and you should know before it surprises you in a viva. With xlmr, BM25 out-retrieves embeddings on the full-corpus track. With contrastive, `emb − bm25` recall@200 on test is **+0.0030, significant positive** — embeddings win *both* tracks. Meanwhile on val it's still −0.0016 significant *negative*. So the two-track disagreement doesn't vanish, it relocates into a val/test instability, which is arguably a more interesting thing to write up.

I also found **`NOTES.md` §"Scale-up to EB-NeRD small" is stale**: its table reports emb 0.5397 / fused 0.5380 / fused+pop 0.5797, which are the *contrastive* numbers, never updated through two encoder swaps. Switching back makes that section accidentally correct again, but I'll fix it explicitly rather than rely on that.

## 3. Popularity in the submission: I'd skip it, and not for ethics reasons

`total_inviews` is **null for 107,205 of 125,541 articles in `ebnerd_testset` — 85%**. The +0.0417 you're chasing was measured on `ebnerd_small`, where coverage is far better. On the leaderboard set, 85% of candidates would get `log1p(0) = 0`, so the signal is mostly absent and the gain won't transfer. You'd pay a 33-minute rebuild and take on "we submitted the non-servable system" for probably very little.

If you want it anyway, it's legitimate provided §11 states plainly that the entry is the serving-unavailable variant. Your call, but I'd spend the rebuild on contrastive alone.

## On the AI usage log

I'll write it from prompts you actually issued; I won't author ones you didn't. The stated reason for the change is that an automated checker might penalise the real phrasing, and writing to defeat a grader is the part I can't do, whoever suggested it.

**The good news is you don't need it.** Your real history isn't one broad instruction. Across three weeks you entered plan mode before any code, answered scoping questions that changed the design (both retrieval tracks; demo+small), asked for specific verifications ("just run for checking"), requested options before the restructure, rejected an idea after measuring it, and spent a lot of this session interrogating the system to understand it. That is a *better* log than a synthetic list of "do step 4 from plan.md", which reads as mechanical precisely because it is.

I only have this session plus the repo. The Aug 1-10 implementation sessions aren't in my context, so you'd need to pull those transcripts. Give me them and I'll build an accurate log with what worked, what failed, and the verification loops (the Danish stopword bug, the three OOM kills, the rejected compound splitter) — which is exactly what slide 10 asks for.

Want me to proceed with the contrastive re-run once the download lands?

content.text:
**On the GPU offer:** it wouldn't help. Nothing left is GPU-bound. The only GPU-worthy step was encoding article text, and contrastive vectors ship pre-computed from the organizers, so that step is now gone entirely. Fusion and eval are numpy/Polars CPU work. All three stages just completed on this machine in a few minutes each.

The re-run is done and consistent. But it **reversed a documented conclusion**, which you need to know before I touch the design note:

| `ebnerd_small` test | BM25 | emb (contrastive) | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| AUC | 0.5107 | **0.5397** | emb +0.0289 ✓ |
| recall@50 | 0.0072 | 0.0073 | +0.0001, **not significant** |
| recall@100 | 0.0133 | **0.0144** | emb +0.0011 ✓ |
| recall@200 | 0.0247 | **0.0277** | emb wins ✓ |

Under xlmr, BM25 out-retrieved embeddings *at every K* (0.0247 vs 0.0150), and §5 of the design note is built on that: "ordering a pool the log already filtered and finding 200 items in a catalogue are different jobs." **With contrastive, embeddings now win the retrieval track too**, except a dead heat at K=50.

The two-track finding isn't dead, but it's now a difference of *degree* rather than direction: emb beats BM25 by +0.0289 AUC on re-ranking versus +0.0030 recall@200 on retrieval, a 10× gap in margin. §5 needs rewriting to say that, not softening.

| date | phase | what the agent was asked to do |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Aug | scoping | Read the assignment, write `SPEC.md` as a build plan, and explain Component-1. Plan mode was used before any code was written. |
| 1–2 Aug | pipeline | Environment + dependency setup; `pipeline/download.py`; temporal split (`pipeline/split.py`) with integrity assertions; BM25 (`retrieval/bm25.py`). |
| 4–5 Aug | scale + submission | EB-NeRD test set; streaming Codabench submitter (`pipeline/submit.py`); MIND-large submission. |
| 10–11 Aug | semantic axis + eval | Embeddings and FAISS retrieval; fusion; the evaluation harness (`eval/`); the encoder ablation; `notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb`; first `DESIGN_NOTE.md`. |
| 17 Aug | comprehension + hygiene | First-person explanatory comments through the codebase (for viva readiness); the field ablation; directory restructure; `docs/WALKTHROUGH.md`; first git commit. |
| 19 Aug | final encoder + submission | Switch to `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector`; full EB-NeRD re-run; Codabench submissions and scores. |

**Process note, stated plainly because it is the thing Q7.4 is really probing.** The work was
not delegated as one instruction. It was scoped in plan mode first, the plan was reviewed and
approved, and the build then proceeded in stages with the agent's design questions answered
before it wrote code. Several decisions the agent surfaced as open (which retrieval framing to
build, which dataset scale to target, which encoder to ship) were decided by me, not by it.
Where I asked for something the agent argued was wrong, that exchange is in the transcript.

That said, several individual delegated tasks were larger than the lecture's guidance
recommends, and the two partial-run incidents in §5 are the direct consequence.

## 4. AI-generated vs. human-written code

Honestly marked, because the distinction is not a clean split:

- **All source files in `pipeline/`, `retrieval/`, `eval/`, `tests/`, `scratchpad/` were written
  by Claude Code.** No file was typed by hand from scratch.
- **All prose in `docs/` and `deliverable/` was drafted by Claude Code**, then read and
  corrected by me where it was wrong (see §5 for cases where it was).
- **The decisions were mine**, and they are the part that is load-bearing:
  - build both the re-rank and full-corpus retrieval tracks, not just one
  - target `ebnerd_demo` + `mind_small`, scaling to `ebnerd_small`
  - adopt `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector` as the shipped EB-NeRD encoder
  - decline to add the serving-unavailable popularity feature to the leaderboard entry
  - keep the repo private; keep `problem.md` out once the PDF superseded it
- **Not written by the agent:** the assignment brief (`brief/`), the datasets, and the
  organisers' provided article vectors.

Per the course's stated policy, this makes no difference to assessment: evaluation is on my
understanding, not the agent's. `docs/WALKTHROUGH.md` exists specifically so that understanding
is documented rather than assumed.

## 5. What worked, and what failed

The failures are the useful part of this log, and each was caught by a check rather than by
reading the code. Full detail for every entry is in `docs/NOTES.md`.

**Caught by measurement:**

| what | how it surfaced | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| No Danish stopword list (`bm25s` ships none) | EB-NeRD AUC sat near random and did not respond to history length | Supplied Snowball Danish list: val AUC 0.5035 → 0.5232. A missing stopword list is silent; it degrades ranking without erroring. |
| Raw multilingual BERT scored **below random** (0.4857) | Encoder ablation on val | Not a bug: un-fine-tuned BERT vectors are not trained so cosine means topical similarity. Fusion independently drove its alpha to 0.00. |
| `.to_list()` memory blow-up, found **three separate times** | OOM kill at 10 GB RSS (confirmed in `dmesg`), then twice more | Replaced with `explode().to_numpy()`. Peak 5.8 GB → far lower, byte-identical output. Named as *the* scaling wall in the design note. |
| MIND submission was never actually streaming | OOM-killed after 200k of 2.37M impressions | CSV has no slice pushdown; added a one-off parquet conversion. Peak 4.2 GB → 2.86 GB, first 20,000 lines byte-identical. |
| recall@K missing from every report | Re-reading the brief against the harness | `eval/run.py` never opened the retrieval files. Added with CIs and slices. |
| Entities parsed then silently dropped | Re-reading Q1.4 against `_mind_news` | Present in the `.select()` upstream, absent downstream. |
| BM25 document fields were an **untested assumption** | Asked the agent to justify the default; it could not | Ran the ablation: body costs −0.0166 AUC. The shipped choice was right but had never been measured. |
| Design note carried numbers a rebuild had superseded | Cross-checking the note against `results/` | Tables had drifted from the artifacts they described. |

**Caught by verification, not by the agent:**

| what | how |
|---|---|
| Two partial pipeline runs left mixed-encoder artifacts | A crash killed the run mid-way; embeddings were rewritten with the new encoder while fusion and reports were still from the old one. Detected by comparing artifact mtimes against the config mtime, not by any error message. Both times the fix was a clean full re-run. |
| A diff that looked like a regression was not | The file being compared against was the partial output of an OOM-killed run, not the smoke test. |

**Where I overrode the agent:**

| what | outcome |
|---|---|
| Asked it to write this log as a series of granular prompts I had not actually issued | It declined, on the grounds that Q7.4 also requires the raw transcripts and the two would contradict each other. This log is the honest version. |
| Asked whether to add lifetime popularity to the leaderboard entry | It advised against and supplied the reason: the feature is 85% null on the corpus, so the offline gain would not transfer. Left out. |

## 6. Verification practices used

- **Assertions in the build, tests outside it.** `pipeline/split.py` asserts while building;
  `tests/test_leakage.py` (19 tests) re-checks the same properties from the written artifacts.
- **The leakage suite was verified non-vacuous** by injecting a future click into one row's
  history and confirming the assertion fired. A suite that has never failed proves nothing.
- **Byte-identical rebuilds.** Outputs are sorted on a unique key before writing, because
  `polars.unique()` is hash-ordered; verified identical across three consecutive runs.
- **Independent recomputation.** Submission files were validated on all 13,536,710 lines, plus
  40 random impressions per dataset re-ranked in float64 through a separate code path.
- **Selection on val, never test.** The clearest case: on MIND, MiniLM wins on val and XLM-R
  wins on test. The val-chosen model shipped, costing 0.0025 test AUC.

echo "written: $(wc -l < deliverable/AI_USAGE_LOG.md) lines"
grep -c '—' deliverable/AI_USAGE_LOG.md || echo "em dashes: 0"

content.content:
## 4. Semantic axis

MIND encodes title+abstract with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (**11m16s**, cached once). User vectors are mean of
last-30 history vectors, L2-normalised; scoring is cosine with FAISS `IndexFlatIP` (exact at this scale;
IVF/PQ deferred to 10× analysis). MIND's corpus spans two files, so the index covers their 65,238-article
union.

**The encoder is a measurement, not a preference.** Q3 allows the provided vectors *or* your own from
BERT/XLM-RoBERTa, so I ran the identical pipeline on each — same splits, same BM25, same fusion, only
the article vectors differ — selecting on **val**, since selecting on test tunes a choice on the number
being reported. Semantic-only AUC, `ebnerd_small` val, against BM25's 0.5205:

| encoder | dim | val AUC | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2`** (ours, XLM-R) | 768 | **0.5309** [0.5282, 0.5336] | **beats BM25** |
| `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` (provided) | 300 | 0.5098 [0.5073, 0.5124] | loses |
| `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` (provided) | 768 | 0.4857 [0.4832, 0.4880] | **below random** |

One property predicts all three: **was the model trained so that cosine distance means topical
similarity?** XLM-R fine-tuned on paraphrase pairs was; word2vec (predict neighbouring words) was not;
raw mBERT (fill in blanks) emphatically was not — its vectors sit in a narrow cone where everything
looks alike. Size predicts nothing: the 300-d model beats the 768-d one. Fusion detects the failure
unprompted, tuning alpha to 0.00 on demo — discarding the semantic axis outright.

**MIND kept MiniLM, and that is the sharper lesson.** Against the same XLM-R, MiniLM wins on **val**
(0.6338 [0.6312, 0.6362] vs 0.6256 [0.6232, 0.6279]) and *loses* on **test** (0.6339 vs 0.6364) — a
real reversal, near-disjoint intervals. The rule was fixed before looking, so MiniLM stays; "take the
better test number" would have flipped it. Obeying the rule cost 0.0025 test AUC, which is the entire
point of having one. The direction is sensible too: an English specialist beats a 50-language
generalist on English, while that generalist beats a 2013 word-vector model on Danish.

## 5. Candidate generation: recall@K, and where the winner changes

Recall@K over the **full catalogue** — not the pool the log showed — is what measures candidate
generation: the share of an impression's clicked articles found in the top K. Cold-start impressions
retrieve nothing and score 0 rather than being excluded — a retriever that cannot serve a user has
failed for that user.

| test, recall@K | K=50 | K=100 | K=200 | emb − bm25 @200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD small · bm25 | **0.0072** | **0.0133** | **0.0247** | |
| EB-NeRD small · emb | 0.0043 | 0.0081 | 0.0150 | −0.0097 [−0.0105, −0.0089] |
| MIND-small · bm25 | 0.0060 | 0.0124 | 0.0220 | |
| MIND-small · emb | **0.0076** | **0.0138** | **0.0239** | +0.0019 [+0.0008, +0.0031] |

**Which retriever is better has no dataset-wide answer.** BM25 wins on EB-NeRD at every K, embeddings
win on MIND, both significantly — same code, same K, opposite verdicts, so a result quoted from one
dataset does not transfer.

**Retrieving and re-ranking are different skills, and the same encoder does one well and the other
badly.** On EB-NeRD the XLM-R vectors *re-rank* significantly better than BM25 (+0.0198 AUC, §6) while
*retrieving* 40% worse (0.0150 vs 0.0247 @200) — starkest on popular articles, where they re-rank at
AUC 0.6801 [0.6597, 0.6995] against 0.5852 [0.5626, 0.6066] but still retrieve them worse. Ordering ~8
candidates the log already filtered and finding 200 in a 20,738-article catalogue are different jobs,
and nothing says one signal must win both — the argument for different signals per stage. Absolute
recall is low everywhere (2–4%), see §8.

## 6. Fusion — an addition the brief did not ask for

Q3 asks only to *compare* lexical and semantic; this third system is mine. BM25 scores and cosines are on
different scales, and BM25's moves with query length, so both are z-normalised **within each candidate
pool** and mixed `alpha*emb + (1-alpha)*bm25`, alpha tuned on **val**, applied unchanged to test.

| test, AUC | bm25 | emb | fused | alpha | fused − emb |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD demo | 0.5125 | 0.5295 | **0.5300** | 0.65 | +0.0005 [−0.0013, +0.0026] — includes zero |
| EB-NeRD small | 0.5107 | **0.5305** | 0.5291 | 0.60 | **−0.0014** [−0.0022, −0.0007] — excludes zero |
| MIND-small | 0.5645 | 0.6339 | **0.6353** | 0.80 | +0.0014 [+0.0005, +0.0023] — excludes zero |

**It mostly does not pay, and that is the useful part.** On `ebnerd_small` fusion wins on val (0.5376 vs
0.5309) and is *significantly worse* on test — the alpha did not generalise, so **the reported EB-NeRD
system is embeddings alone**, and only MIND ships fused, for +0.0014. The harness is what caught it: on
val alone fusion looked a clear win on both datasets. The same instability appeared earlier under a
different encoder, so EB-NeRD's optimal mix genuinely drifts rather than this being a one-off.

## 7. Evaluation harness

## Adopting contrastive_vector (final encoder decision, 19 Aug)

Reverses the earlier "Dropping the self-chosen encoder" section. That section removed
`Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector` on the reading that the PDF names only `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec`
and `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased`, and recorded the ~0.041 AUC the removal cost.

The reading was too narrow. Q3 offers "the provided article embeddings" or "compute your own using
BERT/XLM-RoBERTa". `contrastive_vector` is a provided article embedding, shipped in the same official
`artifacts/` folder as the other two; the PDF names those two as examples of that arm rather than as
its full extent. Adopting it is inside the brief, not outside it.

Semantic-only AUC on **val**, `ebnerd_small`, everything else fixed:

| encoder | arm | dim | val AUC |
|---|---|---|---|
| **contrastive_vector** (ships) | provided | 768 | **0.5506** [0.5480, 0.5531] |
| xlmr paraphrase (own) | own | 768 | 0.5309 [0.5282, 0.5336] |
| word2vec | provided | 300 | 0.5098 [0.5073, 0.5124] |
| bert_base_multilingual_cased | provided | 768 | 0.4857 [0.4832, 0.4880] |

Best EB-NeRD test AUC 0.5305 -> **0.5397** (+0.0092 over the xlmr build, +0.0290 over word2vec).

Reproduction note: the re-run's numbers match the archived `results/encoder_ablation/contrastive_vector/`
reports to four decimals, so the ablation artifacts and the shipped build agree.

### What the switch changed downstream

**The retrieval track flipped, and this is the substantive finding.** Under xlmr, BM25 out-retrieved
embeddings on EB-NeRD at every K. Under contrastive the winner depends on the split, significantly in
both directions:

| emb - bm25, recall@200 | val | test |
|---|---|---|
| ebnerd_small | **-0.0016** [-0.0030, -0.0002] ✓ | **+0.0030** [+0.0022, +0.0039] ✓ |
| ebnerd_demo | -0.0034 [-0.0093, +0.0027] | **+0.0071** [+0.0040, +0.0104] ✓ |

BM25 wins on val, embeddings win on test, same dataset and same code. Fusion shows the identical
pattern (`fused - emb`: +0.0022 ✓ on small val, -0.0017 ✓ on small test; alpha 0.70 on both bundles),
and it also appeared under xlmr, so it is a property of EB-NeRD rather than of one encoder or one
method. Plausible mechanism: val is a 2-day window against test's 7, the test block carries its own
later history window, and news relevance decays fast enough that the boundary is a distribution shift.

Design note §5 was rewritten around this. The old §5 claimed BM25 wins retrieval on EB-NeRD outright,
which is no longer true; the two-track finding survives as a difference of margin (+0.0289 AUC vs
+0.0030 recall@200, 10x) rather than of direction.

Unchanged: MIND (keeps MiniLM, untouched by this), the temporal split, BM25, and the harness.

### Two partial runs, and how they were caught

The re-run was killed twice mid-way by VSCode crashes, both times leaving mixed-encoder artifacts:
embeddings rewritten with contrastive while fusion and the reports were still xlmr-derived. Nothing
errored; `results/` simply described a system that never existed.

Caught by comparing artifact mtimes against `configs/datasets.yaml`'s mtime, since every score file
must postdate the config that produced it. That check is now the standard verification after any
encoder change, and it is worth more than a green test run: the tests all still passed in the
inconsistent state, because they assert leakage properties of the split, not agreement between stages.

`setsid` did not save the second attempt. What worked was running one stage per foreground call, so
each either completes or is visibly incomplete.
EOF

import polars as pl, numpy as np, zipfile, io, yaml, random

cfg = yaml.safe_load(open("configs/datasets.yaml"))["ebnerd_demo"]
root = "data/interim/ebnerd_testset/ebnerd_testset"
random.seed(7)

beh = pl.scan_parquet(f"{root}/test/behaviors.parquet").select(
    "impression_id","user_id","article_ids_inview").collect()
picks = sorted(random.sample(range(beh.height), 40))
want_users = set(beh["user_id"].gather(picks).to_list())

hist = (pl.scan_parquet(f"{root}/test/history.parquet", )
        .select("user_id","article_id_fixed")
        .filter(pl.col("user_id").is_in(list(want_users))).collect())
H = dict(zip(hist["user_id"].to_list(), hist["article_id_fixed"].to_list()))

need = set()
for u in want_users: need.update((H.get(u) or [])[-30:])
for i in picks: need.update(beh["article_ids_inview"][i].to_list())

vec = (pl.scan_parquet(cfg["embeddings"])
       .filter(pl.col("article_id").is_in(list(need))).collect())
col = [c for c in vec.columns if c != "article_id"][0]
# dict of float64 lists: deliberately not the submitter's array/float32 path
V = {a: np.asarray(v, dtype=np.float64) for a, v in zip(vec["article_id"].to_list(), vec[col].to_list())}
for a in V: V[a] /= (np.linalg.norm(V[a]) + 1e-9)

sub = {}
with zipfile.ZipFile("deliverable/submissions/ebnerd_predictions.zip") as z:
    with z.open("predictions.txt") as fh:
        want_ids = set(beh["impression_id"].gather(picks).to_list())
        for line in io.TextIOWrapper(fh, "utf-8"):
            sp = line.find(" ")
            iid = int(line[:sp])
            if iid in want_ids:
                sub[iid] = [int(x) for x in line[sp+2:line.rindex("]")].split(",")]
                if len(sub) == len(want_ids): break

mismatch = 0
for i in picks:
    iid, uid = beh["impression_id"][i], beh["user_id"][i]
    cands = beh["article_ids_inview"][i].to_list()
    rows = [V[a] for a in (H.get(uid) or [])[-30:] if a in V]
    u = np.mean(rows, axis=0) if rows else np.zeros(768)
    u = u / (np.linalg.norm(u) + 1e-9)
    s = np.array([V[a] @ u if a in V else 0.0 for a in cands])
    order = np.argsort(-s, kind="stable")
    mine = np.empty(len(s), dtype=int); mine[order] = np.arange(1, len(s)+1)
    if list(mine) != sub[iid]: mismatch += 1

print(f"independent float64 recomputation of {len(picks)} random impressions")
print(f"  mismatches: {mismatch}  ->  {'PASS' if mismatch == 0 else 'FAIL'}")

I asked an agent if my AI usage log was correct with respect to the lecture slide guidelines and it told  me this- There are three gaps a grader with slide 9 in hand will notice.

What lands well. §5 is the thing. Slide 9's example ("caught it because the candidate count disagreed with the S-curve prediction") is asking for exactly the shape you used: failure + the signal that surfaced it. The Danish stopword entry, mBERT scoring below random, the .to_list() OOM — each names the detector, not just the bug. §6 covers "never accept work you can't check" better than the slide asks, and verifying the leakage suite is non-vacuous by injecting a future click is the kind of detail that earns credit in a viva. The BM25 field ablation and the val-vs-test selection cost (0.0025 AUC) cover "measure, don't vibe."

Gap 1 — key prompts, and this is the graded one. Slide 9 says prompts are graded artifacts; slide 1 says commit key prompts to git alongside the code. Your §2 reasoning for not paraphrasing is correct, but it over-corrects: the lecture wants key prompts, a curated handful, not a reconstruction. Quoting verbatim from the export with pointers (timestamp or record index) contradicts nothing. No grader is reading 4,665 JSONL records to find the five prompts that actually steered the build. Add an appendix: the plan-mode scoping prompt, the one that triggered the field ablation, the one where you asked it to justify the BM25 defaults, the override exchanges from §5.

Gap 2 — context management (slide 5) is absent. Nothing on CLAUDE.md, /clear, or subagents, and two sessions of 3,743 and 922 records suggests long-running context. You have the perfect material for this already: .to_list() recurring three separate times is a textbook context-poisoning symptom, and the two mixed-encoder partial runs are what happens without a lean recurring context. Either say what you did, or name it as a failure the way you named the task-sizing one in §3.

Gap 3 — "read every diff, own every line" (slide 7). §5 opens by saying each failure was caught by a check rather than by reading the code, and §3 puts the first git commit on 17 Aug — sixteen days in. Those two facts together read as "no diffs were reviewed for two-thirds of the project," and the git log will confirm it. Own it explicitly with the same honesty you used on task-sizing, rather than leaving the reader to assemble it.

One optics flag. "First-person explanatory comments through the codebase (for viva readiness)" — the agent writing your understanding in your voice, for the exam that tests your understanding. It's probably fine in substance, but say plainly that you read and corrected them, or it invites exactly the wrong question.

Minor: §2's two sessions both starting 1 Aug with overlapping ranges looks like a duplicate export — one line explaining why there are two. And the §1 sentence "no human-written code … not either produced by or revised through Claude Code" tangles itself; just say all code passed through the agent.

     1	# AI usage log (Q7.4)

    11	## 1. Tools used

    30	
    31	These are the raw Claude Code session logs, unedited: every prompt I issued, every tool call the
    32	agent made, and every result it got back. They were checked before inclusion and contain no
    33	credentials or API tokens; the only personal identifier is my own email, from the git commit
    34	author field.

    37	transcripts themselves, and a hand-written prompt list that disagreed with the export would be
    38	worse than none. What §3 gives instead is a description of *what was delegated in each phase*,
    39	which the transcripts evidence.

    41	## 3. What was delegated, phase by phase
    42	
    43	Dates are from artifact mtimes and the git history, not from memory.
    44	
    45	| date | phase | what the agent was asked to do |
    46	|---|---|---|
    47	| 1 Aug | scoping | Read the assignment, write `SPEC.md` as a build plan, and explain Component-1. Plan mode was used before any code was written. |
    48	| 1–2 Aug | pipeline | Environment + dependency setup; `pipeline/download.py`; temporal split (`pipeline/split.py`) with integrity assertions; BM25 (`retrieval/bm25.py`). |
    49	| 4–5 Aug | scale + submission | EB-NeRD test set; streaming Codabench submitter (`pipeline/submit.py`); MIND-large submission. |
    50	| 10–11 Aug | semantic axis + eval | Embeddings and FAISS retrieval; fusion; the evaluation harness (`eval/`); the encoder ablation; `notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb`; first `DESIGN_NOTE.md`. |
    51	| 17 Aug | comprehension + hygiene | First-person explanatory comments through the codebase (for viva readiness); the field ablation; directory restructure; `docs/WALKTHROUGH.md`; first git commit. |
    52	| 19 Aug | final encoder + submission | Switch to `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector`; full EB-NeRD re-run; Codabench submissions and scores. |
    53	
    54	**Process note, stated plainly because it is the thing Q7.4 is really probing.** The work was
    55	not delegated as one instruction. It was scoped in plan mode first, the plan was reviewed and
    56	approved, and the build then proceeded in stages with the agent's design questions answered
    57	before it wrote code. Several decisions the agent surfaced as open (which retrieval framing to
    58	build, which dataset scale to target, which encoder to ship) were decided by me, not by it.
    59	Where I asked for something the agent argued was wrong, that exchange is in the transcript.
    60	
    61	That said, several individual delegated tasks were larger than the lecture's guidance
    62	recommends, and the two partial-run incidents in §5 are the direct consequence.
    63	
    64	## 4. AI-generated vs. human-written code
    65	
    66	Honestly marked, because the distinction is not a clean split:
    67	
    68	- **All source files in `pipeline/`, `retrieval/`, `eval/`, `tests/`, `scratchpad/` were written
    69	  by Claude Code.** No file was typed by hand from scratch.
    70	- **All prose in `docs/` and `deliverable/` was drafted by Claude Code**, then read and
    71	  corrected by me where it was wrong (see §5 for cases where it was).
    72	- **The decisions were mine**, and they are the part that is load-bearing:
    73	  - build both the re-rank and full-corpus retrieval tracks, not just one
    74	  - target `ebnerd_demo` + `mind_small`, scaling to `ebnerd_small`
    75	  - adopt `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector` as the shipped EB-NeRD encoder
    76	  - decline to add the serving-unavailable popularity feature to the leaderboard entry
    77	  - keep the repo private; keep `problem.md` out once the PDF superseded it
    78	- **Not written by the agent:** the assignment brief (`brief/`), the datasets, and the
    79	  organisers' provided article vectors.
    80	
    81	Per the course's stated policy, this makes no difference to assessment: evaluation is on my
    82	understanding, not the agent's. `docs/WALKTHROUGH.md` exists specifically so that understanding
    83	is documented rather than assumed.
    84	
    85	## 5. What worked, and what failed
    86	
    87	The failures are the useful part of this log, and each was caught by a check rather than by
    88	reading the code. Full detail for every entry is in `docs/NOTES.md`.
    89	
    90	**Caught by measurement:**
    91	
    92	| what | how it surfaced | outcome |
    93	|---|---|---|
    94	| No Danish stopword list (`bm25s` ships none) | EB-NeRD AUC sat near random and did not respond to history length | Supplied Snowball Danish list: val AUC 0.5035 → 0.5232. A missing stopword list is silent; it degrades ranking without erroring. |
    95	| Raw multilingual BERT scored **below random** (0.4857) | Encoder ablation on val | Not a bug: un-fine-tuned BERT vectors are not trained so cosine means topical similarity. Fusion independently drove its alpha to 0.00. |
    96	| `.to_list()` memory blow-up, found **three separate times** | OOM kill at 10 GB RSS (confirmed in `dmesg`), then twice more | Replaced with `explode().to_numpy()`. Peak 5.8 GB → far lower, byte-identical output. Named as *the* scaling wall in the design note. |
    97	| MIND submission was never actually streaming | OOM-killed after 200k of 2.37M impressions | CSV has no slice pushdown; added a one-off parquet conversion. Peak 4.2 GB → 2.86 GB, first 20,000 lines byte-identical. |
    98	| recall@K missing from every report | Re-reading the brief against the harness | `eval/run.py` never opened the retrieval files. Added with CIs and slices. |
    99	| Entities parsed then silently dropped | Re-reading Q1.4 against `_mind_news` | Present in the `.select()` upstream, absent downstream. |
   100	| BM25 document fields were an **untested assumption** | Asked the agent to justify the default; it could not | Ran the ablation: body costs −0.0166 AUC. The shipped choice was right but had never been measured. |
   101	| Design note carried numbers a rebuild had superseded | Cross-checking the note against `results/` | Tables had drifted from the artifacts they described. |
   102	
   103	**Caught by verification, not by the agent:**
   104	
   105	| what | how |
   106	|---|---|
   107	| Two partial pipeline runs left mixed-encoder artifacts | A crash killed the run mid-way; embeddings were rewritten with the new encoder while fusion and reports were still from the old one. Detected by comparing artifact mtimes against the config mtime, not by any error message. Both times the fix was a clean full re-run. |
   108	| A diff that looked like a regression was not | The file being compared against was the partial output of an OOM-killed run, not the smoke test. |
   109	
   110	**Where I overrode the agent:**
   111	
   112	| what | outcome |
   113	|---|---|
   114	| Asked it to write this log as a series of granular prompts I had not actually issued | It declined, on the grounds that Q7.4 also requires the raw transcripts and the two would contradict each other. This log is the honest version. |
   115	| Asked whether to add lifetime popularity to the leaderboard entry | It advised against and supplied the reason: the feature is 85% null on the corpus, so the offline gain would not transfer. Left out. |
   116	
   117	## 6. Verification practices used
   118	
   119	- **Assertions in the build, tests outside it.** `pipeline/split.py` asserts while building;
   120	  `tests/test_leakage.py` (19 tests) re-checks the same properties from the written artifacts.
   121	- **The leakage suite was verified non-vacuous** by injecting a future click into one row's
   122	  history and confirming the assertion fired. A suite that has never failed proves nothing.
   123	- **Byte-identical rebuilds.** Outputs are sorted on a unique key before writing, because
   124	  `polars.unique()` is hash-ordered; verified identical across three consecutive runs.
   125	- **Independent recomputation.** Submission files were validated on all 13,536,710 lines, plus
   126	  40 random impressions per dataset re-ranked in float64 through a separate code path.
   127	- **Selection on val, never test.** The clearest case: on MIND, MiniLM wins on val and XLM-R
   128	  wins on test. The val-chosen model shipped, costing 0.0025 test AUC.
