**I want to state the process plainly, because it's what Q7.4 is really probing.** I didn't
delegate this as one instruction. I scoped it in plan mode first, reviewed and approved the
plan, then had the build proceed in stages, answering the agent's design questions before it
wrote code. Several decisions it surfaced as open, which retrieval framing to build, which
dataset scale to target, which encoder to ship, I decided, not it. Where I told it something was
wrong, or it refused me outright, that exchange is in the transcript (§3 has one example of the
second kind).

That said, I gave it several individual tasks that were larger than the lecture's guidance
recommends, and the two partial-run incidents in §7 are the direct consequence.

runs from 1 Aug; my first commit is dated 19 Aug. Two separate things sit inside that gap and I

Why I hadn't pushed a GitHub repo before 19 Aug: this course originally used GitHub Classroom
for submission. GitHub Classroom got discontinued, and the TA only told us on 18 Aug that we
should push to our own repos in the meantime while they look for an alternative. I created a

Why I still only made one commit once a repo existed: that part is a genuine gap, and I'm
recording it as one. I could have kept a local git history from day one regardless of whether I
was pushing anywhere, and I didn't; my single 19 Aug commit covers all 87 files and 16,424 lines

build, because there was no git history to diff against. What stood in for that, imperfectly,
was the harness's own diff view on each edit, plus the verification practices in §8 (assertions,

don't substitute for me reading every line as it landed, which is what slide 7 actually asks
for.

## 5. Context management

Slide 5 asks for a lean, recurring `CLAUDE.md`, for `/clear` on contradiction, confusion,
poisoning, or a context that's grown too long, and for subagents to isolate work. Here's what I
actually did:

- **I used `CLAUDE.md`, but only from 17 Aug on** (`docs/NOTES.md` / repo history). Before that
  date I ran the project with no persistent instruction file at all. Once I created it, I edited
  it in place rather than rewriting it, and kept it short: project rules plus the global
  behavioral guidelines, not accumulated detail.
- **I didn't use `/clear`, but I did compact the context manually.** Per §2, both transcript
  files share one start timestamp: this was one long, continuously resumed session across the
  whole 19-day project, not a sequence of fresh contexts. Within that one session, though, I
  deliberately compacted the context rather than letting it grow unchecked. The export confirms
  **two** manually triggered compactions, both in `session-1`:

  | when | trigger | tokens before -> after |
  |---|---|---|
  | 2 Aug, 03:53 | manual | 287,337 -> 12,736 |
  | 10 Aug, 06:28 | manual | 386,823 -> 12,746 |

  I recall triggering a third compaction later in the project, but I can't find it as a
  `compact_boundary` record in either exported file. Maybe that session segment never got
  flushed to disk before a crash, or my own count is off by one. I'm recording two **confirmed**
  and a third **I remember but can't find in this export**, rather than rounding up to match my
  memory. Even the two I can confirm fall short of the slide's `/clear`-on-signal practice: I
  wasn't resetting on a specific trigger like contradiction or distraction, both confirmed
  compactions look reactive, sitting near 290-390k tokens rather than proactive. But it's real
  context hygiene, not none.
- **I didn't use subagents to isolate any of this project's own work.** (The `Agent` tool exists
  in the toolset and I've used it elsewhere in this account, just not to fork off pieces of this
  build.)

**What I think this plausibly cost me, stated as a hypothesis rather than something I can
prove:** the `.to_list()` -> boxed-Python-float memory blow-up in §7 got fixed once, then I had
the agent write the same bug again from scratch in two more files later in the same session
(`retrieval/embeddings.py`, then `pipeline/submit.py`). I don't have direct evidence this was
context "poisoning" in the slide's specific sense, an early mistake it stayed fixated on, rather
than the same gap in its Polars knowledge just showing up three times in a long session with
nothing forcing it to recheck earlier fixes against new code. Either way, a fresh context per
module, or an explicit instruction to check prior fixes before writing similar code, is the kind
of thing that would plausibly have caught it after the first instance instead of the third. I'm
recording this as a candidate cost of not managing context better, not a confirmed one.

## 6. AI-generated vs. human-written code

I'm marking this honestly, because the split isn't clean:

- **Claude Code wrote every source file in `pipeline/`, `retrieval/`, `eval/`, `tests/`,
  `scratchpad/`.** I didn't type any of them by hand from scratch.
- **Claude Code drafted every piece of prose in `docs/` and `deliverable/`**, and I read and
  checked each one against the underlying artifacts (`results/`, `NOTES.md`'s own measured
  numbers) rather than accepting it on the agent's say-so. §7 has the specific cases where that
  check found the prose wrong.
- **I want to call out the first-person explanatory comments through `pipeline/`, `retrieval/`,
  `eval/` directly**, since they're written to represent *my* understanding, for a viva that
  tests exactly that. I asked for them, then verified each one against the surrounding code and
  the design note's own numbers instead of shipping them unread. The field-ablation question in
  §3 is one example of that verification surfacing something the code didn't actually justify.
- **The decisions were mine**, and they're the part I think actually matters:
  - I chose to build both the re-rank and full-corpus retrieval tracks, not just one
  - I chose to target `ebnerd_demo` + `mind_small`, scaling to `ebnerd_small`
  - I chose to adopt `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector` as the shipped EB-NeRD encoder
  - I chose not to add the serving-unavailable popularity feature to the leaderboard entry
  - I chose to keep the repo private, and to drop `problem.md` once the PDF superseded it
- **The agent didn't write:** the assignment brief (`brief/`), the datasets, or the organisers'
  provided article vectors.

Per the course's stated policy, none of this changes how I'm assessed: I'm evaluated on my own
understanding, not the agent's. That's why `docs/WALKTHROUGH.md` exists, so that understanding
is written down rather than assumed.

## 7. What worked, and what failed

I think the failures are the most useful part of this log, and I caught every one of them with a
check, not by reading the code myself. Full detail for every entry is in `docs/NOTES.md`.

**Caught by measurement:**

| what | how it surfaced | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| No Danish stopword list (`bm25s` ships none) | EB-NeRD AUC sat near random and didn't respond to history length | I supplied the Snowball Danish list: val AUC 0.5035 -> 0.5232. A missing stopword list is silent; it degrades ranking without erroring. |
| Raw multilingual BERT scored **below random** (0.4857) | Encoder ablation on val | Not a bug: un-fine-tuned BERT vectors aren't trained so cosine means topical similarity. Fusion independently drove its alpha to 0.00. |
| `.to_list()` memory blow-up, found **three separate times** | OOM kill at 10 GB RSS (confirmed in `dmesg`), then twice more in different files | Replaced with `explode().to_numpy()`. Peak 5.8 GB -> far lower, byte-identical output. See §5 for why I think it recurred. |
| MIND submission was never actually streaming | OOM-killed after 200k of 2.37M impressions | CSV has no slice pushdown; I added a one-off parquet conversion. Peak 4.2 GB -> 2.86 GB, first 20,000 lines byte-identical. |

| Entities parsed then silently dropped | I re-read Q1.4 against `_mind_news` | Present in the `.select()` upstream, absent downstream. |

I caught it by comparing artifact mtimes against the config mtime, not from any error message. Both times I fixed it with a clean full re-run. |
| A diff that looked like a regression wasn't one | The file I was comparing against was the partial output of an OOM-killed run, not the smoke test. |

- **Assertions in the build, tests outside it.** `pipeline/split.py` asserts while building;

content.text:
All confirmed. Two things worth knowing before the list: Q3 in the actual PDF names exactly **"BERT/XLM-RoBERTa"** for the self-encoded arm, and this clause governs both datasets, so it's the same fidelity question the `contrastive_vector` decision already dealt with. And MIND's history is short (median 19, mean 32.6) against EB-NeRD's 258, which is directly relevant to one of the ablations below.

## Ablations worth running on MIND

Ranked by how cheap they are given the infra you already have, and what's genuinely untested.

**1. History-length sweep, specific to MIND.** The `HISTORY_LEN=30` sweep in `NOTES.md` was only ever run on EB-NeRD val, where it came back flat (0.4967→0.5059 across 1 to 100 clicks) because EB-NeRD's median history is 258 clicks, so cutting at 30 barely changes the query. MIND's median is 19. Thirty is close to "use everything" there, so the sweep could behave completely differently, and nobody's checked. Cheapest ablation on the list: sweep `HISTORY_LEN` on `mind_small` val only.

**2. The query/document field asymmetry, on MIND.** Already flagged in `NOTES.md` as untested: BM25's query is titles-only, documents are title+abstract. On EB-NeRD that asymmetry flipped the title-only-document setting into the retrieval winner. MIND's abstract coverage is 94.8% and pools are ~3× larger, so this could land differently, and it's a straight extension of the field ablation you already built (`scratchpad/field_ablation.py`).

**3. Entity overlap as a signal.** MIND ships Wikidata-linked entity annotations, currently parsed into the schema and never scored ("nothing scores on entities yet," per `NOTES.md`). A Jaccard overlap between a candidate's entities and the union of the user's recent-history entities, z-scored and blended in like the fusion weight, is a genuinely new axis, not a re-run of something already tried. EB-NeRD has entities too but MIND's are cleaner (canonical Wikidata IDs vs EB-NeRD's `ner_clusters`), so MIND is the better place to try it first.

**4. User-vector pooling.** Right now it's mean-of-last-30, re-normalized. The obvious alternative is max-similarity: score a candidate by its best match to *any* history item rather than to the average. Mean pooling blurs a user with genuinely diverse interests into a bland centroid; max-pooling could catch "this matches the one thing they read about yesterday" even if it's unlike everything else in their history. Purely a content-side scoring change, same vectors, so it stays inside C1 rather than drifting into C2's behavioral territory.

**5. Cold-start fallback, measured rather than just conventioned.** MIND has real cold-start users (1.8–3.0% across splits, unlike EB-NeRD's demo bundle which has none). The current convention is an all-zero score and empty retrieval for them. You already have `train_click_counts` built for the novelty metric; testing "fall back to train-popularity ranking for cold-start users" against the current "score nothing" convention, on the cold slice specifically, is cheap and answers a real design question. Worth being careful with the framing if you report it: it's a controlled ablation, not a silent swap into the servable system, same honesty the popularity feature already gets in §9.

**6. Whether `fused` can actually ship on the MIND leaderboard.** This is the expensive one, but it's the one with a real payoff. The leaderboard entry is embeddings-only because dense `get_scores` is ~10¹¹ operations at MIND-large scale. But the leaderboard task is re-ranking a given candidate pool, not full-corpus retrieval, so BM25 there only ever needs to score the handful of candidates in each impression, not the whole 120,961-article corpus. If that's right, a version of `submit.py`'s streaming path that scores BM25 restricted to just the candidate ids per batch (rather than calling `index.get_scores` over the full vocabulary) could make `fused` tractable at scale, closing the +0.0014 AUC gap that's currently left on the table. Worth checking whether that reasoning holds before spending the implementation time, since it's the one item here that touches the actual submission pipeline rather than just the offline harness.

Skip: re-running the stemming or compound-splitting ablations on MIND, those already ran on both datasets and MIND's conclusion (+0.0019 AUC, significant) is settled.

## Alternatives to MiniLM

Three real candidates, but all come with the same scope question `contrastive_vector` already raised, and I'd flag it the same way rather than skip it.

| model | dim | family | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2` | 768 | MPNet | the strongest model in the same "all-*" SBERT family MiniLM belongs to; general-purpose, not retrieval-specialized |
| `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5` | 768 | BERT | trained specifically for retrieval with hard-negative mining, not general sentence similarity, which is a better match for what you're actually doing (cosine ranking) than MiniLM's STS-style training |
| `intfloat/e5-base-v2` | 768 | BERT | also retrieval-trained; needs `"query: "` / `"passage: "` text prefixes to work correctly, easy to forget and it silently tanks quality if you do |

**The scope question, stated plainly:** MiniLM is a distilled transformer, not literally BERT or XLM-RoBERTa, and it already shipped without this being litigated. mpnet is architecturally closer to BERT than MiniLM is; BGE and E5 are both built on BERT backbones, so arguably more clearly inside Q3's wording than what's already running. I'd apply the same rule the `contrastive_vector` decision used: it's a defensible reading, but it's a reading, and it belongs in the design note as a stated choice rather than something assumed.

**What I won't claim:** that any of these will actually beat MiniLM on *this* task. General MTEB/retrieval-benchmark superiority is a reasonable prior, not proof for mean-pooled, L2-normalized cosine similarity over MIND titles+abstracts specifically. The EB-NeRD encoder ablation already demonstrated this exact trap: the 768-d model lost to the 300-d one, and size predicted nothing. Same protocol applies here: encode with `notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb` (swap `MODEL`), select on val, report test, and let the numbers decide rather than the parameter count.

Want me to run any of these? Cheapest first would be #1 (history-length sweep) or #2 (field ablation on MIND), both reuse code you already have and need no new downloads.

content.text: Cached MiniLM embeddings exist, so no re-encoding needed. Writing a non-destructive sweep script, same pattern as `field_ablation.py`, covering both BM25 and embeddings since MIND's shipped system leans on both (`fused` is the reported headline there):

input.command:
cat > /home/neemon/Desktop/semesters/sem-5/ire/assignments/ass-1/scratchpad/history_len_sweep.py <<'PYEOF'
"""HISTORY_LEN sweep on MIND, both scorers.

The original sweep (docs/NOTES.md, "BM25 results") only ran on EB-NeRD val, where it came back
flat because EB-NeRD's median history is 258 clicks and cutting at 30 barely touches the query.
MIND's median history is 19 (mean 32.6), so HISTORY_LEN=30 is close to "use everything" there,
and the shipped value was never actually checked against MIND's own history distribution.

Non-destructive: monkeypatches the HISTORY_LEN each module reads at call time and never writes
to data/processed. Verify with `md5sum data/processed/mind_small/{bm25,emb}_val.parquet` before
and after.

    .venv/bin/python scratchpad/history_len_sweep.py
"""
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import retrieval.bm25 as bm25mod                    # noqa: E402
import retrieval.embeddings as embmod                # noqa: E402
from eval import bootstrap, metrics                  # noqa: E402

DATASET = "mind_small"
SPLIT = "val"
SWEEP = [1, 3, 5, 10, 30, 100]          # same grid as the EB-NeRD sweep, for comparability
SHIPPED = 30

cfg = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml").read_text())[DATASET]
proc = ROOT / "data/processed" / DATASET
articles = pl.read_parquet(proc / "articles.parquet")
impressions = pl.read_parquet(proc / f"impressions_{SPLIT}.parquet")

print(f"{DATASET} {SPLIT}: {impressions.height:,} impressions, {articles.height:,} articles")
hist_len = impressions["history"].list.len()
print(f"history length: median {hist_len.median():.0f}, mean {hist_len.mean():.1f}, "
      f"max {hist_len.max()}\n")

position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
published = None  # MIND carries no publication dates

labels = [
    np.fromiter((c in set(k) for c in cand), bool, len(cand))
    for cand, k in zip(impressions["candidates"].to_list(), impressions["clicked"].to_list())
]

# --- BM25: index is independent of HISTORY_LEN, build once ---
index, stemmer = bm25mod.build_index(articles, cfg, ("title", "abstract"))

# --- embeddings: vectors are independent of HISTORY_LEN, load once (cached) ---
vectors = embmod.load_vectors(DATASET, cfg, articles)
print()

results = {"bm25": {}, "emb": {}}
for n in SWEEP:
    bm25mod.HISTORY_LEN = n
    embmod.HISTORY_LEN = n

    t0 = time.time()
    bm25_scores, _ = bm25mod.score_split(index, stemmer, cfg, impressions, articles, position, published)
    bm25_scores = [np.asarray(s, dtype=np.float64) for s in bm25_scores]
    v, keep = metrics.per_impression(bm25_scores, labels)
    results["bm25"][n] = {"auc": v["auc"], "ndcg10": v["ndcg@10"]}

    emb_scores, _ = embmod.score_split(impressions, articles, vectors, position, published)
    emb_scores = [np.asarray(s, dtype=np.float64) for s in emb_scores]
    v, keep = metrics.per_impression(emb_scores, labels)
    results["emb"][n] = {"auc": v["auc"], "ndcg10": v["ndcg@10"]}

    print(f"  HISTORY_LEN={n:<4} done in {time.time()-t0:.0f}s")

bm25mod.HISTORY_LEN = SHIPPED
embmod.HISTORY_LEN = SHIPPED

print(f"\n{'HISTORY_LEN':<12} {'bm25 AUC':<26} {'emb AUC':<26} {'bm25 nDCG@10':<26} {'emb nDCG@10':<26}")
print("-" * 116)
for n in SWEEP:
    row = [str(n) + ("  (shipped)" if n == SHIPPED else "")]
    for scorer in ("bm25", "emb"):
        row.append(bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(results[scorer][n]["auc"])))
    for scorer in ("bm25", "emb"):
        row.append(bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(results[scorer][n]["ndcg10"])))
    print(f"{row[0]:<12} {row[1]:<26} {row[2]:<26} {row[3]:<26} {row[4]:<26}")

print(f"\npaired differences vs HISTORY_LEN={SHIPPED} (95% CI; significant if it excludes zero)")
print("-" * 116)
for scorer in ("bm25", "emb"):
    for n in SWEEP:
        if n == SHIPPED:
            continue
        mean, lo, hi, sig = bootstrap.paired(results[scorer][n]["auc"], results[scorer][SHIPPED]["auc"])
        print(f"  {scorer:<6} n={n:<4} AUC {mean:+.4f} [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]  {'SIG' if sig else '   '}")
PYEOF

content.text:
**This is the opposite result from EB-NeRD, and it's not close.** Where the EB-NeRD sweep was flat (AUC moved 0.009 across the whole 1→100 range), MIND's is steeply monotonic and every single point is statistically significant against the shipped value:

| HISTORY_LEN | bm25 AUC | emb AUC |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.5165 | 0.5576 |
| 3 | 0.5377 | 0.5910 |
| 5 | 0.5483 | 0.6064 |
| 10 | 0.5637 | 0.6220 |
| **30 (shipped)** | **0.5801** | **0.6338** |
| 100 | 0.5840 | 0.6356 |

## What this means for the shipped MIND system

**Truncating to `HISTORY_LEN=30` costs real accuracy on MIND, and the sweep shows exactly how much.** Cutting the query at 1 click instead of the full history throws away 0.076 AUC on embeddings and 0.064 on BM25, both far outside the confidence interval. That's larger than the entire encoder-choice decision (MiniLM vs XLM-R was a 0.0025-0.008 AUC question) and comparable to the entire lexical-vs-semantic gap this project has spent the most effort on.

**Going the other direction, from 30 to 100, still helps and is still significant** (+0.0039 bm25, +0.0018 emb), just by a much smaller margin. Given MIND's mean history length is 33.3, a cutoff of 100 is already "almost everyone's whole history" for most users, so the curve is visibly flattening but hasn't gone flat yet, unlike EB-NeRD where it was flat from 1 click onward.

**Why the two datasets disagree, and it comes down to what the constant is actually doing on each.** On EB-NeRD (median history 258, mean 33-ish is a different regime entirely), a cutoff of 30 is a real truncation that discards the vast majority of history, and it turns out that discarding didn't matter, older clicks weren't adding useful signal there. On MIND (median history 20, mean 33.3), a cutoff of 30 is close to *no* truncation at all for a typical user. So "the same constant, 30, tuned once and reused across both datasets" wasn't tuned on MIND at all in any meaningful sense, it just happened to sit near the natural history length there.

## The actionable finding

`HISTORY_LEN=100` (or higher, un-swept) is very likely to beat 30 on MIND, by a real and significant margin, and the sweep hasn't found the ceiling since AUC was still rising at 100. Worth extending the grid to 200/558 (max) to see where it plateaus.

Given the fusion weight and the leaderboard both depend on this constant, and it's currently shared globally between both datasets, this is a genuine, measured improvement available on MIND specifically, distinct from anything in `NOTES.md` so far. Want me to extend the sweep to find where it actually plateaus, or move straight to making `HISTORY_LEN` per-dataset in the config and re-running the full MIND pipeline at the better value?

def mean_pool(histories: pl.Series, article_row: np.ndarray,
              vectors: np.ndarray, dim: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """User vectors: mean of the last HISTORY_LEN article vectors, L2-normalised.

    Row i corresponds to histories[i]. Users with no usable history stay all-zero, which
    is the cold-start convention the offline scorer uses too.
    """
    users = np.zeros((len(histories), dim), dtype=np.float32)
    for i, history in enumerate(histories):
        if history is None or len(history) == 0:
            continue
        rows = article_row[np.asarray(history[-HISTORY_LEN:], dtype=np.int64)]
        if len(rows):
            users[i] = vectors[rows].mean(axis=0)
    users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9
    return users


def write_lines(handle, impression_ids: np.ndarray, scores: np.ndarray,
                lengths: np.ndarray) -> None:
    """Split the flat score array back per impression, rank, and emit one line each."""
    offset = 0
    for imp_id, n in zip(impression_ids, lengths):
        ranks = ranks_from(scores[offset:offset + n])
        offset += n
        handle.write(f"{imp_id} [{','.join(map(str, ranks.tolist()))}]\n")


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------- EB-NeRD

def stream_ebnerd(cfg: dict, limit: int | None):
    root = INTERIM / "ebnerd_testset/ebnerd_testset"
    articles = pl.read_parquet(root / "articles.parquet", columns=["article_id"])
    ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy().astype(np.int64)

    # Integer ids let us use a lookup array instead of a dict of 125k strings — and,
    # more importantly, keep 206M candidate ids out of Python entirely.
    # A plain array indexed BY article id, holding its row in `vectors`. Ids are dense ints,
    # so this is an O(1) lookup with no hashing and no Python objects, and it vectorises:
    # article_row[flat] resolves millions of candidates in one call.
    article_row = np.full(int(ids.max()) + 1, -1, dtype=np.int64)
    article_row[ids] = np.arange(len(ids))

    vectors = _provided_vectors(cfg, articles)
    dim = vectors.shape[1]
    # Unknown candidates land on a trailing zero row: score 0, no crash, no silent
    # misalignment onto some other article's vector.
    vectors = np.vstack([vectors, np.zeros((1, dim), dtype=np.float32)])
    article_row[article_row < 0] = len(vectors) - 1

    print("  building user vectors from history.parquet")
    history = pl.read_parquet(root / "test/history.parquet",
                              columns=["user_id", "article_id_fixed"])
    users = mean_pool(history["article_id_fixed"], article_row, vectors, dim)

def stream_mind(cfg: dict, limit: int | None):
    root = INTERIM / "MINDlarge_test/MINDlarge_test"
    news = pl.read_csv(
        root / "news.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False, quote_char=None,
        new_columns=["article_id", "category", "subcategory", "title", "abstract",
                     "url", "title_entities", "abstract_entities"],
    ).select("article_id", "title", "abstract")

    vectors = _encoded_vectors(news, cfg["model"])
    dim = vectors.shape[1]
    vectors = np.vstack([vectors, np.zeros((1, dim), dtype=np.float32)])
    article_row = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(news["article_id"])}
    unknown = len(vectors) - 1

    prepared = _mind_parquet(root, article_row, unknown)
    scan = pl.scan_parquet(prepared)
    total = scan.select(pl.len()).collect().item()
    if limit:
        total = min(total, limit)
    print(f"  {total:,} impressions, {len(article_row):,} articles, dim {dim}")

    for offset in range(0, total, BATCH):
        batch = scan.slice(offset, min(BATCH, total - offset)).collect()
        # Histories are already row indices, so deduplication is over tuples of ints.
        # Dedup is per slice: across slices identical histories are recomputed, which is
        # the trade streaming makes for bounded memory. Mean-pooling 30 vectors is cheap.
        order: dict[tuple, int] = {}
        index = np.fromiter(
            (order.setdefault(tuple(h[-HISTORY_LEN:]), len(order))
             for h in batch["history_rows"]),
            dtype=np.int64, count=batch.height,
        )
        users = np.zeros((len(order), dim), dtype=np.float32)
        for key, i in order.items():
            rows = np.asarray(key, dtype=np.int64)
            rows = rows[rows != unknown]

"""BM25 over article text, on the two tracks the assignment asks for.

  re-rank    score the candidate pool the log already shows for an impression.
             Comparable to the leaderboards, which rank within the given pool.
  retrieval  ignore the pool and pull the top-K from the whole corpus.
             This is the "candidate generation to a few hundred" half of the spec.

The query for both is the user's recent click history: the titles of their last
HISTORY_LEN clicked articles, concatenated. History is already guaranteed strictly
earlier than the impression by pipeline.split, so the query cannot leak.

Both tracks come out of a single scoring pass. Queries are deduplicated first — history
is constant per user within a split, so the ~230k MIND impressions collapse to far fewer
distinct queries, and BM25 runs once per distinct query rather than once per impression.

    python -m retrieval.bm25                       # both datasets, all splits
    python -m retrieval.bm25 ebnerd_demo --fields title

Writes, per dataset and split:
    bm25_<split>.parquet       impression_id, bm25        aligned to `candidates`
    retrieval_<split>.parquet  impression_id, retrieved   top-K ids, best first
"""

import argparse
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import bm25s
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import Stemmer
import yaml
from tqdm import tqdm

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
PROC = ROOT / "data/processed"

# Most recent clicks forming the query, per dataset config (`history_len`). News interest
# decays fast, so how far back to look is a real per-dataset question, not one constant:
# the sweep in docs/NOTES.md found EB-NeRD flat but MIND rising significantly to 100.
TOP_K = 200        # "a few hundred candidates"
OVERFETCH = 3      # fetch TOP_K*OVERFETCH before the publication-date filter thins it

FIELDS = {
    "title": ("title",),
    "title_abstract": ("title", "abstract"),
    "title_abstract_body": ("title", "abstract", "body"),
}


def document_text(articles: pl.DataFrame, fields: tuple[str, ...]) -> list[str]:
    present = [f for f in fields if articles[f].null_count() < articles.height]
    missing = set(fields) - set(present)
    if missing:
        print(f"  note: {'/'.join(sorted(missing))} is empty for this dataset, skipping")
    return (
        articles.select(
            pl.concat_str([pl.col(f).fill_null("") for f in present], separator=" ")
        )
        .to_series()
        .to_list()
    )


def stopwords_for(cfg: dict):
    """bm25s ships lists for some languages only; others come from configs/."""
    if cfg.get("stopwords_file"):
        lines = (ROOT / cfg["stopwords_file"]).read_text().splitlines()
        return [w for w in (ln.strip() for ln in lines) if w and not w.startswith("#")]
    return cfg.get("stopwords")


def build_index(articles: pl.DataFrame, cfg: dict, fields: tuple[str, ...]):
    # Stemming and stopwords are per-language (EB-NeRD is Danish, MIND is English), so both
    # come from the dataset config. Getting this wrong silently degrades BM25 rather than
    # erroring: a Danish corpus stemmed as English just matches worse.
    stemmer = Stemmer.Stemmer(cfg["language"])
    texts = document_text(articles, fields)
    tokens = bm25s.tokenize(
        texts, stopwords=stopwords_for(cfg), stemmer=stemmer, show_progress=False
    )
    index = bm25s.BM25()
    index.index(tokens, show_progress=False)
    return index, stemmer


def build_queries(impressions: pl.DataFrame, title_of: dict[str, str], history_len: int) -> list[str]:
    """Last `history_len` clicked titles per impression. Empty for cold-start users."""
    # I treat "what this user recently read" as the query and the corpus as documents, which
    # turns recommendation into ordinary ad-hoc retrieval. Titles only, and only the most
    # recent history_len, because news interest decays fast and older clicks add drift.
    return [
        " ".join(title_of.get(a, "") for a in hist[-history_len:])
        for hist in impressions["history"].to_list()
    ]


def score_split(index, stemmer, cfg, impressions, articles, position, published):
    """One pass over distinct queries, filling both tracks."""
    queries = build_queries(impressions, dict(zip(articles["article_id"], articles["title"])), cfg["history_len"])

    # A user's history is fixed within a split, so the same query text recurs across all of
    # that user's impressions. I map each distinct query to an id, then invert it into
    # query -> [rows that share it], so BM25 scores each query once and I fan the result out.
    # setdefault gives me "look up or assign the next id" in one step.
    order: dict[str, int] = {}
    per_impression = []
    for q in queries:
        per_impression.append(order.setdefault(q, len(order)))
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = defaultdict(list)
    for row, q_id in enumerate(per_impression):
        groups[q_id].append(row)
    print(f"    {len(order):,} distinct queries for {impressions.height:,} impressions")

    tokenized = bm25s.tokenize(
        list(order), stopwords=stopwords_for(cfg), stemmer=stemmer,
        return_ids=False, show_progress=False,
    )

    candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
    timestamps = impressions["timestamp"].to_list()
    article_ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy()
    n_fetch = min(TOP_K * OVERFETCH, len(article_ids))

    cand_scores: list = [None] * impressions.height
    retrieved: list = [None] * impressions.height

    for q_id, tokens in enumerate(tqdm(tokenized, desc="    scoring", unit="q", leave=False)):
        rows = groups[q_id]
        if not tokens:
            # Cold start: no history, so BM25 has no query. Zero scores and an empty
            # retrieval, rather than an arbitrary ranking that would look like a result.
            for row in rows:
                cand_scores[row] = np.zeros(len(candidates[row]), dtype=np.float32)
                retrieved[row] = []
            continue

        # One dense score vector over the whole corpus, which both tracks then read from.
        scores = index.get_scores(tokens)
        # argpartition to find the top n_fetch is O(corpus); fully sorting 125k scores when
        # I only need 600 of them would not be. I sort only that small slice afterwards.
        top = np.argpartition(-scores, n_fetch - 1)[:n_fetch]
        top = top[np.argsort(-scores[top])]

        for row in rows:
            # Re-rank track: just look up the pool's articles in the same score vector.
            cand_scores[row] = scores[[position[a] for a in candidates[row]]].astype(np.float32)
            hits = top
            if published is not None:
                # An article published after the impression could not have been shown.
                # I over-fetched by OVERFETCH precisely so this filter still leaves TOP_K.
                hits = hits[published[hits] <= np.datetime64(timestamps[row])]
            retrieved[row] = article_ids[hits[:TOP_K]].tolist()

    return cand_scores, retrieved


def run(name: str, cfg: dict, fields: tuple[str, ...], splits: list[str]) -> None:
    print(f"\n{name}  fields={'+'.join(fields)}")
    articles = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / "articles.parquet")
    index, stemmer = build_index(articles, cfg, fields)
    print(f"  indexed {articles.height:,} articles")

    position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
    published = None
    if articles["published_time"].null_count() < articles.height:
        published = articles["published_time"].to_numpy()
    else:
        print("  note: no publication dates; retrieval cannot filter unpublished articles")

    for split in splits:
        impressions = pl.read_parquet(PROC / name / f"impressions_{split}.parquet")
        print(f"  {split}: {impressions.height:,} impressions")
        cand_scores, retrieved = score_split(
            index, stemmer, cfg, impressions, articles, position, published
        )

        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "bm25": [s.tolist() for s in cand_scores],
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"bm25_{split}.parquet")
        pl.DataFrame({
            "impression_id": impressions["impression_id"],
            "retrieved": retrieved,
        }).write_parquet(PROC / name / f"retrieval_{split}.parquet")

        # Recall@K here is a build-time sanity signal, not the reported metric.
        clicked = impressions["clicked"].to_list()
        hit = sum(
            bool(set(c) & set(r)) for c, r in zip(clicked, retrieved) if c
        )
        print(f"    recall@{TOP_K} (full-corpus retrieval): {hit / impressions.height:.4f}")


def main() -> None:
    config = yaml.safe_load(CONFIG.read_text())
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", default=list(config))
    parser.add_argument("--fields", choices=list(FIELDS), default="title_abstract")
    parser.add_argument("--splits", nargs="+", default=["train", "val", "test"])
    args = parser.parse_args()

    for name in args.datasets:
        run(name, config[name], FIELDS[args.fields], args.splits)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

1	"""Semantic counterpart to retrieval/bm25.py — same two tracks, same output shape.
2	
3	Deliberately mirrors bm25.py: same CLI, same query-deduplication pass, same file naming.
4	Only the scorer differs, so the lexical and semantic axes stay directly comparable.
5	
6	  re-rank    cosine between the user vector and each candidate in the given pool
7	  retrieval  FAISS inner-product search over the whole corpus for the top-K
8	
9	The user vector is the mean of the L2-normalised vectors of their last `history_len` clicked
10	articles. History is guaranteed strictly earlier than the impression by pipeline.split.
11

13	  EB-NeRD  the organisers' 300-d word2vec document vectors (config `embeddings`), picked
14	           over bert_base_multilingual_cased by the val-only ablation in NOTES.md

16	           to data/processed/<dataset>/embeddings.parquet, so encoding happens once

18	    python -m retrieval.embeddings

63	    ).astype(np.float32)
64	
65	
66	def _unnest(column: pl.Series, rows: int) -> np.ndarray:

1	"""Codabench leaderboard submissions for both competitions.
2	
3	The leaderboards score held-out test sets that are far larger than anything the offline
4	harness touches — EB-NeRD 13.5M impressions (206M candidate pairs), MIND-large 2.4M — so
5	this cannot reuse `retrieval/embeddings.py`, which materialises every impression at once.
6	The scoring *semantics* are identical (mean of the last HISTORY_LEN article vectors,
7	L2-normalised, cosine against each candidate); only the execution is streamed.
8	
9	    python -m pipeline.submit ebnerd            -> submissions/ebnerd_predictions.zip
10	    python -m pipeline.submit mind              -> submissions/mind_prediction.zip
11	    python -m pipeline.submit ebnerd --limit 50000     smoke test on a prefix
12	
13	Format, from each competition's Submission Guidelines (fetched from the Codabench API):
14	
15	    <impression_id> [r1,r2,...,rn]
16	
17	`ri` is the rank *of the i-th candidate as listed in the test file*, an integer in 1..n
18	where 1 is the best. Row order must match the test file. The zip must contain the text
19	file and nothing else — no folders, no __MACOSX.
20	
21	Only the embedding scorer ships here, on both datasets, because BM25's `get_scores` is dense
22	over the whole corpus per distinct query and does not survive these sizes (DESIGN_NOTE §10).
23	
24	**So the leaderboard entry is not the reported headline system, and the gap is not free.**
25	Offline, `fused` beats embeddings alone by +0.0014 AUC on MIND and +0.0095 on EB-NeRD; on
26	EB-NeRD embeddings alone also lose to BM25 alone, making the submitted system the weakest of
27	the three measured. Reported as two different systems rather than letting the better number
28	stand in for the one actually uploaded — see DESIGN_NOTE §11.
29	
30	Which article vectors get used comes from `configs/datasets.yaml`, the same key
31	`retrieval/embeddings.py` reads, so the encoder chosen by the ablation cannot silently
32	diverge between the report and the submission.
33	"""
34	
35	import argparse
36	import zipfile
37	from pathlib import Path
38	
39	import numpy as np
40	import polars as pl
41	import yaml
42	
43	
44	ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
45	CONFIG = ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml"
46	INTERIM = ROOT / "data/interim"
47	OUT = ROOT / "deliverable/submissions"
48	
49	# Impressions per streamed slice. Peak memory is one slice, not the dataset.
50	BATCH = 200_000
51	# Candidate pairs per vectorised dot-product block. A block materialises two
52	# (PAIR_BLOCK, dim) float32 arrays, so this is the real memory knob: 65536 x 768 x 4 x 2
53	# is ~400 MB, which is what keeps a 206M-pair run inside a 15 GB machine.
54	PAIR_BLOCK = 65_536
55	
56	
57	def ranks_from(scores: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
58	    """Rank of each candidate, 1 = highest score.
59	
60	    Stable sort, so equal scores keep the order the test file listed them in and the
61	    output is reproducible. A cold-start user scores every candidate 0 and therefore
62	    gets the identity ranking — no ordering is invented from nothing.
63	    """
64	    order = np.argsort(-scores, kind="stable")
65	    out = np.empty(len(scores), dtype=np.int64)
66	    out[order] = np.arange(1, len(scores) + 1)
67	    return out
68	
69	
70	def score_pairs(article_rows: np.ndarray, user_rows: np.ndarray,
71	                vectors: np.ndarray, users: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
72	    """Cosine for every (candidate, user) pair, in blocks so the gather stays bounded."""
73	    out = np.empty(len(article_rows), dtype=np.float32)
74	    for start in range(0, len(article_rows), PAIR_BLOCK):
75	        sl = slice(start, start + PAIR_BLOCK)
76	        # einsum "ij,ij->i" is a ROW-WISE dot product: pair i of the left with pair i of the
77	        # right. I want 206M individual (candidate, user) dots, not a 206M x 206M matrix,
78	        # which is what a plain @ would attempt. The fancy-index gather is what actually
79	        # allocates, so PAIR_BLOCK caps that rather than the arithmetic.
80	        out[sl] = np.einsum(
81	            "ij,ij->i", vectors[article_rows[sl]], users[user_rows[sl]]
82	        )
83	    return out
84	
85	
86	def mean_pool(histories: pl.Series, article_row: np.ndarray,
87	              vectors: np.ndarray, dim: int, history_len: int) -> np.ndarray:
88	    """User vectors: mean of the last `history_len` article vectors, L2-normalised.
89	
90	    Row i corresponds to histories[i]. Users with no usable history stay all-zero, which
91	    is the cold-start convention the offline scorer uses too.
92	    """
93	    users = np.zeros((len(histories), dim), dtype=np.float32)
94	    for i, history in enumerate(histories):
95	        if history is None or len(history) == 0:
96	            continue
97	        rows = article_row[np.asarray(history[-history_len:], dtype=np.int64)]
98	        if len(rows):
99	            users[i] = vectors[rows].mean(axis=0)
100	    users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9
101	    return users
102	
103	
104	def write_lines(handle, impression_ids: np.ndarray, scores: np.ndarray,
105	                lengths: np.ndarray) -> None:
106	    """Split the flat score array back per impression, rank, and emit one line each."""
107	    offset = 0
108	    for imp_id, n in zip(impression_ids, lengths):
109	        ranks = ranks_from(scores[offset:offset + n])
110	        offset += n
111	        handle.write(f"{imp_id} [{','.join(map(str, ranks.tolist()))}]\n")
112	
113	
114	# ------------------------------------------------------------------------- EB-NeRD
115	
116	def stream_ebnerd(cfg: dict, limit: int | None):
117	    root = INTERIM / "ebnerd_testset/ebnerd_testset"
118	    articles = pl.read_parquet(root / "articles.parquet", columns=["article_id"])
119	    ids = articles["article_id"].to_numpy().astype(np.int64)
120	
121	    # Integer ids let us use a lookup array instead of a dict of 125k strings — and,
122	    # more importantly, keep 206M candidate ids out of Python entirely.
123	    # A plain array indexed BY article id, holding its row in `vectors`. Ids are dense ints,
124	    # so this is an O(1) lookup with no hashing and no Python objects, and it vectorises:
125	    # article_row[flat] resolves millions of candidates in one call.
126	    article_row = np.full(int(ids.max()) + 1, -1, dtype=np.int64)
127	    article_row[ids] = np.arange(len(ids))
128	
129	    vectors = _provided_vectors(cfg, articles)
130	    dim = vectors.shape[1]
131	    # Unknown candidates land on a trailing zero row: score 0, no crash, no silent

content.content:
## 11. Leaderboard submissions

Both competitions score held-out sets far larger than the splits above (`ebnerd_testset` (13,536,710
impressions and MIND-large test impressions, and MIND-large test 2,370,727), so `pipeline/submit.py` streams them (§10) with unchanged
scoring semantics. **Both entries are embeddings-only rather than `fused`**: on EB-NeRD that *is* the
reported system (§6), and on MIND it costs a known 0.0014 AUC, reported as a different system rather
than letting the stronger fused number stand in for the one uploaded. The reason is the §10 scaling
wall, not preference: BM25's `get_scores` is dense over the corpus per distinct query, which at ~2M
distinct MIND histories is ~10¹¹ operations.

| | submission | AUC | MRR | nDCG@5 | nDCG@10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD (RecSys 2024, comp. 2469) | 893893 | **0.5336** | 0.3412 | 0.3779 | 0.4576 |
| MIND (comp. 13967) | 892088 | **0.6460** | 0.3160 | 0.3405 | 0.3963 |

**The leaderboard came in above the offline estimate on seven of eight metrics**, against far larger
and genuinely held-out sets: EB-NeRD +0.0031 AUC over its offline 0.5305, MIND +0.0121 over 0.6339.
That is the reassuring direction to be wrong in. A leaky evaluation typically posts offline numbers
that collapse on held-out data; these did the opposite, which is corroboration for §2's split that no
amount of internal assertion could provide.

The one disagreement is MIND's MRR, 0.316 against 0.349 offline, while its AUC and both nDCGs rose.
Recorded as unexplained rather than guessed at. The most likely cause is a definitional difference on
multi-click impressions: `eval/metrics.py` takes the reciprocal rank of the *first* clicked article,
and an implementation averaging over *all* clicked articles scores systematically lower there while
leaving AUC and nDCG largely untouched. Testable only against the organisers' scorer, which is not
published.

EB-NeRD allows five submissions a day and scores for hours, so output is validated offline rather than
by trial: all 13,536,710 lines checked as rank permutations of the right length in the test file's exact
row order, plus 40 random impressions per dataset re-ranked in float64 through an independent code path.

**Leaderboard screenshots:** *(attach the two Codabench result rows)*

Both competitions score held-out sets far larger than the splits above (`ebnerd_testset`, 13,536,710
impressions; MIND-large test, 2,370,727), so `pipeline/submit.py` streams them (§10) with unchanged
scoring semantics. **Both entries are embeddings-only rather than `fused`**: on EB-NeRD that *is* the
reported system (§6), and on MIND it costs a known 0.0012 AUC, reported as a different system rather
than letting the stronger fused number stand in for the one uploaded. The reason is the §10 scaling
wall, not preference: BM25's `get_scores` is dense over the corpus per distinct query, which at ~2M
distinct MIND histories is ~10¹¹ operations.

| | submission | AUC | MRR | nDCG@5 | nDCG@10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD (RecSys 2024, comp. 2469) | 893893 | **0.5336** | 0.3412 | 0.3779 | 0.4576 |
| MIND (comp. 13967) | 892088 | **0.6460** | 0.3160 | 0.3405 | 0.3963 |

**Each submission has to be read against the offline number for the system that actually produced
it, not against whatever the offline harness currently reports.** Both moved since these were built:
EB-NeRD's encoder changed (word2vec/XLM-R -> `contrastive_vector`) and MIND's `history_len` changed
(30 -> 100, this section). Comparing against the *current* offline numbers would silently compare two
different systems.

**EB-NeRD (893893) was built after the `contrastive_vector` switch**, so its correct baseline is the
current offline `emb` row: 0.5397 / 0.3492 / 0.3831 / 0.4627. Against that, the leaderboard came in
**below offline on all four metrics** (AUC −0.0061, MRR −0.0080, nDCG@5 −0.0052, nDCG@10 −0.0051). This
is the expected direction, if anything, a larger and genuinely independent population should regress
slightly toward the population mean rather than repeat a specific split's luck, and it is the opposite
of what an earlier version of this note claimed, which compared 893893 against a stale 0.5305 baseline
left over from the pre-`contrastive_vector` build. Caught while writing this section, corrected here
rather than left standing.

**MIND (892088) predates the `history_len` change above**, so its correct baseline is the *old*
`history_len=30` offline `emb` row: AUC 0.6339, MRR 0.3486, nDCG@5 0.3315, nDCG@10 0.3911, not the
current, better numbers in §6's table. Against that correct baseline, the leaderboard beat offline on
three of four metrics (AUC +0.0121, nDCG@5 +0.0090, nDCG@10 +0.0052) and lost on MRR (0.316 vs 0.349
offline), recorded as unexplained rather than guessed at. The most likely cause is a definitional
difference on multi-click impressions: `eval/metrics.py` takes the reciprocal rank of the *first*
clicked article, and an implementation averaging over *all* clicked articles would score systematically
lower there while leaving AUC and nDCG largely untouched. Testable only against the organisers' scorer,
which is not published.

**Neither leaderboard entry reflects the current shipped pipeline.** Rebuilding and resubmitting both,
now that the encoder and `history_len` fixes are in, is the obvious next step and is not done here:
EB-NeRD allows five submissions a day and both take real wall-clock time to score, so it is a deliberate
choice rather than an oversight.

1	# Component-1 Design Note — lexical & semantic retrieval on EB-NeRD and MIND
2	
3	## 1. What was built
4	
5	A config-driven pipeline from raw archives to metric reports in one command — `make data` for Q1's
6	feature store, `make all` for everything — across **EB-NeRD demo** (49k impressions / 1,590 users),
7	**EB-NeRD small** (478k / 15,143) and **MIND-small** (230k / 50,000). Both datasets normalise into one
8	schema, so every downstream stage has a single code path, not a Danish branch and an English one:
9	
10	```
11	impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet  impression_id, user_id, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[],
12	                                      history[], history_timestamps[], recency_seconds
13	articles.parquet                      article_id, title, abstract, body, category, entities[],
14	                                      published_time, total_inviews, …
15	```
16	
17	`entities` normalises two source shapes — EB-NeRD's `ner_clusters`, MIND's per-field JSON — into one
18	`List(String)` (74% / 87% non-empty); `recency_seconds` derives from `history_timestamps`, null where
19	genuinely unknown. Nothing scores on either yet — the feature store is a contract, and a field added
20	later is a migration.
21	
22	Three scorers run over that schema — **bm25**, **emb**, **fused** — on two tracks: **re-rank** (score the
23	pool the log actually showed; leaderboard-comparable) and **retrieval** (ignore the pool, pull the top-200
24	from the whole corpus — the "candidate generation to a few hundred" the spec asks for). The query for both
25	is the user's last 30 clicked titles. The harness reports AUC / MRR / nDCG@{5,10} with bootstrap CIs,
26	diversity / novelty / coverage, cold-vs-warm and head-vs-tail slices, and paired comparisons.
27	
28	## 2. Temporal split
29	
30	Both datasets ship their own train/test boundary, so I adopted it as `test_start` rather than
31	inventing one, and carved `val` out of the earlier block by time. EB-NeRD's day boundary is
32	**07:00**, not midnight — a detail that only shows up in the data.
33	
34	| | train | val | test |
35	|---|---|---|---|
36	| EB-NeRD small | 168,522 | 64,365 | 244,647 |
37	| MIND-small | 95,071 | 61,894 | 73,152 |
38	
39	EB-NeRD ships a separate `history.parquet` per block whose window ends exactly where its impressions
40	begin, so the behaviour-window boundary is given rather than guessed. (The alternative — all 7 provided
41	train days, halving the provided validation into val/test — buys ~38% more train data at the cost of
42	test history up to 7 days stale; nothing here is trained, so fresh test history wins. NOTES.md, §splits.)
43	
44	**Enforcement, not discipline.** `split.py` asserts on every build and fails rather than warns: strict
45	`train < val < test`; per-item history-precedes-impression; `clicked` is a subset of `candidates`; every
46	candidate resolves; no empty ids. Where a check is impossible it says so — MIND's history has no
47	per-item timestamps, so the harness prints that the guarantee is structural rather than verified,
48	instead of passing vacuously.
49	
50	`tests/test_leakage.py` (`make test`, 19 tests, ~20s) re-checks the same properties from *outside*,
51	reading only `data/processed/`: the build asserts what it meant to write, the tests assert what is on
52	disk. Two checks exist only there — that `datasets.yaml`'s cutoffs still match the artifacts, and that no
53	module outside `eval/run.py` mentions a serving-unavailable column. I verified the suite is not vacuous
54	by injecting a future click into a history and watching it fire.
55	
56	## 3. Lexical axis
57	
58	`bm25s` over title+abstract with a per-dataset Snowball stemmer. (`rank_bm25` scores one query at a
59	time in pure Python — unusable at 65k documents; Pyserini/Lucene scales further but drags in a JVM.)
60	
61	**Stemming is not free, and not what I assumed.** The brief specifies no preprocessing, so this was my
62	choice. On val, `stem - none` is **+0.0019 [+0.0007, +0.0029] AUC on MIND, zero on EB-NeRD, and
63	significantly *negative* on recall@200 for both** (-0.0020, -0.0023): it trades precision for
64	variant-matching — worth it ordering ~8 candidates, harmful picking 200 from 20,738. Kept as right for
65	the headline metric, but a track-dependent trade. Danish compound splitting from corpus vocabulary
66	fired on 15% of tokens and made both **worse**: decompounding needs a lexicon, not statistics.
67	
68	**The finding that mattered.** EB-NeRD first scored AUC **0.5035** — random. Rather than report that, I
69	tested whether it was my bug: an **oracle test** (query = the clicked article's own title) ranked it #1
70	in 300/300 impressions at AUC 0.9990 and a history-length sweep was flat, ruling out misalignment and
71	query dilution. MIND worked at 0.58, and that asymmetry located the cause: **bm25s ships no Danish
72	stopword list**, so thirty concatenated Danish titles were mostly function words. The Snowball list
73	moved EB-NeRD to **0.5232**. A missing stopword list is silent — it degrades without erroring.
74	
75	## 4. Semantic axis
76	
77	MIND encodes title+abstract with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (**11m16s**, cached once). User vectors are mean of
78	last-30 history vectors, L2-normalised; scoring is cosine with FAISS `IndexFlatIP` (exact at this scale;
79	IVF/PQ deferred to 10× analysis). MIND's corpus spans two files, so the index covers their 65,238-article
80	union.
81	
82	**The encoder is a measurement, not a preference.** Q3 allows the provided article vectors *or* your
83	own from BERT/XLM-RoBERTa, so I ran the identical pipeline on each candidate: same splits, same BM25,
84	same fusion, only the article vectors differ. Selection is on **val**, since selecting on test tunes a
85	choice on the number being reported. Semantic-only AUC, `ebnerd_small` val, against BM25's 0.5205:
86	
87	| encoder | arm | dim | val AUC | |
88	|---|---|---|---|---|
89	| **`Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector`** (ships) | provided | 768 | **0.5506** [0.5480, 0.5531] | **beats BM25** |
90	| `paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2` (XLM-R) | own | 768 | 0.5309 [0.5282, 0.5336] | beats BM25 |
91	| `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` | provided | 300 | 0.5098 [0.5073, 0.5124] | loses |
92	| `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` | provided | 768 | 0.4857 [0.4832, 0.4880] | **below random** |
93	
94	**On shipping `contrastive_vector`:** it is an official EB-NeRD artifact from the same `artifacts/`
95	folder as the other two, so it sits in Q3's "provided article embeddings" arm; the brief names
96	word2vec and mBERT as that arm's examples rather than as its full extent. It is the strongest EB-NeRD
97	encoder measured, by +0.0197 val AUC over my own XLM-R vectors, and the gap is far outside both
98	intervals. Stated plainly because an earlier revision dropped it on a narrower reading of the brief
99	and then recorded the 0.041 AUC that reading cost.
100	
101	One property predicts all four: **was the model trained so that cosine distance means topical
102	similarity?** Contrastive training optimises exactly that objective and wins; XLM-R fine-tuned on
103	paraphrase pairs approximates it and comes second; word2vec (predict neighbouring words) does not; raw
104	mBERT (fill in blanks) emphatically does not, its vectors sitting in a narrow cone where everything
105	looks alike. Size predicts nothing: the 300-d model beats one 768-d model and loses to two others.
106	Fusion detects the mBERT failure unprompted, tuning alpha to 0.00 on demo and discarding the semantic
107	axis outright.
108	
109	**MIND kept MiniLM, and that is the sharper lesson.** Against the same XLM-R, MiniLM wins on **val**
110	(0.6338 [0.6312, 0.6362] vs 0.6256 [0.6232, 0.6279]) and *loses* on **test** (0.6339 vs 0.6364), a
111	real reversal, near-disjoint intervals. The rule was fixed before looking, so MiniLM stays; "take the
112	better test number" would have flipped it. Obeying the rule cost 0.0025 test AUC, which is the entire
113	point of having one. The direction is sensible too: an English specialist beats a 50-language
114	generalist on English, while that generalist beats a 2013 word-vector model on Danish.
115

## 11. Leaderboard submissions

Both competitions score held-out sets far larger than the splits above (`ebnerd_testset`, 13,536,710
impressions; MIND-large test, 2,370,727), so `pipeline/submit.py` streams them (§10) with unchanged
scoring semantics. **Both entries are embeddings-only rather than `fused`**: on EB-NeRD that *is* the
reported system (§6), and on MIND it costs a known 0.0012 AUC, reported as a different system rather
than letting the stronger fused number stand in for the one uploaded. The reason is the §10 scaling
wall, not preference: BM25's `get_scores` is dense over the corpus per distinct query, which at ~2M
distinct MIND histories is ~10¹¹ operations.

| | submission | AUC | MRR | nDCG@5 | nDCG@10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD (RecSys 2024, comp. 2469) | 893893 | **0.5336** | 0.3412 | 0.3779 | 0.4576 |
| MIND (comp. 13967) | 892088 | **0.6460** | 0.3160 | 0.3405 | 0.3963 |

**Each submission has to be read against the offline number for the system that actually produced
it, not against whatever the offline harness currently reports.** Both moved since these were built:
EB-NeRD's encoder changed (word2vec/XLM-R -> `contrastive_vector`) and MIND's `history_len` changed
(30 -> 100, this section). Comparing against the *current* offline numbers would silently compare two
different systems.

**EB-NeRD (893893) was built after the `contrastive_vector` switch**, so its correct baseline is the
current offline `emb` row: 0.5397 / 0.3492 / 0.3831 / 0.4627. Against that, the leaderboard came in
**below offline on all four metrics** (AUC −0.0061, MRR −0.0080, nDCG@5 −0.0052, nDCG@10 −0.0051). If
anything this is the expected direction: a larger, genuinely independent population should regress
slightly toward the population mean rather than repeat one split's particular luck. It is also the
opposite of what an earlier version of this note claimed, which compared 893893 against a stale 0.5305
baseline left over from the pre-`contrastive_vector` build. Caught while writing this section,
corrected here rather than left standing.

**MIND (892088) predates the `history_len` change above**, so its correct baseline is the *old*
`history_len=30` offline `emb` row: AUC 0.6339, MRR 0.3486, nDCG@5 0.3315, nDCG@10 0.3911, not the
current, better numbers in §6's table. Against that correct baseline, the leaderboard beat offline on
three of four metrics (AUC +0.0121, nDCG@5 +0.0090, nDCG@10 +0.0052) and lost on MRR (0.316 vs 0.349
offline), recorded as unexplained rather than guessed at. The most likely cause is a definitional
difference on multi-click impressions: `eval/metrics.py` takes the reciprocal rank of the *first*
clicked article, and an implementation averaging over *all* clicked articles would score systematically
lower there while leaving AUC and nDCG largely untouched. Testable only against the organisers' scorer,
which is not published.

**Neither leaderboard entry reflects the current shipped pipeline.** Rebuilding and resubmitting both,
now that the encoder and `history_len` fixes are in, is the obvious next step and is not done here:
EB-NeRD allows five submissions a day and both take real wall-clock time to score, so it is a deliberate
choice rather than an oversight.

EB-NeRD allows five submissions a day and scores for hours, so output is validated offline rather than
by trial: all 13,536,710 lines checked as rank permutations of the right length in the test file's exact
row order, plus 40 random impressions per dataset re-ranked in float64 through an independent code path.

115	
   116	## 5. Candidate generation: recall@K, and a split-dependent winner
   117	
   118	Recall@K over the **full catalogue**, not the pool the log showed, is what measures candidate
   119	generation: the share of an impression's clicked articles found in the top K. Cold-start impressions
   120	retrieve nothing and score 0 rather than being excluded, since a retriever that cannot serve a user has
   121	failed for that user.
   122	
   123	| recall@200 | bm25 | emb | emb − bm25 |
   124	|---|---|---|---|
   125	| EB-NeRD small · **val** | **0.0214** | 0.0198 | **−0.0016** [−0.0030, −0.0002] |
   126	| EB-NeRD small · **test** | 0.0247 | **0.0277** | **+0.0030** [+0.0022, +0.0039] |
   127	| EB-NeRD demo · val | **0.0434** | 0.0400 | −0.0034 [−0.0093, +0.0027] |
   128	| EB-NeRD demo · test | 0.0390 | **0.0462** | **+0.0071** [+0.0040, +0.0104] |
   129	| MIND-small · test | 0.0220 | **0.0239** | +0.0019 [+0.0008, +0.0031] |
   130	
   131	**On EB-NeRD the retrieval winner flips between val and test, and both directions are significant.**
   132	BM25 wins on val, embeddings win on test, on the same dataset with the same code and the same K. That
   133	is not a margin shrinking to noise: it is a sign change with disjoint intervals. MIND does not do this:
   134	embeddings win there at every K on test.
   135	
   136	This matters more than which retriever is nominally better, because it says an EB-NeRD retrieval
   137	result quoted from one split does not transfer to the next one in time. §6 finds the identical pattern
   138	in the fusion weight, which points at the dataset rather than at either method: EB-NeRD's val window is
   139	2 days against test's 7, and the test block carries its own later history window, so the relationship
   140	between lexical and semantic signal genuinely drifts across the boundary. News decays fast enough that
   141	two weeks apart is a different distribution.
   142	
   143	**Re-ranking and retrieving remain different jobs, but by margin rather than direction.** The same
   144	contrastive vectors beat BM25 by **+0.0289** AUC when ordering the given pool and by **+0.0030**
   145	recall@200 when searching all 20,738 articles, a 10x difference in margin for the same encoder on the
   146	same split. Ordering ~8 candidates the log already filtered and finding 200 in a full catalogue reward
   147	different things, which is the argument for allowing different signals per stage rather than assuming
   148	one winner.
   149	
   150	Absolute recall is low everywhere (2–5%); §8 explains why, and it is a property of the corpus rather
   151	than of either retriever.
   152	
   153	## 6. Fusion, an addition the brief did not ask for
   154	
   155	Q3 asks only to *compare* lexical and semantic; this third system is mine. BM25 scores and cosines are on

val, embeddings win test, same code, same K, a sign change with disjoint intervals, not noise. MIND
shows no such flip; embeddings win there at every K. §6 finds the identical pattern in the fusion
weight, pointing at the dataset rather than either method: val is a 2-day window against test's 7, each
with its own history window, so the lexical/semantic relationship genuinely drifts across the boundary,

contrastive vectors beat BM25 by **+0.0289** AUC ordering the given pool and by only **+0.0030**

for different signals per stage rather than one universal winner. Absolute recall is low everywhere
(2–5%); §8 explains why, a property of the corpus, not either retriever.

77	MIND encodes title+abstract with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (**11m16s**, cached once). User vectors are mean of
    78	last-30 history vectors, L2-normalised; scoring is cosine with FAISS `IndexFlatIP` (exact at this scale;
    79	IVF/PQ deferred to 10× analysis). MIND's corpus spans two files, so the index covers their 65,238-article
    80	union.
    81	
    82	**The encoder is a measurement, not a preference.** Q3 allows the provided article vectors *or* your
    83	own from BERT/XLM-RoBERTa, so I ran the identical pipeline on each candidate: same splits, same BM25,
    84	same fusion, only the article vectors differ. Selection is on **val**, since selecting on test tunes a
    85	choice on the number being reported. Semantic-only AUC, `ebnerd_small` val, against BM25's 0.5205:
    86	
    87	| encoder | arm | dim | val AUC | |
    88	|---|---|---|---|---|
    89	| **`Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector`** (ships) | provided | 768 | **0.5506** [0.5480, 0.5531] | **beats BM25** |
    90	| `paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2` (XLM-R) | own | 768 | 0.5309 [0.5282, 0.5336] | beats BM25 |
    91	| `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` | provided | 300 | 0.5098 [0.5073, 0.5124] | loses |
    92	| `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` | provided | 768 | 0.4857 [0.4832, 0.4880] | **below random** |
    93	
    94	**On shipping `contrastive_vector`:** it is an official EB-NeRD artifact from the same `artifacts/`
    95	folder as the other two, so it sits in Q3's "provided article embeddings" arm; the brief names
    96	word2vec and mBERT as that arm's examples rather than as its full extent. It is the strongest EB-NeRD
    97	encoder measured, by +0.0197 val AUC over my own XLM-R vectors, and the gap is far outside both
    98	intervals. Stated plainly because an earlier revision dropped it on a narrower reading of the brief
    99	and then recorded the 0.041 AUC that reading cost.
   100	
   101	One property predicts all four: **was the model trained so that cosine distance means topical
   102	similarity?** Contrastive training optimises exactly that objective and wins; XLM-R fine-tuned on
   103	paraphrase pairs approximates it and comes second; word2vec (predict neighbouring words) does not; raw
   104	mBERT (fill in blanks) emphatically does not, its vectors sitting in a narrow cone where everything
   105	looks alike. Size predicts nothing: the 300-d model beats one 768-d model and loses to two others.
   106	Fusion detects the mBERT failure unprompted, tuning alpha to 0.00 on demo and discarding the semantic
   107	axis outright.
   108	
   109	**MIND kept MiniLM, and that is the sharper lesson.** Against the same XLM-R, MiniLM wins on **val**
   110	(0.6338 [0.6312, 0.6362] vs 0.6256 [0.6232, 0.6279]) and *loses* on **test** (0.6339 vs 0.6364), a
   111	real reversal, near-disjoint intervals. The rule was fixed before looking, so MiniLM stays; "take the
   112	better test number" would have flipped it. Obeying the rule cost 0.0025 test AUC, which is the entire
   113	point of having one. The direction is sensible too: an English specialist beats a 50-language
   114	generalist on English, while that generalist beats a 2013 word-vector model on Danish.
   115

1	# Component-1 Design Note — lexical & semantic retrieval on EB-NeRD and MIND
     2	
     3	## 1. What was built
     4	
     5	A config-driven pipeline from raw archives to metric reports in one command — `make data` for Q1's
     6	feature store, `make all` for everything — across **EB-NeRD demo** (49k impressions / 1,590 users),
     7	**EB-NeRD small** (478k / 15,143) and **MIND-small** (230k / 50,000). Both datasets normalise into one
     8	schema, so every downstream stage has a single code path, not a Danish branch and an English one:
     9	
    10	```
    11	impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet  impression_id, user_id, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[],
    12	                                      history[], history_timestamps[], recency_seconds
    13	articles.parquet                      article_id, title, abstract, body, category, entities[],
    14	                                      published_time, total_inviews, …
    15	```
    16	
    17	`entities` normalises two source shapes — EB-NeRD's `ner_clusters`, MIND's per-field JSON — into one
    18	`List(String)` (74% / 87% non-empty); `recency_seconds` derives from `history_timestamps`, null where
    19	genuinely unknown. Nothing scores on either yet — the feature store is a contract, and a field added
    20	later is a migration.
    21	
    22	Three scorers run over that schema — **bm25**, **emb**, **fused** — on two tracks: **re-rank** (score the
    23	pool the log actually showed; leaderboard-comparable) and **retrieval** (ignore the pool, pull the top-200
    24	from the whole corpus — the "candidate generation to a few hundred" the spec asks for). The query for both
    25	is the user's last 30 clicked titles. The harness reports AUC / MRR / nDCG@{5,10} with bootstrap CIs,
    26	diversity / novelty / coverage, cold-vs-warm and head-vs-tail slices, and paired comparisons.
    27	
    28	## 2. Temporal split
    29	
    30	Both datasets ship their own train/test boundary, so I adopted it as `test_start` rather than
    31	inventing one, and carved `val` out of the earlier block by time. EB-NeRD's day boundary is
    32	**07:00**, not midnight — a detail that only shows up in the data.
    33	
    34	| | train | val | test |
    35	|---|---|---|---|
    36	| EB-NeRD small | 168,522 | 64,365 | 244,647 |
    37	| MIND-small | 95,071 | 61,894 | 73,152 |
    38	
    39	EB-NeRD ships a separate `history.parquet` per block whose window ends exactly where its impressions
    40	begin, so the behaviour-window boundary is given rather than guessed. (The alternative — all 7 provided
    41	train days, halving the provided validation into val/test — buys ~38% more train data at the cost of
    42	test history up to 7 days stale; nothing here is trained, so fresh test history wins. NOTES.md, §splits.)
    43	
    44	**Enforcement, not discipline.** `split.py` asserts on every build and fails rather than warns: strict

178	bootstrap on shared resamples, since two systems on the same impressions have correlated errors and
   179	comparing two independent intervals is far too conservative.
   180	
   181	**Cold-start needed a defensible definition.** "Empty history" fails on EB-NeRD, which has *zero* such
   182	users (median history 258 clicks), it would select an empty slice and silently report nothing. The
   183	harness uses a per-dataset bottom-decile history-length threshold plus the true zero-history slice where
   184	one exists. On MIND that slice scores 0.5125 identically across all three systems, correctly: with no
   185	history there is no query, so no ranking is invented.
   186	
   187	Beyond-accuracy over the top-10: category intra-list diversity, novelty as self-information against *train*
   188	click shares, and coverage, sobering, at **5–21%** of the catalogue ever surfaced.
   189	
   190	## 8. Observations
   191	
   192	**Content signals are weak here, and that is the result, not a failure.** MIND reaches 0.6381, within
   193	reach of published neural baselines for MIND-small (~0.65–0.67) from an entirely unsupervised system.
   194	EB-NeRD tops out at 0.5397, for a structural reason: its pools are much smaller (median 8–9 vs MIND's
   195	23–26) and drawn from a tight recency window, so every candidate is already plausible and topically
   196	close, there is little for content to separate.
   197	
   198	**Simple behavioural features are not the shortcut they look like.** Train-click popularity scores *below*
   199	random on EB-NeRD (0.459), the pool is already popularity-filtered.
   200	
   201	**Demo was representative.** Every system landed within 0.002 of its demo value at 10× the users; the
   202	extra data bought precision, CIs tightened from ±0.0040 to ±0.0013, which is what decided fusion.
   203	
   204	**The retrieval track is weak regardless of scorer** (recall@200 of 2–5%): EB-NeRD's corpus spans
   205	1998–2023 while impressions are one week in May 2023, and `published_time <= impression_time` removes only
   206	*future* articles, not stale ones. A recency window on the retrievable corpus is the obvious lever, and
   207	belongs with the behavioural signals in C2.
   208	
   209	## 9. Anti-gaming and serving availability
   210	
   211	`total_inviews`/`total_pageviews`/`total_read_time` are lifetime aggregates over the whole collection
   212	period, they embed the future and cannot be computed at serving time. They are carried into the
   213	processed corpus **only** so the harness can quantify them; no shipped scorer reads them.

4

12	                                      history[], history_timestamps[], recency_seconds
13	articles.parquet                      article_id, title, abstract, body, category, entities[],

     2	
     3	## 1. What was built
     4	
     5	A config-driven pipeline from raw archives to metric reports in one command — `make data` for Q1's
     6	feature store, `make all` for everything — across **EB-NeRD demo** (49k impressions / 1,590 users),
     7	**EB-NeRD small** (478k / 15,143) and **MIND-small** (230k / 50,000). Both datasets normalise into one
     8	schema (`impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet`: id, user, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[],
     9	history[], recency_seconds; `articles.parquet`: id, title, abstract, body, category, entities[],
    10	published_time), so every downstream stage has one code path, not a Danish branch and an English one.
    11	`entities` normalises two source shapes (EB-NeRD's `ner_clusters`, MIND's per-field JSON) into one
    12	`List(String)` (74%/87% non-empty); nothing scores on entities yet, the feature store is a contract.
    13

    15	pool the log actually showed; leaderboard-comparable) and **retrieval** (ignore the pool, pull the
    16	top-200 from the whole corpus, the "candidate generation to a few hundred" the spec asks for). The
    17	query for both is the user's last 30 clicked titles. The harness reports AUC/MRR/nDCG@{5,10} with
    18	bootstrap CIs, diversity/novelty/coverage, cold-vs-warm and head-vs-tail slices, and paired comparisons.
    19	
    20	## 2. Temporal split
    21	
    22	Both datasets ship their own train/test boundary, so I adopted it as `test_start` rather than
    23	inventing one, and carved `val` out of the earlier block by time. EB-NeRD's day boundary is
    24	**07:00**, not midnight — a detail that only shows up in the data.
    25	
    26	| | train | val | test |
    27	|---|---|---|---|
    28	| EB-NeRD small | 168,522 | 64,365 | 244,647 |
    29	| MIND-small | 95,071 | 61,894 | 73,152 |
    30	
    31	EB-NeRD ships a separate `history.parquet` per block whose window ends exactly where its impressions
    32	begin, so the behaviour-window boundary is given rather than guessed. (The alternative, all 7 provided
    33	train days, halving validation into val/test, buys ~38% more train data at the cost of 7-day-stale test
    34	history; nothing here is trained, so fresh test history wins. NOTES.md, §splits.)
    35	
    36	**Enforcement, not discipline.** `split.py` asserts on every build and fails rather than warns: strict
    37	`train < val < test`; per-item history-precedes-impression; `clicked` is a subset of `candidates`; every
    38	candidate resolves; no empty ids. Where a check is impossible it says so — MIND's history has no
    39	per-item timestamps, so the harness prints that the guarantee is structural rather than verified,
    40	instead of passing vacuously.
    41	
    42	`tests/test_leakage.py` (`make test`, 19 tests, ~20s) re-checks the same properties from *outside*,
    43	reading only `data/processed/`: the build asserts what it meant to write, the tests assert what is on
    44	disk. Two checks exist only there — that `datasets.yaml`'s cutoffs still match the artifacts, and that no
    45	module outside `eval/run.py` mentions a serving-unavailable column. I verified the suite is not vacuous
    46	by injecting a future click into a history and watching it fire.
    47	
    48	## 3. Lexical axis

    50	`bm25s` over title+abstract with a per-dataset Snowball stemmer. (`rank_bm25` scores one query at a
    51	time in pure Python — unusable at 65k documents; Pyserini/Lucene scales further but drags in a JVM.)
    52	
    53	**Stemming is not free, and not what I assumed.** The brief specifies no preprocessing, so this was my
    54	choice. On val, `stem - none` is **+0.0019 [+0.0007, +0.0029] AUC on MIND, zero on EB-NeRD, and
    55	significantly *negative* on recall@200 for both** (-0.0020, -0.0023): it trades precision for
    56	variant-matching — worth it ordering ~8 candidates, harmful picking 200 from 20,738. Kept as right for
    57	the headline metric, but a track-dependent trade. Danish compound splitting from corpus vocabulary
    58	fired on 15% of tokens and made both **worse**: decompounding needs a lexicon, not statistics.
    59	
    60	**The finding that mattered.** EB-NeRD first scored AUC **0.5035** — random. Rather than report that, I
    61	tested whether it was my bug: an **oracle test** (query = the clicked article's own title) ranked it #1
    62	in 300/300 impressions at AUC 0.9990 and a history-length sweep was flat, ruling out misalignment and
    63	query dilution. MIND worked at 0.58, and that asymmetry located the cause: **bm25s ships no Danish
    64	stopword list**, so thirty concatenated Danish titles were mostly function words. The Snowball list
    65	moved EB-NeRD to **0.5232**. A missing stopword list is silent — it degrades without erroring.
    66

    70	last-30 history vectors, L2-normalised; scoring is cosine with FAISS `IndexFlatIP` (exact at this scale;
    71	IVF/PQ deferred to 10× analysis). MIND's corpus spans two files, so the index covers their 65,238-article
    72	union.
    73

    75	own from BERT/XLM-RoBERTa, so I ran the identical pipeline on each candidate: same splits, same BM25,
    76	same fusion, only the article vectors differ. Selection is on **val**, since selecting on test tunes a
    77	choice on the number being reported. Semantic-only AUC, `ebnerd_small` val, against BM25's 0.5205:
    78	
    79	| encoder | arm | dim | val AUC | |
    80	|---|---|---|---|---|
    81	| **`Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector`** (ships) | provided | 768 | **0.5506** [0.5480, 0.5531] | **beats BM25** |
    82	| `paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2` (XLM-R) | own | 768 | 0.5309 [0.5282, 0.5336] | beats BM25 |
    83	| `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` | provided | 300 | 0.5098 [0.5073, 0.5124] | loses |
    84	| `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` | provided | 768 | 0.4857 [0.4832, 0.4880] | **below random** |
    85	
    86	**On shipping `contrastive_vector`:** it is an official EB-NeRD artifact from the same `artifacts/`
    87	folder as the other two, so it sits in Q3's "provided article embeddings" arm, word2vec and mBERT are
    88	that arm's named examples, not its full extent. Strongest EB-NeRD encoder measured, by +0.0197 val AUC
    89	over my own XLM-R, gap well outside both intervals.
    90
