    92	similarity?** Contrastive training optimises exactly that objective and wins; XLM-R fine-tuned on
    93	paraphrase pairs approximates it and comes second; word2vec (predict neighbouring words) does not; raw
    94	mBERT (fill in blanks) emphatically does not, its vectors sitting in a narrow cone where everything
    95	looks alike. Size predicts nothing: the 300-d model beats one 768-d model and loses to two others.
    96	Fusion detects the mBERT failure unprompted, tuning alpha to 0.00 on demo and discarding the semantic
    97	axis outright.
    98	
    99	**MIND kept MiniLM, and that is the sharper lesson.** Against the same XLM-R, MiniLM wins on **val**
   100	(0.6338 [0.6312, 0.6362] vs 0.6256 [0.6232, 0.6279]) and *loses* on **test** (0.6339 vs 0.6364), a
   101	real reversal, near-disjoint intervals. The rule was fixed before looking, so MiniLM stays; "take the
   102	better test number" would have flipped it. Obeying the rule cost 0.0025 test AUC, which is the entire
   103	point of having one. The direction is sensible too: an English specialist beats a 50-language
   104	generalist on English, while that generalist beats a 2013 word-vector model on Danish.
   105	
   106	## 5. Candidate generation: recall@K, and a split-dependent winner
   107	
   108	Recall@K over the **full catalogue**, not the pool the log showed, is what measures candidate
   109	generation: the share of an impression's clicked articles found in the top K. Cold-start impressions
   110	retrieve nothing and score 0 rather than being excluded, since a retriever that cannot serve a user has
   111	failed for that user.
   112	
   113	| recall@200 | bm25 | emb | emb − bm25 |
   114	|---|---|---|---|
   115	| EB-NeRD small · **val** | **0.0214** | 0.0198 | **−0.0016** [−0.0030, −0.0002] |
   116	| EB-NeRD small · **test** | 0.0247 | **0.0277** | **+0.0030** [+0.0022, +0.0039] |
   117	| EB-NeRD demo · val | **0.0434** | 0.0400 | −0.0034 [−0.0093, +0.0027] |
   118	| EB-NeRD demo · test | 0.0390 | **0.0462** | **+0.0071** [+0.0040, +0.0104] |
   119	| MIND-small · test | 0.0220 | **0.0239** | +0.0019 [+0.0008, +0.0031] |
   120	
   121	**On EB-NeRD the retrieval winner flips between val and test, both directions significant**: BM25 wins
   122	val, embeddings win test, same code, same K, a sign change with disjoint intervals, not noise. MIND
   123	shows no such flip; embeddings win there at every K. §6 finds the identical pattern in the fusion
   124	weight, pointing at the dataset rather than either method: val is a 2-day window against test's 7, each
   125	with its own history window, so the lexical/semantic relationship genuinely drifts across the boundary,
   126	two weeks is a different news distribution.
   127	
   128	**Re-ranking and retrieving stay different jobs, but by margin now, not direction.** The same
   129	contrastive vectors beat BM25 by **+0.0289** AUC ordering the given pool and by only **+0.0030**
   130	recall@200 searching all 20,738 articles, a 10x gap for the same encoder on the same split, evidence
   131	for different signals per stage rather than one universal winner. Absolute recall is low everywhere
   132	(2–5%); §8 explains why, a property of the corpus, not either retriever.
   133	
   134	## 6. Fusion, an addition the brief did not ask for
   135	
   136	Q3 asks only to *compare* lexical and semantic; this third system is mine. BM25 scores and cosines are on
   137	different scales, and BM25's moves with query length, so both are z-normalised **within each candidate
   138	pool** and mixed `alpha*emb + (1-alpha)*bm25`, alpha tuned on **val**, applied unchanged to test.
   139	
   140	| AUC | bm25 | emb | fused | alpha | fused − emb |
   141	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
   142	| EB-NeRD small · **val** | 0.5205 | 0.5506 | **0.5528** | 0.70 | **+0.0022** [+0.0010, +0.0033] |
   143	| EB-NeRD small · **test** | 0.5107 | **0.5397** | 0.5380 | 0.70 | **−0.0017** [−0.0023, −0.0011] |
   144	| EB-NeRD demo · val | 0.5234 | 0.5602 | **0.5627** | 0.70 | +0.0026 [−0.0011, +0.0065] |
   145	| EB-NeRD demo · test | 0.5125 | **0.5418** | 0.5384 | 0.70 | **−0.0035** [−0.0054, −0.0016] |
   146	| MIND-small · test | 0.5685 | 0.6369 | **0.6381** | 0.75 | **+0.0012** [+0.0005, +0.0018] |
   147	
   148	**On EB-NeRD fusion wins on val and significantly loses on test, on both bundles.** The alpha chosen on
   149	val does not generalise across the split boundary. This is the same reversal §5 finds in the retrieval
   150	track, arrived at through a completely different measurement, which is what makes it a property of
   151	EB-NeRD rather than an artefact of either method. It also survived an encoder change: the earlier
   152	XLM-R build showed it too, so it is not one encoder's quirk.
   153	
   154	Consequently **the reported EB-NeRD system is embeddings alone**, and only MIND ships fused. Fusion
   155	still earns its place in the note: it is the mechanism that *detected* the instability, and on MIND it
   156	is a real if small win. Had I judged it on val alone, as the tempting shortcut, I would have shipped
   157	fusion on all three and been wrong on two of them.
   158	
   159	**`history_len` was shared across datasets and shouldn't have been.** A sweep on MIND val found the
   160	constant (30) truncating a real tail: MIND's median history is 20, not EB-NeRD's 258, so 30 discarded
   161	signal rather than noise. AUC rose significantly to 100 clicks (bm25 +0.0039, emb +0.0018) then
   162	plateaued exactly there. EB-NeRD's own sweep (§3) was flat over the same range, so it stays at 30;
   163	`history_len` is now per-dataset in config. This table reflects the corrected MIND value.
   164	
   165	## 7. Evaluation harness
   166	
   167	Metrics are computed **per impression**, which makes everything else possible: slicing is a mask over
   168	that vector, bootstrapping resamples it. Resampling is over impressions, the approximately-independent
   169	unit, resampling candidates within one would badly understate variance. Comparisons use a **paired**
   170	bootstrap on shared resamples, since two systems on the same impressions have correlated errors and
   171	comparing two independent intervals is far too conservative.
   172	
   173	**Cold-start needed a defensible definition.** "Empty history" fails on EB-NeRD, which has *zero* such
   174	users (median history 258 clicks), it would select an empty slice and silently report nothing. The
   175	harness uses a per-dataset bottom-decile history-length threshold plus the true zero-history slice where
   176	one exists. On MIND that slice scores 0.5125 identically across all three systems, correctly: with no
   177	history there is no query, so no ranking is invented.
   178	
   179	Beyond-accuracy over the top-10: category intra-list diversity, novelty as self-information against *train*
   180	click shares, and coverage, sobering, at **5–21%** of the catalogue ever surfaced.
   181	
   182	## 8. Observations
   183	
   184	**Content signals are weak here, and that is the result, not a failure.** MIND reaches 0.6381, within
   185	reach of published neural baselines for MIND-small (~0.65–0.67) from an entirely unsupervised system.
   186	EB-NeRD tops out at 0.5397, for a structural reason: its pools are much smaller (median 8–9 vs MIND's
   187	23–26) and drawn from a tight recency window, so every candidate is already plausible and topically
   188	close, there is little for content to separate.
   189	
   190	**Simple behavioural features are not the shortcut they look like.** Train-click popularity scores *below*
   191	random on EB-NeRD (0.459), the pool is already popularity-filtered.
   192	
   193	**Demo was representative.** Every system landed within 0.002 of its demo value at 10× the users; the
   194	extra data bought precision, CIs tightened from ±0.0040 to ±0.0013, which is what decided fusion.
   195	
   196	**The retrieval track is weak regardless of scorer** (recall@200 of 2–5%): EB-NeRD's corpus spans

   199	belongs with the behavioural signals in C2.
   200	
   201	## 9. Anti-gaming and serving availability
   202	
   203	`total_inviews`/`total_pageviews`/`total_read_time` are lifetime aggregates over the whole collection
   204	period, they embed the future and cannot be computed at serving time. They are carried into the
   205	processed corpus **only** so the harness can quantify them; no shipped scorer reads them.
   206	
   207	| test, AUC | without | with popularity | difference |

     2	
     3	## 1. What was built
     4	
     5	A config-driven pipeline from raw archives to metric reports in one command — `make data` for Q1's
     6	feature store, `make all` for everything — across **EB-NeRD demo** (49k impressions / 1,590 users),
     7	**EB-NeRD small** (478k / 15,143) and **MIND-small** (230k / 50,000). Both datasets normalise into one
     8	schema (`impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet`: id, user, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[],
     9	history[], recency_seconds; `articles.parquet`: id, title, abstract, body, category, entities[],
    10	published_time), so every downstream stage has one code path, not a Danish branch and an English one.
    11	`entities` normalises two source shapes (EB-NeRD's `ner_clusters`, MIND's per-field JSON) into one
    12	`List(String)` (74%/87% non-empty); nothing scores on entities yet, the feature store is a contract.
    13	
    14	Three scorers run over that schema, **bm25**, **emb**, **fused**, on two tracks: **re-rank** (score the
    15	pool the log actually showed; leaderboard-comparable) and **retrieval** (ignore the pool, pull the
    16	top-200 from the whole corpus, the "candidate generation to a few hundred" the spec asks for). The
    17	query for both is the user's last 30 clicked titles. The harness reports AUC/MRR/nDCG@{5,10} with
    18	bootstrap CIs, diversity/novelty/coverage, cold-vs-warm and head-vs-tail slices, and paired comparisons.
    19	
    20	## 2. Temporal split
    21	
    22	Both datasets ship their own train/test boundary, so I adopted it as `test_start` rather than
    23	inventing one, and carved `val` out of the earlier block by time. EB-NeRD's day boundary is
    24	**07:00**, not midnight — a detail that only shows up in the data.
    25	
    26	| | train | val | test |
    27	|---|---|---|---|
    28	| EB-NeRD small | 168,522 | 64,365 | 244,647 |
    29	| MIND-small | 95,071 | 61,894 | 73,152 |
    30	
    31	EB-NeRD ships a separate `history.parquet` per block whose window ends exactly where its impressions
    32	begin, so the behaviour-window boundary is given rather than guessed. (The alternative, all 7 provided
    33	train days, halving validation into val/test, buys ~38% more train data at the cost of 7-day-stale test
    34	history; nothing here is trained, so fresh test history wins. NOTES.md, §splits.)

    37	`train < val < test`; per-item history-precedes-impression; `clicked` is a subset of `candidates`; every
    38	candidate resolves; no empty ids. Where a check is impossible it says so — MIND's history has no
    39	per-item timestamps, so the harness prints that the guarantee is structural rather than verified,
    40	instead of passing vacuously.

    43	reading only `data/processed/`: the build asserts what it meant to write, the tests assert what is on
    44	disk. Two checks exist only there — that `datasets.yaml`'s cutoffs still match the artifacts, and that no
    45	module outside `eval/run.py` mentions a serving-unavailable column. I verified the suite is not vacuous
    46	by injecting a future click into a history and watching it fire.

    54	choice. On val, `stem - none` is **+0.0019 [+0.0007, +0.0029] AUC on MIND, zero on EB-NeRD, and
    55	significantly *negative* on recall@200 for both** (-0.0020, -0.0023): it trades precision for
    56	variant-matching — worth it ordering ~8 candidates, harmful picking 200 from 20,738. Kept as right for
    57	the headline metric, but a track-dependent trade. Danish compound splitting from corpus vocabulary
    58	fired on 15% of tokens and made both **worse**: decompounding needs a lexicon, not statistics.

## Summary

The `history_len` sweep and its consequences are fully shipped:

**Code**: `history_len` moved from a hardcoded `HISTORY_LEN=30` constant to a per-dataset config value (EB-NeRD stays 30, MIND is now 100), threaded through `retrieval/bm25.py`, `retrieval/embeddings.py`, and `pipeline/submit.py`. The sweep script itself was rewritten to match the new interface and re-verified to reproduce identical numbers.

**Pipeline**: Full re-run across all three dataset bundles. EB-NeRD came back byte-identical (regression check passed); MIND's `fused` test AUC moved 0.6353 → 0.6381. One OOM died mid-`eval.run`, diagnosed precisely (killed entering `mind_small val`, `ebnerd_small` had already written cleanly) and resumed as a fresh process rather than blindly retried.

**Documentation**: `NOTES.md` and the design note updated with the new numbers. While updating the design note I found and fixed **two real, pre-existing errors** unrelated to today's change: a stale offline baseline in §11 that had the leaderboard-vs-offline comparison backwards for EB-NeRD (claimed the leaderboard beat offline; corrected version shows it came in below on all four metrics, which is actually the expected direction), and a stale wall-time (33m28s instead of the current build's 13m30s) in §10.

**Page limit**: Found the design note at 6 pages against a 4-page hard limit — pre-existing, not caused by today's edits alone, but I own having caught it late. Fixed through real content trimming (whole sentences and redundant table rows, not just word-shaving) plus a small, defensible margin adjustment (1.5cm → 1.3cm), landing at exactly 4 pages with every number verified against source.

Test suite: 19/19 passing throughout.

One open item I'm flagging rather than fixing: the MiniLM-vs-XLM-R encoder choice for MIND (§4) was measured at the old `history_len=30` and hasn't been re-validated at 100. It's presented accurately as what that specific ablation found, but whether MiniLM still wins at the new history length is an unverified assumption carried forward. Also, per §11, neither leaderboard submission reflects today's fixes yet — that's a deliberate, not-yet-taken next step given the daily submission cap.

"""MIND encoder ablation: mpnet vs BGE vs E5 vs the shipped MiniLM, on val.

Encoding happens on Kaggle (notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb, §4) because a single 768-d model
over 65,238 articles is ~2.4h on this machine's CPU (measured); three of them is a GPU job, not
a laptop one. This script only scores the vectors once they're downloaded.

    mkdir -p data/interim/mind_encoders
    # copy the three downloaded *_vectors.parquet files there, then:
    .venv/bin/python scratchpad/mind_encoder_ablation.py

Non-destructive: reads retrieval.embeddings' own functions, never writes to data/processed.
Reports val AUC with bootstrap CI for each encoder, paired against the shipped MiniLM baseline,
plus the resource cost (encode time, dim, file size) each one costs, since the brief asks for the
best AUC-vs-resource tradeoff, not just the best AUC.
"""
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import retrieval.embeddings as embmod          # noqa: E402
from eval import bootstrap, metrics             # noqa: E402

DATASET = "mind_small"
SPLIT = "val"
ENC_DIR = ROOT / "data/interim/mind_encoders"

# Measured once, by hand, on Kaggle's T4 (see notebook §4 print output) — filled in after the
# encoding run; used only to print the resource side of the tradeoff, not to score anything.
KNOWN_COST = {
    "minilm (shipped)": {"dim": 384, "kaggle_min": None, "cpu_min_local": 11.3},
}

CANDIDATES = {
    "mpnet": ENC_DIR / "mind_small_mpnet_vectors.parquet",
    "bge": ENC_DIR / "mind_small_bge_vectors.parquet",
    "e5": ENC_DIR / "mind_small_e5_vectors.parquet",
}

cfg = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml").read_text())[DATASET]
proc = ROOT / "data/processed" / DATASET
articles = pl.read_parquet(proc / "articles.parquet")
impressions = pl.read_parquet(proc / f"impressions_{SPLIT}.parquet")
position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}

labels = [
    np.fromiter((c in set(k) for c in cand), bool, len(cand))
    for cand, k in zip(impressions["candidates"].to_list(), impressions["clicked"].to_list())
]

print(f"{DATASET} {SPLIT}: {impressions.height:,} impressions, {articles.height:,} articles\n")


def score(vectors: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    cand_scores, _ = embmod.score_split(impressions, articles, vectors, position, None, cfg["history_len"])
    cand_scores = [np.asarray(s, dtype=np.float64) for s in cand_scores]
    v, keep = metrics.per_impression(cand_scores, labels)
    return {"auc": v["auc"], "ndcg10": v["ndcg@10"]}


# --- baseline: the shipped MiniLM vectors, already cached ---
baseline_vectors = embmod.load_vectors(DATASET, cfg, articles)
baseline = score(baseline_vectors)
print(f"minilm (shipped)   dim=384   val AUC {bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(baseline['auc']))}")

results = {"minilm (shipped)": baseline}
for tag, path in CANDIDATES.items():
    if not path.exists():
        print(f"{tag:<10} SKIPPED — {path} not found (download it from Kaggle first)")
        continue
    table = pl.read_parquet(path).with_columns(pl.col("article_id").cast(pl.String))
    wanted = articles["article_id"].to_list()
    found = dict(zip(table["article_id"], range(table.height)))
    missing = [a for a in wanted if a not in found]
    assert not missing, f"{tag}: {len(missing)} articles missing from {path}"
    raw = table["vector"].explode().to_numpy().astype(np.float32).reshape(table.height, len(table["vector"][0]))
    vectors = raw[[found[a] for a in wanted]]
    vectors = vectors / (np.linalg.norm(vectors, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)
    dim = vectors.shape[1]

    t0 = time.time()
    results[tag] = score(vectors)
    dt = time.time() - t0
    size_mb = path.stat().st_size / 1e6
    print(f"{tag:<10} dim={dim}   val AUC {bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(results[tag]['auc']))}   "
          f"(scored in {dt:.0f}s, vectors {size_mb:.0f} MB on disk)")

print("\npaired vs minilm (shipped), val AUC (95% CI; significant if it excludes zero)")
print("-" * 80)
for tag in results:
    if tag == "minilm (shipped)":
        continue
    mean, lo, hi, sig = bootstrap.paired(results[tag]["auc"], baseline["auc"])
    verdict = "beats MiniLM" if sig and mean > 0 else ("loses to MiniLM" if sig and mean < 0 else "no significant difference")
    print(f"  {tag:<10} {mean:+.4f} [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]   {verdict}")

print("\nResource side of the tradeoff (dim is the ongoing cost: FAISS index size, cosine flops,")
print("candidate-scoring memory; all scale with dim, not with which encoder produced it):")
print(f"  minilm  384-d, 11.3 min to encode locally on CPU (already shipped, sunk cost)")
print(f"  mpnet/bge/e5  768-d (2x minilm's index size and per-query cost), ~2.4h CPU-equivalent each")
print("\nDecide by: does the AUC gain (if any, and only if significant) justify permanently doubling")
print("the semantic index's memory and per-query cost for every future run, not just this one.")
PYEOF

content.text:
Everything is wired and tested end-to-end — baseline scores correctly, gracefully reports which candidates are missing. It's ready for you to run on Kaggle.

## What to do

1. Open `notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb` on Kaggle (T4 GPU, per its existing setup instructions), upload `data/encode_inputs/mind_small.parquet` as the input dataset.
2. Run through cell 4, the new section I added (**"MIND encoder ablation — mpnet vs BGE vs E5 vs shipped MiniLM"**). It encodes only MIND (not the EB-NeRD corpora) with all three candidates and writes `mind_small_{mpnet,bge,e5}_vectors.parquet` to the Kaggle output.
3. Download those three files into `data/interim/mind_encoders/` here.
4. Tell me when they're in place — I'll run `scratchpad/mind_encoder_ablation.py`, which is already written and tested.

## What it will report

Val AUC with bootstrap CI for each of the three against the shipped MiniLM baseline, paired significance, and — since you asked for AUC-vs-resource, not just best-AUC — the actual tradeoff: all three candidates are 768-d against MiniLM's 384-d, meaning **2× the FAISS index size and 2× the per-query cosine cost forever**, not just during this one comparison. A candidate only wins if its AUC gain is both statistically significant *and* judged worth permanently doubling that ongoing cost.

## One caveat baked into the E5 run

E5's `"query: "`/`"passage: "` prefix convention doesn't map cleanly onto this architecture — there's no literal query text anywhere, a "query" is the mean of a user's history *article* vectors, and every article is encoded once, used both as a scored candidate and as a component of user vectors. I've encoded every article uniformly as `"passage: "`, which is the only defensible choice here, but it means E5 isn't exercising the asymmetry its training actually optimized for. If E5 underperforms, that's a plausible reason, not necessarily a mark against the model itself, and I'll flag it as such rather than let it stand as a clean loss.

content.text:
Decisive and unambiguous — **none of the three alternatives beat MiniLM, and two lose badly.** MiniLM's actual val AUC is 0.6356; working back through the paired differences:

| encoder | dim | val AUC (point est.) | vs MiniLM |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MiniLM (shipped)** | 384 | **0.6356** | — |
| mpnet | 768 | 0.6344 | −0.0012, not significant (tie) |
| e5 | 768 | 0.6067 | **−0.0289, significant loss** |
| bge | 768 | 0.5899 | **−0.0457, significant loss** |

There's no tradeoff to weigh here — MiniLM wins on *both* axes simultaneously. It ties or beats every 768-d candidate on AUC while costing half the FAISS index size and half the per-query cosine cost. **Keeping MiniLM is the correct call outright**, not a close call decided by resource preference.

The E5 caveat I flagged (uniform `"passage: "` prefix, no real query/passage asymmetry in this architecture) is a plausible partial explanation for e5's loss, but bge's loss is larger and bge has no such excuse — a straightforward retrieval-tuned model still lost decisively to a small general-purpose one on this exact task, which is worth recording rather than hand-waving. Writing this up properly:

input.command:
cd /home/neemon/Desktop/semesters/sem-5/ire/assignments/ass-1
cat >> docs/NOTES.md <<'EOF'

## MIND encoder ablation: mpnet / BGE / E5 vs shipped MiniLM (21 Aug)

Three retrieval-shaped alternatives to `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, tested to see whether a bigger or
retrieval-tuned model beats it on MIND specifically, given size predicted nothing in the EB-NeRD
ablation. Encoded on Kaggle T4 (`notebooks/encode_articles.ipynb` §4): 65,238 articles, ~1.3-1.6
min each on GPU against an estimated 2.4h each on this machine's CPU (measured on a 500-article
sample of mpnet before deciding to move the job to Kaggle).

| model | dim | trained for |
|---|---|---|
| `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (ships) | 384 | general sentence similarity |
| `all-mpnet-base-v2` | 768 | general sentence similarity, MiniLM's own family, larger |
| `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5` | 768 | retrieval, hard-negative mined |
| `intfloat/e5-base-v2` | 768 | retrieval; needs `"query: "`/`"passage: "` prefixes |

E5 has no literal query text in this architecture (a "query" is the mean of history article
vectors), so every article was prefixed uniformly `"passage: "` rather than exploiting the
query/passage asymmetry it was trained on. Noted as a real limitation on the E5 result, not
retroactively explaining it away.

Semantic-only AUC, `mind_small` val, same `history_len=100`, same protocol as every other encoder
ablation (`scratchpad/mind_encoder_ablation.py`, non-destructive, verified via checksum against
`data/processed/mind_small/emb_val.parquet` before/after):

| encoder | dim | val AUC | vs MiniLM (paired, 95% CI) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MiniLM (shipped)** | 384 | **0.6356** [0.6331, 0.6380] | — |
| mpnet | 768 | 0.6344 | -0.0012 [-0.0029, +0.0004], not significant |
| e5 | 768 | 0.6067 | **-0.0289** [-0.0312, -0.0266], significant loss |
| bge | 768 | 0.5899 | **-0.0457** [-0.0481, -0.0432], significant loss |

**No candidate wins, and the AUC-vs-resource question has a clean answer: MiniLM dominates on
both axes at once.** It ties the best 768-d alternative (mpnet) on AUC while costing half the
FAISS index size and half the per-query cosine cost, and it beats the two retrieval-tuned models
outright and by a wide margin. There is no tradeoff to weigh; MiniLM was already the better
choice before resource cost even enters the argument.

**BGE's loss is the more surprising one.** E5's loss has a stated architectural reason (the
prefix mismatch); BGE has no equivalent excuse; it is a straightforward retrieval-tuned model
that lost decisively (-0.0457 AUC, the largest single-encoder gap measured anywhere in this
project) to a small general-purpose one on exactly the task it should suit. Consistent with the
EB-NeRD finding that neither model size nor stated training purpose reliably predicts performance
on mean-pooled cosine over short news text; only measurement does.

No config change: `mind_small` keeps `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`. Recorded because a rejected idea with
numbers is worth more than an untried one, same reasoning as the compound-splitting ablation.
EOF
echo "appended, NOTES.md now $(wc -l < docs/NOTES.md) lines"

## Result: keep MiniLM, no change shipped

The ablation is complete, verified, and recorded in `docs/NOTES.md`. Summary:

| encoder | dim | val AUC | vs MiniLM |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MiniLM (shipped)** | 384 | **0.6356** | — |
| mpnet | 768 | 0.6344 | tie (not significant) |
| e5 | 768 | 0.6067 | significant loss |
| bge | 768 | 0.5899 | significant loss |

**MiniLM dominates on both axes at once**, so there's no actual tradeoff to resolve: it ties the best 768-d alternative on accuracy while costing half the FAISS index size and half the per-query cost, and it beats the two retrieval-tuned models by a wide margin. Config is untouched — `mind_small` keeps `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`.

The most useful finding for the report is the BGE result specifically: it's a model built and trained for exactly this kind of task, and it still lost decisively (−0.0457 AUC, the largest single-encoder gap measured anywhere in this project) to a small general-purpose model. That's the same lesson the EB-NeRD encoder ablation already taught (mBERT scoring below random, word2vec beating a 768-d model) — training objective and task fit predict performance, not size or stated purpose, and only measuring settles it.

content.text:
Checked against `NOTES.md` — the stemming ablation, `history_len` sweep, and encoder ablation are all done for MIND. Here's what's genuinely still open, ranked by cost:

**1. Re-validate the MiniLM-vs-XLM-R choice at the new `history_len=100`.** That comparison (MiniLM 0.6338/0.6339 vs XLM-R 0.6256/0.6364 val/test) was measured back at `history_len=30`, before the sweep. The just-finished four-way ablation ran at the corrected 100 and confirmed MiniLM beats mpnet/bge/e5 there — but XLM-R itself was never re-tested at 100. Cheapest item on this list, same script pattern, one more model to add.

**2. The query/document field asymmetry, on MIND.** Flagged as untested back when the field ablation ran on EB-NeRD only: BM25's query is built from titles alone, but documents are indexed as title+abstract. On EB-NeRD that asymmetry mattered (title-only documents won re-ranking). MIND's abstract coverage is 94.8% and pools are ~3× larger, so it could land differently — untouched so far. Reuses `scratchpad/field_ablation.py` directly.

**3. Entity overlap as a signal.** MIND ships clean Wikidata-linked entity annotations, currently parsed into the schema and never scored. A Jaccard overlap between a candidate's entities and the user's recent-history entities, blended in alongside BM25/embeddings, is a genuinely new axis — nobody's tried it on either dataset.

**4. User-vector pooling: mean vs max-similarity.** Currently mean-of-last-100 (post-sweep), re-normalized. Max-similarity — score a candidate by its best match to *any* history item rather than the average — could catch a user with genuinely diverse interests that a centroid blurs. Pure content-side change, same vectors, stays in C1.

**5. Cold-start fallback, measured rather than just conventioned.** MIND has real cold-start users (1.8–3.0% across splits). Current convention: all-zero score, empty retrieval. `eval/slicing.py` already builds `train_click_counts` for the novelty metric — testing "fall back to train-popularity for cold-start users" against the current convention, on the cold slice specifically, reuses existing infra.

**6. Whether `fused` can actually ship on the MIND leaderboard.** The expensive one. Current leaderboard entry is embeddings-only because dense `get_scores` is ~10¹¹ operations at MIND-large scale. But the leaderboard task re-ranks a *given* pool, not full-corpus retrieval — so BM25 there only ever needs to score the few candidates per impression, not the whole 120,961-article vocabulary. If that reasoning holds, a pool-restricted BM25 pass could make `fused` tractable, closing the +0.0012 AUC currently left on the table. Worth checking the reasoning before spending implementation time.

Want me to run #1 (cheapest, closes a stated gap) or #2 next?

import polars as pl, numpy as np, zipfile, io, random

HISTORY_LEN = 100  # deliberately hardcoded here, not read from config, to stay an independent check
random.seed(11)

root = "data/interim/MINDlarge_test/MINDlarge_test"
news = pl.read_csv(f"{root}/news.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False, quote_char=None,
                    new_columns=["article_id","category","subcategory","title","abstract","url",
                                 "title_entities","abstract_entities"]).select("article_id")
vecs_all = np.load("data/processed/mindlarge_test_embeddings.npy")
V = {a: vecs_all[i] for i, a in enumerate(news["article_id"])}
for a in V: V[a] = V[a] / (np.linalg.norm(V[a]) + 1e-9)

beh = pl.scan_csv(f"{root}/behaviors.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False, quote_char=None,
                   new_columns=["impression_id","user_id","time","history","impressions"]).collect()
picks = sorted(random.sample(range(beh.height), 40))

sub = {}
want_ids = set(int(beh["impression_id"][i]) for i in picks)
with zipfile.ZipFile("deliverable/submissions/mind_prediction.zip") as z:
    with z.open("prediction.txt") as fh:
        for line in io.TextIOWrapper(fh, "utf-8"):
            sp = line.find(" ")
            iid = int(line[:sp])
            if iid in want_ids:
                sub[iid] = [int(x) for x in line[sp+2:line.rindex("]")].split(",")]
                if len(sub) == len(want_ids): break

mismatch = 0
for i in picks:
    iid = int(beh["impression_id"][i])
    hist = (beh["history"][i] or "").split(" ")
    hist = [h for h in hist if h][-HISTORY_LEN:]
    rows = [V[a] for a in hist if a in V]
    u = np.mean(rows, axis=0) if rows else np.zeros(384)
    u = u / (np.linalg.norm(u) + 1e-9)
    cands = [p.split("-")[0] for p in beh["impressions"][i].split(" ")]
    s = np.array([V[a] @ u if a in V else 0.0 for a in cands])
    order = np.argsort(-s, kind="stable")
    mine = np.empty(len(s), dtype=int); mine[order] = np.arange(1, len(s)+1)
    if list(mine) != sub[iid]: mismatch += 1

print(f"independent float64 recomputation of {len(picks)} random impressions")
print(f"  mismatches: {mismatch}  ->  {'PASS' if mismatch == 0 else 'FAIL'}")
PY

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import numpy as np, polars as pl, yaml
import retrieval.embeddings as embmod
from eval import bootstrap, metrics

cfg = yaml.safe_load(open("configs/datasets.yaml"))["mind_small"]
proc = "data/processed/mind_small"
articles = pl.read_parquet(f"{proc}/articles.parquet")
impressions = pl.read_parquet(f"{proc}/impressions_val.parquet")
position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
labels = [np.fromiter((c in set(k) for c in cand), bool, len(cand))
          for cand, k in zip(impressions["candidates"].to_list(), impressions["clicked"].to_list())]

def score(vectors):
    cand_scores, _ = embmod.score_split(impressions, articles, vectors, position, None, cfg["history_len"])
    cand_scores = [np.asarray(s, dtype=np.float64) for s in cand_scores]
    v, keep = metrics.per_impression(cand_scores, labels)
    return v["auc"]

baseline = score(embmod.load_vectors("mind_small", cfg, articles))
print(f"minilm (shipped)  val AUC {bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(baseline))}")

xlmr_cfg = {**cfg, "embeddings": "data/interim/xlmr/mind_small_vectors.parquet"}
xlmr_vectors = embmod.load_vectors("mind_small", xlmr_cfg, articles)
xlmr_auc = score(xlmr_vectors)
print(f"xlmr              val AUC {bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(xlmr_auc))}")

mean, lo, hi, sig = bootstrap.paired(xlmr_auc, baseline)
verdict = "beats MiniLM" if sig and mean > 0 else ("loses to MiniLM" if sig and mean < 0 else "no significant difference")
print(f"\nxlmr - minilm: {mean:+.4f} [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]  {verdict}")
PY

content.text: Real, clean finding: on MIND, **title-only documents beat the shipped title+abstract on both AUC (+0.0024) and recall@200 (+0.0017), both significant, with no cost on nDCG@10.** This is different from EB-NeRD, where the trade was direction-dependent (title-only won re-ranking, lost retrieval). I'll hold this as a candidate to ship and keep going through the list; noting it in `NOTES.md` now so it isn't lost, then continuing to #3.

cat >> docs/NOTES.md <<'EOF'

## MIND field ablation and XLM-R re-check, and three new candidate ablations (23 Aug)

### XLM-R re-validated at history_len=100

The MiniLM-vs-XLM-R comparison (docs/NOTES.md, "Computing our own embeddings") was measured at the
pre-sweep `history_len=30`. Re-run at the shipped `history_len=100`:

| encoder | val AUC | vs MiniLM |
|---|---|---|
| **MiniLM (shipped)** | 0.6356 [0.6331, 0.6380] | - |
| xlmr | 0.6265 [0.6241, 0.6288] | -0.0090 [-0.0110, -0.0071], significant loss |

Same conclusion as before (MiniLM wins), same order of magnitude gap (-0.0090 vs the earlier -0.0082
at history_len=30). The choice was never actually in doubt at the new history_len; now confirmed
rather than assumed. No change.

### Field ablation on MIND (title vs title+abstract), previously untested

`scratchpad/field_ablation.py mind_small`, val, `history_len=100`, non-destructive:

| variant | vocab | AUC | nDCG@10 | recall@200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **title** | 24,681 | **0.5864** [0.5840, 0.5887] | 0.3489 [0.3464, 0.3515] | **0.0388** [0.0374, 0.0402] |
| title+abstract (ships) | 44,264 | 0.5840 [0.5814, 0.5865] | 0.3494 [0.3468, 0.3522] | 0.0371 [0.0357, 0.0384] |

Paired, `title - title+abstract`: AUC +0.0024 [+0.0006, +0.0041] significant; nDCG@10 -0.0005
[-0.0020, +0.0011] not significant; recall@200 +0.0017 [+0.0007, +0.0028] significant.

**Different pattern from EB-NeRD.** There, title-only won re-ranking and *lost* retrieval (a real
trade). Here, title-only wins both accuracy metrics that moved, and the one that didn't move
(nDCG@10) shows no cost either way. No downside found. Candidate to ship: switch `mind_small`'s BM25
document fields to title-only. Not yet applied, pending the fields-are-per-dataset config plumbing
(currently `--fields` is a shared CLI flag, not a per-dataset config value like `history_len` is).

Mechanism, consistent with the stemming/field findings elsewhere: MIND abstracts run longer relative
to titles than EB-NeRD's, and the query is always title-only regardless of the document setting, so
adding abstract text to the *document* side while the *query* stays short-form dilutes the register
match on both tracks here, where on EB-NeRD's much smaller candidate pools the retrieval track still
benefited from the extra vocabulary.
EOF

    for cand, k in zip(impressions["candidates"].to_list(), impressions["clicked"].to_list())
]


def jaccard(a: set, b: set) -> float:
    if not a or not b:
        return 0.0
    inter = len(a & b)
    return inter / (len(a) + len(b) - inter)


def zscore(values: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    spread = values.std()
    return np.zeros_like(values) if spread < 1e-12 else (values - values.mean()) / spread


print(f"{DATASET} {SPLIT}: {impressions.height:,} impressions")
print(f"entity coverage: {sum(1 for e in entities_of.values() if e):,}/{len(entities_of):,} articles\n")

      for cand, k in zip(impressions["candidates"].to_list(), impressions["clicked"].to_list())]
keep_mask = np.array([y.any() and not y.all() for y in ys])


def mean_auc(alpha):
    aucs = []

        if not ok:

"""User-vector pooling: mean vs max-similarity, on MIND (previously untested).

Shipped: user vector = mean of last history_len clicked article vectors, re-normalised; score a
candidate by cosine(user_vector, candidate_vector). That collapses a user with genuinely diverse
interests into one blurred centroid.

Alternative: score a candidate by its *best* match to any single history item,
max_h cosine(vector(h), candidate), never forming a user vector at all. Might catch "this matches
the one thing they read yesterday" even when it's unlike the rest of their history.

Non-destructive: reads only data/processed/ and the cached embedding vectors, writes nothing.

    .venv/bin/python scratchpad/max_pool_ablation.py
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import retrieval.embeddings as embmod  # noqa: E402
from eval import bootstrap, metrics     # noqa: E402

DATASET = "mind_small"
SPLIT = "val"

cfg = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml").read_text())[DATASET]
proc = ROOT / "data/processed" / DATASET
articles = pl.read_parquet(proc / "articles.parquet")
impressions = pl.read_parquet(proc / f"impressions_{SPLIT}.parquet")
position = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(articles["article_id"])}
history_len = cfg["history_len"]

vectors = embmod.load_vectors(DATASET, cfg, articles)

labels = [
    np.fromiter((c in set(k) for c in cand), bool, len(cand))
    for cand, k in zip(impressions["candidates"].to_list(), impressions["clicked"].to_list())
]

print(f"{DATASET} {SPLIT}: {impressions.height:,} impressions\n")

max_scores, mean_scores = [], []
for cand, hist in zip(impressions["candidates"].to_list(), impressions["history"].to_list()):
    hist_rows = [position[a] for a in hist[-history_len:] if a in position]
    cand_rows = [position[a] for a in cand]
    cand_vecs = vectors[cand_rows]  # (n_cand, dim)

    if not hist_rows:
        max_scores.append(np.zeros(len(cand)))
        mean_scores.append(np.zeros(len(cand)))
        continue

    hist_vecs = vectors[hist_rows]  # (n_hist, dim)
    sims = cand_vecs @ hist_vecs.T  # (n_cand, n_hist): every candidate x every history item
    max_scores.append(sims.max(axis=1).astype(np.float32))

    u = hist_vecs.mean(axis=0)
    u = u / (np.linalg.norm(u) + 1e-9)
    mean_scores.append((cand_vecs @ u).astype(np.float32))

v_mean, keep = metrics.per_impression(mean_scores, labels)
v_max, _ = metrics.per_impression(max_scores, labels)

print(f"mean pooling (shipped)  val AUC {bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(v_mean['auc']))}")
print(f"max-similarity          val AUC {bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(v_max['auc']))}")

mean_d, lo, hi, sig = bootstrap.paired(v_max["auc"], v_mean["auc"])
verdict = "beats mean pooling" if sig and mean_d > 0 else ("loses to mean pooling" if sig and mean_d < 0 else "no significant difference")
print(f"\nmax - mean: {mean_d:+.4f} [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]  {verdict}")

"""Cold-start fallback: current zero-score convention vs train-popularity backoff, on MIND.

Shipped convention: a user with no history gets an all-zero score vector on every scorer (no
query, no ranking invented from nothing). Tests whether falling back to train-click popularity
for these specific users beats that convention, on the cold slice only.

Non-destructive: reads only data/processed/, writes nothing.

    .venv/bin/python scratchpad/cold_start_fallback_ablation.py
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from eval import bootstrap, metrics, slicing  # noqa: E402

DATASET = "mind_small"
SPLIT = "val"

proc = ROOT / "data/processed" / DATASET
impressions = pl.read_parquet(proc / f"impressions_{SPLIT}.parquet")
train_clicked = pl.read_parquet(proc / "impressions_train.parquet")["clicked"].to_list()
counts = slicing.train_click_counts(train_clicked)

history_lengths = np.array([len(h) for h in impressions["history"].to_list()])
cold = history_lengths == 0
print(f"{DATASET} {SPLIT}: {impressions.height:,} impressions, {cold.sum():,} true cold-start ({cold.mean():.1%})")

candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()
clicked = impressions["clicked"].to_list()
labels = [np.fromiter((c in set(k) for c in cand), bool, len(cand)) for cand, k in zip(candidates, clicked)]

# current convention: all-zero score for cold-start users (only meaningful ones evaluated below)
zero_scores = [np.zeros(len(c)) for c in candidates]
# fallback: score by train click popularity (log1p to stop one blockbuster dominating)
pop_scores = [np.log1p(np.array([counts.get(a, 0) for a in c], dtype=np.float64)) for c in candidates]

v_zero, keep = metrics.per_impression(zero_scores, labels)
v_pop, _ = metrics.per_impression(pop_scores, labels)

cold_scored = cold[keep]
n_cold = cold_scored.sum()
print(f"{n_cold:,} cold-start impressions survive the all-clicked/none-clicked filter\n")

if n_cold < 30:
    print("too few cold-start impressions with ranking signal for a meaningful bootstrap CI")
else:
    zero_cold = v_zero["auc"][cold_scored]
    pop_cold = v_pop["auc"][cold_scored]
    print(f"cold slice, zero-score (shipped)   AUC {bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(zero_cold))}")
    print(f"cold slice, popularity fallback    AUC {bootstrap.fmt(*bootstrap.ci(pop_cold))}")
    mean, lo, hi, sig = bootstrap.paired(pop_cold, zero_cold)
    verdict = "beats zero-score" if sig and mean > 0 else ("loses to zero-score" if sig and mean < 0 else "no significant difference")
    print(f"\npopularity - zero: {mean:+.4f} [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]  {verdict}")

The MIND leaderboard entry is embeddings-only because `index.get_scores(tokens)` is dense over

just those candidate positions, the ~10^11 wall may not apply to the submission at all.

This checks two things, in order:
  1. correctness: does a pool-restricted BM25 give *identical* scores to the dense path?
  2. cost: what does it actually cost per impression, and does it extrapolate to 2.37M?

import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml

sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

import retrieval.bm25 as bm25mod  # noqa: E402

SPLIT = "val"
N_CHECK = 300     # impressions to verify identical scores on
N_TIME = 2000     # impressions to time the two paths over

cfg = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml").read_text())[DATASET]
proc = ROOT / "data/processed" / DATASET
articles = pl.read_parquet(proc / "articles.parquet")
impressions = pl.read_parquet(proc / f"impressions_{SPLIT}.parquet")

index, stemmer = bm25mod.build_index(articles, cfg, ("title", "abstract"))
title_of = dict(zip(articles["article_id"].to_list(), articles["title"].to_list()))
queries = bm25mod.build_queries(impressions, title_of, cfg["history_len"])
candidates = impressions["candidates"].to_list()

import bm25s  # noqa: E402
tokenized = bm25s.tokenize(queries[:max(N_CHECK, N_TIME)], stopwords=bm25mod.stopwords_for(cfg),
                           stemmer=stemmer, return_ids=False, show_progress=False)

print(f"{DATASET} {SPLIT}: verifying pool-restricted BM25 against the dense path\n")

# --- 1. correctness ---
mismatches = 0
for i in range(N_CHECK):
    toks = tokenized[i]
    if not toks:

    dense = index.get_scores(toks)
    cand_rows = [position[a] for a in candidates[i]]
    dense_pool = dense[cand_rows]

    restricted = np.array([dense[r] for r in cand_rows])

n_scored = 0
for i in range(N_TIME):
    toks = tokenized[i]
    if not toks:

    n_scored += 1
dense_t = time.time() - t0
per_query = dense_t / max(n_scored, 1)

print(f"  corpus here: {articles.height:,} articles")

print("Extrapolation to the MIND-large leaderboard set:")

MIND_LARGE_DISTINCT = 2_000_000   # ~2M distinct histories, per NOTES.md
scale = MIND_LARGE_ARTICLES / articles.height

print(f"  x ~{MIND_LARGE_DISTINCT:,} distinct histories = ~{est_total_h:.1f} hours")

print("only ~39 candidates are ever read. A pool-restricted scorer would need bm25s to expose")
print("per-document scoring (score(query, doc_ids)); its public API is get_scores over the full")
print("corpus, so this is a library limitation, not an arithmetic one.")

This is a genuinely important result, and it contradicts a claim currently in the design note. **The measured cost is ~1.6 hours, not "impractical."** `NOTES.md` and DESIGN_NOTE §10/§11 both assert BM25 can't back the MIND submission because it's ~10¹¹ operations — but that arithmetic counts *operations*, not wall time, and `bm25s` is sparse and vectorized enough that 2M queries extrapolates to about 1.6 hours single-threaded.

That's slow, but it is emphatically not the hard wall the write-up describes. Recording it accurately:

cat >> docs/NOTES.md <<'EOF'

### Can `fused` ship on the MIND leaderboard? The "not practical" claim was wrong

`NOTES.md` ("MIND submission is embeddings-only") and DESIGN_NOTE §10/§11 both assert BM25 cannot
back the MIND leaderboard entry: `get_scores` is dense over the corpus per distinct query, and at
~2M distinct MIND-large histories x 120,961 articles "that is ~10^11 operations and is not
practical". That claim was argued from an operation count and never timed.

Measured (`scratchpad/pool_restricted_bm25.py`, MIND val, single-threaded):

| | |
|---|---|
| dense `get_scores` | **1.6 ms/query** over 65,238 articles (1,957 queries in 3.1s) |
| extrapolated to MIND-large's 120,961-article corpus | ~2.9 ms/query |
| x ~2M distinct histories | **~1.6 hours** |

**~1.6 hours is slow, but it is not "not practical", and the earlier claim overstated the wall.**
10^11 *operations* is not 10^11 *seconds*; `bm25s` is sparse and vectorised, so the per-query cost
is milliseconds, not the seconds the operation count implies if read as scalar work. The honest
statement is that BM25 at this scale is expensive enough to be an annoyance (comparable to the
EB-NeRD submission's own 13m30s, but ~7x that), not that it is infeasible.

What that means for the submission: **`fused` is very likely shippable on MIND** for the +0.0012 AUC
it is worth offline, at a cost of roughly 1.6h of extra compute on top of the current 5m01s embedding
run. Not done here, it needs `pipeline/submit.py` to grow a BM25 path (it currently streams the
embedding scorer only) and that is a real code change, not a rerun. Recorded as a corrected estimate
and a live option rather than a closed door.

The pool-restriction idea specifically (score only the ~39 candidates per impression instead of all
120,961 articles) does **not** work as a shortcut with `bm25s`: its public API is `get_scores` over
the full corpus, with no per-document scoring entry point. That is a library limitation rather than
an arithmetic one; a real inverted index with early termination (WAND) would expose exactly that,
which is the §10 conclusion and still stands. The correction here is only to the *size* of the wall,
not to its existence or to the direction of the fix.
EOF

**Yes, #3 was measured on top of `fused`** — it blends entity overlap against `fused_val.parquet`, so the +0.0011 is "fused+entity vs fused", not "emb+entity vs emb". That makes it the wrong measurement for your purposes.

Two consequences worth being clear about:

1. **The +0.0011 doesn't transfer to an embeddings-only system.** `fused` already carries BM25's lexical signal, and entity overlap is partly lexical in nature (shared named entities usually means shared words). Against `emb` alone, entity overlap has more unique signal to contribute — so the gain could be *larger*. But it could also be smaller. It has to be re-measured, not assumed.

2. **#2 and #3 don't currently interact at all.** #2 changes BM25's document fields; #3 blends entities onto a score. If you're not shipping `fused`, then **BM25 isn't in your submission pipeline either** — which means #2's finding, however real, doesn't affect what you upload. It only affects the offline `bm25` and `fused` rows in your reports.

So the combination that actually matters for an embeddings-only submission is **`emb + entity`**. Let me measure that:

content.text:
## Answering your two questions

**Is #3 on a fused system?** Yes — it blended against `fused_val.parquet`, so the +0.0011 was "fused+entity vs fused." Since you don't want a fused submission, I re-measured it against `emb` alone: **+0.0023 [+0.0018, +0.0027], significant** — about twice the gain.

That gap is the interesting part. `fused` already contains BM25, and entity overlap is partly lexical (shared named entities usually means shared tokens), so blending entities onto `fused` was double-counting signal BM25 already supplied. Against `emb` alone the entity axis is more nearly orthogonal, so it contributes more. Worth remembering: "what is signal X worth" has no answer independent of what you're adding it to.

**Can #2 and #3 be combined?** Not usefully, and given your constraint they barely interact:

- **#2 changes BM25's document fields.** If BM25 isn't in your submission, this finding doesn't touch what you upload at all — it only moves the offline `bm25` and `fused` rows in your reports.
- **#3 is the one that matters**, because it stacks directly onto the embeddings-only system you're actually shipping.

So the answer is that #2 is a reporting-accuracy improvement, #3 is a shippable one. They're independent, not combinable.

## Scaling claims fixed

Corrected in all three places, and I made a deliberate choice about *how*:

- **DESIGN_NOTE §10** — rewritten to say I overstated it, with the measured 1.6 ms/query → ~1.6 h, and the note that operation counts aren't wall-clock when the kernel is sparse and vectorized. The §10 conclusion (WAND-style early termination is the right fix) still stands.
- **DESIGN_NOTE §11** — reframed from "the §10 scaling wall" to a deliberate cost trade, since that's now the honest description.
- **`submit.py` docstring** — "does not survive these sizes" → the measured figure plus what's actually missing (a BM25 path in that file).
- **`NOTES.md`** — I left the original claim intact and added a `> Superseded` block above it rather than editing it away, so the correction is visible as a correction.

Nothing shipped yet from #2 or #3 — both remain val-only findings. If you want #3 in the submission, that needs an entity-scoring path in `submit.py` and a test-set verification first.

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import yaml

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))

from eval import bootstrap, metrics  # noqa: E402

DATASET = "mind_small"
ALPHAS = np.round(np.arange(0.0, 0.51, 0.05), 2)

cfg = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "configs/datasets.yaml").read_text())[DATASET]
proc = ROOT / "data/processed" / DATASET
articles = pl.read_parquet(proc / "articles.parquet")
entities_of = dict(zip(articles["article_id"].to_list(), articles["entities"].to_list()))
history_len = cfg["history_len"]


def jaccard(a: set, b: set) -> float:
    if not a or not b:
        return 0.0
    inter = len(a & b)
    return inter / (len(a) + len(b) - inter)


def zscore(v: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    s = v.std()
    return np.zeros_like(v) if s < 1e-12 else (v - v.mean()) / s


def load(split):
    imp = pl.read_parquet(proc / f"impressions_{split}.parquet")
    emb = pl.read_parquet(proc / f"emb_{split}.parquet")
    cands = imp["candidates"].to_list()
    hists = imp["history"].to_list()
    clicked = imp["clicked"].to_list()
    ys = [np.fromiter((c in set(k) for c in cand), bool, len(cand)) for cand, k in zip(cands, clicked)]
    ez, fz = [], []
    for cand, hist in zip(cands, hists):
        ue: set = set()
        for a in hist[-history_len:]:

def stream_mind(cfg: dict, limit: int | None):
    root = INTERIM / "MINDlarge_test/MINDlarge_test"
    news = pl.read_csv(
        root / "news.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False, quote_char=None,
        new_columns=["article_id", "category", "subcategory", "title", "abstract",
                     "url", "title_entities", "abstract_entities"],
    ).select("article_id", "title", "abstract")

    vectors = _encoded_vectors(news, cfg["model"])
    dim = vectors.shape[1]
    vectors = np.vstack([vectors, np.zeros((1, dim), dtype=np.float32)])
    article_row = {a: i for i, a in enumerate(news["article_id"])}
    unknown = len(vectors) - 1

    prepared = _mind_parquet(root, article_row, unknown)
    scan = pl.scan_parquet(prepared)
    total = scan.select(pl.len()).collect().item()
    if limit:
        total = min(total, limit)
    print(f"  {total:,} impressions, {len(article_row):,} articles, dim {dim}")

    for offset in range(0, total, BATCH):
        batch = scan.slice(offset, min(BATCH, total - offset)).collect()
        # Histories are already row indices, so deduplication is over tuples of ints.
        # Dedup is per slice: across slices identical histories are recomputed, which is
        # the trade streaming makes for bounded memory. Mean-pooling history_len vectors is cheap.
        order: dict[tuple, int] = {}
        index = np.fromiter(
            (order.setdefault(tuple(h[-cfg["history_len"]:]), len(order))
             for h in batch["history_rows"]),
            dtype=np.int64, count=batch.height,
        )
        users = np.zeros((len(order), dim), dtype=np.float32)
        for key, i in order.items():
            rows = np.asarray(key, dtype=np.int64)
            rows = rows[rows != unknown]
            if len(rows):
                users[i] = vectors[rows].mean(axis=0)
        users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9

        lengths = batch["cand_rows"].list.len().to_numpy().astype(np.int64)
        rows = batch["cand_rows"].explode().to_numpy().astype(np.int64)
        scores = score_pairs(rows, np.repeat(index, lengths), vectors, users)
        yield batch["impression_id"].to_numpy(), scores, lengths

helpers = '''def _mind_entity_sets(root: Path, article_row: dict, n_rows: int) -> list[set]:
    """Entity surface forms per article row, parsed exactly as pipeline/split.py does.

    Returned as a list indexed by the same row ids `article_row` maps to, so the streaming
    loop can look entities up by row without going back through article_id strings.
    The trailing row (the unknown-article sentinel) gets an empty set.
    """
    dtype = pl.List(pl.Struct({"Label": pl.String}))

    def labels(col: str) -> pl.Expr:
        return (pl.col(col).fill_null("[]").str.json_decode(dtype)
                .list.eval(pl.element().struct.field("Label")))

    ent = pl.read_csv(
        root / "news.tsv", separator="\\t", has_header=False, quote_char=None,
        new_columns=["article_id", "category", "subcategory", "title", "abstract",
                     "url", "title_entities", "abstract_entities"],
    ).select(
        "article_id",
        pl.concat_list(labels("title_entities"), labels("abstract_entities"))
        .list.unique(maintain_order=True).alias("entities"),
    )

    out: list[set] = [set() for _ in range(n_rows)]
    for aid, ents in zip(ent["article_id"].to_list(), ent["entities"].to_list()):
        row = article_row.get(aid)
        if row is not None:
            out[row] = set(ents)
    return out


def _zscore_blocks(values: np.ndarray, lengths: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Z-normalise within each impression's candidate pool, vectorised over a flat array.

    The offline scorer z-scores *within each pool* (retrieval/fuse.py) because that is the
    only scope where two scorers' scales need to agree. Same here. A pool with no spread
    gets zeros rather than a division by ~0.
    """
    idx = np.repeat(np.arange(len(lengths)), lengths)
    sums = np.bincount(idx, weights=values, minlength=len(lengths))
    means = sums / lengths
    dev = values - means[idx]
    var = np.bincount(idx, weights=dev * dev, minlength=len(lengths)) / lengths
    std = np.sqrt(var)
    safe = np.where(std[idx] < 1e-12, 1.0, std[idx])
    out = dev / safe
    return np.where(std[idx] < 1e-12, 0.0, out)


'''

        users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9

        lengths = batch["cand_rows"].list.len().to_numpy().astype(np.int64)
        rows = batch["cand_rows"].explode().to_numpy().astype(np.int64)
        scores = score_pairs(rows, np.repeat(index, lengths), vectors, users)
        yield batch["impression_id"].to_numpy(), scores, lengths'''

new = '''    entity_alpha = cfg.get("entity_alpha", 0.0)
    entity_sets: list[set] = []
    if entity_alpha:
        entity_sets = _mind_entity_sets(root, article_row, len(vectors))
        covered = sum(1 for s in entity_sets if s)
        print(f"  entity blend on: alpha={entity_alpha}, "
              f"{covered:,}/{len(article_row):,} articles carry entities")

    prepared = _mind_parquet(root, article_row, unknown)
    scan = pl.scan_parquet(prepared)
    total = scan.select(pl.len()).collect().item()
    if limit:
        total = min(total, limit)
    print(f"  {total:,} impressions, {len(article_row):,} articles, dim {dim}")

    for offset in range(0, total, BATCH):
        batch = scan.slice(offset, min(BATCH, total - offset)).collect()
        # Histories are already row indices, so deduplication is over tuples of ints.
        # Dedup is per slice: across slices identical histories are recomputed, which is
        # the trade streaming makes for bounded memory. Mean-pooling history_len vectors is cheap.
        order: dict[tuple, int] = {}
        index = np.fromiter(
            (order.setdefault(tuple(h[-cfg["history_len"]:]), len(order))
             for h in batch["history_rows"]),
            dtype=np.int64, count=batch.height,
        )
        users = np.zeros((len(order), dim), dtype=np.float32)
        for key, i in order.items():
            rows = np.asarray(key, dtype=np.int64)
            rows = rows[rows != unknown]
            if len(rows):
                users[i] = vectors[rows].mean(axis=0)
        users /= np.linalg.norm(users, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9

        lengths = batch["cand_rows"].list.len().to_numpy().astype(np.int64)
        rows = batch["cand_rows"].explode().to_numpy().astype(np.int64)
        scores = score_pairs(rows, np.repeat(index, lengths), vectors, users)

        if entity_alpha:
            # User entity set is per distinct history, computed once per `order` entry for
            # the same reason the user vector is: identical histories give identical sets.
            user_entities: list[set] = [set() for _ in range(len(order))]
            for key, i in order.items():
                acc: set = set()
                for r in key:
                    if r != unknown:
                        acc |= entity_sets[r]
                user_entities[i] = acc

            ent = np.empty(len(rows), dtype=np.float64)
            per_cand_user = np.repeat(index, lengths)
            for k in range(len(rows)):
                ue = user_entities[per_cand_user[k]]
                ce = entity_sets[rows[k]]
                if ue and ce:
                    inter = len(ue & ce)
                    ent[k] = inter / (len(ue) + len(ce) - inter)
                else:
                    ent[k] = 0.0

            # Blend on z-scores within each pool, matching retrieval/fuse.py's convention.
            scores = (entity_alpha * _zscore_blocks(ent, lengths)
                      + (1 - entity_alpha) * _zscore_blocks(scores.astype(np.float64), lengths))

        yield batch["impression_id"].to_numpy(), scores, lengths'''

assert old in t
t = t.replace(old, new)
p.write_text(t)
print("entity blend wired into stream_mind")

input.command:
cd /home/neemon/Desktop/semesters/sem-5/ire/assignments/ass-1
.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
import polars as pl, numpy as np, zipfile, io, random, json

ALPHA = 0.20
HISTORY_LEN = 100
random.seed(23)
root = "data/interim/MINDlarge_test/MINDlarge_test"

news = pl.read_csv(f"{root}/news.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False, quote_char=None,
    new_columns=["article_id","category","subcategory","title","abstract","url",
                 "title_entities","abstract_entities"])

# independent entity parse: plain json.loads, not polars json_decode
ents = {}
for aid, te, ae in zip(news["article_id"].to_list(),
                        news["title_entities"].to_list(),
                        news["abstract_entities"].to_list()):
    s = set()
    for blob in (te, ae):
        if blob:
            try:
                for rec in json.loads(blob):
                    if "Label" in rec: s.add(rec["Label"])
            except Exception: pass
    ents[aid] = s

vecs_all = np.load("data/processed/mindlarge_test_embeddings.npy")
V = {a: vecs_all[i]/(np.linalg.norm(vecs_all[i])+1e-9) for i, a in enumerate(news["article_id"])}

beh = pl.scan_csv(f"{root}/behaviors.tsv", separator="\t", has_header=False, quote_char=None,
    new_columns=["impression_id","user_id","time","history","impressions"]).slice(0,20000).collect()
picks = sorted(random.sample(range(beh.height), 40))

sub = {}
want = set(int(beh["impression_id"][i]) for i in picks)
with zipfile.ZipFile("deliverable/submissions/mind_prediction.zip") as z:
    with z.open("prediction.txt") as fh:
        for line in io.TextIOWrapper(fh, "utf-8"):
            sp = line.find(" "); iid = int(line[:sp])
            if iid in want:
                sub[iid] = [int(x) for x in line[sp+2:line.rindex("]")].split(",")]
                if len(sub) == len(want): break

def z(v):
    s = v.std()
    return np.zeros_like(v) if s < 1e-12 else (v-v.mean())/s

mismatch = 0
for i in picks:
    iid = int(beh["impression_id"][i])
    hist = [h for h in (beh["history"][i] or "").split(" ") if h][-HISTORY_LEN:]
    cands = [p.split("-")[0] for p in beh["impressions"][i].split(" ")]

    rows = [V[a] for a in hist if a in V]
    u = np.mean(rows, axis=0) if rows else np.zeros(384)
    u = u/(np.linalg.norm(u)+1e-9)
    emb = np.array([V[a] @ u if a in V else 0.0 for a in cands], dtype=np.float64)

    ue = set()
    for a in hist: ue |= ents.get(a, set())
    ent = np.array([ (lambda ce: (len(ue&ce)/(len(ue)+len(ce)-len(ue&ce))) if (ue and ce) else 0.0)(ents.get(a,set()))
                     for a in cands], dtype=np.float64)

    s = ALPHA*z(ent) + (1-ALPHA)*z(emb)
    order = np.argsort(-s, kind="stable")
    mine = np.empty(len(s), dtype=int); mine[order] = np.arange(1,len(s)+1)
    if list(mine) != sub[iid]: mismatch += 1

print(f"independent recomputation (separate entity parser, float64) of {len(picks)} impressions")
print(f"  mismatches: {mismatch}  ->  {'PASS' if mismatch==0 else 'FAIL'}")

All six ablations done, and the shippable one is shipped and verified.

## What changed

**Scaling claims corrected** in three places. DESIGN_NOTE §10 now says I overstated it, with the measured 1.6 ms/query → ~1.6 h and the reason the original was wrong (operation counts aren't wall-clock for a sparse vectorised kernel). §11 reframed from "scaling wall" to a deliberate cost trade. `submit.py`'s docstring updated. In `NOTES.md` I left the original claim standing and added a `> Superseded` block above it, so the correction reads as a correction rather than a quiet edit. PDF still 4 pages.

**Your two questions, answered by measurement:**

#3 *was* on `fused` — wrong baseline for you. Re-measured against `emb` alone: **+0.0023 val**, roughly double. `fused` already carried BM25's lexical signal and entity overlap is partly lexical, so blending onto `fused` double-counted.

#2 and #3 don't combine, and with no fused submission #2 doesn't affect what you upload at all — BM25 isn't in your pipeline. It's a reporting-accuracy finding only.

**Entity signal shipped.** Selected alpha on val (0.20), reported once on test: **+0.0022 [+0.0018, +0.0026], significant**. It generalises (val +0.0023, test +0.0022) — which is exactly what EB-NeRD's fusion alpha failed to do, so that's the meaningful check, not the raw size.

New `mind_prediction.zip`: 2,370,727 lines, 4m38s, 2.0 GB peak, all validation passing. Before the full run I smoke-tested 20k impressions against a fully independent recomputation (different JSON parser, float64, separate z-scoring) — zero mismatches over 40 impressions, which checks parse, blend, z-scoring scope and ranking together.

**EB-NeRD is untouched** — `entity_alpha` defaults to 0.0 there, verified. Its `ner_clusters` have different coverage and the signal is untested, so I didn't assume it transfers. 19/19 tests pass.

Both prior builds preserved: `mind_prediction.EMBONLY-history_len100-unsubmitted.zip` and `mind_prediction.STALE-history_len30-scored-0.6460.zip`.

One thing to flag: this is still an embeddings-only submission in the lexical sense — the entity blend is a second *content* axis, not BM25 returning under another name. Worth being precise about that in a viva, since "embeddings-only" now means something slightly more specific than it did.

content.content:
## Dropping the self-chosen encoder (assignment fidelity)

The semantic axis originally used `Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector`. It is an official EB-NeRD
artifact from the same `artifacts/` folder, but **the assignment PDF does not name it** — it names
`Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` and `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased`, and marks the pair optional.
Choosing a third one was a decision the brief did not offer, so the system now uses the better of the
two it does, chosen by the val-only ablation in "Choosing the EB-NeRD encoder" above.

This costs accuracy and the cost is recorded rather than hidden: contrastive scored 0.5506 on
ebnerd_small val against word2vec's 0.5098. It was also the only EB-NeRD configuration where the
semantic axis beat BM25. Reporting a number produced by an encoder the brief never offered would
have been the worse trade.

**What the swap changed downstream**, all of it re-derived rather than edited by hand:

- every EB-NeRD row in the results table above, and all four `results/ebnerd_*.{md,json}`
- the fusion alphas: 0.70 -> 0.30 (demo) and 0.20 (small), because the semantic axis now deserves
  less weight
- three conclusions in `deliverable/DESIGN_NOTE.md` that reversed sign, rewritten rather than softened:
  §5 (BM25 now out-retrieves embeddings on EB-NeRD at every K), §6 (fusion is no longer rejected on
  EB-NeRD — it now wins where the comparison is powered), §11 (the submitted EB-NeRD system is now
  the *weakest* of the three measured, since embeddings-only lost to BM25)
- the EB-NeRD leaderboard zip, rebuilt from scratch; the superseded one was renamed
  `ebnerd_predictions.STALE-contrastive.zip` rather than deleted in place, so a half-finished
  rebuild could never be mistaken for a valid submission

`retrieval/embeddings.py` gained one flag, `--embeddings <parquet>`, to override the configured
vector file. That is the whole of the code change: because the encoder was already a config value
and `pipeline/submit.py` reads the same key, the leaderboard run cannot silently diverge from the
reported system. Verified the flag is a faithful no-op by pointing it at the config's own file and
confirming byte-identical output.

### The download was the slow part, not the compute

attachment.snippet:
1	# Component-1 Design Note — lexical & semantic retrieval on EB-NeRD and MIND
2	
3	## 1. What was built
4	
5	A config-driven pipeline from raw archives to metric reports in one command — `make data` for Q1's
6	feature store, `make all` for everything — across **EB-NeRD demo** (49k impressions / 1,590 users),
7	**EB-NeRD small** (478k / 15,143) and **MIND-small** (230k / 50,000). Both datasets normalise into one
8	schema (`impressions_{train,val,test}.parquet`: id, user, timestamp, candidates[], clicked[],
9	history[], recency_seconds; `articles.parquet`: id, title, abstract, body, category, entities[],
10	published_time), so every downstream stage has one code path, not a Danish branch and an English one.
11	`entities` normalises two source shapes (EB-NeRD's `ner_clusters`, MIND's per-field JSON) into one
12	`List(String)` (74%/87% non-empty); nothing scores on entities yet, the feature store is a contract.
13	
14	Three scorers run over that schema, **bm25**, **emb**, **fused**, on two tracks: **re-rank** (score the
15	pool the log actually showed; leaderboard-comparable) and **retrieval** (ignore the pool, pull the
16	top-200 from the whole corpus, the "candidate generation to a few hundred" the spec asks for). The
17	query for both is the user's last 30 clicked titles; the harness's own metrics are in §7.
18	
19	## 2. Temporal split
20	
21	Both datasets ship their own train/test boundary, so I adopted it as `test_start` rather than
22	inventing one, and carved `val` out of the earlier block by time (EB-NeRD small train/val/test:
23	168,522/64,365/244,647; MIND-small: 95,071/61,894/73,152 impressions). EB-NeRD's day boundary is
24	**07:00**, not midnight, a detail that only shows up in the data.
25	
26	EB-NeRD ships a separate `history.parquet` per block whose window ends exactly where its impressions
27	begin, so the behaviour-window boundary is given rather than guessed (NOTES.md, §splits, for the
28	alternative considered and rejected).
29	
30	**Enforcement, not discipline.** `split.py` asserts on every build and fails rather than warns: strict
31	`train < val < test`; per-item history-precedes-impression; `clicked` is a subset of `candidates`; every
32	candidate resolves; no empty ids. Where a check is impossible it says so — MIND's history has no
33	per-item timestamps, so the harness prints that the guarantee is structural rather than verified,
34	instead of passing vacuously.
35	
36	`tests/test_leakage.py` (`make test`, 19 tests, ~20s) re-checks the same properties from *outside*,
37	reading only `data/processed/`: the build asserts what it meant to write, the tests assert what is on
38	disk, plus two checks that exist only there (`datasets.yaml` cutoffs still match the artifacts; no
39	module outside `eval/run.py` mentions a serving-unavailable column). Verified non-vacuous by injecting
40	a future click and watching it fire.
41	
42	## 3. Lexical axis
43	
44	`bm25s` over title+abstract with a per-dataset Snowball stemmer (`rank_bm25` scores one query at a
45	time in pure Python, unusable at 65k documents; Pyserini/Lucene scales further but drags in a JVM).
46	
47	**Stemming is not free, and not what I assumed.** The brief specifies no preprocessing, so this was my
48	choice. On val, `stem - none` is **+0.0019 [+0.0007, +0.0029] AUC on MIND, zero on EB-NeRD, and
49	significantly *negative* on recall@200 for both** (-0.0020, -0.0023): it trades precision for
50	variant-matching — worth it ordering ~8 candidates, harmful picking 200 from 20,738. Kept as right for
51	the headline metric, but a track-dependent trade. Danish compound splitting from corpus vocabulary
52	fired on 15% of tokens and made both **worse**: decompounding needs a lexicon, not statistics.
53	
54	**The finding that mattered.** EB-NeRD first scored AUC **0.5035**, random. Rather than report that, I
55	checked whether it was my bug: an **oracle test** (query = the clicked article's own title) ranked it
56	#1 in 300/300 impressions at AUC 0.9990, and a history-length sweep was flat, ruling out misalignment
57	and query dilution. MIND worked at 0.58; that asymmetry located the cause: **bm25s ships no Danish
58	stopword list**, so thirty concatenated Danish titles were mostly function words. The Snowball list
59	moved EB-NeRD to **0.5232**. A missing stopword list is silent, it degrades without erroring.
60	
61	## 4. Semantic axis
62	
63	MIND encodes title+abstract with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (**11m16s**, cached once, 65,238-article union
64	across its two files). User vectors are the mean of last-30 history vectors, L2-normalised; scoring is
65	cosine with FAISS `IndexFlatIP` (exact at this scale; IVF/PQ deferred to 10× analysis).
66	
67	**The encoder is a measurement, not a preference.** Q3 allows the provided article vectors *or* your
68	own from BERT/XLM-RoBERTa, so I ran the identical pipeline on each candidate: same splits, same BM25,
69	same fusion, only the article vectors differ. Selection is on **val**, since selecting on test tunes a
70	choice on the number being reported. Semantic-only AUC, `ebnerd_small` val, against BM25's 0.5205:
71	
72	| encoder | arm | dim | val AUC | |
73	|---|---|---|---|---|
74	| **`Ekstra_Bladet_contrastive_vector`** (ships) | provided | 768 | **0.5506** [0.5480, 0.5531] | **beats BM25** |
75	| `paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2` (XLM-R) | own | 768 | 0.5309 [0.5282, 0.5336] | beats BM25 |
76	| `Ekstra_Bladet_word2vec` | provided | 300 | 0.5098 [0.5073, 0.5124] | loses |
77	| `google_bert_base_multilingual_cased` | provided | 768 | 0.4857 [0.4832, 0.4880] | **below random** |
78	
79	**On shipping `contrastive_vector`:** it is an official EB-NeRD artifact from the same `artifacts/`
80	folder as the other two, so it sits in Q3's "provided article embeddings" arm, word2vec and mBERT are
81	that arm's named examples, not its full extent. Strongest EB-NeRD encoder measured, by +0.0197 val AUC
82	over my own XLM-R, gap well outside both intervals.
83	
84	One property predicts all four: **was the model trained so cosine distance means topical similarity?**
85	Contrastive training optimises exactly that and wins; XLM-R paraphrase fine-tuning approximates it and
86	comes second; word2vec (predict neighbouring words) does not; raw mBERT (fill in blanks) emphatically
87	does not, its vectors sitting in a narrow cone where everything looks alike. Size predicts nothing: the
88	300-d model beats one 768-d model. Fusion detects the mBERT failure unprompted, tuning alpha to 0.00 on
89	demo, discarding the semantic axis outright.
90	
91	**MIND kept MiniLM, and that is the sharper lesson.** Against the same XLM-R, MiniLM wins on **val**
92	(0.6338 vs 0.6256) and *loses* on **test** (0.6339 vs 0.6364), a real reversal, near-disjoint intervals.
93	The rule was fixed before looking, so MiniLM stays; "take the better test number" would have flipped
94	it, costing 0.0025 test AUC to obey, the entire point of having a rule. An English specialist beats a
95	50-language generalist on English, while that generalist beats a 2013 word-vector model on Danish.
96	
97	## 5. Candidate generation: recall@K, and a split-dependent winner
98	
99	Recall@K over the **full catalogue**, not the pool the log showed, is what measures candidate
100	generation: the share of an impression's clicked articles found in the top K. Cold-start impressions
101	retrieve nothing and score 0 rather than being excluded, since a retriever that cannot serve a user has
102	failed for that user.
103	
104	| recall@200 (small; demo tracked it within noise, §8) | bm25 | emb | emb − bm25 |

## 6. Fusion, an addition the brief did not ask for

Q3 asks only to *compare* lexical and semantic; this third system is mine. BM25 scores and cosines are on
different scales, and BM25's moves with query length, so both are z-normalised **within each candidate
pool** and mixed `alpha*emb + (1-alpha)*bm25`, alpha tuned on **val**, applied unchanged to test.

| AUC (small; demo tracked it within noise, §8) | bm25 | emb | fused | alpha | fused − emb |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EB-NeRD small · **val** | 0.5205 | 0.5506 | **0.5528** | 0.70 | **+0.0022** [+0.0010, +0.0033] |
| EB-NeRD small · **test** | 0.5107 | **0.5397** | 0.5380 | 0.70 | **−0.0017** [−0.0023, −0.0011] |
| MIND-small · test | 0.5685 | 0.6369 | **0.6381** | 0.75 | **+0.0012** [+0.0005, +0.0018] |

**On EB-NeRD fusion wins on val and significantly loses on test, on both bundles**: the alpha chosen on
val does not generalise across the boundary. This is the same reversal §5 finds in retrieval, reached
through a different measurement, a property of EB-NeRD, not an artefact of either method.

Consequently **the reported EB-NeRD system is embeddings alone**, and only MIND ships fused. Fusion
still earns its place: it is the mechanism that *detected* the instability, and on MIND it is a real if
small win. Judged on val alone, the tempting shortcut, I would have shipped fusion on all three and
been wrong on two.

**`history_len` was shared across datasets and shouldn't have been.** A sweep on MIND val found the
constant (30) truncating a real tail: MIND's median history is 20, not EB-NeRD's 258, so 30 discarded
signal rather than noise. AUC rose significantly to 100 clicks (bm25 +0.0039, emb +0.0018) then
plateaued exactly there. EB-NeRD's own sweep (§3) was flat over the same range, so it stays at 30;
`history_len` is now per-dataset in config. This table reflects the corrected MIND value.

**A second MIND-only signal, entity overlap, ships alongside `emb`.** MIND's entities are clean and
Wikidata-linked; a candidate's Jaccard overlap with the user's recent-history entities, blended onto
`emb` (`alpha*entity + (1-alpha)*emb`), was selected on val (0.20) and checked once on test: **+0.0022
